title: Trafficked to Myanmar
oneLiner: They left for Thailand on the promise of lucrative jobs, now 32 South Africans are stuck in a military compound in Myanmar - the victims of a sophisticated international trafficking syndicate
summary:
Lucille was offered a work visa, accommodation and a one year contract to work in sales in Thailand, for a company that needed English speaking employees. Unable to find work in South Africa, she jumped at the opportunity. It took three days to recruit her, and fly her out to Thailand after she responded to an online ad. Her mother dropped her at the airport, while there R10 000 was deposited into her account, and she was told to which gate she had to go to pick up her plane ticket. SA citizens don't need visas to fly to Thailand. Once there, she was escorted by armed men during an 8 hour car drive, had to cross a river at night when no one could see, still under armed guard, and then driven to the "compound" where she would work. The experience left her frightened, and once at the compound her passport was taken and she was told she could not leave because she owed the traffickers money. Then she was forced into working on the scams.

We have exclusive access to Lucille Janse Van Vuuren, a 32 year old single mother from Pretoria who fell victim to the traffickers. She is communicating with us from where she is being held on a military compound in Myanmar - one of 7000 thousand victims who were recently rescued from a large scale trafficking operation by a massive crackdown on online scamming sites by the Myanmar authorities. Now, Lucille is stuck in limbo - lured to Thailand under false pretences she was held in Myanmar since July last year and forced to work for the traffickers in online romance scams. But the authorities in Myanmar are refusing to release the South African citizens being held there unless the South African Government steps in to repatriate them. So far the government is silent on the issue, and have not reached out to the South African victims.

title: A Marathon a day for 35 days
oneLiner: Running a marathon is hard enough... but what about 30 marathons in 35 days?
summary:
The “Running Wild” Fundraising Campaign is the initiative of Matthew Murray and Charles Raw. These adventure, running – and conservation enthusiasts have decided to do a mammoth run to help raise funds for Velakukhanya Primary School based in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The pair will be running in South Africa from Port Alfred to Cape Town, spanning 1, 222 km in 35 consecutive days - just shy of a marathon each day! Charles and Matt chose Velakukhanya Primary School as a project in their beloved province of KwaZulu-Natal, where they want to make a difference to the KwaNgwenya community and to the learners at this school, who did not have the same opportunities as they had growing up. Matt and Charles began their epic quest at the beginning of February and are about halfway to achieving their goal. If all goes according to plan, they'll finish on the 7th March in Cape Town. They’re running around 42km per day and are already dealing with the stresses and strains of running a marathon a day. Pushing through the pain of blistered feet, strained achilles tendons, damaged knees and the physical and mental fatigue is the desire to raise R2.3 million for the school.

We look at the physical and mental toll a journey of this magnitude takes on the minds and bodies of lifelong friend Matt and Charles and they undertake the adventure of a lifetime. Will they make it all the way to Cape Town? and what price will they pay for daring to run such an arduous race?
caseStudies: Matthew Murray Charles Raw
experts: Nelfrie Kemp

title: E-hailing Hell
oneLiner: An unregistered driver on the inDrive e-hailing app has been arrested after allegedly causing an accident that claimed the lives of three people.
summary:
E-hailing services provide easy access to transport for thousands of people across South Africa. But, how safe are you when you use them? And is it possible that your driver has simply bought or rented an account on one of the e-hailing platforms, and not registered properly. In this investigation, we uncover an alarming increase in accidents involving e-hailing drivers, and the scandalous advertising of e-hailing accounts for sale.

Police arrested a foreign national who had used the inDrive e-hailing platform to drive passengers around. On Sunday, 16 February, he was driving a 21 year old passenger when he sped through red lights and rolled the car. Two pedestrians, a two year old boy and his aunt, were hit. The child died on the scene, while his aunt died two days later. The passenger was also declared dead on the scene. The company inDrive confirmed that the drive was taken through their platform, but said the driver's details did not match the driver on their system.

title: Foreign Special | Flight MH 17: Who's responsible?
oneLiner: 298 dead, perpetrators identified, convictions nil
summary: 298 dead, perpetrators identified, convictions nil Flight MH17: Who's Responsible? A decade since the passenger flight MH17 was shot down, the guilty - convicted in absentia - remain protected in Russia. This Al Jazeera report investigates the last 10 years of evidence and Putin's direct involvement in the incident. Since 2014, investigators operating out of the Netherlands have been gathering evidence to claim justice for the victims and their families. Elliot Higgins, founder of Bellingcat - an Amsterdam based research group that does open-source investigation - states: "we were able to show definitively that the missile launcher came from Russia...and the exact route that was taken on the day." Digna Van Boetzaeler, chief prosecutor on the case, shows how social media implies the hit was a mistake originally celebrated by Russian troops who were convinced they'd hit a Ukrainian warplane; "After the plane was shot down, 65,000 tweets were sent out from the troll factory in St Petersburg saying #Ukraine, Kyiv and I." Since then, Russian media have changed their tune - claiming that MH17 was shot down by a Ukrainian military jet. Higgins raises an interesting point: "Perhaps if the world had reacted to MH17 at the time, there wouldn't have been such a permission structure for Putin to invade Ukraine in 2022."

title: De Klerks Scamster Couple
oneLiner: This couple are allegedly career conartists, we have a long list of alleged victims who we will interview, and we can confront them.
summary:
Legal Expert Insights: • Lawyer Hechter Hansel, representing the Vogels, has extensive experience in evictions but has never seen tenants as evasive and manipulative as the de Klerks. • The de Klerks have allegedly weaponized legal loopholes, dodging sheriffs and delaying proceedings for months. • The Vogels have filed a criminal case for the theft of their furniture, and the total financial losses—including unpaid rent, water, and electricity—are estimated at over R300,000. Family Insight & Criminal Past: • Christine’s estranged cousin has revealed shocking details: o Christine inherited a fortune from her mother and previously owned a luxury guesthouse in Potchefstroom. o Things took a dark turn when she met Stephen, a former policeman who was found guilty of culpable homicide after killing a passenger while driving drunk. o Christine allegedly bought Stephen’s law degree, only for him to later be disbarred for misappropriating trust funds. o The couple fled Potchefstroom under suspicious circumstances, allegedly after stealing money from guests via fraudulent card transactions. The De Klerks’ Next Move: Despite their extensive history of fraud and evictions, Christine and Stephen are already setting up their next venture—a new wedding venue in Pretoria called De la Mas. We have arranged a meeting with Christine under the pretense of booking a wedding, providing a unique opportunity for an undercover sting operation. Why This Story Matters: • The de Klerks are repeat offenders, with a clear pattern of deception spanning more than a decade. • Their scams have devastated families, destroyed businesses, and cost victims millions of rands. • Victims are desperate for justice and willing to speak out. • By exposing their tactics, we can help prevent future victims and hold the de Klerks accountable. We propose an in-depth investigation featuring exclusive interviews with victims, legal experts, and undercover footage. This is not just a rental scam—it’s a career built on fraud. It’s time to stop them.

Introduction: A dream home turned nightmare, a school hijacked, brides left in the lurch, and a mountain of unpaid rent—this is the story of Stephen and Christine de Klerk, a couple who have left a devastating trail of financial and emotional ruin in their wake. Through a series of carefully orchestrated scams, they have manipulated landlords, homeowners, business owners, and even unsuspecting brides. Now, with eviction proceedings underway and multiple victims speaking out, it’s time to expose their elaborate web of deception. Key Case Studies: 1. Charlene and Duan Vogel – Tierpoort Property Scam o The Vogels, returning expats, rented out their beautifully restored home to the de Klerks in 2021. For 18 months, things seemed fine—until the payments stopped. o After months of trying to resolve the issue amicably, the Vogels were forced to take costly legal action. Their final eviction hearing is scheduled for next Friday. o During their tenancy, the de Klerks allegedly sold the Vogels’ antique furniture and racked up massive unpaid bills. o Further investigation uncovered that this was at least the third property where the de Klerks had pulled the same stunt. 2. Bianca Honeyman – Aftercare Centre Hijacking o Bianca and her husband moved to Australia in 2016 and rented out their aftercare centre in Garsfontein to the de Klerks, who promised to buy the business. o The couple soon began redirecting emails, taking over bank accounts, and even RICA-ing the business phone number in their name. o They never paid rent, sent fake proof of payments, and used the business’s name to take out fraudulent contracts. o Financially and emotionally drained, Bianca and her husband were left with a failing business, massive debts, and ongoing legal battles. 3. Anzette Kleynhans – Rental Scam & Fake Hospital Payments o The de Klerks rented her property in 2016 but stopped paying rent within months. o She eventually got them evicted in 2018 after a lengthy legal battle. o She also alleges that they sent a fake proof of payment to Pretoria East Hospital for treatment of their baby. 4. Bev Untiedt – Stoneybrook Farm Scam o In 2018, the de Klerks moved into Bev’s guest farm with their two children, 12 cats, and 2 dogs. o After paying a small deposit, they never made another payment. o When Bev attempted to reclaim her property, Christine allegedly pushed and threatened her. o After removing items from the house, Bev was forced by police to return them due to a court order obtained by the de Klerks. Beyond Rental Scams: Business Fraud & Wedding Hoaxes • Wedding Venue Scams: o Jacques Kriel booked Luz Blanca at Esperanza, allegedly owned by Christine, for his wedding. After paying a R15,000 deposit, he later discovered the venue was not even theirs. o Christine allegedly scammed multiple couples by accepting bookings and payments for non-existent weddings. • Event Rental Scams: o Business owners like Kobus from B House Building Suppliers and Mary from Krchnavy Décor report that the de Klerks placed fraudulent orders, sent fake EFTs, and never paid for goods and services.

title: Sex offenders in schools
oneLiner: Sex offenders stay in schools due to failed vetting exercise
summary:
Pitch: Sexual abuse by teachers against learners makes regular headlines in South Africa - whether in the form of annual statistics or shocking individual cases. I have established that few teachers were subjected to criminal background checks when they were originally hired. In 2023, the Department of Basic Education announced a drive to “vet” all teachers and school staff in the country - almost half a million people - against the national sex offenders register. More than a year after the vetting project’s initial deadline of December 2023, progress statistics from the Department of Justice (DOJ) - which hosts the register - and the nine provincial education departments - which employ teachers - show that still fewer than 10 percent of teachers have been vetted. My access to- and interpretation of the consequence of these statistics is exclusive and original. Few people in education civil society have picked up on the extent of the failed vetting drive. If the progress stats from Gauteng - where they found 9 convicted rapists and sex offenders out of 11,000 police checks - are extrapolated across the whole teacher population it means that perhaps as many as 350 convicted sex offenders were in schools when the vetting drive started. I have been investigating the issue of sexual abuse in schools for years. Two major facts lend urgent to this vetting exercise: No accountability. Once sex abusers are in the schooling system, it is incredibly difficult to get them out. This is because the oversight mechanisms - which I have studied closely, and can expound on - often fail. This means that many sex abusers stay in the schooling system, even if complaints against them are filed. A staggering statistic to consider is that the South African Council of Educators (SACE) have registered 1,216 rape and sexual misconduct cases against teachers between 2014 and 2024. During that same period it be-registered at most 174 teachers for such offenses. This means that it is particularly important that convicted sex offenders not enter the schooling system, in the first place. No prior vetting. The majority of teachers currently employed in public schools were not subjected to criminal background checks when they were hired. This is another original investigative hypothesis, which I have provisionally substantiated, partly through looking at the collated responses of the nine provincial education departments to point blank queries. In a pertinent case from 2022, the Western Cape High Court ordered that province’s department to pay damages to a learner who was raped by a convicted sex offender teacher it had employed years prior, without checking his criminal background. Why has the vetting exercise failed? There is a lack of capacity at the DOJ to process thousands of clearance certificate requests. But, the vetting procedure at provincial level is also poorly conceived and was vulnerable to derailment from the start. For one thing, it appears to have depended on the proactive individual cooperation of hundreds of thousands of teachers to present themselves at police stations for fingerprinting - this was never going to happen. While some provincial education departments seek to blame DOJ backlogs and teacher non-cooperation for the slow progress, these departments bear ultimate responsibility for the failed vetting drive. This week, the Minister of Justice Mamoloko Kubayi said she would make public the national sex offenders register, to alleviate these challenges to vetting. This is HUGE, but is it really a silver bullet for the failed teacher vetting exercise? Or, will the DOJ simply now outsource its own “inefficient” - in the Minister’s words - vetting process to the nine provincial departments? Kubayi’s spokesman has responded to initial queries. But, he has offered an exclusive sit-down interview with the Minister, on her decision and the need for vetting teachers against the NRSO. I can also feature pertinent real life case studies - like a teacher who was found out for having resigned from his post to quash a sexual harassment case against him in Gauteng, only to be re-employed and to reoffend! I am also working on getting an interview, through her lawyers, with the woman who took the Western Cape Education Department to court in the above mentioned damages case. But, this is so far not secured.

an exclusive finding that a much touted national teachers vetting drive - to ensure there aren’t registered sex offenders in schools - has been a dismal failure. Likely scores of sex offenders remain in schools as a result (backed up by known stats)! Background showing why the vetting drive is urgent based on months of research by Viewfinder: because when sex offenders are in the system it is very hard to get them out because historically teachers weren’t subjected to criminal background checks when they were hired Another established relationship and likely sit-down interview - with Grant Butler the head of the South African Principals Association - who will defend teachers and principals and say that the failure of the vetting process is the fault of provincial education departments and DBE Case studies, illustrating some of the above.

title: Contraception Question
oneLiner: We show how standard government-issue contraception may need to be rethought following a BMJ study published last year
summary:
See above

We have access to individuals in the medical world who are reacting to new information in the way of a study which may change the approach to a contraceptive drug globally, in particular in low income countries. The studies highlight a possible link between the three month injection Depo-Provera, which is made of the synthetic hormone, MPA, and devastating brain tumours. This new information, while not conclusive, could have direct impact on the lives of millions of women who rely on discreet contraception to manage family planning in poorer settings. The case studies we interviewed who were suffering from meningiomas and had been on Depo-Provera for a length of time - sometimes decades - are sufficiently angry to start planning for a class action against the manufacturer of the drug, Pfizer. Their health, independence and livelihoods have been severely impacted by the Meningiomas and they are angry about the suffering they have experienced. This association has direct consequences for contraception across the developing world.

title: Sam Nujoma obit
oneLiner: We examine the legacy of Namibia's first president, Sam Nujoma.
summary:
Samuel Nujoma was a founding member and the first president of the South West Africa People's Organization (SWAPO) in 1960, campaigning for Namibian independence from South Africa. He established the People's Liberation Army of Namibia (PLAN) in 1962 and led SWAPO during a guerrilla war, the Namibian War of Independence, against the apartheid government from 1966 to 1989. When Namibia achieved independence and held its first democratic elections in 1990, SWAPO won and Nujoma was elected President. He served three terms, and retired as SWAPO president in 2007. Nujoma has been awarded the Lenin Peace Prize, the Indira Gandhi Peace Prize, and the Ho Chi Minh Peace Prize. The Parliament of Namibia named him "Founding President of the Republic of Namibia" and "Father of the Namibian Nation". In 2007 SWAPO named him "Leader of the Namibian Revolution."

95 year-old Sam Nujoma was admitted to hospital in late January with some reports describing him as being in critical condition. We examine and recognise his legacy as one of the last members of Southern Africa's liberation movements.
experts: Greg Mills

title: Limpopo: The Baobab Bomb
summary: Hundreds of thousands of indigenous trees – including baobabs and other specially protected species – are set to be the first casualties of a massive heavy industrial plan in Limpopo. It’s a scheme driven by the provincial government and Chinese developers who have touted it as the ‘ the most competitive energy metallurgy special zone in the world’. This is the Musina-Makhado Special Economic Zone (MMSEZ) one of 9 operational zones and three planned zones, that were approved – originally by President Zuma’s government in 2017. The MMSEZ envisages two main developments, one in the northern Musina area focusing on light manufacturing and agro-processing, the other in the southern Makhado (formerly Louis Trichardt) area focusing on coal mining, coal-fired power generation and steel manufacture. It's project that is being fought against by different sectors of the community. Three ( or two) people’s stories we will tell, who are fighting against this are: Lauren Liebenberg, a prominent activist fighting the MMSEZ development, Lauren, her two sisters and parents are part of a private nature reserve, Herd Reserve. This development could jeopardise the biodiversity in the Unesco-designated Vhembe Biosphere Reserve in Northern Limpopo and so strike a blow for the tourism industry in the area. And Makoma Lekalakala( Director Earthlife Africa) who lobbied against this project .As a direct result of his efforts the United Nations Development Programme ( UNDP) withdrew their support’ saying human and environmental rights including well-being of communities must be prioritised. And Mphatheleni Makaulule and her organisation, Dzomo La Mupo,( the voice of Creation) a grassroots community-based organisation that has been one of the strongest and most vocal (and courageous) opponents of the planned expansion of coal mining and development of the MMSEZ in the Vhembe. We will bring in other voices for specifics of the irregularities/controversies. Question the powers that be in the Limpopo Province to get clarity on a project that despite it’s enormous costs seems to be flying by the seat of its’ pants We will be examining the economic, environmental community and political implications of this enormous scheme over the coming months, drawing South African’s attention to the range of issues impacting lives and livelihoods. We will investigate the roots of the MMSEZ, how the project is still on going: Despite no feasibility on the project. Despite an environmental pre -feasibility study identifying critical environmental issues (like high water requirements in a water scarce area. Despite unexamined environmental risks a patch of SA soil has been handed over for 90 years to a foreign country. A project that will have major impact on the use of scarce resources, exports, pollution, greenhouse gas emissions ,local employment market and economic market.

title: Uncle Ben's Hell Hole
summary:
Uncle Ben's Den has been widely criticised on social media and Hello Peter. In an email, UBD director Ronel van Dyk has invited Carte Blanche to visit the facility at any time unannounced. According to the Department of Social Development UBD was registered as an NPO in 2007 but has since been deregistered. If a facility is not registered as an NPO and advertises as an NPO it is operating illegally. It should comply or face closure. Social workers from the department and SAPS have tried to get access to the facility but has been denied entry.

Uncle Ben’s Den is a care facility for elderly, homeless , mentally and physically disabled people. The facility director is Ronel van Dyk. Although the facility has appeared on Kyknet and received money from Lottoland there have been many complaints about the ill treatment, neglect and verbal abuse. Residents are crammed into houses without hot water and electricity. There is not much supervision and residents are often not given required medication . They would get into fights often harming each other or themselves. Residents complain that they are fed bread with no butter and mostly receive pap and spinach or a bit of rice with vegetables leaving many malnourished. Ronel has been accused of being verbally abusive . (Voice clip available) A meeting was called in the hall and 180 people attended. Ronel proceeded to , verbally abuse some of the residents. The rooms have no electricity or hot water. 8-13 people live in a house sharing 1 bathroom The bathroom has no door or curtain . There is a small chair where they can sit to wash themselves with cold water. . A family member of one of the residents paid the facility a visit after her aunt had passed away as she needed the funeral policy. On being questioned about the policy and her aunt’s bank accounts an altercation ensued and Ronel van Dyk assaulted the family member . She reported it to the police . A previous worker at the facility provided photos of residents with bedsores and says that van Dyk was often verbally abusive. Audio recordings of verbal abuse and altercation available. Police and social workers have visited the facility but were not allowed on the premises. VryheidsFront Plus and the Department of Social Development are actively looking into the allegations and have tried to gain access to the facility. It has always been denied will be visiting the facility. Mrs Mamabula from Social Development confirmed that no facility may refuse access by social workers or the police. Residents who have managed to leave the facility have complained of a lack of food some weighing less than 50kg.

title: UPDATE: GEKCO SLAPP suit
oneLiner: The biggest SLAPP suit in South African history has been withdrawn.
summary:
GEKCO is a conservation organisation working outside Johannesburg's northern boundary - which also happens to be one of the most rapidly developing areas in South Africa. The developments are mostly under Century, which is building commercial zones and housing such as Riversands Commercial Park and Helderfontein residential estate. In 2021, GEKCO lodged objections against these developments as part of the public participation process, and in return, Century brought a massive R197 million damages suit against GEKCO and its chair, Kristin Kallesen, in her personal capacity. Century claimed this was the cost of the delays that GEKCO's objections had caused. But legal experts and activists said this was not a legitimate case, but a SLAPP suit. SLAPP, or Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation, is a worrying growing trend globally: big corporates abusing court process and leveraging their greater resources to silence and intimidate communities, activists and journalists. But in the wake of a series of positive developments in South African law, Century has agreed to withdraw its claim against GEKCO. Activists hope it will mark a landmark in the battle against SLAPP in South Africa.

In 2021, we reported on the R197 million suit that Century Property Developments had brought against the Greater Kyalami Conservany (GEKCO) and its chair, Kristin Kallesen. In January this year, that suit was withdrawn.

title: Rabid Seals
summary:
On 4th January last year a young seal attacked a child in the water on Clifton Beach and an visiting America actress. People put this behaviour down to a bacterial infection of the brain caused by red tide bloom called Domic acid poisoning. It causes swelling around the brain and heart. But the last 4 seals the SPCA tested have tested positive for rabies. It’s an alarming finding as there is no cure for rabies in either humans or animals. If you get bitten on an extremity and immediately have a rabies vaccination you have a chance but if you get bitten on the face or upper body that’s a different matter.

Over the last two years there have been several reports of divers and surfers being attacked by seals in the waters around Cape Town. The latest was on 26th May in Muizenberg. 3 surfers were attacked by a young seal who “hunted” them. Biting through the wetsuit of one surfer and latching onto his board. He manged to fight him off by punching it, but it went on to attack 2 more surfers. Dion Bing was on the beach at the time and recorded the event on his surf report.

title: Educor crisis
oneLiner: Educor proud history of independent colleges has collapsed- what now for the students desperate for a decent qualification
summary:
The Education Department informed Educor at the end of last year that they were not allowed to register new students in 2024 until they complied. But despite this very public announcement covered by all the major TV stations City Varsity in Cape Town is in denial. Last week they told staff and lecturers it was business as usual, and the media had got it all wrong. What now for the staff and lecturers who have been struggling with the collapsing college? The Education Department have given them till the end of 2025 to complete the 2nd and 3rd year course. But the state of the facilities and already in a dire situation. Ashton Solomon senior lecture in Multimedia Digital design from 2019 has seen it all, he resigned last week when City Varsity blatantly lied to students. He will speak to the appalling situation of having to work for weeks without electricity due to unpaid bills. Students being admitted to courses they were clearly not qualified to take simply to bring in fees. Computer equipment that does not work and 15 students sharing the few computers that do work. He recorded the zoom meeting where staff discussed passing students on attendance rather than exam results and where the senior lecturer was fired when he opposed this. He will also speak to the fact that the staff are not paid, and do not receive support from the academic management and are expected to string students along. “Acting for Camera” is one of the courses on offer at City Varsity and will set you back R48,000. Irate 3rd year student Billy Shumba Brighton says it’s false advertising. He was promised he would ”experience meaningful mentorship by the best academics in the industry who keep close ties to their field of focus. Our students’ learning experience is enhanced by state-of-the-art equipment and facilities. Boasting studios, an infinity wall, dark room, casting rooms and fully equipped labs, our campus is sure to give you that VIP experience.“ There was no camera to act in front of, for most of his 1st year, they had to use the lecturers’ cell phones and their own cell phones to do their final assessments, says Billy. They had a great lecturer for a couple months, but he was never paid so he left and so there was no end-of-year performance, the students filmed their own final performance and the lecturer returned briefly to assess their submissions. Now there is one dysfunctional camera instead of acting in front of 3 cameras. So many lecturers left during the year that they felt completely demoralized. Exams are required to have external examiners, but City Varsity is known for not paying, so now there are no independent assessments done. Billy’s mother is a domestic worker and he can’t face telling her about the shocking state of the course, and now the news that City Varsity has been deregistered he fears that his qualification is worth nothing. Mazwaneni Fani is a first year student, he paid he registration fee and a pre assessment fee to get into the Multi media course. His mother is a nurse and extremely distressed at the situation and says Mazwaneni mental state is really bad since the announcement – he was so exited to get into City Varsity because last year he didn’t qualify for any of the technical colleges. She is unable to get any answers out of City varsity and simply referred to Damlin College, which has also been deregistered. She will make an very strong interview.

Finally the Department of Education has taken action against Educor, deregistering City Varsity, Damelin, ICESA and Lyceum College. For the last couple of years these institutions have been in financial trouble, but they failed to submit the 2021/2022 Financial records and Tax Clearance certificates to the Department of Education and despite being given several extensions they failed to comply. They lied about their student numbers, saying they had 50 000 students when records show closer to 13 000 and the quality of the education is below standard and does not comply with the CITA regulations. Students are getting marks based on attendance rather than exams. The staff turnover is extremely high due to salaries not being paid. Electricity and rental bills are not paid and Braamfontein campus was simply closed without notice to staff or students.

title: The Decay of Urban Spaces
oneLiner: The influx of homeless people into the suburbs is leading to the urban decay of public spaces. How does one balance compassion for the homeless a with the needs of communities that feel under existent
summary:
A failing economy is driving more and more people into poverty leading to an influx of desperate people to middle-class suburbs in search of opportunity. The result is that residential streets, urban parks and other public spaces are becoming overrun by a mixture of homeless people, substance abusers and illegal immigrants. The problem is being exacerbated by the failure of the authorities to enforce by-laws hastening the degradation of these important public spaces. People can be found loitering illegally on sidewalks, sleeping in front of shops and inside city parks themselves. In the worst cases, abandoned buildings are hijacked and transformed into squalid informal settlements that threaten the safety of residents, the environment and the fiscal sustainability of small businesses - that are so vital to the South African economy. How does one balance compassion for the homeless a with the needs of communities that feel under existential threat?

Carte Blanche grapples with the impact of homelessness on public spaces, a complex problem with no obvious and easy solutions

title: Shack City
oneLiner: A world Class City building shacks for millions of Rands
summary:
Shack City *All visuals in a shared Google Drive What is the story? The City of Johannesburg is actively building shacks for millions of Rands. Why is this a problem? According to the City’s Guidelines for Emergency Housing, the municipality must proactively conduct assessment of possible buildings to determine the extent they can be converted and refurbished to meet conditions for transitional accommodation, including condition of structure and existing services. This has not been happening for years. There are abandoned and unsecured buildings in the inner the City has had years to renovate. In addition, there is valuable infrastructure which is not being refurbished and maintained which would eliminate unnecessary costs to fiscus. What are these costs? Usindiso Cost of Usindiso building fire, the market value of the building which will be demolished (still awaiting these costings from the City), the R 4.2 million water bill never collected by the City will only impact the ever increasing rates bill Denver Shalazile Lot Land was bought for R 40 million - 2020 for purposes of JMPD impound and never used. Now it’s been repurposed for shacks for survivors of fire and other former inner city building residents. City insider says he was in a heated meeting in 2020 where JMPD execs were angry with Helen for not consulting on the purchase as its near the hostel and there are concerns about crime. Requested interview and information from JMPD - they shut it down saying Floyd Brink will respond. Highlights waste of taxpayer Rands on untested pursuits The shacks In an emergency housing plan the department of human settlements indicated it needed over R 68 million for 1000 shacks which includes the electrification, sanitation and civil engineering of the land. This would equate to approximately R 68 000 per shack. When we put in a question to DHS, it stated it had paid R 4.2 million for 300 shacks thus far. The total of 1000 shacks will cost an estimated R 14 million. It would be interesting if the shacks cost more than R 500 000 to build. Why the discrepancy? I asked if the R 14 million total includes water and electrification, demolishing exiting structures on the land and civil engineering. The City states it will get back to me. City Power I contacted City Power to ask what the planned cost to electrify the camp will be - it stated R 88 million for the informal settlement. This brings us closer to the original estimates. Important to note: the informal settlement includes the existing formal settlement in Denver as the Shalazile Camp will form part of the Upgraded Informal Settlement Program. Last year, R 4 billion was set aside to upgrade informal settlements. Inordinate amounts are being spent to implement electricity and water infrstructure on shacks - prone to fires - while the City ignores the infrastructure in the inner city. The Contractor To highlight a further waste of money and the questionable decisions of the City, the contractor awarded the tender to build the shacks is Laphinda Security & Cleaning Services. There is no internet traceability of construction projects executed by Laphinda Security only a Facebook page with a single image of two security guards standing by a branded Laphinda Security vehicle. Laphinda Security has an expired MBD Grading 1 - PE 1GB. It expired in February 2022. PE 1GB means the contractor cannot even receive a contract valued at R 1 million yet it received a contract of R 4.2 million. This may explain why residents of the camp are getting cut on the corrugated material and why the shacks are flooding - an incompetent contractor from a police panel. Using JMPD panel for Human Settlement project Why is the department of human settlements using a JMPD contractor to execute its work of providing human settlements Shack quality standards The department of human settlements under its mandate does not build shacks. The NHBRC does not quality assure shacks. Highlighting the pure waste of taxpayer Rands on structures which are temporary in nature. In the guidelines for temporary housing, temporary Relocation Units or Temporary Emergency Accommodation is meant to be up to 12 months. How can the City justify building shacks for millions of Rands for up to 12 months? In fact, the City is actively building an informal settlement from scratch. Is this how the City will be tackling the 500 000 housing backlog moving forward? Did the City have options? Yes. - To secure and maintain its own buildings in the inner City. To proactively identify buildings suitable for potential emergencies in order to drastically minimise the capital outlay on emergency accommodation - To upgrade and maintain available inner city infrastructure instead of investing in mega cities outside the economic hub. Mega Cities are huge mixed use property development projects able to house over 10 000 units. These megacities have cost billions and have remained incomplete and often mostly empty for decades. Mayors wasting money on pipe dreams Herman Mashaba - Inner city rebirth - R 20 billion Parks Tau - Project Kopanong - R 5 billion to revitalise inner city buildings. Who will help tell the story Andy Chinnah - Human rights activist Andy has been a human rights activist for over 20 years. He has worked intimately with the survivors of the Usindiso building fire from day one. He ha attended every single day of the commission and has amazing insights into the City’s failings Heather of Savage Dodd Architects Heather Dodd has been renovating buildings in the inner city for the last 20 years. Dodd’s firm also developed Elangeni across from Usindiso. She will give insights into the cost to revamp these city abandoned buildings and the city’s failure to protect its assets including the inner city infrastructure. We’ll go to Cresthill and Vannin court in the same street. One revamped by the firm and the other they did all the ground work for but it never took off due to unnecessary project delays. Sithembiso Dlamini Sithembiso is a mother of two children - a teenage daughter and a 10 year old special needs son. They survived the fire and were relocated to the one room 3x3 m tin shacks at Shalazile. Since the fire, her son stopped walking - the state gave her an old wheelchair with faulty wheels. For years. Sithembiso struggled to secure a place for her son at a special needs school but finally managed to do so in the South. Unfortunately, it costs her R 1500 to transport her child to school daily. This takes up the bulk of the R 2090 social grant she receives. In an effort to survive - Sithembiso began selling refreshments from her shack - this drew the attention of two armed men who knocked on her cardboard shack door at 1 a.m a few weeks ago - she managed to fight them off. A week later, four knife-wielding men knocked at her cardboard door at an ungodly hour…smashing it in with ease. One attempted to stab her and she screamed which drew the attention of other shack dwellers who assaulted the assailant. He has been hospitalized and she receives regular death threats - if he should die, she will die too. She says her assailants are from the nearby Denver Hostel. She reported the matter to the DHS and the police - nothing has been done to move her to safety. This despite the fact there is a disability grant in the emergency guidelines meant to cater to survivors like Sithembiso. She has nowhere to go and is suicidal. Shacks by Teboho Teboho has been building decent shacks for over 5 years. These Denver shacks are shoddy even for shacks. How could the City get shacks wrong? It demonstrates the complete lack of care for the survivors and demonstrates their disdain for the inner city. Teboho will assess the shack standards since the NHBRC - understandably doesn't quality assure shacks. We will also get a quote from Builders Warehouse in order to get an accurate value on how much was actually spent. Official Interview - awaiting confirmation from the City

The City of Johannesburg building shacks for million of Rands

title: Capturing the Court

Research by the MHCAC released earlier this year found that if the move went ahead, one-third of Makhanda’s businesses would lose so many customers that they would have to shut down. Makhanda would become a “ghost town” where unemployment would skyrocket from 38.3% to above 50%, significantly higher than the national average of 33.6%. The research also found that more than 5000 people associated with different aspects of running and supplying the court would lose their jobs. In Bhisho SKG Africa has been buying up office buildings and land, building an elaborate new office complex at Independence Avenue Office Park, and promising to refurbish the dilapidated Amatola Sun hotel and golf course for a cool R3 billion! But what it is it about Bhisho? Could he be positioning himself to accommodate the the dozens of new offices needed to accommodate the High Court move? 1. 25 offices for advocates 2. 40 offices for attorneys 3. 50 offices for the Master's Office 4. 20 offices for the NPA 5. 10 offices for the Legal Resources Centre 6. 10 offices for Legal Aid 7. 4 offices for the Sheriff

An interview with Jean du Plessis the owner of SKG and 50+ other companies. He owns the luxury Ebenhaeser Guest House spread over 3 properties overlooking the Nahoon River. SKG Africa is a massive property company based in East London. They own well over 600 properties throughout the country and have over 500 leases with government departments. For this, they earn well over R1.2 billion per annum. In East London SKG built the massive Waverley Office Park which houses 22 public entities, including the Amathole District Municipality. They also house the Buffalo City Municipality in various city offices. So why did the ANC-led municipality agree to write off R50m owed to them by SKG Africa? And when the DA requested that the decision be rescinded, why did the ANC Mayor refuse to allow a vote?

title: Milking Kimberley Psychiatric
oneLiner: Five years after it's openend, the Kimberley Mental Health Hospital, is in shambles, risking staff and patient safety.
summary:
In the early 2000s, the Northern Cape faced a severe shortage of psychiatric facilities, forcing patients to await placement in prisons due to insufficient hospital beds. Despite plans to build a modern mental health hospital in Kimberley, corruption scandals ensued, delaying construction and causing building costs to skyrocket. The hospital finally opened its doors in 2019, but five years later, the rot of corruption is running deeper than ever, as the facility continues its struggle to provide even basic services and adequate mental health care. When issues are raised, staff hears “there’s no money”, but Carte Blanche gold hold of a number of documents proving that inflated payments by the Department of Health in the province are eating away at the mental health budget meant for vulnerable patients. Nepotism among high-ranking officials have further worsened the situation. The failure to fulfil promises to improve mental health services underscores the need for accountability and proper management to address the dire conditions affecting patients and staff in the Northern Cape.

title: 30 Years of Democracy - South Africa as our home
oneLiner: South Africans reflect on how the democratic South Africa has served them as their home over the last thirty years
summary:
The history of SA is one of migration, displacement, belonging, exile, leaving home to seek new opportunities elsewhere. So our focus will be on the landscape and the different challenges experienced by the citizens of five of our main provinces. We propose dividing the 72 minute documentary into six parts (of about 12 minutes each), with an introduction and conclusion making up one part, and five longer parts where we get to know people who have been part of the democratic journey in different areas of the country, but who we find in their homes. To develop a picture of that journey we propose to separate each part or segment with poetic visuals – drones, wide shots, close up shots, stills, time lapses – of transport infrastructure: roads, railways, runways, traffic, taxis, cars, aeroplanes, potholes, broken bridges, contrasting both the sophisticated infrastructure that works and that which is broken. The images will also speak to what binds us, what connects us to the landscape. Much of this will be without voice over or narrative and will paint a verbal picture. They will also provide a dynamic tension with the homes we visit. We will need to film in both rural and urban spaces, across five provinces - Gauteng, Eastern Cape, Western Cape, Kwazulu-Natal and maybe Northern Cape. In locating our characters at home, we will also, by default, highlight the issues of migration, and displacement, isolation, belonging, disillusionment, loss, hope and love which are also common in the country’s experience. The infrastructure segways will contribute to that effect. We propose a narrative voice to link the parts but will keep the wording sparse. It will be a voice to link and create context rather than an explaining voice. We will focus the interview on three main questions: 1) How are you feeling about South Africa as your home? 2) What events have happened to make you feel like that? 3) What are your hopes for the future South Africa? Those questions will be set in an interview which also asks them questions about who they are and how they live their life. The answers will be threaded through the documentary with broader context provided by political and social experts. The characters and experts selected will be given licence to answer in seriousness but also with humour. We hope to interview approximately three to four people and expert in each province, with some specifically identified for a slightly different Afrikaans version.

We have a unique opportunity to feel the pulse of South Africa's democracy through the lived experience of a range of people across South Africa. This is a story about South Africa and her people: A reflection on how we are doing, what brought us to this point and how do we feel about the future.

title: Gibson Nzimande
oneLiner: From wastepicker to Master's degree graduate, Gibson Nzimande is a steadfast student who excelled despite adversities.
summary:
This is the story of Gibson Nzimande who grew up in a blended family, living a normal life of a middle-class family in a house in Katlehong, the East of Johannesburg. One day his normal life was turned upside down. This was four years ago. He not only lost his mother but was thrown to the streets, abandoned by his six siblings and father. He was forced into street life, during the day collecting recyclables from the streets of Sandton and getting paid for it in Alex where there are several recycling centers. At night he slept under a tree on Rivonia Road. He decided the only thing that would save him from the street life was education so he went to a local library and enrolled at the University of Johannesburg to study. Today he holds a Masters's degree in History, with plans to pursue his PhD. He cleaned up with the help of petrol attendants who would sneak in to get hot water for him to bathe, he would buy food and study materials with the money from recycling and study at a bench near the garage. He says during the day he would collect waste and at night he studied with the help of the petrol station's lights. His former lecturer took him out of the streets after hearing his story and helped him scrap his debt with the university while getting more funding for him to study further and get accommodation. He fought hard to stay away from crime and drugs that he was constantly exposed to, in street life. That was not the only challenge he was faced with but the severe poverty, but through it all he preserved and became the success he is today. - I would tell the story through a recreation of images by following the day in the life of a waste picker. We met with one of his old friends who has agreed to this. This includes close-up shots of the sack they use to carry the recyclables, him getting up to go collect, long shots of him passing through places like Sandton City pulling his trolley and later delivering them to be weighed so he can get paid. This is against the backdrop of his interview about his old life. - An interview with a petrol attendant (Johannes) who also helped him with food and water near where he used to sleep. I would like to film the petrol station at night to show what lighting Gibson had to work with. Perhaps a timelapse would be a creative way to demonstrate this. - A childhood friend (Tumelo Ntoyi) who can refer us to the background story of Gibson, how they grew up, and his account of how the transition affected Gibson. This is the closest person to being family as his whole family abandoned him and did not even reconcile with him post-graduation as one would expect. I would like to film them revisiting where they used to live, where they would go by bread for example, generic shots of a playground or park they used to visit. Just to reminisce of their old lives in the township growing up. - The lecturer Prof Thembisa at the university, general cutaways of the lecture hall and them wokring and of the university. - Additional shots are of the city life, the hustle and bustle, moving taxis, and street vendors. - General shots of the groups of the waste-pickers sitting down and eating or moving together with their trolleys in groups, also shots of them at the scrap yards. - The new life of Gibson in his small room at the student res, and shots of him going to the library living his new life. He stays in a residence in the city. - Additional pictures of him in his old life. - Graduation pictures.

Only 6% of South Africans have university degrees, and in numbers that is 1,7 million people in a country of 59,39 million. This is according to the Higher Education Department in 2021. One of those people is Gibson Nzimande, with all odds stacked against him, he made it through and is on his way to a PhD.

title: Amapanyaza
oneLiner: Are Gauteng's new Crime Prevention Wardens the Premier's illegal private army?
summary:
Hastily trained over s few weeks, questions have been raised about the wide-ranging powers the AmaPanyaza have to fight crime. The province calls them "peace officers" but were they constituted properly under the law? The justice ministry says they did not gazette this as required in legislation. Since they have hit the streets allegations have emerged that they have beaten residents of Ekurhuleni including a young man who has been left unable to urinate on his own and uses a catheter. The wider question is also about the money and whether funds were diverted from NGOs looking after the elderly and disabled to create this unit.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi says his 6000 newly employed officers are still in training as they wait the gazetting of their duties by various departments. So why have they been deployed to various crime hotspots around the province? On what basis did they allegedly assault "Sipho" who sustained extensive injuries that have left him barely able to walk and reliant on a catheter to urinate? If not yet properly constituted, how is this force being paid? By what authority? Is the money allocated to them being used properly? "Sipho" will share his dramatic assault by these wardens and how it has nearly destroyed his life.

title: Hysterectomy Hell
oneLiner: One in four women undergo a hysterectomy by the age of 55 years old, according to American statistics. In many cases, its unnecessary.
summary:
Melanie Verwoerd was diagnosed with an ovarian tumour in 2021. She was told that there was a 70 to 80% chance that it was cancerous and a radical hysterectomy was performed. Turned out, the tumour was benign, and she needn't have had a hysterectomy after all. Eight months of a gruelling recovery process followed. Hundreds of women have contacted her since her book was published, and her podcast broadcast, detailing their experiences. Verwoerd has become somewhat of an activist, urging women to obtain second opinions and spreading awareness about the difficult mental and physical recovery after a radical hysterectomy.

One in four women undergo a hysterectomy by the age of 55 years old. In some cases, its entirely unnecessary. A Cape Town woman, Melanie Verwoerd, has written a book and produced a podcast "Never Waste A Good Hysterectomy" detailing the trauma of her experiences.

title: Saving Private Rhino
oneLiner: We reveal the fate of the largest privately owned white rhino herd in the world
summary:
African Parks has one clear objective: to rewild these rhino over the next 10 years to well-managed and secure areas, establishing or supplementing strategic populations, thereby de-risking the future of the species. The breeding programme will be phased out and the project will end once all the rhino are released into the wild. This is one of the largest continent-wide rewilding endeavours to occur for any species.

Africa’s beleaguered rhinos have been thrown a significant lifeline with the announcement that nearly 2,000 semi-wild rhinos owned by South African rhino breeder John Hume will be “rewilded” into reserves across South Africa and other parts of the continent over the next 10 years. African Parks, a private Johannesburg-based conservation NGO that manages 22 protected areas in partnership with 12 governments across Africa, confirmed on Monday, 4 September that it had “stepped in as the new owner of the world’s largest private captive rhino breeding operation”, the Platinum Rhino project, a 7,800-hectare property in North West.

title: Bajaj Qute
summary: Bajaj e-hailers have been promised hell if they enter certain areas with their cars to pick up or drop off customers. Actually, Bajaj is not classified as a car but a quadricycle and recently a number of them got impounded by the JMPD due to them not being in possession of operator’s licenses. Some drivers are now operating in fear. The E-hailing industry regards them as a big disaster waiting to happen as they consider them unsafe and not fast enough to escape violence that could be unleashed on them and the mini-bus taxi industry commented that “we don’t even want to see those things here”. Bajaj Qute is a quadricycle originally from India that has been introduced to the e-hailing industry by Bolt South Africa. It is regarded as the most affordable for consumers and drives at a top speed of 70km per hour. It is supposed to take trips not more than 4km with only one passenger. The E-hailing industry association believes the introduction of Bejaj into the market is just another exploitation by the big apps and they swear that Bejaj won’t last in South Africa. They believe that these cars will be abused on the road and will leave a number of drivers with a huge debt. The Bejaj is an improved version of a Tuk-Tuk and even though Tuk-Tuks are located in limited areas, it seems the Bejaj will be able to move around the city. The Bajaj has been approved by the SA regulator, The National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications (NRCS) as it meets the specification of a quadricycle. To acquire a Bajaj for Bolt, a driver pays R1500 a week for 3 years. The company supplying Bejaj, MyNextCar, takes care of the insurance and maintenance. On our visit to MyNextCar offices, a long queue of drivers was signing up for a car that even its own industry, the ehailing industry, believes is not welcomed in South Africa. They feel the app giant is just adding a problem on top of all the other problems they are experiencing. What is Bajaj and can it survive the South Africa tough and hostile e-hailing industry?

title: Westbury Violence
oneLiner: It is a gangster paradise, Westbury a community filled with drugs, guns, and gangs.

A fight between gangsters, Now pastors who are former gangsters are being targeted Community violence bleeds into schools Centers accommodating young people. PART ONE The segment starts with clips of heavy police presence, and police arresting people. Followed by a line explaining that Westbury is a community enveloped in violence, drugs, and gangsterism. Clip of gunshots Number of people get caught in the crossfire. Gang rivals battle over streets and territories, leaving the community in fear. But Westbury wasn't like that. Some say it all changed when drugs were introduced in the community. PART TWO Move to Church. Pastor Eugine comes in and explains what Westbury used to look like as a young boy playing soccer. Pictures of him as a young soccer player. He explains how the gangs operated in the late 1960s and early 1970. Him being part of one of the gangs. PART THREE Move to Reverend Peter Faver. He will explain how the 1999 peace treaty was short lived. He will speak on how the operations of the gangs changed. He will talk about how gangs are the core in the business of selling drugs, and how young people are recruited by these gangs, which is different from what they did back then. He then talks about how they are targeted as former gangsters, and why he believes they are a target. He explains about how he was shot at the gym by a 16-year-old. PART FOUR Back to pastor Eugine. Just like Reverend Peter, he will explain how he was target while at a cemetery during a funeral Highlights Pastor Eugine: shots of him in the church. We took a walk with him to the graveyard. This is a place where he survived a drive through shooting, but also where he buries these young people. Also why people are afraid to go to funerals. Reverent Peter: Shoots of him at Kofifi Radio station. Him working with youngsters who are former drug users. PART FIVE Three months ago one of the alleged gang leaders was gunned down. Since then there has been a heavy police presence in the area. Here SAPS explains the strategy in place to deal with the violence. SAPS will also address the allegations of corrupt police officers who work with these gangsters, where in some instances some police officers were arrested. PART SIX A clip of students at Westbury High School We explain that the violence in the community bleeds into schools, and Westbury High School is not an expansion. Acting Principal Mr Dickson explains how some students bring weapons to school. Also how one student tried to shoot him in his office. PART SEVEN Clips showing what Westbury looks like. People standing in corners, taxi’s hooting, street vendors. We ask where do young people in Westbury go, to get away from the chaos. We introduce Westbury Youth Centre, managed by Brigit Munnik. Brigit will talk about the plenty of resources available for young people in the community. How the center replaces drugs and guns, with skills development. Highlights: Brigit: Shots of different activities available at the center, that’s dancing, drama, singing, computer skills. We walk with Brigit as she talks to young people who are not in school, and sitting by the corners. Overall: Painting Westbury. Environmental noise. Hero shots

For many years, Westbury has been engulfed with violence. There are constant shootings, with innocent community members being caught in the crossfire. But Westbury’s gang violence is not a new phenomenon, it has been going on for decades. It dates back to the late 1960s, and early 1970s. The gangs: Fast guns, Varados, and Vultures were formed during this time. At that time these gangs were joined by individuals who were interested in soccer and Boxing. But soon that changed when drugs were introduced in the community. Selling drugs became a lucrative business. The gangs moved to fighting and killing each other over territories to sell drugs. After many years of back and forth between the three gangs, in 1999 they decided to call a truce. They met at Cecile Payne stadium and agreed on a peace deal. They handed over their guns, and burned flags associated with their gangs. Some of the gang members went to church and became pastors, but others went back to their old ways and revived the gangs. Since then Westbury has been prone to violence. In late February and March this year violence erupted in the community when an alleged leader of one of the gangs was shot dead. Currently there is a heavy police presence in the area. This story will look at the current targets of these gangs, pastors who were once gangsters. They are targeted under the notion of revenge, as people who once killed and went to jail, and therefore they need to pay for what they did. One of the pastors' who is targeted is Pastor Eugene Wheats. He is a former gangster, who was saved after the 1999 peace agreement. Last year when he was performing a graveside service, gangsters drove through and started shooting. He jumped into the grave hole. When these kinds of drive through shootings happen, it is innocent community members who are caught in the crossfire. The story will also feature a mother who lost her child because of the violence. The current gangs use young people to carry out the crimes. This includes the selling of drugs, hijackings, and killing the targets. As a result, the drugs and weapons end up at schools. Acting principal Westbury high School, who was also threatened with a gun by one of his students, will explain what the school is doing to fight violence. Young people in Westbury are exposed to drugs and violence, where do they go to get away from the chaos. Westbury Youth Center provides skills development to young people in the community. It is run by Brigit Munnik. She works with young people who are in school, those who left the gangs, and those who are unemployed and are recruited by the gangs. She replaces guns and drugs with skills development programs.

title: Pussyfooting around Putin
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche we examine why the South African government is pussy-footing around Putin and why it may be dangerous for the country
summary:
The ANC’s political allegiance to its Cold War friend, Russia, is causing a political rumpus as a potential visit to South Africa by Russian President Vladimir Putin forces the South African government to make choices, including whether or not it leaves the International Criminal Court, which may reset its already damaged global reputation for the worse. The ICC has issued a warrant of arrest for Putin for the kidnapping of thousands of Ukrainian children during the conflict between the neighbours. As South Africa is a signatory to the Rome Statute which underpins the ICC, it would be obliged to arrest Putin if he comes to South Africa. Putin was expected to arrive for the BRICS summit in August this year along with leaders of the countries aligned with South Africa in this economic block – Brazil, India and China. The Premier of the Western Cape, Alan Winde, says he will get his unarmed LEAP officers to arrest Putin if strays into the Western Cape, a province under the political control of the opposition. While this throws up the spectacle of the absurd – unarmed para-police officials arresting one of the world’s militaristic strong men – it has set the cat further among the pigeons, sending the government into a legal huddle as it tries to work out what to do. Already the issue is being passed from ministry to ministry as the legal ramifications of a potential Putin visit are examined, the tension between the political party, the ANC, the government and the interests of the economy and South Africa’s citizens are weighed up, not to mention South Africa’s constitutional commitment to a human rights based foreign policy. This political hot potato is just one more milestone in South Africa’s slow drift to isolationism, which has been compounded by greyl-isting, industrial-scale corruption, poor governance, loss of investor confidence and a clumsy foreign policy which appears to be biased ideologically to the allies of the ANC, rather than drawn from a strategic positioning of South Africa to get the maximum benefit from trade and political opportunities from the Global North. We look at the event, the discussions around it and the consequences of pussy-footing around Putin, in the context of this dangerous drift, in which so much of the country’s moral and financial capital could be squandered.

This is the hot topic of the moment which has engaged two government ministries, and both wings of the Presidency plus numerous civil society bodies and commentators - and the brouhaha around Putin's potential visit throws South Africa drift into isolationism into sharp focus.

title: Bester Update
oneLiner: Carte Blanche sits down with Judge Edwin Cameron to unpack the investigation that exposed the Thabo Bester saga. Also, nee details have emerged of the man whose body was used to fake Thabo Bester’s
summary:
The benefit of the previous insert is that some of our speakers, including the hidden inmate, speak extensively and passionately about the issues at Mangaung prison. Those previously unheard parts of the interview are hugely informative. With the judge and DCS brought into the conversation the story is a great opportunity to explore the future possibilities when it comes to the DCS-G4S contract. The question here being: if the department failed to listen and act on the repetitive warnings of JICS, how can the public trust that the department will act accordingly and in its best interests when it comes to the G4S contract? The department has said that it is in talks with its legal department about the contract. We expect the department to take the viewers into its confidence and give the status of thos talks.

The audacious Thabo Bester prison break, the mystery of the unidentified body in cell 35 and the watchdog with no teeth – as they are uncovered, the details of the recent escape from Mangaung prison continue to shock the public both locally and internationally. For authorities, the focus has been on rounding up all the suspects and figuring out who had what role in the grand plan. And the biggest question in that regard remains: who did the charred remains wheeled out of cell 35 belong to? What seems to have escaped the spotlight is the fact that before the GroundUp exposé, there was an investigation by an independent body that was instrumental in piecing the bizarre facts together. Despite having almost limitless investigating powers, unfortunately this state organ has no authority to lay charges with law enforcement and initiate criminal investigations. It's core functions are to “facilitate the inspection of correctional centres” and “report on the treatment of inmates in correctional centres and on the treatment of inmates in correctional services.” Such reports are then sent to the Minister of Justice, Correctional Services and the portfolio committee. This body, tasked with overseeing these investigations, is the Judicial Inspectorate of Correctional Services (JICS), headed by Inspecting Judge Edwin Cameron. At the parliamentary portfolio committee recently, he was at pains to explain the limits to the powers of JICS.

title: Ouma Karina last survivor of an ancient tongue Nluu
summary:
As a child growing up on a farm at the edge of the Kalahari, Katrina was forced to stop speaking her language, Nluu – later in life, even her husband told her her language was ugly. But in the early 1990s, Elsie Vaalbooi, a N|uu speaker made a public radio call for other speakers of the language to come forward, attracting about 29 speakers from the Northern Cape area - today Katrina is the sole survivor. She is determined her language and culture will not die with her- she has spent the last 20 years working with linguists who have made hours of recordings while she has painstakingly repeated each work and story she recalls. But it’s a complex language and Karina is literate and so relies on visiting academics and her granddaughter to capture the language. She is determined her language will survive and has written a children’s book the ”Tortoise and the Ostrich” and various academics have written basic readers to teach the children in her community. But late last year a comprehensive Nluu dictionary was released – a culmination of over 25 years of work, in Nama, English and Northern Afrikaans. This has given Ouma Kartina hope that her language will survive, she herself has spent years teaching children in a school out the front of her house along with her granddaughter Claudia Snyman. But promises are plenty and funding scare. She is not short of awards and acclaim. In 2014 she was awarded the Order of the Baobab Silver, in 2017 the Deputy Minister of Arts and Culture Rejoice Mabudafasi declared Nluu would be taught in schools up to university- in 2023 she was awarded an Honorary doctorate in Literature from the University of Cape Town for her enormous contribution to preserving her language and her culture by being awarded this honorary doctorate. 90-year-old Esau stood on the UCT stage for the entire award speech – she was an incredible presence embodying so much history. But despite the acclaim and recognition, the State have not provided for her in any way, not even funding her school. Kartina at 90 lives in a small home in a dusty suburb of Upington along with her 26 members of her family. She is the sole breadwinner providing for them with what she earn from various academics for her expertise. There are over 6,500 languages and dialects still spoken in the world - 25 disappear every year, and with them heritage and culture.

This week 90-year-old Katrina Esau was awarded an honorary Doctorate of Literature by the University of Cape Town in recognition of her contribution to the preservation of her language, Nluu. She is the sole surviving speaker of her 25,000-year-old language. Largely an oral as opposed to written language, Nluu is extremely complex with 114 distinct sounds, including 45 clicks, 30 non-click consonants and 39 vowels. To place this in context, English, Russian and Chinese have about 50 sounds.

title: The Arch Angels
oneLiner: The are a group of unlikely seafarers brought together by fate ,they are the Arch Angels and they are taking the world of sailing by storm.
summary: - In a history-making voyage, the first complete crew from the Royal Cape Yacht Club Sailing Academy hailing from marginalised communities has crossed the finish line of the 50 th Cape2Rio yacht race, after a thrilling battle to gain third position. The dreams of five young South Africans came true on Thursday as their boat, the AArchAngel, arrived in Rio de Janeiro after 24 days and a 3,300 nautical mile ocean crossing from Cape Town to Guanabara Bay. Skipper Sibusiso Sizatu (30), first mate Daniel Agulhas (29), Renaldo Tshepo Mohale (29), Azile Arosi (22) and Justin Peters (21) departed on January 2, with the backdrop of the historic Robben Island reminding them of Nelson Mandela’s words, "It always seems impossible until it's done”. The final hours of ArchAngel’s race saw the boat neck and neck with their closest competitor, Argonaut, eventually beating them by 23 minutes. This is the achievement of their lives. So many years, so many obstacles, yet they kept moving forward. Born into disadvantaged communities, the crew have broken stereotypes of race and class and demonstrated that it is possible for people from diverse backgrounds to participate in sports such as yachting, previously accessible only to the privileged few. Sizatu says in the future, he hopes to see an all-female crew from the Academy doing a race of similar stature, empowering more women in the sport. The Alexforbes ArchAngel crew have made history in the golden anniversary of the iconic race. Sixteen teams lined up at the start, hailing from South Africa, Brazil, India, Italy and the United States of America, with three boats withdrawing during the challenging event. The overall race was won by Atalanta, with Ray of Light in second position.
