title: Reading crisis
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche we investigate how government inaction is driving the illiteracy crisis
summary:
Executive summary Being able to read is one of the most important ways for a child to break out of a cycle of intergenerational poverty. As many as 80 percent of Grade 4 children in SA cannot read. Despite the president and government’s commitment that every Grade 4 child should be able to read for meaning by 2030, SA’s children are making pitifully slow progress towards this goal. Using the findings of the Reading Panel 2030’s recent report on government’s progress, we have identified that the lack of planning, implementable literacy programs and budgets at both the national and provincial departmental levels is an important driver of the literacy crisis in South Africa. We have gained access - through permission from a principle - to a school in a township outside Makhanda in the Eastern Cape. With this and other access in Makhanda, we will be able to report the literacy crisis via educators and activists working at the coalface. We have also identified experts to interview and started a right-of-reply engagements with the national and provincial education departments - asking them to respond to the finding of lacking plans, programs and budgets for improved reading outcomes. Overview: Government failures are driving the literacy crisis in South Africa Being able to read is one of the most important determinants for children to break the cycle of intergenerational poverty. In 2014, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation published findings that if all students in low income countries left school with basic reading skills, 171 million people could be lifted out of extreme poverty, equivalent to a 12% reduction in the world total (UNESCO, 2014). In his 2019 State of the Nation Address, President Cyril Ramaphosa said that reading comprehension for children was “possibly the single most important factor in overcoming poverty, unemployment and inequality”. And, in his first State of the Nation Address after being re-elected later that year, the President reiterated the need to “mobilise the entire nation behind a massive reading campaign” towards the goal of ensuring that every 10-year-old will be able to read by 2030. The President’s comments came against a backdrop of a steady improvement in the percentage of children who could read in recent years (Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS) trends for SA 2006, 2011, 2016). But, these gains have been very slow. At this trajectory it would take more than 80 years to reach government’s goal. And, though there have been improvements. The most recent results from leading international study for figures show that nearly 80 percent of grade 4 children could not read in 2016, placing South Africa way behind reading outcomes in much poorer countries such as Kenya and Swaziland. The results for the 2021 edition of the PILRS are not out yet, but projections are not good. If learning losses due to the Covid-19 are taken into account, experts project that fewer children can read today than was the case before the pandemic. A panel of civil society leaders and education experts was convened in 2022 by Dr. Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, the former United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of UN Women, to monitor South Africa’s progress towards the 2030 goal. The Reading Panel 2030’s latest report, published in February, has concluded that failures within government are also important drivers of the literacy crisis in South Africa. Though Basic Education Minister Angie Motshekga has stated her Department’s commitment to realising the President’s 2030 literacy goal. The Department’s plans have been vague, and its budget allocations negligible. Last year, the Department’s Director General Hubert Mweli told Parliament that a “National Reading Plan” was being implemented by all Provincial Education Departments and a number of other “line functions” within the Department. But, experts on the Reading Panel 2030 have noted that the National Reading Plan had not been published, throwing doubt on whether it even exists We queried the Department, and filed records requests for a copy of the reading plan and the minutes of progress meetings touted by the Department of Parliament last year. To date, DBE’s spokesperson Elijah Mhlanga has not responded and our records request is pending. In last year’s budget vote, the Minister reiterated the importance of “improving reading in the early grades”. But, the only budget line item dedicated to reading for Early Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA) had been allocated R11.1 million, amounting to well below 1 percent of the Department’s annual budget. The DBE’s Primary School Reading Improvement Program (PSRIP) also draws a relatively small budget and its goals and interventions, the panel have concluded, fall well short of what is needed. The lack of a budget for reading is not because the budget is not nuanced. A number of other Department specific priority areas have been allocated conditional grants to which are disbursed directly to provinces, there is no such grant for reading. Indeed, the bulk of the education sector’s budget is spent at the level of provincial departments of education, which run schools and employ teachers. The Reading Panel concluded that most provincial departments have also not planned, developed programs or allocated budgets specifically for improved reading outcomes. Also, a major shortcoming hampering the effective teaching of reading is that teachers and classrooms are not equipped with the physical materials and resources that are needed. In his 2019 SONA, President Ramaphosa said that “[Government] will be substantially expanding the availability of these early reading resources across the foundation phase of schooling”. In 2008, the Department published a list of ten minimum resources needed for literacy teaching, but only DBE “workbooks”, leaving a massive resource gap. Field reporting from the coalface of the literacy crisis Further to this high-level picture, this story will be produced on the ground in the Eastern Cape - the country’s poorest province with a history of poor basic education outcomes . Provincial education departments: We have submitted queries to each provincial education department asking them to outline what reading interventions and budgets they have in place, and to respond to the Reading Panel 2030 finding that there are no such funded programs at the provincial level, except programs in the Western Cape and Gauteng.

Our story of “accountability failure” hinges showing that the Provinces and Department of Basic Education has done very little to plan, budget or implement literacy programmes in spite of the President and the Department’s commitment to the 2030 goal that all kids should be able to read for meaning by 2030. Through records requests I have secured a copy of what the Department touts as its “National Reading Plan” - in reality this document is just a table of “activities” and “targets”. Access to this document is exclusive and significant, because even education sector experts have never seen it, and have been calling for its release. Analysing it shows that it is actually not an implementable plan, because it has no delegation of responsibilities, means for measuring progress towards targets or budgets for executing activities associated with it. We have now submitted further records requests for the department to provide us with the monitoring and evaluation reports to show what - if any - progress has been made. I have some ideas for how to build outrage in narration and graphics in support of this point.

title: Gift of the givers - How to save a life
oneLiner: Not your average NGO, this is the largest disaster response organisation on the continent.
summary:
Treatment Overview Opening and setup: 2 minutes We start the insert with a collection of disasters, wars, earthquakes and water shortages. From there we go into a link - we hold the audience in suspense - we explain where we are. In Pietermaritzburg. The reason why we visit a seemingly ordinary town is for an extraordinary individual. All will be revealed soon. Our presenter meets our hero. Dr Sooliman. Known for his NGO - Gift of the givers. We find ourselves in a warehouse. It’s massive. We conduct the interview in one of the main distribution centers of GOTG. We talk about Dr Sooliman’s history, from Potch to Maritzburg. Gift of the Givers: 4 Minutes Dr Sooliman is synonymous with Gift of the Givers. He has been all over the world, saving lives. Most recently, drilling hundreds of boreholes for the water crisis in the Eastern Cape. He talks to us about a variety of disasters his NGO was involved in. Lots of action and pace is fast. Then We find out GOTG is much more than we thought… We visit a school that GOTG built, the lives of children touched by the good doctor are evident here in a small school near Maritzburg. But there’s more… We also see a medical center they built, to help the less fortunate. We see Dr Sooliman talk at another unveiling of a ward at the Charlotte Maxeke hospital in Joburg… He is a very busy man. We cover a lot of these with photos. But then, we slow the pace again…. title: The Village Genius
oneLiner: From Venda village to MIT marvel, meet the remarkable Mulalo Doyoyo: engineer, inventor, and award-winning researcher. He has now invented LICEM, a game-changing liquid cement that looks set to shake
summary:
He grew up in Vondwe village with his grandparents and attended the local schools. A scholarship from the NG Kerk saw him sent to Mbilwi Secondary School – a school strong in science and mathematics - where he became Head Boy and matriculated in 1988. With a bursary from Anglo American he attended the University of Cape Town, obtaining a BSc in Mechanical Engineering in 1993. He obtained his Honours degree in 1994 at Brown University in the USA, then two Master’s degrees: solid mechanics in 1995 and applied mathematics in 1996. In 1999 he defended his Doctoral thesis in Ballistics and went on to accept a post-doctoral research position at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). In 2004 he started lecturing at Georgia Institute of Technology (Georgia Tech). He returned to South Africa in 2015 to contribute to the building of a democratic country and has lectured at UJ, and TUT. He founded an experimental laboratory for environmentally friendly chemicals and has come up with several inventions: Ahifambeni: A hydrogen powered motorbike: Amoriguard: Environmentally friendly paint https://amoriguard.co.za Ecocast: Brick making machines that use less water and energy https://www.engineeringnews.co.za/article/locally-developed-low-water-brickmaking-machine-uses-industrial-waste-2016-07-08 Runza: A stainless steel motor vehicle suitable for SA’s terrain https://www.news24.com/citypress/business/locally-manufactured-runza-car-comes-with-many-benefits-20200319 Cenocell: Cementless concrete https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenocell Doyoyo says his inspiration for Cenocell came from his grandmother. She made pots from river clay, but with the addition of her ‘secret ingredient’ (frog urine) her pots were unbreakable. He found a substitute chemical that did the same job. His grandfather built stone structures which sparked his interest in structural engineering.

Interview with Mulalo Doyoyo, as well as Roland Gustafson, former head of Volvo Concept Center and Chairman of the Next Generation Vehicles (NGV) initiative. Demonstration of LICEM liquid cement strength test Journey to Venda, Doyoyo's childhood home

title: Affinity Ponzi Scam
oneLiner: Investing for your nest egg can be scary, so who do you trust with your money? A respected Johannesburg accountant takes members of his community for tens of millions of rands and then disappears.
summary:
Johannesburg accountant Michael David Ash allegedly scammed community members out of at least R60 million, and then fled to Israel. A case of fraud was opened at the Sandringham Police Station in 2019. There have been around 55 victims who were taken by this respected accountant, a trusted member of the Jewish community. He presented himself as a pious man whose son is a leading charismatic Rabbi in Johannesburg. But why does Rabbi Eitan Ash claim no knowledge of the fraud, when he tried to broker a settlement with one of the victims Andi Colley? The rabbi signed a sworn affidavit at the Sandringham Police station stating that he had no knowledge after supposedly trying to broker a settlement. According to the investigator who has 8 victims under this case, these were just stalling tactics until Michael Ash fled the country. Once he disappeared, the Rabbi closed ranks and told them to do what they had to do – that is, lay charges. Before fleeing the country Chad Thomas confronted Michael Ash, recorded on video, where he admits that the money was not invested in Steinhof which is what he told one of the victims, quickly changed his story to it was invested in the President’s game farm, and then said no it wasn’t invested and he would pay the money back. This of course did not happen. We will try and confront the Rabbi to get some answers. A call to Michael Ash in Israel and speak to some of the victims who have lost their savings.

A classic ‘affinity fraud’ - a crime which targets a specific community, generally a religious community, often taking the form of a Ponzi scheme. In this case the majority of the members who were scammed were Jewish, but other people who were referred by family and word of mouth were also scammed. We see how easily people gave over their hard earned money and inheritance to a respected accountant Michael David Ash, whose son is a prominent charismatic Rabbi. How the victims were ostracised by the community for speaking out. This is South Africa’s Bernie Madoff story.

title: DATING APP CRIMES
oneLiner: Looking for love online has led some dating app users down a path of blackmail, assault, and a extortion.
summary:
In recent years, users of popular dating apps, Tinder and Grindr, have reported falling victim to scams related to catfishing, extortion, harassment, assault, sextortion, and in some cases, even rape. The global issue seems to have embedded itself in South African dating culture of late, where gay users of Grindr - a notorious ‘hookup’ app - have repeatedly fallen prey to assault and extortion - crimes which the police have largely failed to remedy. Similarly, there have been a number accounts of abuse off Tinder - by primarily heterosexual users. But some victims claim they’ve been unable to seek any support from authorities to solve these crimes, whilst receiving no responses from the app developers themselves. Yet despite these online dangers and the very real consequences of anonymous connections, these apps have continued to grow in popularity. We explore the stories of victims who have fallen prey to unscrupulous and violent criminals who’ve exploited these apps for nefarious gain; speak to experts about the psychological aspects of online dating and how dating apps have reshaped our romantic and sexual connections; and explore the elements of online dating that’s fraught with dangers and deception.

It’s a 21st century crime that targets dating app users.

summary:
Please view the video here: please watch in file Who is Gino? His father, Jo Sanchez, runs a construction company https://www.sanjo.co.za/ with alleged ties to organizations such as Cosatu https://www.sanjo.co.za/clients/, who have a lot of political influence in South Africa. They live a life of luxury ferarri’s, yachts, trips to Greece… After the case and all evidence being collected including video footage of the assault and medical reports, the case was assigned to Prosecutor Mr David Jacobs. Despite the video evidence showing Gino, the affidavits confirming it was him, the prosecutor declined to prosecute without providing any reason. Then de Barros hired lawyer William Booth – well known criminal attorney. He questioned the NPA. Prosecutor David Jacobs then lost the docket, but then when he found out there were hard copies, the docket re-appeared. With Booth’s intervention the NPA decided to prosecute Gino for attempted murder on one count. (I have the email)… But its been over a year, and Gino still haven’t had his day in court, because they didn’t arrest him. They sent him a subpoena to appear in court, and the police say they haven’t been able to serve it on him because Gino is in Johannesburg – and doesn’t live in cape town. The police are just dragging their feet, and Booth has now asked for an arrest warrant – which is yet to be signed by the NPA. The PI is willing to speak, Booth, Charl Norman who was with de Barros is willing to speak, we have the affidavits of the witnesses and we can call them (ive been hesitant because these kids are gino’s social group – despite them giving evidence saying he did it) We would obviously confront Gino – we know where he lives. But his dad’s house is in a complex near sandton city. We have MANY pictures of Gino and his family. All the evidence and affidavits is in the folder provided.

Paulo de Barros is a French and Portuguese national. He came to South Africa in 2018 to work at a tech company providing internet access via Opera. They provided access specifically to those who cannot afford it – they became the browser of choice in Africa for 100m people. Then 2 years ago he was assaulted one evening in Bantry Bay, hit in the head and nearly died. • He sustained a skull fracture, brain hemorrhage, brain contusion and nose fracture – and permanent brain damage. He also had permanent hearing loss (Autophony – person's own speech or other self-generated noises (e.g. heartbeat, eye movements, creaking joints, chewing) are heard unusually loudly in the affected ear; Dizziness/ vertigo/ chronic disequilibrium caused by the dysfunction of the superior semicircular canal; Tullio phenomenon – sound-induced vertigo, disequilibrium or dizziness, nystagmus and oscillopsia; Pulse-synchronous oscillopsia; Hyperacusis – the over-sensitivity to sound; Extreme sound distortion ( broken stereo); A feeling of fullness in the affected ear, Pulsatile tinnitus; Brain fog ;Fatigue ;Headache/migraine; Tinnitus – high pitched ringing in the ear Brain damage This means for the past 2 years he couldnt anywhere where there is noise, noise became his “handicap, it's everywhere. I haven't been able to travel, socialize or even go to restaurants or malls without suffering… I simplify cannot live a normal life since then. I basically do nothing all day and most of the days besides sitting at home and working in front of my computer… Since then I have had a limited life, reduced to being always alone where there is no noise.” He knew something was wrong, but no one listened to him, so he went to France to see a specialist and he was then diagnosed with Semicircular canal dehiscence (SCD) which is a crack of the fracture that never healed, sustained by the attack which is the root/source of all the problems. I am now awaiting for surgery from a Professor in Belgium. This is so rare, that he is likely the only person currently living with this extreme rare disorder – most people are sent into a vegetative state. The surgery requires the doctors to open his skull, fill in the gap with a bony material taken from other parts of his skull to plug the defect and then resurface the area. Then his skull is glued back together. The recovery for this is a month – he will be put into a coma, and then woken up. You can see the crack – very hard to diagnose His surgery is going to take place towards the end of March. And his life hangs in the balance. So how did this happen? And why? It all began that fateful night when he was assaulted. Obviously in the hospital, Paulo was reliant on his friend and the police to investigate. Paulo’s friend said that the Sea Point Police officer assigned the case M. Mgolozeli denied that anything happened after visiting the house and was going to dismiss the case, but then Paulo hired a PI – Ben from Unisure who collected the video of the incident and got affidavits from all the witnesses present – all of which point the finger at one man. A 25 year old from St. Johns named Gino Sanchez. The video shows Gino walking up to de Barros (randomly) and gino punches him in the face, then twice more while he’s unconscious on the floor. For the 2 hours before the incident from when De Barros arrived, the two of them never spoke or interacted according to the CCTV we have. There was no explanation as to why Sanchez beat him. And none has been forthcoming.

Not many 11 year olds can brag about playing golf with President Cyril Ramaphosa. But golf prodigy Simthandile Tshabalala did that and more. He has well over 20 trophies and came second in his age group in the Australian Open 2020 in January. In November 2019 he was presented with the Sports Minister’s Excellence Award at the SA Sport Awards. He says he wants to be the best like Tiger Woods. It’s only been a year since he’s gained a professional coach and a sponsor – manufacturer, TaylorMade. Otherwise it is his father, Bonginkosi Tshabalala, who has been funding his career, making sure his son reaches his full potential. For father and son it’s been an incredible journey, spending lots of quality time together… something which Sim's father never had. His father says he grew up with an absent father, with no male guidance or exposure to many things, so it’s very important that he provides this platform for his son. The only thing that he cannot get over, is his own son beating him at the game of golf. in addition to his achievements, Sims also gives back to the community. He was recently been named the official Global Honorary Youth Ambassador for 67 Blankets for Nelson Mandela Day.

In just under three years of playing competitive golf, eight-year-old Simthandile Tshabalala has made his mark on the sport, representing South Africa internationally and winning a plethora of trophies. Tshabalala, who learned the game from YouTube videos and has only been professionally coached for the last few years, has already played at the Australian Open, where he came fourth, has played in Malaysia and Scotland, and won the local US Kids Tour last year. He has also showcased his talent in the United States, England and Canada. Fondly known as ‘Sim Tiger’, Tshabalala has grabbed the attention of notable sponsors like TaylorMade, but the rest of his increasingly expensive career is being funded by his father. Tshabalala emerged victorious in the Junior Africa 2021 Challenge. This story will look into Tshabalala’s career and bumpy road to success, the relationship he shares with his caddy (who also happens to be his father) and we probe efforts to make the sport more diverse, which many say aren't enough. What more needs to be done to make it more accessible to kids like Sims?

He was also working on an Investec case where the bank is owed millions.

title: Manenberg - Batting for change
oneLiner: A gangster turned coach - changing lives of many. One over at a time.
summary:
We follow Shahied Adonis and discover how a single person, can change the lives of many.

Research call with Shahied Adonis | Dlala Africa Shahied Adonis Battingpro@gmail.com 064 411 5988 BACKGROUND: Shahied Adonis grew up in the Cape Flats. When he was four years old, his father passed away which eventually led him to a life of drugs that he later kicked. He’s a professional cricket coach. He worked for Old Mutual and was helping with their Sports program until Old Mutual wanted to stop the program which was helping a lot of kids. Adonis got into a disagreement with Old Mutual around this which eventually went to the Appeals court. He won at the Appeals court and was dismissed by Old Mutual. He was then employed by Cricket SA. How this started – in 2012, his son wanted to get a bursary to get into Bishops but his son played soccer. Adonis told him that he would need cricket or rugby to help him get noticed by Bishops so for three years – he started training him, focusing on cricket and in 2015 his son got the Bursary. During this time, he realised that he could apply this to other children and try help them as well. He built relationships with different schools and the community. He offered the coaching clinics for free. Coming from the Cape Flats, he had always wanted to find ways of giving back and this was his opportunity. This program was the cricket excellence program and he had a lot of kids from middle- income family who came from a disadvantaged background. In 2019, they moved to Primrose Park and he decided to take the program into a more disadvantaged community. He didn’t really know much about Manenberg at the time – just that it was a gang ridden, drug driven community. He decided to introduce himself to the children there and immediately realised that that this was going to be a very different challenge. The children weren’t interested at all and he quickly realised that their issues were different. The children were rude, they did drugs and lived with gangsters. On top of that, these children were hungry. In the first year, they didn’t even play any cricket – they got some soccer balls and offered them a meal. He got some help from the community and some volunteers. With time, the children started coming. Initially they had a very relaxed atmosphere, allowing the children to do what they want in this now safe environment. They could chill and listen to music… In Manenberg – they used to use the school field but they often found bullet casings on the field so they very quickly realised that they needed to move the program elsewhere. In 2020, they started with the learning aids – food, cricket and soccer – and they could come as and when they wanted. They are up against the gangs in this area because the gangs want them as runners and the gangs pay them like R100 a day and these kids use this money to take care of the families they do have – mainly grandparents. The Children struggle with reading right up to Grade 7. Most don’t have fathers and some mothers themselves are drug addicts. In Manenberg, there were no cricket nets so they got together with the community and they built cricket pitches and had nets donated by Bishops (I think that’s the school he mentioned). With time, when they realised that the children would stay – that they would have a structure. So in 2020, they started paying the senior youths a stipend – they stepped up and became part of the program and these kids who used to ‘bully’ them, became their role models. The key was that to be allowed in the program they now had participate in academic lessons and play cricket. The key was providing them with food first and eventually these kids started to buy into the program. They’ve helped some children learn cricket and get Bursaries at Bishops, SACs and Rondebosch as well. One of their seniors got into club cricket as well.

title: Mesh Action
oneLiner: South African women take big Pharmaceutical company Johnson and Jonson to court over mesh defects
summary:
In October last year, a class-action lawsuit was filed at the Johannesburg High Court against Johnson and Johnson, for manufacturing, and selling transvaginal mesh devices used in health facilities across the country. These women claim that the mesh which was used when they underwent operations to treat either dislocated pelvic organs or urine problems had defects and was not properly tested. Transvaginal mesh like other mesh products, is made from polypropylene. Polypropylene is simply described as a plastic that is soft and flexible. When the mesh which contains this polypropylene is implanted in the pelvic area it causes complications in some women. This is because the muscle in the pelvic area is thin, and struggles to accommodate the mesh. This triggers foreign body reaction. The body identifies the mesh as a foreign body. As a result, the body fights the mesh, and the mesh starts to break down into pieces, and folds itself, causing erosion or failure. It is this erosion that causes constant pain in the pelvic area. This is why the mesh is labeled as a defect. The applicants claim that Johnson and Johnson was aware of these defects, and failed to implement measures to protect the safety of women. Therefore the company is liable for the suffering, income loss and the psychiatric injuries they suffered due to the faulty mesh. Johnson and Johnson is accused of providing misleading information about the safety and the effectiveness of these meshes, and continued to manufacture, market, and distribute the mesh implants.

Multi-billion dollar pharmaceutical giant, Johnson and Johnson faces yet another class-action lawsuit for manufacturing and distributing mesh defects. This time the lawsuit is brought forth by South Africa women. The tale is told by two women from different parts of the country, who came together after realizing they have one common enemy. Through social media and other means of communication, they discovered that they are experiencing similar health complications. They all started experiencing these complications after undergoing an operation where transvaginal mesh was used. Their lives changed forever. They are now part of a class-action lawsuit aiming to make the big pharma pay for concealing evidence about the mesh defects.

title: UFS student housing chaos
summary:
Neo is very clear that students are desperate for accommodation, and she goes out of her way to welcome them to the community- ensuring she leaves pamphlets in every student house with useful numbers, aware that many of the students are coming from rural areas and need support. But they feel like they are drowning- studentification has caused spatial restructuring and the needs of the student sub-culture dominate. She has no plans to move, but the value of her property has decreased by 60%. The University has accommodation for 5000 in hostels on campus and the other 20000 students must find accommodation elsewhere. The University has an accreditation process which sets out standards and does inspections but students are still getting exploited. One residence has 56 students on the property, no proper building plans have been passed and there is two toilets and 4 showers for 42 students. The conflict arises when student life clashes with suburban life and the parties run from Friday night till late Sunday. The police are no longer responding to noise disturbance call outs, its left up to community policing forums or private security. Tensions came to a head in January when residents signed a petition to close down all the student houses. Now the University and the Municipality are meeting with Landlords to try and reach an amicable agreement. The other issue is the densification of suburbs without the necessary improvement of infra structure. Building plans have not been approved, Sewers are over flowing, rubbish is piling up and spaza shops are popping up in residential areas without business rezoning. NSFAS pays R39700 annually for accommodation and so business is booming. Many of these homeowners don’t live in Bloem and so residents struggle to get them to get the students to comply. Houses built with single phase electricity and not adapted to accommodate 40 students drawing power are blowing. Universitas residents clean their own streets and sidewalks fully understanding that the Municipality can’t keep up, but they resent having to clean up endless condoms, liquor bottles and their children can no longer play in the parks As soon as the for-sale sign on a house goes up they bought and the next week the building begins, garages and even the parking areas turned into bedrooms, and backyards into dormitories. The municipality has been conducting inspections - but follow up action of closing them hasn’t happened. The Mungahung Municipality Mayor resigned, there is an acting CFO and there are two building inspectors. Landlords are complaining that even if they try and comply they can't get their plans passed or their businesses certified . The Municipality has clear bylaws about what a legal student accommodation requires but its overwhelmed. Crime is on the rise and the main targets are the students who are on foot carrying phones and laptops. Neo’s son had his backpack ripped off his back walking home from school.

Residents of Universitas in Bloemfontein lives have been turned upside down by the student accommodation that has taken over their suburb. Universitas and Brandwag are suburb adjacent to the University which have become an extension of the campus but without the protection of the security and control that university residence do. Retired advocate Neo Sephoti bought a house in Universitas in Bloemfontein in 2005, it was a quite upmarket residential area near University of the Free State and Central University of Technology, but over the last 5 years it has radically transformed. It is now home to 702 student houses, eradicating the residential fabric of the neighbourhood.

title: Zuko Nonxuba
summary:
In early 2016 investigative journalist Sabelo Skiti wrote what he thought would be a Christmas story about how the grinch of Christmas, Litigation Lawyer Zuko Nonxuba, stole a RAF plaintiffs’ money. But it turned out to be so much bigger than that, his story fueled an SIU investigation into Nonxuba, who to date has been awarded nearly a half million rand by the WC and EC DOH, with hundreds of thousands of it unaccounted for. For nearly a decade Nonxuba has managed to evade the arms of the law, but as the net finally starts to tighten, we put all the building blocks of his illustrious scam together, to give a holistic picture that will leave even the most cynical South African shocked. Nonxuba painted himself as a brilliant litigation lawyer for the people, going into underprivileged communities and offering to help families with disabled children, and in many cases he did. He got huge medical negligent pay outs for children with CP, and he in some cases he paid the money over to the plaintiffs. But it appears that he was also trying to scam poor, illiterate moms with disabled children, so that he could make millions for himself. Modus operandi varied, but what we can prove is that he would get touts to go into the community and find him families with special needs children. He would then create totally fraudulent medical negligence claims in their names, that they were not even aware of, whether some of these cases were awarded money from the DOH we can’t say, but we have the facts about the few that were stopped by the SIU in the EC and the WC DOH. When he wasn’t creating fraudulent claims and the plaintiff actually won their case against the department, what we can prove is that he was then either opening a trust and only paying them a tiny percentage and claiming the rest on exorbitant legal fees, which the LPC reprimanded him for. Or there was never a trust opened, and he would simply pay the plaintiff a small amount of cash and maybe a monthly amount like 2k for “groceries”. These plaintiffs were largely unaware of how much they had been awarded, which in most cases was 5million up.

As South Africans it’s like we’ve almost become numb to corruption or people stealing millions from the government. But this time it’s different, Nonxuba is not just allegedly stealing from the state, he is stealing from these desperate special needs children, taking money meant to give them a fighting chance at LIFE, and using it to make himself richer and richer and richer.

title: Wheelchair Boxer
oneLiner: A fighter who won't give up on his dreams.. even from a wheelchair
summary:
He is a fighter who won't give up on his dreams. He wakes early in the morning in Johannesburg and begins training. He begins with push up and sit-ups and then does laps around the block of his Turffontein home. Tony is a competitive wheelchair sprinter and mid-distance competitor, as well as a champion weightlifter. His real dream, though, is unique. He wants to be South Africa's first competitive wheelchair boxer. When he's not working at the hair salon which is his day job, and where, despite his handicap, he stands for most of the day, he is at the gym training with his coach and able-bodied boxers, learning how to box better and how to pit himself against opponents who have so many advantages over him. His life is a voyage of self-discovery, where, as he says, "You want to be a champion, but not a champion for yourself, but a champion for others too." He works hard at the salon and develops himself into as multifaceted a human being as he can be. He attends church, plays the saxophone and trains to beat himself and the handicaps that he carries bravely with him. He hasn't persuaded sporting authorities to recognise wheelchair boxing yet, but he is not giving up on his dream. He trains, boxes at the gym and competes in racing and weightlifting in the South African Sports Association for the Disabled championships (SASAPD) in wheelchair racing and weightlifting, keeping his many goals alive and working towards his ultimate challenge. Like all disabled people, he too, has times when things have seemed difficult, perhaps even unmanageable, but he refuses to give up. In this way he hopes to touch people's lives and inspire them to better their own and to find a way to fight for their own dreams. Living in SA for more than a decade and he sends money home to his wife and children in Nigeria, and he says South Africa is a land of opportunity, a place where he has been able to follow his dreams. Tony will be competing in the SASAPD championships in late March so we will spend a day with Tony, starting early in the morning on Friday 10 March, filming him and interviewing him as he goes about his day, from training in the early morning to playing the sax to going to the salon and the gym where he trains and boxes with other able-bodied opponents. Then on March 21 we will film him at the final day of the SASAPD championships down in Cape Town where he competes in the 800m wheelchair race and the final results are announced. He may not win the actual race, but this will provide a nice narrative arc to follow him through his journey into his own success and his personal best.

Adesanya “Tony” Adebayo is a man who won’t let life beat him. And he doesn’t particularly like other people beating him either. This Nigerian immigrant to South Africa contracted polio as a child which made his left leg extremely weak, forcing him to use a wheelchair as his main way of going about the world.

title: Diabetes Technology
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche, we take a look at the most exciting technological advancements in the management of type 1 diabetes.
summary: Type 1 diabetes affects millions of people around the world. It's a chronic autoimmune condition in which the body attacks and destroys the insulin producing beta cells in the pancreas. Insulin is a hormone that regulates the amount of glucose or sugar in the blood, and without it, glucose builds up in the bloodstream. If not diagnosed and treated, it's deadly. The condition typically develops in children and teenagers, but can also develop in adults. In 1921, the discovery of insulin was a game-changer for this once fatal disease. Fast forward a century, and the advances in technology have revolutionised the management of type 1 diabetes, transforming the lives of those living with the condition. The condition requires 24/7 management, and can be particularly challenging for children, who can experience isolation, depression and health complications. But, with the new developments in management, some of that burden is eliminated. We take a look at some of the most exciting advances, and how that's impacting the lives of children, from toddlers to teenagers.

title: Equatorial Guinea
oneLiner: Equatorial Guinea: Behind bars in Africa's hellhole...48 Hours after a super yacht belonging to the vice president of Equatorial Guinea is confiscated, two engineers from South Africa are put behind b
summary:
Early reports on a local news station in Equatorial Guinea reported Police arrested Potgieter and Huxham after they found a black bag of cocaine on a flight from Singapore. On a national broadcast station you can hear the men saying “we are innocent” The Department of International Relations and Communications have been in touch with the families and although there have been no formal charges against them in a statement from DIRCO they were charged with “possession of drugs.” Huxham and Potgieter, employees of SBM Offshore, a Dutch oil and gas company, work in two different departments and until their arrest have not known one another. They were thrown in Africa’s hellhole, Black Beach at first while the Dutch company’s legal team gathered evidence for the case. The two men have been moved to Oveng Asem, a maximum-security prison on the eastern side of the mainland, and worse than Black Beach in terms of isolation, says an Equatorial judge, Ondo Angue Jaun Carlos, who has since fled Equatorial Guinea. “There is there is little hope for them in Oveng Asem as it is ruled by the Defense Force. The Vice President of Equatorial Guinea, Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, known as Teodorin Obiang is Minister of Defense and National Security in Equatorial Guinea. Obiang decides on your fate, says the judge.

Two South African engineers, Frederic Potgieter (53) from George and Peter Huxham (55) from Langebaan, were arrested at a hotel in the Equatorial Guinean capital Malabo on Bioko island on the 9th of February. They were detained in the notorious Black Beach prison - the same prison Hoekwil local Daniel Janse van Rensburg spent more than 400 days after he was illegally detained in 2013. The link in both cases is the vice president of Equatorial Guinea, Teodorin Obiang, known for his lavish lifestyle and squandering of state funds.

title: Coalitions
oneLiner: In November 2021 we voted for new councils, and many metros rely on coalition governments to get things done. But are voters getting what they signed up for?
summary:
The Ekurhuleni Council is a mess. It’s coalition government, or what’s left of it, has seen mayor Tania Campbell ousted, then re-elected, and then the speaker ousted, and right now, council is waiting to re-elect a new speaker. The PA and Action SA have both left the coalition, leaving the DA along with a handful of rats and mice parties in power. For how long, nobody knows. Speaker Raymond Dhlamini was ousted in Ekurhuleni last week, by design of the City Manager who illegally called a council meeting, and illegally got the speaker ousted and replaced by an acting member. City Managers have no executive authority based on the Systems Act (32 of 2000) – they are going to court tomorrow to thrash it out. Dhlamini may be back in office.... and by the time we air the insert, the whole DA led coalition may be gone. a City Manager acting beyond her paygrade, a crumbling coalition and while service delivery was never spectacular, and lacking in most instances, it’s now much worse. And while the ANC is no longer in power, for now, in the city, behind the scenes, they are… Then, the City Manager was appointed by the previous ANC mayor, and most of the heads of department that report to her, too. It’s a legacy municipality with a fresh, previously in opposition coalition. This is the picture of how a coalition can go terribly wrong on so many levels. And then, the one man band parties, who have as little as a single seat in council, can sway the direction of government, despite the fact that they have no real constituency.

We have access to the City of Ekurhuleni, notably the worst minority coalition government in SA, and investigate why its simply not working.

title: Tender fraud in the City of Cape Town
oneLiner: It's a story of death threats, kidnapping and tender fraud within the City of Cape Town's housing Departmnet
summary:
In 2020 Good Hope Construction GHC was awarded a tender by the City of Cape Town to fix stairways on the city council Flats which had deteriorated badly, and people had fallen and been badly injured. The tender was for R26 Million odd rand. GHC was in the process of finalising the paperwork with the City when the contract got stalled for a bunch of technical reasons and GHC began to investigate. Then Mayor Dan Plato instigated an investigation and there is a report that says R300 million was spent irregularly but the City has refused to release this report. During the investigation the head of City Safety and Security Investigation Unit Reynold Talamakies approached GHC director and offered him R30 million rand by TCC to drop the investigation against the City and TCC. Raziek has this recording. Talamakies has subsequently been arrested and will turn State Witness. TCC Construction was awarded a tender by the City of Cape Town made up of 49 different projects and over charged for scaffolding. For example TCC would charge R800 000 million and a comparative quote for the same scaffolding for the same period of time was R18 600. TCC construction were not only paid excessively for scaffolding but it should normally be included as part of any job, but TCC charged for it over and above. These invoices were approved by a City official Alistar Standbul who has subsequently been arrested. We have the paper trail to prove this. Good Hope Construction have a letter from the city manager where they agreed their tender was terminated irregularly but states that it needs to be fought out in court, GHC cannot afford the court case, and the stairways have yet to be repaired. In that period R26 million that should have been spent rebuilding the stairways has been spent by TCC on various inflated and irregular building projects. When the City is pressed to release the report that reveals R300 million was irregularly spent the City say they are investigating, and have not released the report.

This story sounds like plot from soapy. Muslim brother in laws in the construction industry in Cape Town fight it out for lucrative City of Cape Town Tenders. Raziek Rajah exposes his brother in laws Asif Khan corruption and the consequences: Death threats, kidnapping of his father, bribes, and the bankrupting of his successful construction company. The directors of TCC and 2 COCT officials have been arrested and charged with fraud over a construction projects- the trail comes to court on the 12th March. But we have documents relating to inflated scaffolding costs which do not form part of the trial and be fresh evidence which the rest of the press do not have

They also offer homework support to some of the most vulnerable children in Alldays... Come rain or shine, meals are cooked in the open and kids sit there on the dusty ground enjoying what is often their only meal for the day. In 2013 Rahmqvist swooped in as the saviour of these children. He founded the Mapungubwe Foundation Centre (NPO) and Stephen and Paulina were given positions on the board. (along with other municipal officers). And the building was built on Municipal land right next to the Alldays Primary School.

Swedish national Lief Rahmqvist is one of the biggest private landowners in the Limpopo Province. In 1994 he bought up a bunch of farms on the Botswana border, North of Alldays, in the Blouberg Local Municipality. He consolidated them into what he called the Mapungubwe Private Nature Reserve (PTY) Ltd. The property borders the Mapungubwe National Park. In 2013 decided to "give back" to the community of Alldays. He founded the Mapungubwe Foundation Centre NPO. In essence, he took over the established Dirisang Drop-in centre that has been around for years... And he proceeded to get donations from far and wide

title: Steytlerville Follies
oneLiner: A unique theatrical experience in the middle of the Karoo
summary:
Mark has a background in theatre and worked in the circus as a white-faced clown for many years across Europe. Jacques was working in the corporate world in Cape Town. They met at Hinds’ little theatre in De Waterkant and fell in love. In 2003 they moved to Tulbach, enjoying the countryside. Then an advert in the newspaper drew their attention, a derelict building in… Steytlerville. They took great care to restore the old building and today it is a beautiful victorian-esque haven… But the big attraction at their hotel is the Steytlerville Follies. By day Mark and Jacques run their hotel, and by night… they transform into Dame Layla Lamborgini and Freddie Ferrari and entertain guest with excerpts from the musicals, classical song and dance. Jacques designs and makes all their costumes, and choreographs the drag shows, and is also the main performer, while Mark accompanies on piano. They are absolute characters! They even inherited custody of an eccentric old lady’s “son” — a ventriloquist dummy and now Charlie (the puppet) is part of the show. Their lives are filled with stories and laughter.

It smacks of "Pricilla, Queen of the Desert" (for those old enough to remember it) — Mark Hinds and Jacques Rabie, a couple of middle aged white gentlemen gave up their lives in the city and decided to move to the sleepy Karoo Town of Steytlerville. They discovered a little hotel, which they bought and restored, the Karroo Theatrical Hotel - an oasis in the desert.... and they entertain their guests with a one-of-a-kind drag show... in the middle of the Karoo!

title: Cash Caterpillar- Mopane Worms
summary: Masontja (Mopane worm) While Dutch farmers face the mass culling of livestock because of an overload of nitrogen pollution, in Africa the humble mopane worm gives off less greenhouse gases and contains protein levels of 60%, higher than meat or fish. Yet while we relish blood seeping steak, hideous looking prawns and crayfish that feed on effluent, we squirm at the thought of eating these nutritious caterpillars, which have been part of the African diet for centuries. The Gonimbrasia Belina is a species of moth, native to Botswana, parts of the North West province, Limpopo, Zimbabwe and Namibia. It feeds almost exclusively on the mopane tree and its offspring is slowly making its way onto mainstream menus. This story will also look at the trade in mopane worms – from the tree to the plate – their sustainability (shrinking mopane forests) and carbon footprint (they need less space – 3 kg of mopani leaves equals 1kg of worms, while cattle farmers need 10 kg of feed to make 1kg of beef). Locations: Harvesting/cultivation in Limpopo/Venda or Botswana/North West Journey to cities via traders Street sellers Online sellers Manufacturers Cooking & eating Sustainability & carbon footprint Characters: Dr James Sekonya – did his PhD on the mopani worm trade – and found that the market was concentrated in urban areas and supplied by imports from Botswana and Zimbabwe, with most of the value going to traders, rather than harvesters. With villages expanding in Limpopo, mopane forests are being chopped down for fencing & firewood, increasing the reliance on worms from Botswana. Botswanan worms are bigger, being harvested when they reach a particular size, which means lots more meaty goodness and less leaf matter. To protect our wild population of worms in SA, commercial farming needs to be implemented and we need to learn from Zimbabwe & Botswana, he says. He’s willing to accompany a CB team to harvesting and trading sites in the Vhembe and Mopani districts of Limpopo in December, which is when they are harvested and transported to market. Or just across the border to Botswana, where availability is greater. james.sekonya@mandela.ac.za https://open.uct.ac.za/bitstream/handle/11427/36554/thesis_sci_2022_sekonya%20james%20george.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y Wendy Vesela-Ntimbani – chemical engineer who grew up in Limpopo and learnt the art of harvesting worms with her parents in the mopani forests and is trying to ensure their sustainability in that part of the world: Over the years there has been over-harvesting of the mopanes. We need to regenerate the population of the mopane worms to ensure the life cycle of the emperor moth continues, for future generations to enjoy what I’ve enjoyed. She has a company called Matomane (Tsonga for mopani worm) that turns them into flour used in savoury biscuits, protein bars and cereals. Her website says they are a cost-effective alternative to meat, fish & chicken – but her products look expensive. https://www.matomani.com/products/ Compare her price of unprocessed worms to price of meat per gram. 067 641 2139; info@matomani.com Phuthi Kabasa calls herself the Mopane Bites Queen and turns mopani worms into ‘banting-friendly’ snacks like tortillas & crisps. https://www.mopanibites.com/blog 063 802 4194 sales@mopanibites.com Other interviews: Dept of Agriculture about sustainability projects and plans – wild worms or worm farms? They had a project near Ganyesa in North West, but the moths disappeared, it’s believed to Namibia and Botswana, because of overexploitation. Tito Mboweni: he’s been approached via Treasury with a view to cooking a worm meal for our presenter. He declined, but let’s not give up on him. Third hand messages can be misinterpreted. https://briefly.co.za/80047-tito-mboweni-cooks-a-storm-mopane-worms-mzansi-reacts.html Alternately, we could get a chef to prepare them for our presenter. They are on the menu of this Cape Town restaurant, along with crickets and ants. https://www.independent.ie/life/food-drink/food-news/south-africans-get-the-bug-inside-the-cape-town-insect-restaurant-where-worms-termites-and-crickets-are-on-the-menu-38462093.html Food sustainability expert: Professor Sheryl Hendriks is a food security policy expert with extensive experience in policy analysis and programme design. She is engaged in high-level global food security policy think tanks and panels and is influential in food security and nutrition policy in Africa. sheryl.hendriks@up.ac.za https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319238779_A_systematic_review_of_sub-national_food_insecurity_research_in_South_Africa_Missed_opportunities_for_policy_insights Media: https://www.news24.com/news24/southafrica/news/healthier-than-most-expensive-steak-entrepreneur-seeks-to-turn-mopane-worms-into-tasty-snacks-20220703 https://www.wantedonline.co.za/food-and-drink/2019-05-03-the-most-lauded-chefs-cant-get-enough-of-them-but-are-are-insects-the-new-it-food/ https://www.iol.co.za/business-report/entrepreneurs/watch-want-mopane-worms-on-that-pizza-a-local-entrepreneur-is-changing-the-face-of-masonja-db62a6de-14a5-42f2-9f6b-bcca849a3308 https://mg.co.za/environment/2022-08-01-vibrant-cross-border-trade-in-mopane-worms-from-botswana-to-south-africa/?amp https://briefly.co.za/80047-tito-mboweni-cooks-a-storm-mopane-worms-mzansi-reacts.html https://briefly.co.za/people/women/130947-local-engineer-turned-entrepreneur-comes-up-with-creative-way-world-try-enjoy-mopane-worms/ https://www.citizen.co.za/news/3156731/mopane-worms-southern-africa-regulations-study-finds/

title: Rocky Road - Juandré Kidson Murder
oneLiner: A father murdered in front of his family, why our roads are dangerous, even when we are not driving.
summary:
We visit the exact location of where Juandré was murdered next to the N4. His brother Marco, tell us how it changed their lives forever. We speak to emergency responders about what is called “Spiking”, putting spikes / nails / screws in the road to get you to stop. They tell us what they see on a regular basis. Bakwena Toll This area is known for being a hotspot for these incidents with police and the MEC for Community Safety well aware of the dangers. We speak to Bakwena Platinum Corridor Concession Toll, they will give us facts about the accidents that occur, not only on the N4 but surrounding roads too. What are being done to curb this? Other incidents We find out that the Kidson incident was the second “Spiking” to occur on that day, on the very same section of road. We hear of other life changing incidents that involved “Spiking” or rocks in the road. A man spent weeks in a coma after perpetrators dropped rocks off a bridge as he passed by.

In early May, the Kidson couple and their baby were travelling on the Bakwena N4 towards Brits in their Hyundai SUV. Around 20:00 they drove over rocks near the R512/Randburg exit. Knowing it was unsafe, Juandré Kidson kept driving. Until he couldn’t anymore. He had no other option than to stop. He get out of the car to change the wheel. Whilst changing the tyre, 3 men approached their car. Armed and dangerous. Whilst pleading with the men to let his wife and baby go, they shot him in the head in cold blood, in-front of his family. What lead to the brutal murder? We speak to the Kidson family, at the centre of this tragedy. We will hear in detail what happened on that fateful night.

title: Desperately seeking sperm [6170]

Couples and single women are all now able to find donors with more ease than ever before. So much so, that some male donors have the potential to father over 100 children within just a few years... Ari Nagel is an American super sperm donor, fast approaching his 100th child. ‘I can help them have a lifetime of joy and happiness with little or no effort on my part’, says Ari, who travels around the world and asks for no payment for his ‘services’. For Karolina and Agnieszka, a same-sex couple in Poland, their choices are limited. Same-sex couples cannot access sperm donations in the country, so Ari was their last hope. But what does the lack of regulation mean for a generation of donor-conceived kids? Erin Jackson started an online community for donor-conceived people and has conducted surveys on this issue, her findings are startling and could change how this industry is regulated.

One man in the USA has the potential to father over 100 children... all because of a poorly regulated industry.

title: Dizu Plaatjies [6162]

summary:
One of his most promising students, Zinzi Najova, is now starting to make her names as a traditional performer, in particular of the uHadi, and ancient calabash and bow instrument which hails from the Eastern Cape and Kwazulu-Natal. It is traditionally played by older women, and Dizu has promoted older players from the rural areas, and then passed the gift of playing down to women like Zinzi, who is grew up in an urban environment but still reaches out to past traditional sounds and customs. Dizu still tours globally in university holidays with a traditional band called the Ibuyembo Ensemble and teaches at schools, using a collection of traditional instruments he has at his home in Langa. We will film Dizu showing us his instruments and telling us his story, with some use of archive, which is limited. And we will interview Zinzi Najova briefly about her journey and what Dizu has taught us and why that is important to young people, even in an urban setting. The filming will take place in Langa, at Dizu's house with a drone shot of the environment.

Dizu Plaatjies is a giant in South African traditional music. He grew up the son of a Sangoma in Pondoland, and learned traditional ways and music at his knee. As a young man he mastered the marimbas through a church band and then developed a style of using marimbas and traditional instruments to play indigenous music, forming the band Amanpondo which toured the world during apartheid, bringing indigenous sounds and African music and melodies to European audiences. Since then, he has developed as a teacher and maker of indigenous instruments, and has been promoted to a Professor at the University of Cape Town where he manages a course in traditional musical performance, and hands his skills down to students in the Music Faculty.

title: Vaccine Vexation
oneLiner: The plan was for 67% of the population to get Covid -19 vaccines by the end of this year. But while some nations have reached 40% coverage, we ask why are lagging at less than 1%
summary:
To achieve the 67% target, we would need to ramp up daily vaccinations to about 250 000 doses, while at best we are currently only at about 10 000 a day. On Saturday Minister of Health Dr Zweli Mkhize confirmed the total number of vaccines administered to date stood at 182 983 - most of these going to front-line health care workers. That is a far cry from the estimated 1.5 million doses needed to cover all our health care providers, a target that was set for the end of April this year. So what is the hold up and how can it be fixed? That's a question only government can answer at this stage. There is a confirmed world wide shortage of vaccines, and many first world countries have been accused of ordering too many vaccines ( countries like the US have ordered 1 billion for their 330 million population) and hoarding vaccines not needed. There are also issues over the question of vaccine efficacy and safety, as well as which ones to procure for SA. We have only recently concluded the sale of the Astra-Zeneca vaccines we bought to AU member countries, after it was decided to halt the use of the vaccine because of questions around its usefulness against the South African strain of Covid-19 (A decision that has been questioned by many experts). Meanwhile, government has said they will NOT force anyone to take the vaccine - but there is a growing worldwide trend to require people to have "vaccine passports", proving they've been vaccinated before they are allowed to enter work premises, hotels etc. So while the government might not force us, could private institutions soon require it? And will South Africans who have not been vaccinated be allowed to work and travel to countries where such restrictions are in place?

Vaccination Vexation The South African Government has promised to have 67% of our population, or about 40 million South Africans vaccinated by the end of the year. This weekend President Cyril Ramaphosa, speaking at a Human Rights Day commemoration, again assured South Africans that every single person in the country would get access to a vaccine, and called for patience. But there are growing concerns that the government's promised two thirds target by the end of the year won't happen. Especially since no one seems to be able to tell us how this will be achieved. In one of the worst public health disasters of the century, why all the secrecy? Or is it simply that they themselves don't know?

title: NSFAS Corruption
oneLiner: While everyone is looking at what's happening in the student protests, we should also be looking at NSFAS - because a closer look reveals R7 billion in irregular expenditure.
summary:
NSFAS has R7.5 billion in irregular expenditure. There is a further R50bn that the auditor general is concerned is irregular expenditure. This is the third year in a row that NSFAS has a qualified audit (bad audit outcome). Student protests come at the end of a chain of administrative actions that do not get performed timeously. In essence the Fees Must Fall protests are budget advocacy and a financial issue. If one reverses from the moment of Mthokozisi Ntumba's incredibly sad death, there has been a slow violence in the institutional failings at NSFAS. It may not be immediately apparent that social justice can looks like administrative justice and everyday actions that public officials must take require exercising their mandate in alignment with the Constitution and the Public Finance Management Act. The institution and its systems have been under enormous additional pressure since the 2015 fee free tertiary education announcement, as it would have suddenly needed to do a lot more than previously. It has emerged that there has been syndicated fraud and corruption. One of the types of fraud that have been discovered is that there have been ghost students who have been paid, because NSFAS wasn't doing enough to ensure that the students who were approved were indeed eligible to receive the funding. There are thousands of records of this nature, where students were approved without the correct documentation and checks being done. Only 40% of these records had been checked by the time the latest audit report was completed. To eradicate this syndicated fraud requires proper IT systems, good internal controls, integrity by those in key positions at NSFAS. A number of criminal complaints have been referred to the Special Investigating Unit to investigate. Parliament's Standing Committee on Public Accounts is frustrated with the pace of addressing these issues at NSFAS.

Parliament’s portfolio committee on Higher Education, Science and Technology has described the National Students Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) audit outcomes under administration as the “worst ever”. The latest NSFAS annual report has revealed irregular expenditure of R7.5 billion. Irregular expenditure is actually even higher, with the Auditor General saying that an additional R50bn in irregular expenditure 'should have been disclosed as a result of disbursements made against eligibility criteria and conditions that were set without consultations with the minister or eligibility criteria and conditions not gazetted'. Part of the problem that has given rise to the irregular expenditure is that there has been syndicated fraud and corruption where "ghost students" have been getting paid without proper checks being done before payments are made. Irregular expenditure is not corruption per se - it means that the proper procedures required by legislation have not been followed. The extent of corruption will be quantified when the amount lost due to 'material irregularity' - the Auditor General's new audit category that gives the AG teeth - is determined. However at the time of the audit, the amount lost due to material irregularity had not been determined by the NSFAS administrator, Randall Carolissen. It is clear that since his arrival as Administrator there are some new controls that have been put in place and cases of fraud have been handed over to law enforcement, whereas previously the irregular expenditure wasn't even being detected.

August drives on the R555 once a week and has lost many tyres over the years at huge cost. It is well known in the area as a very dangerous road – a main problem being rain, if it rains the R555 becomes extremely dangerous because drivers cannot see the potholes. The road has been in a state of disrepair for years. We have planned to go on a road trip on the R555 with August. Another case study is a location, the JRA Asphalt factory in Johannesburg. R 63 million was spent on refurbishing the existing plant – it has not produced anything since March 2020, has never met production targets and is still an empty yard – even though the JRA has put out ads for plant supervisors. Additionally in Johannesburg, JRA depots are under-resourced – people doing nothing. We can go on site visits with Sean Kreusch (DA). There are other examples to pepper the story with, and also, how does the pothole situation relate to the economy, who is to blame and what can be done about it?

This year's season of heat waves and rain, a stormy cocktail perfect for cracking up South Africa's roads, has exposed the country's state of disrepair. A nationwide plague of potholes has become the physical representation of the accelerating decay of South Africa’s infrastructure. After our social media call for viewer submissions we have almost four hundred photos and videos from all over the country. Potholes are everywhere and what better way to illustrate this than the viewers’ submissions. We start the story with light-hearted moments - from the pothole fishing competition in KZN to the man bathing waste deep in a pothole. But, Potholes are a serious matter...

title: SAFFRON
oneLiner: At R200,000 rand for 1 kg, Saffron is the most expensive spice. However, SA farmers have tried and failed for years to produce a viable, sellable crop. But that was until now.
summary:
He is doing this to solve a two fold problem: 1. To ensure that the market grows and assists developing farmers – this week he is in northern pretoria assisting up and coming potential farmers beginning their crops, ad 2. To find out where else in south Africa it will grow successfully. Within three years, peak production should deliver between 1kg and 5kg saffron a hectare. While the sterile flowers are delicate, they only need 250mm to 300m in irrigation, are frost resistant and can withstand temperatures of minus 15 degrees Celsius. Engelbrecht believes the plants are best suited to the Karoo, but Saffricon is currently testing in KwaZulu-Natal and elsewhere as well. Plans are in place that could see South Africa becoming a significant player in the farming and export of saffron. For the South African economy, this offers an invaluable source of foreign income from exports, whilst also assisting in establishing emerging, small-scale farmers - Furthermore, it offers commercial farmers an alternative source of income through diversification.

The land of Saffron In 2016 Northern Cape farm Bennie Englebrecht decided to try planting SAFFRON. Despite previous farmers trying and abandoning the challenge quite quickly in South Africa. Bennie managed to grow excellent crops (based on both smell and flavour). Saffron is the MOST expensive spice in the world at R200,000 for one kilogram. Englebrecht however took several years to make the saffron profitable because the downer about it is that it takes 150,000 crocus sativus flowers to yield ONE kilogram – and that means you need labour – each corm/flower/bulb producers 3 red threads (stigma’s - tiny thin red threat part of the flower) The production is very labour intensive, however the flowers are frost resistant and don’t need much water – but lots of heat – which is perfect for karoo like conditions. Engelbrecht created “Saffricon” and is the managing director – he has tried and tested his crop over 4 years (his farm is between Williston and calvinia in the northern cape (about 4.5 hours from cape town). Based on his quality – he had interest from Bahrain who believes there is a strong demand for this product internationally. The only other country that has been successful is Iran – and that’s because the majority of its labour force are woman who are paid $5 per day. But its not just used as a spice. Its also used for medicine, dyes and cigarettes. Englebrecht came up with an idea to assist local farmers to start their own crops – his company company is now making saffron bulbs available for around R450,000 for 150,000 of these so-called corms, which should cover a quarter hectare, as part of growing contracts.

title: Single Dad Birth Register_Girl With No Name
summary:
Wesley Hayes legal career started taking off when he was taken on by the Mandela family in various legal cases, and finally he had the finances to fulfil his dream of becoming a father. He always wanted a child but witnessing the trauma children experience when divorce and custody battles get ugly, he knew he wanted to do this on his own. So at 35 he went through all the psychological, social and medical examinations at the Stellenbosch fertility clinic, chose an egg donor and had six embryos successfully frozen. He signed a contract with the surrogate mother that she would not have any involvement in the child’s life. She willingly handed over Justine into his arms as soon as she was born. But a month later when the proud father went off to register his baby, he hit a brick wall. Children cannot be registered if the mother’s ID is not on the birth certificate. A single mother can register a birth without the father’s ID but it’s impossible for a father to register his child without the mother’s ID, despite DNA evidence that it is his, and despite there being provision in the Children’s Act that women can be anonymous egg donors, the Birth and Death Registry makes this impossible.

Wesley is a successful attorney and decided to fulfil a life long dream of becoming a father, but he was clear he wanted to do this on his own. The fertility clinic took him through all the very expensive procedures and his sperm fertilized an anonymous donors egg and 6 embryos were frozen. Finding a surrogate mom to carry the embryos wasn't as easy, but 6 years later baby J was born. But she remains nameless and identity less nearly a year after her birth no matter what her dedicated dad does, he simply is unable to register her birth because her mothers identity is unknown. South Africa's birth and death registration simply does not recognize that a man can chose to have a child without the mothers identity being known. A woman can have an anonymous sperm donor and register her child's birth but not a man.

title: Police Impersonation
oneLiner: We take a look at the alarming rise in police impersonation cases in Gauteng, and ask what, if anything, can be done to stop this disturbing crime trend.
summary:
After our last blue lights gang story aired last year, we were inundated by submissions from viewers who had similar experiences. In some of our latest cases, the MO seems to be almost identical, although attacks are happening all over Gauteng. In one interesting case, Chris Cronje was hijacked by men dressed as police officers who were driving a police vehicle. He was kept hostage for hours, as the hijackers drove around with him held at gunpoint in the back of the car, stopping at various ATM's and withdrawing an eventual total of R16k. He was later dropped off in a veld near Heidelberg. His vehicle was recovered two weeks later, near the Mozambican border - indicating it was most likely going to be shipped cross border. But the blue light gangs are not the only police impersonators doing the rounds. In the past year a new police impersonation scam, one that targets men who have visited sex workers or strippers, has become very popular. The men are contacted via whatsapp a day or two after their "meetings", and threatened by a man claiming to be a policeman. They are told the women they have met have laid charges of rape and/or assault against them, and the scammers demand amounts between R5000 and R50 000 to make the case "go away". The men are told that they will be arrested, not get bail, and of course warned of the disgrace of rape charges hanging over their heads. The tow truck scam, which we have featured before, also remains popular, as well as cases of extortion against business owners like restaurants, pubs and taverns, all targeted by men pretending to be police.

From "blue light" gangs, to scams and extortion, South Africa has seen an alarming increase in cases where criminals are impersonating police officers to get away with their crimes over the last few years. Gauteng is one of the provinces hardest hit by these types of crimes. Security experts say that they are seeing new cases on a weekly basis, and that multiple gangs, organised crime syndicates and even prisoners, who are currently incarcerated, are behind the crimes. And it's not just people dressed in police uniforms anymore, nowadays criminals even have access to sophisticated software which allows them to duplicate telephone numbers, making it seem as though they are calling you from legit law enforcement telephone numbers.

title: The ANC - A House Divided
oneLiner: The ANC finds itself at the head of crisis-ridden South Africa during a global pandemic. A state of emergency that has exposed deep divisions amid the systemic corruption that has ravaged the country.
summary:
Benevolence The ANC, as the main liberation party in the long struggle of South Africans to break free from colonialism and apartheid, has a history of patronage. During the struggle people grew dependent on the organization for support throughout the decades of racial persecution. Customs that are ingrained in the ANC and ANC supporters that, as for most liberation movements, are hard to break when they get into government. "Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely" In South Africa, the transition to government meant the ANC chose to make certain compromises. Some would regrettably provide opportunities for corrupt activities involving the pillaging of state coffers. Basic services were defined as commodities and the servicing of enterprises that provided them was commercialized. So that still, large state corporates are funded to deliver services countrywide while commercial companies are tendered to service those state owned enterprises. The means for stealing from the state was given by the patronage culture of the ruling ANC, providing networks through which bribes and sweeteners could determine the winners of contracts. And almost inevitably, these opportunities and means for defrauding the state provided the central motive for ‘state capture’, an operation for maximizing the loot and for helping the thieves get away with it. But now, after years of escalating corruption, the state’s coffers are running dry, and with shortages made even more acute by the effect of the Covid-19 pandemic, finally corruption within the ANC has been identified as a critical challenge. The major complication to rooting out the culprits, is that the organization seen by many as best placed to take on the challenge is the ANC itself.

This is a perilous time for South Africa. Mass unemployment and declining tax revenues are widening the scourge of inequality, even with heavy state borrowing. The ANC government is working on vaccinating enough people to reach herd immunity from the Covid-19 virus. Tragically, when the country is desperate for clear direction, divisions within the ANC are ever more apparent with widespread corruption and high profile cases coming to a head. President Ramaphosa is obfuscating, avoiding direct condemnation of former President Zuma’s defiance of the law. And, as a seasoned politician, he is looking after his own back by dithering over tackling the divisions that are splitting his party in two. There are so many senior figures in the ANC accused of corruption, they are almost powerless to expose each other, for fear of bringing the whole house down. At the very top of the ANC, defiant leaders and disdain for the rule of law has paralysed the ruling party, which begs the question, can the ANC and our democracy survive this factionalised leadership?
