title: Kgetlengrivier: Enough is Enough
oneLiner: Residents of Kgetlengrivier took on the local municipality... and won!
summary:
The people of Koster and Swartruggens in North West are rejoicing. They have achieved what no other small community in SA has done. A radical High Court decision has changed their lives from being the victims of Municipal mismanagement to being in charge of their own fate. In December Judge Gura ruled in favour of the Kgetlengriver Concerned Citizens, giving them the power to clean their towns up, and to take service delivery in their own hands. Service delivery in the Kgatlengrivier area has been all but nonexistent for more than 4 years. Sewage was flowing through people’s yards (see pictured attached) and potholes made it difficult to navigate the litter-strewn roads. Only the lucky had water for a few hours per day. 30litres of sewage per second ran into the river. By 2018 the community had enough. The final straw that broke the camel’s back was when the mayor had the road to her mansion paved, this, while most of the community were struggling just to get basic services. Riots broke out and protesters burnt doen several businesses and properties owned by the then-mayor. The municipality was declared disfunctional and the North West was placed under administration. The community approached the court and were granted a temporary order to step in and help repair some of the damaged infrastructure. But the local municipality was adamant that it would sort out the problems…. at a cost of some R144 million, Kgetlengrivier Local Municipality embarked on a project to build a new sewage works. But residents say it never worked. Despite the Municipality’s interventions residents became desperate, regularly reaching out to the media with pleas for help. The stench was unbearable and sewage was literally flowing through people’s gardens.

At Carte Blanche we do many stories about poor service delivery and regularly our presenters are standing in rivers of sewage flowing down streets, but we seldom get a chance to showcase a real success story. The tale of Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens vs the local municipality is an opportunity to showcase one such victory. The fed-up residents of Swartruggens and Koster in the North West, decided enough is enough and fought for the right to restore service delivery in their towns...

title: Zuma vs Zondo - The Standoff

summary:
Scope of the story: - The Commission - The Accusations - The Avoidance Tactics - The Supporters - The Detractors - The Government - The ANC - The People - The Law - The Outcome

On 28 January 2021 The Constitutional Court of South Africa directed Mr Jacob Gedleyihlekisa Zuma "to appear and give evidence before the [ Zondo ] Commission on dates determined by it". Four days later, on 01 February 2021, Mr Jacob Gedleyihlekisa Zuma released a statement declaring "in advance that the Commission Into Allegations of State Capture can expect no further co-operation from me in any of their processes going forward. If this stance is considered to be a violation of their law, then let their law take its course." The long running standoff between the Zondo Commission and former President Jacob Zuma, who set up the commission, appears to be reaching a head and on 15 February 2021 we will find out if Zuma follows through with his defiance and if the judiciary follow through with the Law. Zuma claims he is being victimized by the State, harking back to Apartheid judicial practices that targetted specific individuals. With his defiance of the Constitution and the Zondo Commission, can Zuma avoid jail for contempt of court or does he even want to? For now the ball is in Zuma's court but depending on how he plays it, who has more to gain and lose in the endgame? The 26 year old fledgeling democracy of South Africa or the 78 year old former statesman Jacob Zuma?

title: The Good Messenger: mRNA's Promise for More Effective Medicine
oneLiner: We examine how the mRNA technology behind several of the COVID vaccines could unlock new ways of fighting other diseases.
summary:
Imagine a species so advanced it’s able to replicate the functioning of the human body at a molecular level, one with the audacity to grow in a lab a crucial element of how human cells function and then inject them into actual, living beings. Well, thanks to breakthroughs in Genome sequencing and advances in other areas of medicine, that is precisely what our species is now able to do. It’s a technology at the cutting edge of science and crucial to our attempts to defeat the SARS-CoV-2 virus. However, this is not a Covid story. mRNA is a molecule containing the instructions by which cells make proteins - essential to how our bodies function. What’s the point of proteins? Well, in scientific terms they “are large, complex molecules that play many critical roles in the body. They do most of the work in cells and are required for the structure, function, and regulation of the body’s tissues and organs.” In other words, they’re very important not only to the healthy functioning of our biological systems but to the development of disease and – hopefully – our body’s ability to deal with it. The use of mRNA as the foundational technology in the development of two of the current generation of Covid vaccines (by which our body is “tricked” into making antibodies by recognising a section of the virus’s now infamous spike protein) has confirmed what many have believed for several decades: it's a natural biological process that can be manipulated to help our bodies fight other viruses and diseases. In the southern African context, HIV is one that often comes to mind. So, how does the technology work in lay terms? How did we stumble upon it? Could the darkness of this global pandemic thrust us into the light of a new and infinitely more successful way of treating those suffering currently incurable diseases? And how close might we be to a HIV vaccine, for example?

Thanks to the extraordinary efforts of leading scientists, the world has been exposed to the wonders of Messenger RNA and its ability to ward off severe COVID19 and, possibly, infection with SARSCoV2. Many, though, are unaware of exactly what mRNA is and how the technology works. We aim to answer those questions while revealing how the success in developing mRNA-based vaccines might lead to new, more effective treatments for other viruses and diseases. It's a case of a unique technology, perfected in unique times, leading to unprecedented advances in modern medicine.

title: Immunotherapy: The living trials
oneLiner: Imagine you didn't need harmful chemotherapy or radiation, and a death sentence could be lifted by having your own immune system killing the cancer? Well that's immunotherapy and the trials are over.
summary:
10 years ago you didn’t meet a melanoma survivor, but when this drug came along, it stimulates a specific pathway in the patient - teaches immune system how to activate its immune system, and it corrects the pathway - only works in 20% of melanoma patients, what is surprising is that they don’t die – 10-15 years – so they had a sustained response… as it has now taught your immune system to fight it naturally. Its simple and quick many patients come in on their lunch breaks and don't have to tell ppl they have stage 4 cancer. Also it doesn't make them feel bad at all - no side effects!

There are traditionally 4 ways to treat cancer, 1. Chemotherapy 2. Radiation 3. Surgery 4. Targeted therapy (developed about 10-11 years ago – found that a certain type of cancer has a mutation – cancer cell’s contain DNA – some cancer like lung and melanoma- has a break which is called a mutation – one single mutation is abnormal – develop a drug that inhibits the abnormality… - almost 100% effective…. A patient on oxygen and then a few days later will be walking around – so amazing – BUT IT doesn’t last forever. Works quickly, but as cancer mutates quickly it comes back after 2-3 years this treatment will fail and return. THEN THERE IS 5. Immunotherapy – The Nobel Prize for Medicine or Physiology 2018 was awarded to James P. Allison of the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center and Tasuku Honjo of Kyoto University for their discovery of cancer therapy by inhibition of negative immune regulation.- i.e. Immunotherapy. It is life changing - and its as simple as going in for a drip for 30 minutes every 3 weeks. Immunotherapy uses your your body's on immune system to recognize the cancer cells and kill them. Basically - put simply cancer forms when your cells do not die - apotosis (cell death) is inhibited. In 2018 two kinds of medicine that these doctors created was trialed in South Africa - and its taken 2 years but not Dr Sze Wai Chan who has headed the trials is giving us exclusive access to meet those patients who should have died. Trials are very interesting in that they usually are comprise of patients who are diagnosed with stage 4 first - this means that doctors have looked at their cancer and concluded they cannot recover from it. But Dr Chan, has tested both medicines to astonishing results.

title: Oxera: Breath of fresh air in 2nd Covid wave
summary:
The standard treatment for COVID patients when admitted to hospital is to have oxygen administered through a basic cannular system, or even a mask but that’s very inefficient only getting 60% of the oxygen in, for extremely sick patients this is simply not a sufficient supply. Patients conditions are deteriorating quickly because of this and people are dying simply because there are not enough ICU beds or ventilators or adequately trained staff and people are dying unnecessarily simply because they can’t get oxygen efficiently into their collapsing lungs. OXera is a simple device that administers high levels of oxygen through a mask, that is inflated and fits securely to the patients face. Using a bag and filter it pushes oxygen into the lungs preventing them from collapsing and making it easier for the intake of oxygen. The oxygen level can be regulated and increased according to the patients needs, it works quickly and does not require highly specialised staff. It can be used in a general wards and attached to the standard oxygen supply. Inspired by diving apparatus it had a valve which increases the pressure of oxygen to the lungs and a filter that prevents the virus being expelled into the air protecting medical staff and filters what the patient breaths in.

The second Covid wave has been far worse than the 1st and there are not enough hospital beds across the country never mind ICU beds or respirators. Afrox and Liquid Air barely have enough medical grade oxygen to keep up with demands having to increase their deliveries from once a week to daily supply consequently cutting back on supplying to their industrial customers. “ Oxera” Oxygen Efficient Respiratory Aid invented by an anesthetises at Frere Hospital has just been licenced by the SA Health Regulatory Authorities uses far less oxygen and has the potential to save lives.

title: The AARTO Amendment Act - Are You Ready?
oneLiner: The Amendment to the AARTO Act, currently only covering Johannesburg and Tshwane, will become countrywide on July 1st and stakeholders are warning of total gridlock and damaging life consequences.
summary:
Currently in Johannesburg and Tswane they have been recording demerit points but not enforcing any consequences regarding the points although fines for traffic infringements still have to be paid. So for our story - the consequences regarding the demerit points system have to be hypothetical at this stage, but we do have real life case studies that will show how their current infringements, be they actual or erroneous as in the incorrect number plate case study, could mean under the demerits point sytem and it's administrative pitfalls they would have their licences suspended. Re-enactment August 2021. Mr Joe Soap travels this road every day to and from work. He doesn't realize, because of inadequate notices, that last week the JMPD changed the speed limit of a short stretch of her route from 80 to 60 kilometres per hour. In 40 working days he will have racked up R 56 000 in fines (not to mention the R 100 payment, the Infringement Penalty Levy (IPL),for the privilege of receiving each fine) and 80 demerit points, enough to be banned from driving for 16 and a quarter years. All because there is a speed camera there and it can take up to 60 days for the notification of offences (if they arrive). The AARTO amendments is a strict consequence-based points system. The AARTO Act has effectively three documents 1. Infringement notice, recording the offence 2. Courtesy letter, a reminder to pay 3. Enforcement order, recording the offences consequences and non-payment penalties There are no Warrants of Arrest, no Administration Marks.

Because it's a pilot phase the points demerit system of the AARTO system doesn't apply yet, the Minister of Transport has not proclaimed the points demerit system to be in force. But this year the Government is instigating a revolution in AARTO, heralded as a mechanism for improving road safety and a way to ease the burden on courts. Once a truffle has been taken from the ground, it has to be cleaned, graded and sold and eaten within 2 or 3 weeks, or they “go off” and can't be used.

Truffles are one of the most expensive delicacies in the world and have earned many titles - The black diamond of the kitchen. The Mozart of mushrooms. The jewel of cuisine. These are some of the labels that the truffle has earned for itself over time. The highly sought after nutty and oniony taste and aroma make Truffles perfect for pastas, eggs, poultry and other dishes! In this insert about the newly emerging truffle industry in South Africa, we will portray how a South African laboratory in Pretoria is now creating a world first – producing truffles in a laboratory, something thought impossible, till now.

title: Drug Patents: Money or Your Life
oneLiner: Essential Cancer medications completely unaffordable for patients in South Africa.
summary:
Lenalidomide in the form of Revlimid, is patented by Celgene (USA). They also hold 32 patents for generics. In countries like India and Iran, it is not possible for one company to hold all the patents of a drug's generics, so there, competitors can manufacture alternatives, often at a fraction of the cost. In SA no-one can manufacture generics and importing generics have been very restricted. Up until 2016, SA patients could apply to import a generic of Lenalidomide from India at around 4% of the cost of the original. At the time the generic cost about R27,000 per year, compared to the R730,000 of the original, Revlimid. This import was done via Section 21 authorisations from the Medicine Control Council for importations. But noticing the loophole, Celgene, with the assistance of a South African pharmaceutical company (Key Oncologics (Pty) Ltd) stepped in and registered Lenalidomide with SAHPRA, The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority. This meant that importing a generic became illegal. So at the moment Lenalidomide can only be bought in SA through Key Oncologics. On top of that, South Africa’s patent system is geared towards monopoly holders and is at odds with the government’s constitutional obligation to take reasonable legislative steps to protect and promote the right to health of people living in South Africa. A revision in South Africa’s intellectual property policy could see the prices of medicines drop by as much as 90%, say Cancer Alliance and other NGO's fighting for the change in SA legislation. In SA, granting a patent is a simple administrative process. You pay a fee, tick the boxes and complete the paperwork. Big companies are taking advantage of this and acquiring patents for medicines, which blocks competition, thus creating situations where they can charge what they like, and patients have no option but to pay... or die.

Many Cancer medications are pricey, with dying patients literally bankrupting themselves to try and stay alive. One good example is Lenalidomide, which is sold under the trade name, Revlimid. This medication is listed as an essential cancer medication by the WHO and is used for patients with Multiple Myeloma (Blood & Bone Marrow cancer) and a variety of other blood cancers. There is no cure for Multiple Myeloma and it's considered a long-term cronic disease. Patients need regular medication to prevent the progression of the disease - often for many years. Lenalidomide t/a Revlimid is priced at over R800,000 for year's supply in South Africa, and very few can afford it. Medical Aids pay up to about 80% (if you're lucky), depending on your medical aid... but co-payments are generally huge and many patients are struggling to afford it. Bear in mind that the patient faces additional expenses, and treatments and co-payments. If you don't have medical aid, you simply have no access to Lenalidomide. The State cannot afford to supply patients with this drug.

title: COVID-19: How Africa kept pandemic at bay
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche we look at Africa's seemingly remarkable escape from COVID-19 which has brought much of the world to its knees.
summary:
There is no single reason for Africa’s seemingly remarkable escape. For one, Africa consists of 54 countries that are ethnically and socially diverse. Yet, across the continent there are some trends that hint at why deaths form Covid-19 remain so low. The median age in Africa, where more than 60 percent of people are under the age of 25, is about half of that in Europe. This, combined with Africa’s warm climate and the potential of pre-existing immunity in some communities, has played a significant role. Thirdly, millions of citizens have developed a degree of immunity to Covid-19. Herd immunity defines the protection of a population from a virus through mild exposure to it. While South Africa may have unintendedly developed herd immunity against Covid-19, the World Health Organisation does not condone achieving herd immunity through public and unmonitored exposure to the virus. In South Africa’s case, the reported potential herd immunity was unintended. After easing lockdown restrictions in September, the country has managed to avoid a second wave of infections unlike other nations around the world. Where countries in Europe are re-entering lockdown as a result of Covid-19 cases increasing, our local government has continued to report an unexpected drop in cases. Studies conducted in Western Cape and Gauteng have shown that up to 40% of people have developed coronavirus antibodies, with the majority unaware that they had ever been infected. The studies are ongoing to determine how much protection antibodies offer and for how long.

In April, as Covid-19 shut down country after country, the United Nations issued a stern warning: Africa might be next. Officials said Covid-19 could directly kill at least 300,00 people in Africa and possibly as many as 3.3. Million. In May, with infections and deaths still surprisingly low, the World Health Organisation revised that prediction down to between 83,000 and 190,000. There has been much speculation for Africa’s seemingly remarkable escape from a pandemic that has brought much of the world to its knees. To date, just over 40,000 Africans have lost their lives to Covid-19

title: The coming population implosion
oneLiner: ...........the world is facing a population implosion by the end of teh century
summary:
Continued global population growth through the century is no longer the most likely trajectory for the world's population. By contrast, world population might peak just after mid-century and substantially decline by 2100. Since 1950, the total global fertility rate has dropped by half (reasons – better education for women, lower child mortality, access to contraception, increased societal prosperity, economic uncertainty, unaffordable housing, etc). Though the global population is currently rising — mostly due to high fertility rates in African countries — experts have also observed falling fertility rates around the world. Replacement fertility is around 2.1 children per woman. The US, Denmark, China, and Singapore all have low fertility rates: 1.87, 1.73, 1.6, and 0.81, respectively. Japan, one of the most extreme cases of population implosion, has a fertility rate of 1.41. Its population has been declining for the past few years. This is concerning for demographers and economists because countries must hit what's known as "replacement fertility" in order to keep their populations — and their economies — stable.

Fresh new research, important to all of us.

title: DIGITAL DISINFORMATION
oneLiner: How vulnerable are we to digital propaganda and misinformation? We reveal how digital misinformation is being used to manipulate ordinary South Africans
summary:
Digital disinformation and propaganda is becoming an increasing problem all over the world. We've seen how disinformation campaigns have been used to affect the outcome of the Brexit referendum and the 2016 US presidential election. Closer to home, we've seen the damage wrought by the white monopoly capital/ radical economic transformation campaign of PR firm Bell Pottinger Over the past 4 years, the problem has only gotten worse with more sophisticated and insidious campaigns being launched against an unsuspecting public. We've seen the rise of Q-Anon in America while here in South Africa, xenophobic and overtly racist sentiment is being used to target ordinary South Africans. The #PutSoutAfricansFirst hashtag has been weaponised and used to disseminate vile afrophobic propaganda that could possibly incite real world violence. In this story we reveal several of disinformation campaigns and how they were uncovered through the world of the Digital Forensic Research lab, an organization based in Cape Town who are a part of international think-tank The Atlantic Council We'll visit their lab in the the Mother City to see the forensic techniques they employed to reveal the true perpetrators of these digital campaigns. We'll see the technology they have at their disposal and how it is used to join the dots and unmask the real culprits behind these fake news campaigns We'll also speak with EFF MP Naledi Chirwa who was attacked by one of these digital campaigns with fake posts that threatened to expose her alleged fraudulent citizenship We'll also speak with William Bird from Media Monitoring Africa. They've launched a campaign called the Real411, which provides a platform for members of the public to report disinformation and gain his insights into how prevalent the problem is in South Africa. Finally we provide solutions to the problem: What can be done to stop disinformation campaigns?

We look at the sinister motives of digital disinformation through several compelling case studies 1. We look at how afrophobic and xenophobic sentiment was spread on social media by the fake "Lerato Pillay" twitter account. We look at the weaponizing of the #putsouthafricansfirst hashtag through the work of the DFR Lab - who unearthed and exposed the true identity of the Lerato Pillay 2. Similarly we look at the fake Tracey Zille twitter account. A South African government official posing as a racist white woman on Twitter posted several racially incendiary tweets that were designed to spark outrage. The furor generated by these tweets was used to funnel users to at least three of his websites, where he hoped to net an income off the back of the outrage caused by his tweets. 3. Finally, A network of racially charged websites used narratives of white victimhood in South Africa to turn a profit. The website domains are owned by a South African company called CoZaNic, operated by a man named Deon Venter.

Another central interview is Judge President Dunstan Mlambo who can talk about the fact that you cannot appear in court if you don’t have the rights granted by an appearance certificate – and he will go into ramifications and accountability. We also have recordings as evidence of Pretorius’s deception, including a Legal Practice Council phone call that says she is not registered, and UNISA stating she has not finished her studies towards a Bachelor of Law degree (which she purports to have).

Possibly never attempted before - an elaborate online bust of an impostor masquerading as an advocate. Pauline Pretorius, AKA Johanna Petronella Jansen Van Vuuren, stole the identity of her alias, a long standing member of the bar, and has profited from this for years. Pauline Pretorius’s maiden name, she claims, is Johanna Petronella Jansen Van Vuuren, co-incidentally the same as Advocate Johanna Petronella Jansen Van Vuuren. Even more remarkable is that both women are in possession of certificates, awarded on the same day in August 2013, qualifying them to be admitted and authorised “to practice and to be enrolled as an advocate of the High Court”. There the similarities end, and from amongst Pauline Pretorius’s ranks suspicions led to challenges of her Right to Appear in the High Court… and her assertion that she gained a Bachelor of Law (LL.B.). The whistleblower June Kotze realized there was something fishy in the conduct of Pauline Pretorius and challenged her, leading to emails which we have - and Pretorius furnishing Kotze with her fake advocate certificate as ‘proof’ she was who she claimed she was. The real Johanna Petronella Jansen Van Vuuren was horrified that her identity has been stolen for the deception.

title: Breast Implant Illness [5855]
summary: Breast implant illness (BII) is a term that some women and doctors use to refer to a wide range of symptoms that can develop after undergoing reconstruction or cosmetic augmentation with breast implants. It is also sometimes referred to as autoimmune/inflammatory syndrome induced by adjuvants (ASIA). BII can occur with any type of breast implant, including silicone gel-filled, saline-filled, smooth surface, textured surface, round, or teardrop-shaped.Two possible problems with breast implants: One is the condition Towt developed — breast implant illness (BII) — a cluster of symptoms such as fatigue, memory loss, and joint pain that can occur after getting breast implants and that frequently improve after the removal of the implants (explantation). Many of the symptoms of BII are the same as those of autoimmune and connective tissue disorders, such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. However, only some people who have BII get diagnosed with a specific autoimmune or connective tissue disorder. BII isn’t well understood and isn’t officially recognized as a medical condition, but some experts say it’s likely to be related to an autoimmune reaction to the implants. The other serious risk is a rare form of T-cell lymphoma (cancer of the immune system) called breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) that develops in the scar tissue and fluid surrounding an implant. So far, all the confirmed cases of BIA-ALCL have been in women who had breast implants with a textured surface or whose implant surface type was not known. BIA-ALCL is curable in most patients if it’s diagnosed early and treated appropriately, but at least 33 women have died from the illness as of July 2019.2 Some patient activists call BIA-ALCL a “man-made cancer” because it’s linked to a specific medical device and was identified for the first time in 1997.

title: Poisoned to Death

summary:
On Friday night of the 21st of August, the Ingram family had dinner with their twelve year old daughter Tammy, at their complex Apartment in Port Elizabeth. At around 8.30 pm their 17 year old son Matthew arrived home after having had dinner at a friend’s house. The family spent part of the evening together and then turned in for bed. Later that night the entire family started to get violently ill with vomiting and diarrhea. After trying to deal with the situation themselves it became obvious they needed emergency care and were rushed to the hospital by their eldest son Joshua. Selina and Stanton were so ill they were unable to take care of their children. At first they thought it was something they ate, but later realised it couldn’t have been that, as Matthew had not eaten with them. They were convinced they had some sort of a tummy bug. On arrival at the hospital, the children were convulsing and because the doctors did not know what had caused them to be so ill, they put them both into an induced coma. This was after Matthew had been convulsing and frothing at the mouth in his brother’s arms, Tammy was convulsing continually. Stanton and Selina were too ill to take care of the children and they too were being treated in the hospital. In the early hours of 23rd of August, Tammy passed away, whilst Matthew was still in an induced coma. The toxicology report from their blood tests showed that the family had high levels of the toxin Methyl Bromide in their blood stream, in Tammy and Matthew in fact so high that it was 10 times what is deemed a safe amount. The family were bewildered as they didn’t know how they could have inhaled this toxin. Four weeks later, Matthew died in hospital, four days before his 18th birthday.

On Friday the 21st of August, in a quiet suburban complex in Port Elizabeth, Selina and Stanton Ingram enjoyed the evening together with their children, twelve year old Tammy and seventeen year old Matthew. Little did they imagine that this would be the last time they would be together as a family. Unbeknownst to them they had been attacked by a lethal poison, Methyl Bromide, a substance well known to toxicologists but with no antidote. Stanton and Selina survived, but their children tragically didn’t. How did the poison get in?

title: Koeberg Alarm
oneLiner: We investigate whether South Africa's only nuclear power station should be operating given the country's unreliable electricity supply.
summary:
Africa's only nuclear power station is the ageing Koeberg plant, located right next to a major city. As Koeberg reaches the end of its lifecycle (around 2024) the government (perhaps to avoid the extremely costly decommissioning process) has started to extend the life of the plant for another 20 years (the "PLEX programme") in a process lacking transparency and likely to be very expensive. But experts warn that this piecemeal overhaul is risky. If anything goes wrong, it would be devastating for Cape Town -- and there is little to no disaster preparedness.

Nuclear power stations depend on electricity for cooling, pumps and other key functions... a power cut equals a nuclear meltdown. Koeberg has four levels of back up power, but with Eskom's ongoing power supply issues, there are concerns around Koeberg's nearly-out-of-date power generator (Ankerlig), and technically you just need to lose one back up power level for the plant to be considered unsafe. The Fukishima disaster happened because the tsunami took out the plant's power and back up power (a tsumani could also hit the west coast and engulf Koeberg). New safety recommendations after the Fukushima meltdown of 2011 (including significantly improved measures against power failure) are not being implemented here.

title: Tracking down the Table Mountain Killer
oneLiner: In 2017 and 2018, a spate of muggings, stabbings and murders occurred in the Table Mountain Reserve. We find out how ‘eyes and ears on the ground’ helped to identify the suspected killer.
summary:
Zimbabwean national Blessing Bveni is linked to the series of muggings and stabbings in the Silvermine Nature reserve above Kalk Bay and St James before he was arrested for the murders of pilot Doug Notten on January 28, 2018 and pensioner Ian McPherson, stabbed to death for his bicycle on March 13, 2018. In an ongoing trial in the Western Cape High Court the State alleges Bveni was involved in a number of attacks on cyclists and hikers before he killed Notten, 57, who was hiking with his wife, Julia in Silvermine above their St James home and McPerson who was cycling on the Fish Hoek side of Silvermine. Bveni is also accused of repeatedly stabbing and robbing neighbourhood watch member Malcolm Esterhuizen on February 7, 1918 at the exact spot where McPerson was killed.

Table Mountain Reserve has always been a place of beauty and tranquility for hikers and cyclists. But all this changed in 2017 and 2018 when a man by the name of Blessing Bveni used the park as his hotspot to ambush and kill unsuspected hikers and cyclists. His appearance was misleading as he was dressed as someone who is going for a stroll in the reserve and with a kind smile. This would all change when he would suddenly take out his knife or screwdriver and lunge towards the person slashing and stabbing in a bout of anger that has turned him into a monster. It took two years to gather enough evidence and put him behind bars. He is currently awaiting trial.

title: Fake Law Firm Exposed

summary:

Monies were paid into another scam law firm's account, SPOMOP PTY LTD. Spomop's website has been suspended, their physical address does not exist, and when pushed for answers they stop taking calls. They still have an active Facebook page. But an insider has spilled the beans, and we now know that the person known to our case studies as T Harry, AKA Michael, AKA Harry is actually Tsepiso Harinnyane Hlapi. Hlapi is not a lawyer, lives in an upmarket house in Dainfern, and has a long history of running the same scam. A CIPC search revealed he is the active director of several other labour law firms: Labourdex, Labour Law Assist, Labourzone etc. None of these have active websites, but a HelloPeter search reveals scores of exactly the same complaints about these firms - they got settlements but never paid out.

Imagine you've been unfairly dismissed during the Covid-19 pandemic. You search the web and find what appears to be the perfect law firm to handle your case on https://www.employmentlaw-experts.co.za. Their website looks legit, they promise the world and best of all they take on your case on a "No Win, No Fees" basis. After consulting with you, mostly via Whatsapp, they approach your former employers and get a settlement on your behalf. But the settlement is paid directly to Employment Law Experts accounts, and you never see your money again. That's exactly what's happened to many case studies who have approached Carte Blanche with their stories.

title: Illegal wood cutting
oneLiner: Illegal wood logging causing devastation of the Magaliesberg world heritage site
summary:

Buyers travel from Mbombela, Bloemfontein and as far as Durban to stock up on cheap firewood to resell in their respective provinces. Marketed amongst others as Hardwood, Rooibos and Bushveld Iron wood, the wood sellers here don’t operate small businesses. As soon as bakkies, trucks, minibuses and utility vehicles drive off with their daily loads, bakkies and trucks arrive to fill up the stock. This seems to be happening around the clock. Although the sellers tell you that they receive stock from Botswana every three days, the truth is, the wood is chopped in the Magaliesberg mountains, a UNESCO world heritage site and protected biosphere.

It takes 5 minutes to chop down a tree, but it takes it 25 years to grow back. The Magaliesberg Biosphere world heritage site is slowly losing the battle against illegal wood poachers who sell wood they claim originates from Botswana when in actual fact, they have teams of people chopping down trees seven days a week.

title: Cyril: Clawing back the billions
oneLiner: We all wonder what our president is doing right? But here's the answer: he's using civil litigation to claw back the billions and fighting corruption
summary:
10 months after coming into power the president had instituted the Nugent commission of inquiry, which made way for a new commissioner Edward Kieswetter and several other experts coming back to SARS. He then instituted the Mpati commission at the PIC, and a special team under Judge Yvonne Mokgoro is implementing the recommendations along with a new board. This lead to summons' being issued to past board members. And now several investigative agencies are being pulled together to investigate the alleged PPE tender corruption. Prosecutions: As the wheels of justice turn slowly, they are turning. Zuma has suffered a number of setbacks in various courts. The Hawks are investigating 250 cases of municipal fraud of which 93 are already in court. In June 2002 - 9 suspects were arrested for the VBS Mutual Bank saga - and one of them as turned state witness to secure convictions. 5 of them were sequestrated and their assets seized to repay moneys to the bank, and 2 were declared delinquent and cannot be company directors again. At least consequences are following, even before jail sentences. Dudu Myeni has also been declared a delinquent director after SAA and the Muhlathuzi water board.

So what has Ramaphosa done? Summary: 1. rid of the rot and replaced them with competent office holders, as well as rebuilding institutions 2. A lot of action through civil proceedings (sequestration, asset seizure and civil claims) 3. Progress has been made with some state-owned enterprises, although most of the covid 19 corruption seems to take place at the provincial and local gov level (we'll use examples of eskom, transnet and NPA) 4. Ramaphosa has put the state on a new trajectory, he is trying to ensure that the ANC follows. Eskom retrieved 1 billion from Mckinsey, 150m from Deloitte, they have cancelled coal contracts worth R3.7 billion as well a R14 billion oil supply contract, and other contracts are being investigated. The SIU in august launched proceedings to recover R3.8 billion from 12 individuals connected to eskom. And the SIU are clawing back R400 million from two contracts connected with eskom and transnet for computer software. At Transnet the South China Rail has repaid R618 million, R1,168 billion has been recovered from Gupta entities and assets worth R232 million from a former Gupta associate have been frozen. Prasa has been put under administration. At the land bank there have been people who have gone to jail for fraud. At the NPA, Ramaphosa dismissed its national director and the president appointed a commission to investigate the deputy directors - which were both fired. And now new permanent deputy's have been appointed, and Shamila Batohi has taken office after being recruited from The Hague. In his SONA speech in February, Ramaphosa announced that a special unit would be created within the NPA to prosecute state capture cases: with skills from "within government and the private sector." Hermione Cronje has not been appointed outside the NPA to head this unit, and R38 million has been allocated from Treasury for this unit, and R25 million has been allocated for appoint private sector practitioners and R102 million to fill vacancies - 800 posts were advertised in February 2020. Ramaphosa after consulting top lawyer Wim Trengrove revoked the appointments of five senior prosecutors. In July 2020 regulations on the Zondo commission were changed allowing the NPA to use evidence from the commission in criminal prosecution. At the ANC's National Executive Council (NEC) they resolved to urgently establish a permanent multidisciplinary agency to deal with all cases of white collar crime, organized crime and corruption. The SIU and Special Tribunal - their mandate is to recover public money through civil claims - they do not prosecute. But the SIU can refer a case to NPA to prosecute. * Criminal cases require "beyond reasonable doubt" - while civil claims require the less strenuous test of "on a balance of probabilities." To speed up civil litigation, President Ramaphosa created the Special Tribunal to adjudicate civil proceedings - operation from 1 oct 2019 - chaired by 8 judged and lead by Judge Thami Makhanya. Currently 22 cases are before the tribunal - like luxury care purchases, dodgy scholar transport claims and inflated gov contracts. In 2 cases the tribunal ruled that pension of suspects be frozen, giving the SIU the opportunity to seize the money, meaning resigning and running with ones pension has become more difficult. The SIU has R14.7 billion in cases it wishes to submit to tribunal. AFU (which focus on 10 specific crimes incl fraud, cash smuggling, human trafficking, counterfeit fraud and drug related offences). Although they were deliberately restrained in Zuma era, and now has a new lease on life. It reported last years it recovered nearly R2 billion from economic crimes compared with only R180 million the previous year. Over the past 5 years they've recovered R11.8 billion in 2707 cases. For eg. two weeks ago they seized the bank accounts of R700,000 siphoned off UIF money meant for underemployed workers.

title: What's with the Whales?
oneLiner: What mystery, lurking beneath the waves, is driving whales from the depths and into near-certain death on land? We look into what science is telling us about an increase in whale beachings.
summary:
Of all nature’s unanswered questions, whale beaching is among the most curious and unsettling. Just last week, seven Northern Bottlenose Dolphins died on a popular beach in the west of Ireland despite the best efforts of locals to keep them alive (footage available). At almost the same time, another pod was beaching in the Faroe Islands, although locals there were less inclined to save them. South Africans, too, have seen this tragic phenomenon at first hand: in an incident that made global headlines in 2009, 50 Pilot Whales beached themselves at Kommetjie in the Western Cape. 20 were saved. https://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/31/science/earth/31whales.html A report last year suggested Cetacean beaching had increased by 15% in a six-year period, with 5000 whales and dolphins stranded around the UK between 2011 and 2017. The question is: why? Well, research has yet to provide a satisfactory answer. There are many theories including sonar interference from offshore wind farms, naval weapons testing, blasting by the oil and gas industry, and a myriad other. Each is plausible, but none can be blamed with any conviction. What scientists know for certain is that something is driving these creatures from the ocean depths and - given their precarious numbers – we can’t afford to lose them in these sorts of numbers. Not when fishing nets are claiming their victims, too. This will be an insert filmed largely with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group. We will venture offshore in search of Minke whales and Humpbacks, talking to experts about the beaching scourge and what might be causing it. We will also link up with South African experts who, despite being thousands of km away, share similar concerns to the hardy Irish braving the worst of the Atlantic’s notorious weather to deepen our understanding of whales and - hopefully – figure out why they’re dying. We will also talk to the UK Cetacean Strandings Investigation Programme, the compilers of the study.

Recent research suggests there's been a 15% increase in whale stranding in the past few years in the U.K. A mixture of scientific study and anecdotal evidence tells us that is probably true of other parts of the world. It's something that mystifies the people dedicating their lives to preserving these remarkable creatures, although theories abound: climate change, naval activity, sonar, wind farms... there are as many possible explanations as there are whales. We head to sea to talk to experts about which of these - if any - are most likely.

title: Kitty Killers
summary:
Many cat owners believe their well-fed feline babies don’t kill and just lie around in the sun, but at night they go hunting, and GPS trackers show they can range as far as 3km from their homes. Those living on the edge of the Table Mountain National Park are killing off an astounding number of creatures, just one cat can kill up to 90,000 animals a year. They mostly kill reptiles and amphibians like the endangered Leopard Toad, but also birds and mice. They kill the reptiles, sometimes eating them, but cats like to play with their prey and so they will bring back an injured bird or mouse to play with at home. Most studies to date have been done by surveys and it turns out that most owners are blissfully unaware of what their cats are up to at night. The UCT and SANBI study, which was conducted over the last 10 years, attached “Kittycams” to cats and monitored what they kill and how far they ranged. They discovered that 80% of the prey is never brought home.

Those sweet kitties who are social media darlings and have more YouTube and Instagram followers than most politicians are killing 30 million wild creatures a year on their midnight prowls. A recent paper released by SA National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) and UCT has revealed that it’s not just happening on the urban edge of Table Mountain National Park, but right across Cape Town - 200,000 cats. Could well be far higher cause the kittycam batteries die after 2.30 and the cats hunt easily till 6.30am. Cat are a major contributor to the extinction of 26% of the worlds reptiles, mammals and birds and a threat to a further 25%

title: Getting the Job Dung.
oneLiner: Could a species of insect, well known to us here in Africa, prove a secret weapon in the battle for a more sustainable future?
summary:
One cow produces about 30kg - roughly equivalent to an average 7-year-old boy – of manure every day. There are about 10 million head of cattle in New Zealand, for example, equating to – give or take a pat or two – 300 million kg of dung per day. Multiply that several hundred times over and you have a poo problem of sizable proportions. Now, that might not sound like bad news given our penchant for lathering our own gardens with organic fertilizers but an excess of nitrogen-rich manure is bad news for our rivers and oceans - where much of the dung ends up - and doubly bad news for water absorption in a rain-scarce country like South Africa. Enter the humble dung beetle. If dung removal were an Olympic Sport, these guys would be the Jamaican relay team. They build tunnels up to 20cm beneath the soil's surface and fill them with dung. That has benefits which make everyone - farmers, environmentalists, governments and the beetles - a winner. Who would have thought, in this world of mounting crises and shrinking solutions, this particular problem would have a deployment-ready army, itching to do battle in the fight against dung? Another example of working with nature to help save nature. Enter the humble dung beetle

Dung Beetles don't get the publicity they deserve! For 60 million years they have toiled under a blazing sun, ridding the landscape of somebody else's mess. That "somebody else" is the bovine species we know as the cow: a voracious consumer of grass and depositor of poo. This insert will explain why that's not always good news for the environment and why countries as far afield as Australia and New Zealand are turning to dung beetles to undo the damage.

title: The Senseless Killing of Nathaniel Julies
oneLiner: Police brutality is in the headlines once more, this time with the senseless killing of a sixteen years old Down syndrome boy in Eldorado Park, that has ignited outrage & tension within the community.
summary:
On the night of the killing in Eldorado Park, the police threw Nathaniel Julies into a police van after shooting him, dropped him off at the Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital and by the time the authorities got to the potential crime site it had been cleaned up and contaminated. Police contend that Nathaniel Julies got caught in crossfire between gangs and police but locals dispute this because, for one thing, according to them gang violence has been at a low ebb in Eldorado park. In the immediate aftermath of Nathaniel Julies’s killing we speak to the family of the deceased and local people and campaigners to witness the impact of this horrifying event. On hearing of the circumstances of Nathaniel’s death residents of Eldorado Park took to the streets to protest. On confronting the mass protest, police attempted to stem the tide by arresting local development and economic civil association chairperson Majiet Amiene, under false pretext, calling him to the police station for a meeting and there arresting him. He is currently in police custody. The community believe Amiene was arrested because he is considered a whistle blower by authorities, exposing corruption emanating from Eldorado Park police station, the nature of which includes lost dockets and collusion with gangs. As well as the Eldorado Park community and the Human Rights Commission we try to get answers from SAPS and IPID to why police brutality seems to be unabated and what they are going to do about it.

On Wednesday 26 August, 16 years old Nathaniel Julies, a resident of Eldorado Park with Down Syndrome, left his home to get a packet of biscuits. He never returned home. His life was mercilessly wiped out by a close range shot, from the barrel of a policeman’s gun. With 440 deaths “as a result of police action” tabled in the 2018/2019 IPID Annual Report (page 42) why has police violence remained unchecked in South Africa?

title: cheetah update
oneLiner: ealier this year we broadcast a two year investigation by Ban Animal Trading , exposing unscrupulous animal breeders , we update viewers on the latest developments
summary: Cheetah Cheater – The Wildlife Export Trade Every year thousands of wild animals are exported out of South Africa and traded to zoos, sold as pets or simply disappear abroad – potentially ending up in meat markets. High on the demand list is one of Africa’s favourite short-distance sprinters – the cheetah. Marketed as the “cat most like a dog”, a King Cheetah can cost up to R1.5 million a pop. Raising a cheetah cub as a pet can lead to its death as its diet is too specialised to easily be accommodated. But that doesn’t put off international buyers. Interpol says the illegal wildlife trade is a multi-billion-dollar industry, but overlaying, and probably supporting it, is the legal trade. Earlier this year we exposed HESC , an animal sanctuary run by Lente Roode, which exported cheetah destined for the pet trade.
caseStudies: "Blue"

title: Tuli Elephant man Craig Saunders at it again with animal sanctuary in a wetland
summary: Controversial businessman and owner of 3 elephant Sanctuaries Craig Saunders is applying to open a 4th facility in the Western Cape just outside Kleinmond called Lamlock Animal Sanctuary. He plans to bring 6 elephants, 3 Rhino and various buck onto a farm that incorporates a massive wetland system. Despite huge public opposition to development on this wetland and an extensive EIA which appears to have been halted it appears the permits for 2 Elephants from his Hazyview property are in the final stages of being granted. Part of the opposition is that he has re-established a fence through the wetland initially trapping the herd of wild horses and other wild animals that move freely through the area Craig Saunders was originally charged for animal cruelty for his part in the abuse of the Tuli Elephant saga but charges were later dropped for insufficient evidence. He bought 5 of the Thuli elephants which witnesses said he beat about the head with a stick. Due to mounting international pressure only recently Saunders has stopped elephant back rides in his Hartbeespoort facility. Currently there are containers bordering an small enclosed area on land that has been cleared of aliens. The initial application was that the elephant would be enclosed in this area where visitors could view them, controlled by their elephant handlers and then the elephants would be able to wander through the wetland. Currently the EMS Foundation have engaged their lawyers to get the Department of Environmental affairs land use to concluded the EIA on the land but will Saunders be able to circumvent this through other legislation and move animals?

title: Something's Fishy - Rhodes Research on Vanderkloof Dam
oneLiner: A fishing scheme posing as a research project by Rhodes University at Vanderkloof Dam, is causing the further extinction of the Large Mouth Yellow fish and impoverishing the local fishing community
summary:
A suspicious experimental fishing project at Vanderkloof dam, designed to assess the viability of a small-scale fisheries, is slowly causing the extinction of the globally endangered Large Mouthed Yellow fish (LMY). This, while the project that was designed to uplift the poor Northern Cape fishing communities, is now further impoverishing them. The state funded project implemented by Rhodes University seems to be a commercial operation under the guise of research. Tons of fish have been killed and no research data is being furnished to justify the project. The project is also adding to the collapse of the local tourism industry due to the use of illegal gillnets on South Africa’s second largest dam.

A dubious fishing project spearheaded by Rhodes University and funded with taxpayer’s money, is causing the extinction of the critically endangered Large Mouth Yellow fish in their last remaining habitat in Africa, the Vanderkloof dam. The local impoverished fishing community around the dam that has been dependent on fishing for nearly half a century is also further being deprived of resources by the Rhodes project.

title: Oranges and Lemons
oneLiner: It is almost the end of the orange harvest, and down on a farm deep in rural KZN on the banks of the Blaaukrantz river – the seeds of resilience were sown and now they have borne fruit. Against impo
summary:
In November last year Carte Blanche brought you the story of the Sun Valley citrus estate. With its export quality oranges, this farm was the largest land redistribution project in the area between Weenen in the east, and the foothills of the Drakensburg in the west. Investors managed the farm and exported the citrus. With a turnover of around R60 million, it could bring in profits of R10 million annually if it was managed well. But then in 2019 a violent war broke out between two community families who owned the farm. Forty people in the area were murdered. Management felt unsafe and one evening over a weekend, they packed up their assets under cover of darkness and drove their convoy of tractors and trailers, and fled, never to return. Nothing except an empty packhouse remained. There wasn’t even a chair left in the offices. Carte Blanche arrived a few weeks later to find despair. There was no security, no money, and no formal management. The farm’s future hung in the balance and with it 700 people who depended on it to keep them from starvation. There was petty theft and the farm stood still. Without R12 million rand in emergency funding the farm would close.

A story that against the odds has a happy ending and subtly highlights woman empowerment in Women's month but without being in your face

title: Oscar Chalupsky’s race of his life
oneLiner: SA sporting icon Oscar Chalupsky, without question one of South Africa’s most successful ever sportsmen, is currently engaged in the toughest battle of his life - a fight against bone-marrow cancer.
summary:
Oscar Chalupsky is big on health and diet and besides a minor shoulder operation has never spent a day in hospital throughout his 40 year sporting career. But 2019 things changed for Oscar. He was racing in Australia in the World Championship when he experienced a pain in his ribs that became unbearable. “I was in such pain. I would sleep standing up as the pain was unbearable when I tried to lie down. It was totally debilitating. And I was racing despite this constant pain and still finished,” says Chalupsky. But in typical fashion Chalupsky was determined to not let it stand in his way. He finished 34th, at age 56, in a star-studded fleet of almost 500 paddlers in the 27km Doctor race offshore Perth. After the race Chalupsky flew back home to Porto in Portugal. He immediately went for scans and the radiologist showed Chalupsky a tumour pressing against his spine which is the reason for the pain. Chalupsky contacted a bone-marrow specialist in bone-marrow in Cape Town, Dr. Mike du Toit, who urged him to waste no time and fly to Cape Town immediately. Despite the unbearable pain Chalupsky was not going to cancel his wife Claire’s 60th birthday celebration on the 25th of November. “The day after she turned 60 I got onto a plane and headed for Cape Town”. Further scans and Medical tests revealed Chalupsky had multiple myeloma - a bone-marrow cancer considered to be incurable. His cancer was at a very advanced stage and urgent treatment was needed. Months of heavy chemotherapy followed and a blood transfusion over an arduous three week period.

Oscar Chalupsky is a world-class padler with dozens of trophies and titles to his name. His achievements range from youngest Springbok lifesaver in 1979, South African Junior Sportsman of the Year (1981), South African bodyboarding champion ()1983) and South African Iron Man (1984) to winning the world ski paddle championships at least eight times. Also a coach, he has passed on his skills and techniques to many others in the paddle sports world. Now he is facing his biggest challenge - his battle with multiple myeloma - or more simply put, bone marrow cancer.

title: The Father
oneLiner: Exclusive: A father refuses to let justice slide after his daughter's rape. He goes after the perpetrator himself. Not only does he catch him but turns out he's a serial rapist.
summary:
Meanwhile, William refused to drop the case, and Tshepo's father sent people to the family's house to threaten them and intimidate them. Roux moved William to a new house in cosmos city away from Muldersdrift as he worried for Williams family's safety. He then decided to help fund William's search for justice, giving him time off and money to go find Tshepo. William began paying informers in the local townships, they would track William's father's vehicle, this lead to several other houses they owned, eventually going to one in a township called Madidi (which is near Brits). There William and two of his friends managed to find someone who knew Tshepo and confirmed Tshepo was staying in his father's house. They went from Tavern to Tavern to Tavern... until finally they found Tshepo... they followed him to his house... there they surprised him and found him hiding in the cupboard. William Tasered him, and it took everything in him to do the right thing. He took him to the police station, and finally Tshepo was arrested. When they got Tshepo's DNA back, turns out there were many rapes he was connected to. 16 woman, and 4 children. These are those that we know of. Over the next year William went to every court hearing, some families were paid R50,000 to drop cases against Tshepo by his father, but William stayed the course - refusing to have his daughter "bought off". He gathered community members and got people to go to the court case - all the time Roux assisted where he could. Finally last week Tuesday 28 July Tshepo, who was found guilty earlier this year, was sentenced to life in prison. I told William about the law requiring us to conceal the identity of the child and family, and he said he and his wife want to speak, they dont need to have their real names, but they want to show their faces - they are adamant that he was able to rape their child because so many stayed silent or were happy to be paid off.

We have the story exclusively. The father will speak, and in a TV first in SA, we are going to hide his identity using make up - a prosthetic nose and beard. This will ensure we meet the legal requirements. Dario has approved of this, as has Luke Lamrecht - in terms of the ethics. SHOULD WE CONFRONT THE FATHER OF THE PERPETRATOR? I'LL LEAVE IT UP TO OFFICE. But he is SUUUUUUPER DANGEROUS. I'm happy to, William is happy to, Police say he's very dangerous, and has made witnesses and others disappear. He is also a convicted murderer. STORY: William is a father who has gone all out to catch the man who raped his daughter. He moved to South Africa from Malawi in 1997 and met his wife, who is South African, they have had two girls, Julia and Ennelise - "Nana" as a nickname. When they lived in Muldersdrift, Nana was 11 years old, when a man in a taxi approached her. He wanted her to buy him a cigarette at the tuckshop. She complied. When she came back, he scooped her up onto his lap, and drove away with her. He took her past Lanseria airport and raped her brutally. The man then dropped her off in the bush, throwing a R20 note at her. Hardly able to walk from the pain, she managed to get to the side of the road where another taxi managed to pick her up and drop her nearby her home. Her mother, and aunt immediately took her to a hospital, where they got a rape kit and J88 form done...and then they went through the painful process of her identifying her rapist and retelling the horror story. She was able to give a very good description, and semen was taken and sent for a DNA test. Then her mother called William, he was beside himself with grief. He couldn't believe this had happened, and he decided that no matter what he would get the man. Based on the description, William managed to track down the man who raped her - Tshepo Moeketsi. Turns out, he was a man well known to the community, not only that, but when they went to the Muldersdrift police station seems that there were several other cases of rape against him. However, he'd not been arrested. William insisted. The next thing, Tshepo's father called. A man also well known in the community - he had murdered a 12 year old boy who stole sweets from his tuckshop... he'd spent several years in jail for that crime. Tshepo's father came to William's house to ask if they could remunerate him (admitting his son was guilty) instead of him laying a charge. William said he must bring Tshepo to his house. But instead Tshepo went into hiding, as William had no intention of taking the bribe. William works as a chef and driver for Anthony Roux. Roux was devastated for William and helped him with the hospital bills, as Nana needed an operation after the ordeal. He also hired a PI to help William find the culprit. But the Muldersdrift police tipped off Tshepo's father, who hid Tshepo when the police raided the family home. And Tshepo remained hidden for the next 8 months. William said he had sleepless nights, taking care of Nana, she was in a bad way. She had counselling which her mother took her to in Krugersdorp. But for a long time she couldn't sit, or go to the loo she was in such pain. She also had nightmares. William said it drove him to obsession. So he decided he would do everything to hunt down Tshepo.

title: GBV Vault
oneLiner: an app which has a secret vault to store pics of abuse, to be used in court
summary:
Recently the organisation mobilised to help Nicole who was abused by her fiance. He had left a note saying that he was going to kill himself and then arrived at her home, threatening her. She was on the phone with the crisis counsellor as he threatened her and luckily police arrived in a few minutes. She had taken out a restraining order against him but he is defending it and she has to prove that he was abused her. But he had destroyed her phone and pictures of her abuse were forever lost. Enter a new app developed by SA Fight back - which has special features - an emergency number to press for help and nearby SA Women fight back members can respond immediately, , a private chat room which opens immediately so that the victim can report to nominated people what is happening - and most important a vault where women can record images of their abuse over the years, with notes and even medical reports. Only nominated people will have access to this vault which is stored in the cloud, via a password in the event of her death. It also can be used by the victim in court to show a history of abuse. Nicole's pictures were all lost. They would not have been if she had had the vault.Her partner destroyed her phone.

Last night SA Women Fight back celebrated a year of existence - and the fact that it has just got NPC status -it has 241 000 female members on its private group, and 85 000 facebook members. it has volunteers who have stepped up to support victims through various means - counselling, crisis management, legal assistance, help through the court process. But, and this is the tragic part, the latest statistics show that there has been an increase of domestic abuse and GBV in SA over the last year. This is a story which shows some of the background support it provides and also how it has adapted new technology in the form of a brilliant app which encourages more volunteers to join as "angels" and a system which enables victims - a panic button on the app, and a vault that contains pictures of their abuse. In the private group, women share their sometimes horrific abuse and are supported. Volunteers pour through these messages and reach out to offer support.

title: Lockdown Blue Light Brigade
oneLiner: We investigate a brazen blue light gang operating in JHb, and ask why neither the police nor the national lockdown has stopped them in their tracks
summary:
For the past few years a notorious Blue Light Gang have been terrorising the streets of Johannesburg - and by their unique modus operandi police believe it most likely is the same group of people behind dozens of attacks. Their plan is simple - after identifying vehicles they want to hijack, in most cases expensive double cab bakkies, they follow the victims on the highway in an unmarked white vehicle equipped with blue flashing lights on the dashboard. Motorists think they are being pulled over by legitimate police / traffic police. Once stopped a single man, dressed in police uniform approaches the vehicle. Initially motorists are questioned as if its a real traffic stop - asked for their drivers licence, told they were speeding, asked if they have been drinking etc etc. Then the driver is ordered out of the vehicle, and once that happens several more armed men appear, seemingly out of nowhere, and take the hapless motorist and anyone else in the car hostage at gunpoint. They are driven to an abandoned piece of veldt, held hostage and forced to hand over their bank card details. Their vehicles are also searched for tracking devices. Some victims are assaulted, and almost all of them are held for at least four to six hours. Once the hijackers are ready to leave, the victims are told in which direction to walk to find help. the blue light gang make off with their vehicles, phones, wallets, wedding rings etc.

A brazen gang of car hijackers are operating along the R59 hi-way just south of Johannesburg, pretending to be police and pulling over unwitting motorists in supposed traffic stops, before kidnapping them, holding them hostage while their bank accounts are drained and then making off with their valuables and their vehicles. And while its been an ongoing issue, the most recent cases have all taken place under the national lockdown.

title: Santa Maria Madre de Deus: A Hidden treasure
oneLiner: Hidden treasure of immense archeological value lay undiscovered on the East London seabed for centuries until chanced upon by two local spear fishermen.
summary:
On 19 Sept 2019 while swimming back to shore after a dive, local spear fishermen Hennie Roos and Mathew Fenn encountered three cannon on the seabed off the Nahoon River Mouth, north-east of East London. After the dive they contacted John Barry of Southern Cross Boating and Adrenalin, and a scuba dive on the site was arranged a week later which confirmed the presence of the cannon on the seabed. Subsequent dives have recorded further cannon on the site as well as anchors and pieces of dressed or cut stone that appear to be part of a ship’s ballast. Based on the location of the site and the appearance of the guns it is suggested that the wreck may be that of the Portuguese naveta, Santa Maria Madre de Deus, believed to have been lost in the vicinity of Bonza Bay, in 1643, nine years before Van Riebeeck established the Dutch settlement in Table Bay. A Dive team has been put together that will include the two spear fishermen, who will now learn to scuba dive and can become part of the retrieval endeavour. Carte Blanche gets an exclusive first look at the site of the find and speaks to all the key players who will excavate the site over the next few months. We will take a boat trip and film the divers who will dive to see what more they can find and film some more fresh underwater footage of the cannons.

Two spear fishermen have stumbled on what appears to be a unique archaeological find off the East London Coast. Relics that could possibly belong to the Santa Maria Madre de Deus that went missing in 1643. This wreckage site has remained untouched and unexplored for 377 years. Carte Blanche gets an exclusive first look at this historical find.

title: PROTECTION ORDERS
oneLiner: Victims in possession of protection orders continue to die at the hands of their abusers – we investigate why this document does not provide the protection it promises.
summary:
For many victims, the first line of defence against abuse and harassment is a protection order. Despite campaigns, initiatives, summits and countless budget allocations over the years, victims complain about delays in getting this documents. Many who do eventually get it say that it is not effectively enforced by police. The insert highlights the cracks in the system and interrogates why we are failing dismally to protect victims of GBV.

We speak to victims who share their difficulties in getting protection orders issued and enforced. We also map years of promises to give victims of gender-based violence access to the justice department services aimed at protecting them – the most basic of which is the protection order. Over and above this, we speak to a reformed abuser who explains why in some cases this document could lead to increased abuse and violence being unleashed on the victim.

title: The Woodcutter's Daughter
oneLiner: We visit a third-generation wood-cutter from Knysna with “sawdust in her veins”: Dalena Wolmarans is the last of a rare breed making her living from the southern Cape forest in a dwindling industr
summary:
Dalena Wolmarans said that she loved spending her holidays on the timber trucks and, by the age of 11, her father had taught her how to pull the truck forward to save him a trip down to the hydraulic crane post. At 21, Wolmarans received her heavy duty vehicle licence and, from working as a hostess on Intercape buses she finally drove the buses. On hearing the devastating news that her beloved father had suffered a stroke she headed back to Knysna. "My father having the stroke was the first trigger of a sequence of challenges that life threw my way." She added that, in retrospect, the challenges formed the framework of her life. "I was like the blackwood tree of the family. No-one really wanted me around, because it was the sons' place to take over. I sent out statements when that had to be done, I drove the truck picking up timber from the plantation and did the daughter's job when it was needed." Wolmarans said that looking back at her life she can either see it as a minefield of disasters or a growing forest of opportunity. "My father died, a year later my brother died, one of my loyal workers died when cut in half during a freak accident at the neighbouring sawmill days after I had my first baby and my husband was diagnosed with cancer." She added that every setback also marked a new phase, a new challenge and a new opportunity for her. Earlier this year Wolmarans faced a new but exciting challenge: the Department of Wood and Forest Science at Stellenbosch University under Prof Martina Meincken, asked Wolmarans to select the perfect piece of yellowood in the craftsmanship of violin. After much searching in her pile of this rare species, she found the perfect piece. “I was so surprised when I heard the beautiful sound of the violin made by Hannes Jabocs, an excellent luthier (violin maker) from Pretoria. And he told me how well it compares with the traditional violins made from the imported European Spruce wood.”

Dalena Wolmarans loved her father and as a child she felt most at home deep in the forest where her father would cut the logs to sell to furniture makers in the Knysna area. At 21 she already had a heavy duty truck license, knew how to use a sawmill and cut rare and expensive logs of stinkwood, blackwood and yellowood and even delivered it to customers. She has a passion for the forest and compares the individual species of yellowwood, stinkwood, ironwood, boekenhout and others that grow in the district, to having individual temperaments - just like artists do,” she says. She is one of only a handful of female wood-cutters that knows the different species like the palm of her hand and learnt how to survive in a man’s world. Since the loss of her father thirty years ago, she has turned adversities into a ‘forest of opportunity’ - not easy when rising costs, changing market trends, cost-ineffective and wasteful methods of producing, have taken its toll on the merchants and furniture makers alike. Dalena Wolmarans runs two businesses in the Knysna area that were started by her father in 1958 – Adam Stander Houtverkoper and AJJ Stander Transport. Wolmarans buys indigenous hardwood timber and blackwood, cut it into planks to dry in her kiln at their Knysna premises, before selling it on to customers. On the transport side, Dalena Wolmarans runs two MAN trucks and hauls timber for local sawmills and harvesting contractors

title: Lake Sibaya
oneLiner: South Africa's largest coastal freshwater lake is drying up!
summary:
The Northern KZN coastal plains is a very unique area. The area contains 60% of South Africa's peatlands, with the Mfabeni swamp in iSimangaliso dating back to 45,000 years back, and is recognised as the world's oldest peat-accumulating wetland. The vegetation of the region is complex and exceptionally diverse. The lake supplies water to Sodwana, and Mbazwana & Mseleni communities, and it is the rapid expansion of especially Mbazwana that has raised many eyebrows and is easily blamed for the lake's declining levels. The uMkhanyakude District Municipality has as far back as 2015 realised that Lake Sibaya cannot sustain the increasing extraction levels and they have been working on the Jozini scheme, to supply the area water from the Pongola river... but this is making very little progress. Climate Change has meant that the area receives a lot less rain than historically, and the lake mostly relies on groundwater and the very shallow water table. Unlike other lakes and dams in the area, Lake Sibaya does not have a very big catchment area. So, decreased rainfall and groundwater extraction has a major impact on the lake. But perhaps the biggest concern for Lake Sibaya's future is commercial forests and illegal plantations. The Mbazwana and Manzengwenya plantations border the lake and were planted in the 1950's. They are government plantations but the land has been returned to the locals, so they benefit greatly from the rental paid by government. And this is huge, considering that Mbazwana is considered to be one of the poorest communities in South Africa. In addition many local tribes and land owners want access to the lucrative timber industry and illegal, unlicensed plantations are sprouting all over the region.

The coastal plains of Northern Maputuland are systematically drying out, most evident in the continuing receding levels of Lake Sibaya in the iSimangaliso Wetland Park, South Africa's only World Heritage Site. The entire area is a unique ecosystem, a complex network of groundwater aquifers, ancient peatlands and coastal dune forests. Researchers have recorded a 4-5m drop in water levels at Lake Sibaya since 2010 and the groundwater is said to be decreasing at about 1m per annum. Unlike other lakes (St Lucia) and dams in the Pongola River, Lake Sibaya is not recovering from the severe drought of 2015/6/7. The levels of the Lake Sibhayi (Sibaya) have been dropping at an alarming rate since 2000, creating consternation among scientists, conservationists, tourism organisations, local government and surrounding communities. Research and monitoring in the area are contributing greater detail to formulate strategies to help steer the coastal plain away from a looming environmental crisis.

title: Two Pandemics
oneLiner: Covid-19 has taught us all the ‘new normal’ and a resilience to cope. Tonight we hear the stories from families who experienced the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic, some similarities and how they surviv
summary:
In the early part of 1918 a disease began to sweep around the planet - a lethal virus that infected a third of the world’s population and left upwards of 50 million dead. The ‘Spanish flu’ spread simultaneously in Europe, Asia and North America over a twelve-month period. The First World War, although not the direct cause of its outbreak, contributed to its rapid spread worldwide. It became known as the Spanish flu, only because wartime censorship in other countries meant Spain was the first place it received widespread press attention. Soldiers, were particularly vulnerable to infection. As they were constantly moved between different theatres of war across the globe they spread the virus to many countries. South Africa was not spared. Soldiers came back by ship and docked in Durban and Cape Town; those infected spread the disease as they travelled by train to every corner of the country. In September and October of 1918 the Spanish Flu had killed between 300 000 and 350 000 people: most of them were young adults between 18 and 40. History is about to repeat as we live through another pandemic of global proportion. With Covid-19 we have learnt to live in lockdown; in isolation and have grown accustomed to the word ‘social distancing’. We look back at 1918 and link the past and the present as we make sense of the human experience and how people learnt to cope and came out stronger.

As the world faces social distancing and isolation we go back in history and re-visit a pandemic of similar nature from 1918 - the Spanish flu. We listen to stories of families and their collective memories of how people coped at the time with the disease and their resilience to survive against all odds. A hundred years later, despite facing another pandemic of global proportion, families are learning to cope with the ‘new normal’ and are adapting to a new way of life which ultimately are giving them the tools to come out stronger.
