title: Botswana elephant mystery
oneLiner: While Botswana has been in lockdown for COVID-19 hundreds of elephants have mysteriously died in the Okavango Delta, we investigate why
summary: An unprecedented amount of Elephants have mysteriously died in the Okavango delta, Botswana since May 2020. On the 25th of May Elephants without borders flew over the Okavango and discovered 165 Elephant Carcasses. In June a second flight revealed new carcasses bringing the total, according to them, to 365 mysteriously dead elephants. Mike Chase the director of the project says that some of the animals appeared to have died abruptly and landed face forward. They observed some animals walking in circles, appearing to be disorientated and others dragging their hind legs, which potentially means they were paralysed by whatever was killing the elephants. Poaching has been ruled out, as all the elephants tusks were in place. Some conservationists say it's due to starvation, because of an overpopulation of Elephants in Botswana. Niall from National Park Rescue strongly disagree with this hypothesis, he is gravely concerned as Bots is home to 1/3 of the worlds remaining elephant population and last week more carcasses were found.

title: Debtbuster - a nightmare you cant get out of
summary:
Debt Busters promise that will can negotiate lower interest rates with the banks and your creditors and will handle your debt crisis. Some of the creditors are not being paid at all. The amounts they are paying off of their debt are extremely low so they get stuck in this cycle for far longer than if they had just paid it off themselves. Some people have ended up paying off the debt themselves yet Debtbusters haven’t removed them from their register and so they cannot get finance because their credit record is damaged. Some case studies have found Debtbusters have blatantly lied to them saying they have paid off creditors when in fact they haven’t and have paid them off themselves.. One case study discovered that the interest rate they had negotiated on her behalf saw her paying nearly R80 000 more than she needed to and only when she enquired did she discover this. She had to negotiate with Standard bank and they are paying back R25 000. Another case study lost her job at the beginning of lockdown and informed Debtbusters that she could not pay her monthly instalments and they needed to inform her creditors, they failed to submit her forms and now when any money does get deposited into her account they remove it immediately. She is a widow who supports 5 children and that money is her lifeline. So you think you sign up and pay monthly and Debtbusters are handling your problems but it turns out they not- it’s still up to you to follow up on all the debts and for many this is just not what they signed up for. Have Debtbusters just got too big and greedy to rectify these errors and what’s the impact on peoples lives? With the Debt crisis spiralling out of control are consumers getting ripped off?

Debtbusters: When your debts all become too overwhelming you turn to the professionals to help you out and keep the creditors off your back. Initially the administration process goes quite smoothly but when you have a problem and things have gone horribly wrong it can take months to resolve, if they ever do. People get passed from one consultant to the next and no one seems to remember what they told the last one. If they want to terminate their services, you aren’t released until you can prove all your accounts have been paid up and will still need to pay. Now they can’t even walk into their officers to speak to someone because of Covid 19. Their Debt crisis has just got bigger. This story was repeated in various forms by many people who have complained on Hello Peter and written into us

title: Big Data: Protection Your Personal Information
oneLiner: Big Data is one of the most valuable commodities of the 21st century but how do we go about protecting our right to privacy and our personal information?
summary:
Here in South Africa the Protection of Personal Information Act (Or POPIA) is a landmark piece of legislation that is slowly being rolled out. POPI says that everyone has the right to privacy and looks to protect South African consumers by ensuring that all South African institutions conduct themselves in a responsible manner when collecting, processing, storing and sharing another entity's personal information by holding them accountable should they abuse or compromise personal information in any way. New provisions of the act became law on July 1st 2020 and gives companies in South Africa one year to comply with all the regulations of the law. Businesses that don't comply with the POPI Act, regardless of whether it’s intentional or accidental, can face severe penalties. The Act makes provision for fines of up to R10 million and a jail sentence of up to 10 years, depending on the seriousness of the breach. This affects every single company in SA, from obvious big data collection companies like Discovery to other financial institutions but practically for every business that collects personal information.

Data is becoming one of the most important commodities of the 21st century. In the age of the internet, every one of us generates vast amounts of data about ourselves every day. From our internet browsing history, to the health data our smart watches collect, to the tracking data from our mobile phones, to the transaction history of our credit cards, the data points that we generate can be used to create a fairly accurate and comprehensive profile about us as individuals. That’s why big companies and governments around the world are spending billions of dollars each year to find better ways to harvest and analyse the data we generateThe question is: If our personal data is so valuable, how do we go about protecting it?

title: Convalescent Plasma Therapy
oneLiner: ..... a promising treatment for Covid-19
summary:
Blood from COVID-19 survivors can be a rich source of antibodies or proteins that the immune system makes to attack the SARS-CoV-2 virus, the virus causing COVID-19. Plasma is the part of the blood that contains these valuable antibodies. It has long been the focus of treatment during pandemics and it is surmised that if you give somebody who is really sick a dose of somebody else’s antibodies that it will assist in their recovery. The method has been used during the 1918 Spanish Flu and also for Ebola treatments. There are currently dozens of studies underway across the globe looking at this as a treat possible treatment for Covid. Some results are trickling in and it seems positive. The Mayo Clinic has determined that giving sick Covid patients plasma does not harms them, and seems to have positive effects. Another study from Methodist Hospital in Houston shows a 75% success rate. However, the Houston study was a small one. But it is very encouraging. In the US , the US National COVID-19 Convalescent Plasma Project, a group of physicians and scientists from 57 institutions in 46 states are involved in clinical trials. Here in South Africa people who have recovered from COVID-19 are donating their blood to help others who are trying to fight off the disease. It is part of a South African clinical trial involving 600 volunteers and is headed by the SA National Blood Service.

This could be a game changer in the fight against the virus.
experts: Dr. Marion Vermeulen Dr. Devorah Wineberg Dr. James Musser Dr. Jacob Glanville

title: ILLEGAL LAND SALES
oneLiner: Many of Gauteng's 700 informal settlements were set up illegally – we investigate how syndicates distribute and sell land owned by municipalities or private individuals.
summary:
Covering around 3500 hectares of land, the Crocodile River Reserve used to be home to a range of wildlife including scorpions, birds, frogs, bats and gazelle. About 100 local landowners initiated a process to have the reserve declared a protected area and last year, they succeeded. In October, the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development announced that the reserve in Centurion, outside Pretoria, would be protected from human activity that could cause harm to the flora and fauna as well as the environment. Less than a year later, the area has suffered exactly that – harm caused by human activity, criminal human activity to be exact. Seeing a lucrative market out of people's desperation for land and housing, a man by the name of Baba Sashane, who does not own any land on the reserve, started a land sales business on the conservation area. Sashane sells 20m by 20m plots on protected land that does not belong to him, and business is booming at R10 000 per plot. A large area within the reserve is now a fully-fledged informal settlement with a creche, supermarkets and even a taxi route. Rightful landowners are helpless to remove the squatters. The forest is quickly being stripped of its trees for firewood – there is no formal electricity supply to the settlement so the fast-growing community relies on wood fires to cook and keep warm in the brutal winter. Wildlife including species of buck have been hunted to near non-existence by the newcomers. A local business has reported several robberies in recent months and has had to shut down their evening service offerings due to safety concerns.

title: Paradise Lost - Bazaruto Island View Estate
oneLiner: Crystal clear waters and white sandy beaches, investors were thrilled at the prospect of purchasing property in Mozambique - now they say they've been duped by a South African businessman.
summary:
In 2008, Erasmus established Bazaruto Island View Estate (he is again the sole director) and began to sell property investment opportunities, initially claiming that clients would have full title ownership of the properties, then that they had 99 year leases, and finally demanding that clients pay extra and build on the stands within 5 years. He advertised extensively on Radio Pretoria and Facebook. It seems a number of people invested in BIVE, which was represented as a luxury “security lifestyle estate” in the making, with promises of a medical centre, resort, marina, etc. People invested either to own a holiday home or to build and sell at a profit. In 2016, a string of articles appeared in the Lowvelder, with alleged victims claiming to have invested tens or hundreds of thousands, only to see no return years later. Erasmus admitted that he had started selling plots in 2009 despite receiving permission only in 2012. He claimed perceptions of conflict in the area were slowing development and construction had only started on two houses. He also claimed that 70% of the stands had been sold. Investors claimed they had been charged levies despite no electricity or water connection; the contractor told Lowvelder he had withdrawn because nothing was happening. One Lowvelder article revealed that the images featured on BIVE’s website with its logo were actually taken from the sites of luxury resorts around the world. Similarly, the pictures on BIVE’s website gallery appear to be of a nearby resort called Casa de Lua, as well as a fishing charter company called Big Blue Vilankulo. From about 2014 onwards, Erasmus and his partner Grace Bagnari (Schutte) abandoned the BIVE social media pages and started posting on a variety of other groups and pages, including Mozambique Properties (MozProp), Destination Mozambique, Opportunities in Mozambique, Vilanculos Beach Properties and MozForum. They seem to have been avoiding the BIVE name, but the sales pitch is the same.

Crystal clear waters, white sand and friendly locals – this is the promise sold to willing buyers by Ettienne Erasmus, a prolific businessman who has been selling property opportunities in Mozambique to South Africans since at least 2008. The problem is, after he takes your money, the promised property does not seem to materialise. His sales pitch is that South Africa is a ‘sinking ship’ with a failing economy, whereas Mozambique offers safety, friendly locals keen for investments, and a growing economy.

title: saving the Rhino
oneLiner: Its the biggest dehorning ever undertaken and we got to ride in on their final day
summary: For the past 5 years Nico J from Rhino 911 has been fighting with the government to implement a mass dehorning of the full rhino population in the Pilanesberg, which is a K1 population and one of the most important in the SADC region. He was stone walled for years, even after he offered to pay for the operation himself. Until this year. He was given the go ahead and immediately had to get sponsors on board to cover the 2 million rand operation. It is the biggest operation of its kind ever undertaken in the world. Two helicopters with 15 people per team took 9 days to remove the horns of the entire rhino population. They have one day left, which we can fly in on with them. Lockdown was the perfect time to do the operation, as the park was void of all tourists. But during the operation they battled to find a cow and her calf, only to eventually discover her fresh carcass on the parks border. The calf was never found. They were too late. This wasn’t new to Nico who has run smaller operations in parks across Africa. He says that every time they start an operation they lose at least one rhino, as the syndicates are tipped off. Over the 9 days they removed over ¾ of a billion Rands worth of Rhino horn, which has now been placed in state vaults around the country. - This may be angle too? It’s a debate we have all heard though, whether or not to legalise and control the trade of Rhino horn. Nico documented the entire operation and has sent me the videos. He has some amazing footage. The story would be about the magnitude of the operation and the humans that worked 15 hour days to get it done in order to save the Rhino the only way they know how. - Can add an element of the debate around whether or not Dehorning the right solution though

title: Live Animal Exports Update June 2020
oneLiner: Once again an Al Mawashi Vessel is docked in East London... and 70,000 sheep are awaiting their fate.
summary:
Live Animal Export by Sea Industry is considered by many to be exceptionally cruel. Animals are subjected to dirty living conditions, overcrowding, noise and lack of fresh air for 21 days, and these voyages can become unbearably hot during the Northern Hemisphere Summer. Many sheep die from heat exhaustion, illness and injuries. A whistleblower from Australia took undercover footage of the harrowing conditions aboard Al Mawashi's vessels. But Al Mawashi has repeatedly denied these conditions onboard of their vessels. They claim that it's just a few sheep that suffer and for the most part, the sheep are happy and healthy. Al Mawashi is a major importer of live animals for consumption to the Middle East. A Huge public outcry and Lobbying by Animals Australia led to the shipment of Live Animals from Australia being banned during the Middle Eastern Summer, but then the Kuwatis came knocking on South Africa's door. They intended on importing over a million animals over a 5-year period, a deal that our Government and some farmers found to be lucrative. Al Mawashi has now made three successful shipments of sheep from SA to the Middle East, although the NSPCA keeps up the fight against what they believe to be a gross animal welfare violation. Last week, when the Al Messilah arrived in East London, DALRRD announced that they have advised the Eastern Cape Veterinary Services against any live animal exportation to the Middle East from May to September 2020. The Eastern Cape Veterinary Services have confirmed that they have no intentions of going against the decision from DALRRD. Yet Al Mawashi has made their intentions clear.

Last year we exposed the Live Animal Export by Sea Industry, whereby farm animals (mostly sheep) are transported on large cargo vessels from Australia and South Africa to the Middle East. Although The NSPCA contested the first shipment in 2019, they lost the court battle and about 65,000 sheep left our shores on the Al Suwaikh to be slaughtered in Kuwait and Oman. The NSPCA also tried to stop a shipment earlier this year, but once again failed... However, in a surprise move a Al Mawashi vessel, the Al Messilah arrived at East London last week, and reports indicate that some 70,000 sheep are waiting in Berlin (outside EL) to be shipped to the Middle East. The NSPCA managed to win an urgent Court Application with Costs against Al Mawashi and the case has been postposed until 16 July. No animals may be loaded until then.

title: Triggerfish
oneLiner: We follow the roller-coaster ride to success of Africa’s largest animation studio and go behind the scenes to the creators of award-winning characters that have thrilled audiences across the globe.
summary:
Triggerfish was established in 1996 as a stop-frame animation studio in Cape Town producing TV commercials and animation series for childrens’ programmes. The studio made their name with the popular Takalani Sesami and Sesami Street children’s series. In 2004, one of the junior animators on the series, Stuart Forrest, was made a partner together with Mike Buckland and Anthony Silverston. In 2007, the company moved into computer-generated animation and shifted their focus to motion pictures. Adventures in Zambezia, and Khumba were their first two animation films. They pulled out all the stops, hired more people and worked to extreme deadlines to deliver the films for release in 2012/2013. Forrest and the team were rewarded for their hard work. Both features were box-office successes and received several accolades, including Best Animation at South African Film and Television Awards and a Gold Panda Award for Best Foreign Animation film for Khumba. But the next year, there was no work in the pipeline and no funding and salaries had to be paid. They nearly didn’t survive. 120 staff were retrenched, people they had nurtured for the past 10 years. It was a terribly difficult environment. Two years later though, Triggerfish was back on track. Backed by global distributors, they made their mark again in the animation world. Over the last five years, they have thrived, creating a slate of award-winning films broadcasted on BBC One Christmas Specials and produced by Magic Light Pictures - a UK producer of children’s entertainment. These include Stickman, Revolting Rhymes, The Highway Rat, Zog and The Snail and the Whale.

Triggerfish animation studio has produced two of the five highest-grossing South African feature films of all time - Adventures in Zambezia and Khumba - and, in collaboration with Magic Light Pictures, has animated five multi-award-winning BBC Christmas adaptations, including the Oscar-nominated Roald Dahl adaptation Revolting Rhymes, the Annecy-and-Kidscreen-winning Julia Donaldson adaptationStick Man, and the International Emmy-winning Zog. Triggerfish is currently producing their third feature film, Seal Team, and Netflix’s first African animated TV series, Mama K's Team 4. In 2013, the studio set up a non-profit organisation, the Triggerfish Foundation, with the mandate to create awareness about animation as a career in Africa, train future animators, and help them to make their first animation so that they would be employable, improving diversity and gender equality in the sector. Key initiatives include the pan-African Triggerfish Story Lab, supported by The Walt Disney Company; the all-women Triggerfish Writers Lab with Netflix; the free Triggerfish Academy digital learning platform; and regular bursaries to study at The Animation School.

title: Healthcare Interrupted
oneLiner: Many routine, yet essential healthcare services are impacted on by Covid-19
summary:
Covid-19 has disrupted our lives in many ways. Businesses have closed, people have lost livelihoods, loved ones... The world as we knew it just a few months ago has changed forever. One important, sometimes overlooked, impact is the disruption in routine medical services across the world. Reports from many countries show severe disruption of routine healthcare services in many countries due to lockdowns imposed, diversion of healthcare workforce to COVID-19 response, and disruption of travel and supply chains. Even basic immunization services have come to a grinding halt in many settings. Internationally the Irish National Breast Screening Programme (Breast Check) reports 0 mammograms for the month of April, and a 96% reduction in samples sent to CervicalCheck labs. In the USA, the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association warn that emergency rooms across the country are 40 to 50% less busy when it comes to cardiovascular patients seeking care. People are staying home, ignoring serious symptoms for fear of contracting Covid-19. New figures from University College London suggest there could be 18,000 more cancer deaths in England because of the coronavirus pandemic. A similar situation is playing off in Sub-Saharan Africa. Besides cancer and heart disease we have a set of medical challenges that cannot simply be ignored until we find a vaccine for Covid-19. Prof Sanne (Right to Care) told News24 there had been an increase in missed appointments by HIV patients of between 40% and 60% since the lockdown, and a similar issue was expected for diabetes and other illnesses needing chronic medication.

The world is focussing on Covid-19, and the devastating effects on humanity, but experts are warning that there are other humanitarian crises waiting in the wings. Thousands of people across South Africa depend on regular access to medicine and healthcare, patients with HIV, TB, Diabetes, Heart Disease to name but a few... but Covid-19 is disrupting more and more of the healthcare services that these people depend on. From being harassed by police on their way to the clinic, to being too scared to seek medical help, or to collect medicines... it is becoming evident that we're faced with an imminent disaster.

title: 21st Century Tech on the Covid Front Line
oneLiner: We look into how cutting edge technologies are being harnesses in the battle against SARS-CoV-2.
summary:
Diamond Light Source is at the centre of a global crowd-sourcing experiment. Its owners have made the technology available to scientists all over the world who believe they have the right recipe for a compound capable of neutralising the virus. For a small fee, they're able to submit the molecular make-up to the Diamond team who then create the experiment required to test the interaction between the compound and some of the virus's constituent parts. That interaction is observed in the high-quality x-rays delivered by this high-intensity light-source. It's hoped that this unprecedented crowd sourcing initiative will deliver a compound capable of fighting the virus which can then be manufactured and tested as a new drug. Allied to this is another example of how technology is being used to assist in the fight against Covid19: Artificial Intelligence and its ability to process what's know as "Big Data". It's an application of machine learning that allows researchers to produce accurate models on the impact and behavior of the virus at a speed previously unheard of. At Wits, academics and researchers have built a detailed Covid dashboard that provides the most accurate picture available of the spread of the virus and impact of the disease it causes, Covid19. Crucially, using complex mathematics, it's able to predict future patterns allowing governments to shape policy befitting the reality. It also provides a useful example of the relationship between the technology and the humans using it.

Hospitals and frontline medical staff are the forefront of the struggle against Covid19, but 21st century technologies like Artificial Intelligence and high-powered X-rays are being deployed behind the scenes to bolster our ability to counter this unseen enemy. We get a first-hand insight into one such technology, the so-called Diamond Light Source. It's described as pure light, billions of times brighter than the sun, able to deliver X-Rays of such clarity that researchers are able to watch molecules interacting with the microscopic building blocks that constitute this new Coronavirus.

title: Insurance Pitfalls of the Pandemic

summary:

Locally it seems this is also the case - and businesses like restaurants and hotels, who are going to be the hardest hit in the economic fall out of the lockdown and virus, are getting the short end of the stick. We'll deal with the merits of each case study on a case by case basis, because it all boils down to the fine print. BUT - no matter what the fine print says, all these owners have been docking up thousands of rands in premiums for years, all in the belief that they WERE covered. Even once lockdown is eventually lifted, these businesses, which form an integral part of the economy, are going to be vulnerable. The insurance could have at least covered some of their costs - costs that will impact on thousands of lives as staff, many of them breadwinners, face layoffs and cut salaries.

We have had many web submissions from business owners, particularly in the tourism and hospitality industry, who thought they were covered for exactly the kind of crisis the national lockdown and Corona Virus Pandemic has caused by their business interruption insurance. Most of them were sold on lines from brokers such as "if your business closes for a month, your fully covered" etc. But now that they've been forced to close their lodges, restaurants and B&B's and claimed from insurers like Momentum, Santam and Brite, the insurers have come up with any number of excuses not to pay.

title: LOCKDOWN POLICE BRUTALITY
summary: Throughout the lockdown, we have seen reports of people being wrongfully arrested for contravening the Disaster Management Act. In many cases, people are reprimanded and arrested even when they have done nothing wrong. For example, our case studies include a man who was arrested on his way to buy electricity at a nearby shop, people who were arrested while walking or jogging on the beach during the allocated exercise time between 6am and 9am, and a father who was fined when he collected his children from his parents' home in Mpumalanga after the lockdown extension. We investigate the validity of these arrests and the apparent abuse of power by law enforcers in some of the cases as well as the implications of the criminal records attached to these cases. We also dissect the difference between an admission of guilt and bail – we spoke to people who honestly believed they were paying bail when they were in fact admitting that they were guilty and getting a criminal record. One of our case studies helps illustrate that despite the government assuring them that the relevant department were aware of the changing regulations, the information doesn't filter to some enforcers on the ground – after parents were granted permission to move their children from one province to another, law enforcers told our parent they knew nothing of the sort, and then slapped him with R2000 rand fine. Also, in the KZN incident captured on video, with the father in a scuffle with police over his child, we have learned that the incident was a climax to a situation that was brewing earlier. It turns out that the father was one of eleven people taking in by police after being "caught" walking on the beach during exercise time with his child. The father was among the parents who asked to leave their kids at home before being taken in to the police station for processing. While doing exactly this, he has no idea why the police suddenly went for his son. This is when the video was taken.

title: Sweden Unlocked: A Unique Approach to Combating Covid
oneLiner: As lockdowns and their inevitable economic toll take hold across the globe, Sweden is cutting against the grain by staying open for business and relying on citizens to do the right thing.
summary:
This is the story of a country that has followed its own path in the battle against Covid19. It's relied on a responsible public to do the right thing in helping keeping Sweden open for business. As a result, the pandemic has come at less of a price for Swedes than it has for others. But, it's not without controversy: the death rate is the highest in Scandinavia and there are ongoing warnings of a health system that risks being overwhelmed. But, the Swedes remain resolute that theirs has been the correct approach and that others - South Africa included - have got it wrong. The story will be told through the eyes of Swedish journalist, Marika Griehsel as she ventures through the streets of Stockholm. It's quieter than usual, but notably busier than most other cities around the world. She'll talk to experts and those on the frontline and, as a personal insight, visit the nursing home where her father is being cared for. She's not aloud inside and has to stand in the street and shout to him at his third-floor window. The vulnerable are isolated, the rest of society goes about daily life as best it can.

If lockdowns constitute a global experiment, Sweden is the control group. While the vast majority of states have chosen extreme caution as the best means to combat Covid19 - sacrificing their economies in the process -Sweden has opted for a different path. They haven't insisted on businesses shutting down, they've kept schools and universities open, and public transport has operated as normal. Their most powerful weapon is a responsible citizenry, they say; people who'll keep a social distance because it's the right thing to do. Controversially, many of Sweden's epidemiologists have argued for herd immunity, believing a 60% infection rate will achieve that. They also claim the virus has infected a lot more people than current estimates suggest and that immunity is closer as a result. One of their most outspoken medical scientists has criticised countries like the U.K. for abandoning herd immunity and over-estimating the cost of the virus to human life. It's not a popular position in many quarters - not even in Sweden - but is routinely used by lockdown critics around the world as an example for other countries to follow. Most recently, and surprisingly, Sweden was hailed as a shining light by the WHO. A locally-based crew will film on the streets of Stockholm where life - while far from normal - is continuing lockdown-free. They'll also talk to experts on both sides of the debate, including the country's chief epidemiologist, a hospital clinician working with Covid patients, Sweden's foreign minister and a Swede who is infected with Covid19 and has been for the past 40-odd days. It'll be a first-hand look at the country everyone is talking about. It'll also offer an insight into an issue that is far more complex than many people realise - including those arguing against the lockdown in South Africa.

New Development (Brics) Director General for South Africa, Ratsoma Monale will talk about the loan offering they are providing and conditions there of. As economic activity resumes albeit under limited measures under level 4 lockdown, an interview with a printing and packaging factory owner, on sight, will illustrate what the 'new normal' for business and economy looks like and how South Africa's economic relief efforts are important to keep industry afloat and people employed. These visuals will also illustrate the discussion about how South Africa is going to reimagine an economy that is highly dependent on labour.

Whilst South Africa's health and humanitarian response to COVID 19 response has been lauded around the world, its efforts to save the economy will test its resilience to survive the pandemic. Global financial institutions have made available relief loan facilities to countries at a lower interest rate with minimal conditions. The loans government officials are considering will be channeled for both health efforts and economic stimulus a move that raises concerns about the added debt burden on an already constrained fiscus, a legacy of stringent loan conditions especially on poor countries, corruption and the recovery of the economy.

title: Covid19: the Search for a Silver Bullet.
oneLiner: Is an effective and safe Covid19 treatment any closer within reach, or is our desperation fueling unwarranted optimism?
summary:
There are - at last count - more than 500 clinical trials and research studies underway around the world as part of a desperate search for a possible treatment or cure for Covid19. It's important work because a vaccine - even by the most optimistic estimates - is more than a year away. That's creating significant anxiety because it means the next 12, 18 or possibly 24 months of our lives will be characterised by social distancing and - in the event of a transmissions spike - periods of lock-down. A treatment - or even a cure - would clearly make that a less frightening proposition. the term "game-changer" is overused but, with case fatality rates currently hovering at anywhere between 1 and 10%, anything that makes admission to hospital routine rather than a medical emergency would be deserving of the title. That's why so many people are working so hard to find a new or existing drug that could do precisely that. Trials are already underway and many more are planned and, in some cases, early results are already being published. With luck, one or perhaps several will prove effective and the gap between now and a vaccine will seem a little less daunting. But, there are caveats: there's no guarantee a treatment or cure will be found nor is it a sure thing an effective drug will be safe at the required dosage and there's always the danger that scientific rigour falls by the wayside in the quest for speed. We'll talk to two South African experts about the trials process, the most publicised candidates, the pitfalls and the broader context of the search for a vaccine. We'll canvass them, too, for their views on the ethical dilemmas. We'll also talk to one of several companies using AI to identify existing drugs and compounds that might help in the fight against the pandemic.

We speak to two of South Africa's leading infectious disease experts for insights into the global search for a possible Covid19 treatment, a scientific undertaking spanning more than 500 medical trials involving thousands of volunteers. We also hear from a company harnessing the power of AI to radically speed-up a process that would otherwise take years. And, throughout, we ask: are we discarding scientific rigour in this race against time?

With the massive drop in the number of passenger air flights, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) has updated its analysis of global airline passenger revenues concluding that they will plummet by 314 billion dollars this year, (55% compared to last year). With such a drop in capital coming in not only small airlines will struggle to survive. Even the best positioned airlines have been put under liquidity pressure… with no money coming in, massive pressure has been put on their savings in hand. The savings of the large operators are depleting fast, which is why they are using vouchers for deferred travel so they can hold on to capital. It is also why governments have been put under severe pressure to fund airlines to keep them afloat. Most airlines have about a two month cash flow allowance with bigger airlines having slightly deeper pockets but as time marches on as does the corona virus, casualties are inevitable. The scale of the decline can be seen in the struggles of the once apparently embedded players -like British Airways, who have announced they may have to shed 12000 jobs. Unlike some other European airlines whose governments are rescuing with money, British Airways is not being bailed out by the British government -some say in a tactical maneuver by BA to see off one of its main rivals Virgin Atlantic. There is so much uncertainty in this new coronavirus era that the course of recovery is uncertain. To start with, no-one is clear as to when countries will actually lift travel restrictions as lockdown measures and timetables continue to be revised throughout the world. With such uncertainty people have begun to talk about a return to a “new normal” rather than a pre-COVID 19 normal, which the timescale to attain is now being talked about in terms of ‘years’.

The knock on effect of lockdown has well and truly begun and a snowball of economic deluge is on a roll. Not least in the aviation industry, with the exponential damage of that on the tourism industry. Worldwide travel restrictions to fight COVID-19 mean global aviation is on its knees. From South Africa to the rest of Africa, to the ends of the earth, it looks like all airlines will be in some form of business rescue pretty soon, predicts Guy Leitch editor of SA Flyer Magazine. So how devastating is this collapse and how are countries tackling the crisis of empty skies? And if air flights are already predicted to be half of that a year ago, what is the impact on jobs, GDP and how far does that impact spread and accumulate? Job losses and GDP decline, globally, will be dire indicators of the cost of strict travel restrictions and peoples’ recent reluctance to travel communally.

title: LOCKDOWN Grapes of Wrath
oneLiner: Wine exports represent R9 billion in foreign earnings and stopping wine exports has cost South Africa R3 billion
summary:
They are losing R200 million weekly and 70 to 80 of the smaller wineries are in danger of collapsing. 98% of wine is produced in the Cape and they employ nearly 300 000 people, and that does not include all the other industries they support like tourism and the restaurant trade. Not only have they lost income in March and April but they are likely not to get much income for the next 4 or 5 months as wine sales take 60 to 90 days to pay. The impcats will be felt for years to come as they have already lost valuable listing in Europe. SA is the only wine producing country in the world not allowed to export wine, and wine sales are booming under lockdown in America and Europe. It will take decades to win back those listings as they can’t even send them tastings for this year. Normally at this time of the year they are travelling the European and American markets marketing their wines in the European summer. The wine industry is extremely competitive and their hard-earned market share is disappearing by the day while Chile and Argentina fill the gap.

The wine industry in the Western Cape exports 50% of their wines and so when lockdown was announced, and all their domestic income cut off, they had a lifeline. They could export to the overseas markets which were booming and had taken years to establish. Lockdown came at the end of a bumper harvest where both volumes and quality were excellent and they manged to bring in the crop. Then suddenly 9 days later, Minister Dhlamini Zuma and Minister of Transport Fikile Mbalula shut it all down. Bottle stores were looted and a container hijacked and that was the end of the lifeline. It’s made no sense and as wine farms have pointed out that it takes 3 people to export and none of them have to have any contact with each other. The wine industry has even offered to escort their goods to the harbour under heavy security.

title: Covid19 and Waste Water
oneLiner: With a Covid-19 vaccine still months from being a reality, could our waste water systems prove to be the ultimate early warning systems for detecting viral loads in South African communities?
summary:
Using waste water treatment plants to test for substances ingested by humans is not new technology - the FBI uses it in America to screen large populations for overall drug use, and are able to successfully see if there are spikes in drug intakes in certain areas. The same technology can be used to test for Covid 19 - by testing waste water coming into treatment plants before it is chemically treated. This would allow for large scale analysis of dense populations, like the urban metropols mostly affected by the disease in SA. But our current waste water treatment system is in a state of complete chaos - could the covid19 crisis be the critical turning point in preventing an even larger public health crisis, the collapse of our national water systems.

The South African waste water treatment system is in a state of disaster - but according to Professor Anthony Turton the current Covid19 pandemic might just present the perfect opportunity, created by the perfect storm. Using new technology already available in the Netherlands, we could use our waste water treatment plants to detect Covid 19 viral loads in South Africans - and the best part is international funding is available to kickstart the project, which could see the first testing happen within a month, if the SA Government buys into the idea. The relatively small investment in setting up the systems would offer many benefits - it would be cheaper than trying to test the almost 59 million individuals in South Africa, and would mean we could do continuous testing on high density populations - something that will not be possible with individuals. Meanwhile, while Covid19 is found in human faeaces, the jury is still out on whether it can be transmitted in this way. But experts warn it's better to be safe than sorry.

title: The Doomsday Clock
oneLiner: ....the doomsday clock that shows how far humanity is from selfdestruction
summary:
The Doomsday clock has been in existence since 1947 when the threat that nuclear warfare became real. The cook was introduced as a metaphor to show how critical the situation is, with midnight as Doomsday. The time to midnight is re-assessed every year in the light of nuclear and other threats. Lately, the issue of climate change has also been factored into the scenario. With growing unease between major geopolitical players, new ballistic missile developments by the US and Russia and a growing climate change crisis, the clock was set at 100 seconds to midnight in January this year -- before the pandemic.

A physical metaphor/symbol that serves as a warning to humanity on the road to self-destruction

title: SA Express - We Do Nothing For You
oneLiner: SA Express is pending liquidation. Most employees have not been paid since February. They too are now penniless and who knows, soon to be homeless. A plea to government is falling on deaf ears.
summary:
After being put into business rescue most SA Express employees have been left without salaries since the end of February where some were paid 50% of their salaries, but as of the 25th of March 462 of the 650 employees have received no salary at all. They were told this on the 24th of March through a letter from the Business Rescue Practitioners (BRP). It was a very matter-of-fact letter informing them to speak to the banks that they will not be able to meet their commitments. They were unable to claim from UIF or get benefits from their pensions and medical aids, as those had not been paid. Many of these employees support families and are on chronic medication, they are running out of food and do not know where to turn to. They have written letters to the DPE and to the President and as yet they have had no response. The BRP Daniel Terblanche and Phahlani Mkhombo say their hands are tied as there is no money despite appeals to the shareholder which is government for some cash injection. They have applied for COVID relief for UIF, but that won't even cover some of these employees' actual UIF claims and they are still waiting to hear if there will be any relief from the COVID fund. This afternoon the BRP's managed to get an extension on two of the medical aid schemes until May, but there are still others that have not been covered. SA Express employees have basically been left out in the cold. Pappa Mollo who is acting on behalf of the employees is willing to speak to Carte Blanche And they are trying to see if they can bring charges of fraud against the government with Regards to the fact that their UIF contributions had been deducted from the salaries they Received, as well as pensions and Medical Aid. Is government going to let these loyal Employees fend for themselves?

With the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) keeping their distance and the acting CEO deferring to the Business Rescue Practitioners (BRP), workers have been left holding the can. Business Rescue has revealed the shocking shortcuts taken in the past... UIF not paid, employees' medical aid not uptodate. The COVID19 pandemic was not the cause of this but in the current crisis the SA Express employees have the worst of all head-starts on the rest of South Africa - out of work, money running out, bills unpaid, food running out and no support from the state, banks or erstwhile employers. From the employees' perspective, nobody cares, not the DPE nor the BRPs. There is no money, so can the government come to the rescue of these loyal employees?

title: The Kiffness V SAMRO
oneLiner: A musician takes on SAMRO over a lack of music royalty payouts and wins.
summary:
When he queried this SAMRO said it was “human error”. But when he spoke to other musicians they said ‘doesn’t he know who David Alexander Scott is?’ To his surprise David Alexander (with an N) is strangely a SAMRO board member as well as the founder of Sheer Publishing?!? SAMRO said it was an error, and that David Alexader was an unknown American?!? Scott decided to investigate all his invoices from SAMRO and discovered numerous “human errors” – for example: He had a song that SAMRO said had been paid 14 times, but when he checked on radio monitor (which is very accurate) it was actually played 1300 times. Depending on which station that is, it can be a lot… in that per play is between R60-R400 – and even the amounts were secret and unknown in the industry. SAMRO said it was a “portal error” and that he would be paid for his correct number of radio plays. And when he was paid… it ended up going to “Alexader” again – which they again attributed to “Human error” *we don’t have proof it’s THE David AlexaNder but really? He has all the proof to show that it’s fishy…It’s the same name they constantly keep paying… so it’s worth a question… This is just one example, but he said that it’s a problem rife in the industry. In March this year he wrote open letters to SAMPRA’s CEO Pfanani Lishiva and even woolworths for not paying what was owed to the artists registered with them… (Woolworths haven't broken any rules. They've just opted to use a royalty free service, which they're entitled to do.) These matters were addressed (The SABC are said to be drafting a payment plan with SAMPRA because they received their R2.1 billion government bailout)…and some payments are now forthcoming not just to Scott but other musicians as well… he then created video’s https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=woDGWooQWHY&feature=youtu.be&t=133 and wrote articles

Musician David Scott has a quest: to hold the Royalty music industry to account. He’s quite a character – funny and quirky – our audience would appreciate him - and it’s unique and educational for musicians AND the audience. He has lots of proof and has been quite vocal about it – please see attachments. This Sunday on Carte Blanche: While the Covid-19 out break has caused many freelancers and creatives to lose work (performances), Musician David Scott aka The Kiffness has found an unusual strategy to keep himself afloat… we follow his investigation into royalty pay-outs in South Africa’s secretive music industry. MEET Local musician and social media personality David Scott aka The Kiffness …recently known for his humour surrounding the Corona Virus: https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/236277944217161/, https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/1291362381252238/, https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/203506354047381/ But what he isn’t known well for is his massive battle with the music royalty industry. Towards the end of last year Scott went viral for his stringent stance on non-payment of royalties. He came out swinging, calling out 5FM and other radio stations for playing his music but NOT paying him for its use. He basically told them they could no longer play his music as a protest for not being paid (please see vocal tweets and pictures of him protesting) – The industry that are very dependent on radio play/airtime and for positioning on charts like 5fm’s top 40 began to take note – and as his investigations deepened he realized even some the countries biggest artists didn’t understand or know how royalty payments work: mostly because the industry like it that way and they are very secretive. Scott learned about the fact that the SABC hadn’t paid roughly R100 million to SAMPRA https://www.sampra.org.za/ (SA music performance rights association) for radio plays to its roughly 20,000 registered musicians. And secondly, and more importantly, when he went into his account on SAMRO (SA MUSIC rights organization – which requires proof of radio play to register – once off registration). Scott realized he was not being paying out the correct amounts, or even at all for his performances or needletime (which is another terms for radio plays). Even more disturbing was the fact that someone else –an “David Alexader” (spelt without the N) was being paid his royalties.

title: COVID: The Standoff - Virus vs Townships
oneLiner: Accused of not taking the Covid-19 pandemic seriously, residents in townships and informal settlements say they are doing the best they can with the little they have.
summary:
The challenges in informal settlements are well-known but organisations and individuals are making a difference despite huge and valid concerns about population density. We focus on efforts to contain the spread in Alexandra seeing as it is the most densely populated township in Johannesburg and has most recently confirmed its first case. The organisations we speak to seek to address the two biggest concerns where the virus is concerned in townships – washing hands and people having enough food to minimise the need to go out and potentially expose themselves and others to the virus. Our focus takes a national approach as we use social media videos from other provinces including the Eastern Cape and an interview with Social Juctice Coalition to give an overview of the sanitation challenges associated with densely populated communities across the country. For the KZN perspective, we have a freelance producer and cameraman who is familiar with townships around the Durban area and will be able to take us into an informal settlement home of a family living a small shack and interview them about their water and sanitation challenges as well as the difficulty in maintaining social distancing. They will also tell us if KZN government interventions have filtered to them and if they have been able to access social welfare assistance. We will use a graphic to separate the stories from each province so that they do not pile on top of each other.

Following the first confirmed case of Covid-19 in Alexandra, we speak to residents and organisations who say they are putting up a good fight but might lose due to population density in the area. We spend a day with Linda Twala, a beloved businessman and philanthropist in Alexandra who is known for being hands-on in his community outreach programs. We go from his charity storeroom where food parcels are prepared for distribution among the needy and elderly in Alexandra, and we see him making deliveries and interact with beneficiaries. We also get to interview the beneficiaries about what they are doing to protect themselves from the virus.

title: Lock-down at Two Oceans Aquarium
oneLiner: With the help of some fancy cameras we walk with the penguins; swim with the sharks and feed the baby turtles during lock-down at the Two Oceans Aquarium.
summary:
Since the 20th of March The Two Oceans Aquarium in Cape Town have been on complete lock-down. There are two teams doing alternating day and night shifts. Their top priority? The safety and wellbeing of the more than 10 703 animals in their care. Some of the animals have been at the aquarium since the opening 30 years ago. Chuck, Farrady and Dorris are African Penguins. They came in as rescues but with the help of dedicated hands, they have settled in well, unlike their cousins along the south-western coast of Africa who have been sliding towards extinction due to overfishing. Lock-down means there is more time for the penguins to explore and see what the rest of the animals are up to. This morning Jasmin is heading for the shark tank. It is feeding time. For some of us, self-isolation at home means spending more time with our cats. At the aquarium, it means spending more time with our catsharks! Aquarist, Leigh de Necker takes a hands-on approach. She is making sure that the catsharks and shysharks in her care each get their daily meals. Many animals in the aquarium will only stay for a while. Sharks are released into the ocean after 5 years. The adult turtles that came in as rescues are nursed back to health, tagged to monitor their movements and then set free to roam the oceans across the world, like Joshi who has swam all the way to Australia on her travels. This time of the year is a dangerous time for little hatchling turtles as they are picked up in strong currents and end up on the beaches. The aquarium gives them a fighting chance and when they are strong again they are released back into the wild to fend for themselves.

More than 500 000 people visit The Two Oceans Aquarium in Cape Town every year. For the first time since opening its doors in 1995, urgent measures have called for a complete lock-down of the aquarium in an effort to prevent the spread of the Covid-19 virus from visitors to the staff. A small team of dedicated staff is on duty, taking shifts to make sure that the thousands of animals in their care are fed and healthy.

title: 3D Print Farm

summary:
Then yesterday 27 March the first Corona death was announced and this spurred the group into more action - they got a hold of netcare911 whose ambulance drivers were looking to partner with 3d printers, https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1APqsTqUWrfr1fiIGOFxhZdtYe_sIsXPG?fbclid=IwAR3E0HiqRHmk8wpz9fW8Y_gRjdCgH3g2YKocpMSKZYOm0MGKWONyTU6MP7A (offical netcare letter) But now emergency services - Joburg CBD emergency services - collected from marius, doctor in khalafong (50 units) and department of health (5 in midrand), netcare911 (kevin) are all asking for the masks! So we have a few nice case studies - like a doctor in a government hospital etc. there are various different types of face shields and masks - I have filmed some of them and have seen them being printed. I am in touch with numerous people about getting information. And as they had already mobilized and were already clued up with the approved international designs -the department of health are testing right now. The 3D PRINT FARM already have made 1000s of shields and face masks. And whose paying for this? It's for FREE - the 3D printing community had one goal, if they all help out and share the cost (which is cheap a couple of rands worth of product per print) they were all happy to come together to chip in. There are lots of very nice angles in this. The hospital are happy to speak, the 3d printing community have been filming their efforts for me... and collecting the products using ambulances.

It started two weeks ago when Bernhard Vogt of AMS 3d printers thought if Italian and American doctors can do it, why can't we. Together with other 3d printing companies, and even clients who had bought 1 or two printers he created a whatsapp group which I've been a part of from the beginning. The group called "3d print farm" - began to mobilize anyone from the 3d printing community who wanted to begin practicing through trial and error designs already made available from other countries who were already in the midst of thousands of corona virus infected patients. From watching youtube videos: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ItpExBEieY&feature=youtu.be and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pP7z3iw76GA - the trial and error of printing these designs began. Please see pics i've uploaded to this link: https://drive.google.com/open?id=1-DH3iowLJEmAOqdf8KGCJPgQXE1zZ1je https://cults3d.com/en/3d-model/tool/simplae-face-shield-frame-rsa https://www.thingiverse.com/thing:4225667 From fask masks, protective gear and even ventilator components... the group tried everything out there and were in constant communication. They rallied each other, and shared their successes and failures, taking photo's of settings and examples that worked... tirelessly for the past week, then they had the designs ready, but no where to put them?

title: Flake and Chips- Aussies take a bite out of our sharks
oneLiner: “Flake and Chips- Aussies take a bite out of our sharks” Sharks are protected in Australia so they importing ours for what they call “flake and chips
summary: Demersal long liners are catching sharks, mostly Bronze and Copper sharks but also hammer heads which are protected and exporting them to Australia and Shark Fin mainly to Japan. In 2018 SA exported 113 tons of shark fin to Asia and 56 tons of shark meat. Shark fin is dried before export so you can imagine how many more sharks are being killed. The DEA is not issuing quotas on the number of sharks that fishermen can catch, and despite their own fisheries scientist warning them of the huge drop in numbers the long liners are stripping our waters of shark. 27 of the 30 sharks tagged in PE were caught by a single demersal long line vessel. They have fished out the sharks around PE so have moved to just outside De Hoop Marine protected area. With the demise of the Great Whites, not only due to the Orcas but the demise of the smaller sharks the shark diving tour operators in Gansbaai have paid nearly R1 million rand to local fishermen not catch Bronze/Copper sharks off Gansbaai “watching” zone so they can keep the shark cage diving afloat. But in the last few months this ”deal” has broken down and more and more boats are coming in from Cape Town and catching sharks right in front of tourists. 40 Bronze Whalers were taken out two weeks ago. a month ago fishermen came right up to a shark cage diving boat and caught 4 bronze whaler sharks. A video of 40 smooth-hound sharks and about 12 dozen soupfin sharks and 6 hammerheads was taken just off De Hoop. Sharks reproduce slowly and the copper and hammer heads are listed as endangered species. Over 1 Million sharks are killed annually and not only is this destroying the oceans ecology it’s destroying a local tourist industry, in 2016 we had 85 000 shark cage diving tourist its dropped to below 50 000 now- they say a live shark supports five jobs for every 1 job a dead shark, it’s an industry that employs over 300 local people.

It is all good and well to declare Coronavirus a National Disaster and order business and people to stay at home and practice social distancing, but how is this going to affect small businesses and self employed people, who in South Africa are a major sector working class?

title: Diamond Scammer: Forever Diamonds and Gold
oneLiner: What do the Sicilian Mafia, angry investors and illicit diamonds have in common? They're all connected to South African Louis Liebenberg, the man investors say has cheated them out of millions .
summary:
We have been approached by several investors, one of them who sank R3.2 million into Liebenberg's promised deals and has never seen a scent back, who all say Louis is living the high life in a luxury house in an estate in Bronkhorstpruit off their money. He is constantly bringing in new investors, but we have found none who have actually received any of the promised returns or their initial money back. When they start pressuring Louis for their money, he scares them off in three ways: 1. He threatens that if people approach the media, the company will collapse as Wealth4U did and he will liquidate and no one will see any money, 2: he says he is dealing illegally in diamonds and they are therefore implicated, 3: he comes up with threatening stories about the underworld, gangsters he knows, hits put out on peoples lives etc. We have documentary proof of all of the above via facebook posts, whatsapp messages, etc. From videos that Liebenberg himself makes as marketing material, it is clear that he makes the deals sound legit, he says its done under legal certificates etc, SO INVESTORS ARE NOT INITIALLY AWARE THAT HIS DEALINGS ARE ILLEGAL.

Louis Petrus Liebenberg is a self proclaimed diamond king - the son of a pastor who grew up on the diamonds fields of the west coast in Port Nolloth, Liebenberg claims he is a specialist in the field and currently offers investors in his business Forever Gold and Diamonds returns of between 50% to 100% within 14, 21 or 30 days, supposedly possible by buying small packages of uncut diamonds. The only problem is, very few of the investors ever seem to have received any of the promised returns on their investments. What's worse, they've never even seen their initial capital back either. But this is not the first time Louis has gotten away with taking in millions for investments and failing to return on his promises. In 2005, Liebenberg opened Wealth4U mining and Exploration, raking in at least R130 million in investments from 1700 shareholders. But by 2009 the company was liquidated, and the only assets worth anything amounted to a poorly R7 million - investors lost everything.

title: Bloem Zoo Crisis
oneLiner: Animals at the Bloemfontein zoo left to die as the zoo's doors are closed.
summary:
The Manguang Municipality of Bloemfontein has been adamant that the city's zoo delivers a positive contribution to the community. In the beginning of 2019 they claimed to have adequate capacity in terms of people and funding to keep the zoo running without hiccups - even though there had been public outcries about the state of the animals in the past. By the end of 2019, the municipality admitted that they do not have the necessary resources to keep the facility running and DESTEA stepped in. The zoo was closed down, and the animals were to be relocated to other state facilities. But this never happened and by March 2020 animals were dying. At the moment animals are being moved to other facilities by DESTEA, but there is concern that because it is now an emergency, animals are sent to all kinds of facilities, even private farms where hunting is allowed. So the question is, will these state assets simply be discarded? There are also questions around the SPCA's conduct. On 7 Feb 2020 they issued a statement saying that the animals are fine.. Two weeks later animals are dying, buffalo are so sick that they're losing their hair, and many anilas are limping and listless. They were supposed to check regularly. What happened?

In Feb/March 2019 Carte Blanche looked at the state of zoos around the country and the Bloemfontein Zoo was highlighted as an old fashioned zoo that provides very little educational value and poses a threat to the welfare of the animals. We saw barren, dirty enclosures where animals have very little stimulation and are surrounded by their own waste. Ponds and pools were dirty. The zoo was generally unkept. Then on 17 December 2019 the SPCA together with Free State Department: Economic, Small Business Development, Tourism and Environmental Affairs (DESTEA) closed the zoo down. The conditions had deteriorated to such an extent that the Manguang Municipality was ordered to move the animals and shut down the facility. The SPCA vowed to do regular inspections to check on the welfare of the animals. But by end Feb 2020 animals were dying from hunger and SPCA inspectors were greeted by a horrific scene.

title: Africa Clockwise
oneLiner: We follow the Sampson family who circumvented Africa for 6 years in a big green truck using only vegetable oil.
summary:
Mark Sampson is a South African comedian/climate change activist. In 2013 he, his wife Sam and their two young children, Ruby and Zola set out in the Big Green Truck, a 41 year old Mercedes 911 converted to run on vegetable oil, to make the first carbon neutral circumnavigation of the African continent. They expected the entire journey to take two years and finish before the kids hit high-school. In 2017 they had just finished driving up the West coast, 23000km through 20 countries, breaking down 15 times. This year they finished the journey, six and a half years, 47000km and 38 countries later. They broke down 27 times, got delayed 14 months behind closed borders in Liberia during the Ebola pandemic, and sometimes waited months to gather enough waste oil donations from hotels to fill up with fuel (this was how they ran the truck, showcasing an eco-friendly way of disposing of waste oil). The idea of the trip was to show people (including their kids) how to live without thousands of possessions, and to ring an alarm bell about climate change. They say “In 2013 we thought we were going to be teaching our kids how to cope with extremes of weather and less water so they could pass resilience lessons on to their kids – we didn’t think they would be dealing with climate emergency in their lifetimes.”

A Cape Town family became the first people to cross Africa without petrol or diesel; a journey of over 47 000km crossing 29 African countries in a 1978 Mercedes using only vegetable oil.

title: Male Infertility: There is always hope

Also Carte Blanche has never done a program on male infertility. Also there remains huge stigma surrounding male infertility. Stories we present on Carte Blanche can help reduce the stigma. The context is in 40% of presenting couples at fertility clinics, the issues lie with the men. What are the common causes? 50% of these conditions can be reversed, according to Dr Moata. But he adds 80 to 90 per cent of all male fertility cases can be treated with modern medicine such as our one case study will tell us - Noleen Root's husband Antonie underwent 2 years of specialised hormonal treatment with Prof Kruger because he had zero sperm. The couple conceived twins. The story can be set against SA's and Africa's first fertility show.

When unable to conceive, many couples present themselves at fertility clinics for assessment and treatment. in 40 % of the cases, male infertility is the cause. This is not widely known. Stigma often results in males not presenting themselves for assessment. Male Infertility is a treatable condition. We speak to couples where the men have been infertile and hear how they coped with the stigma, the treatment they had, and the coupe's joy in conceiving. We also hear how some men fall out of male infertility treatment, because of the ongoing stigma, and the length it takes ...and marriages collapse.

title: Child substance abuse
oneLiner: The epidemic of substance abuse is spreading to children as young as primary school age...and rehab services are all but completely absent.
summary:
Meghan and Kevin Botes started trying to help the children of Bosmont when they moved to the area in 2014. They noticed a group of children begging for food and money. The children were dirty, ill-fed and not attending school. A growing number of the kids were also addicted to glue. It soon became clear that most of them lived in one block of flats, where their parents were unemployed and addicts themselves. Legally, children must be removed from situations in which they are harmed or neglected, but unless a foster facility is willing to take them, the court can't remove them from their parents' care. Because no foster homes deal with child addiction, they've been left in this situation. Meghan has met with the DSD, who indicate they've been familiar with these children since 2015. She has also tried to get them into rehab but can't find anywhere that will offer it to kids younger than 12. She got one or two older boys into an outpatient programme but it was designed for adolescents and adults, and they soon refused to attend. One home offered to take the children if they were first detoxed. Having read that glue detox takes around 2 weeks, Meghan raised money to take the children on a two-week camp with their parents' permission. It was a success: the kids were clean for a month, and one girl is still clean over a year later. But when Christmas came most of them relapsed. When Meghan approached DSD for help funding a second camp, she was told she's not a registered NPO and shouldn't run camps. There's also been minimal effort to ensure the kids don't return to the same dysfunctional home environment. The situation is deadlocked. Meghan is trying to register an NPO to provide rehab, and tries to be a constant presence in the kids' lives by spending Tuesday evenings providing food and a short Bible/prayer session. Meanwhile, nothing is fundamentally changing for the children.

A group of children in Joburg's poor western suburbs paints a picture of socio-economic deprivation that, one can only imagine, is all too common in South Africa. These children, whose ages range from around 14 to 6 and even younger, have been a cause for concern for former resident Meghan Botes for over two years. But despite all her efforts to find suitable rehabilitation treatment for the children and social services support for them at home, she is coming up against brick walls in every direction. It seems there simply are no services available for children under the age of 12, which means these kids are simply falling through the gaps in the system. UPDATE: One of the children was hit by a car last week while buying glue, and died. This and the pandemic have brought the situation into new sharp relief.

title: Meerkat Investigation
oneLiner: How easy is it to get your hands on a meerkat for a pet? And would you really want one?
summary:
Solid Earth is a meerkat rehab centre in Victoria West in the Karoo and is run by Alma-Celeste Jeppe. She takes in abandoned, rescued, and confiscated meerkats and tries to rewild them. She works closely with Lucas Lookout, a rehab centre in Krugersdorp where meerkats that cannot be re-released into he wild are kept. Lucas Lookout currently has 53 meerkats, and there are 34 at Solid Earth.

There are many people in South Africa illegally breeding and selling meerkats for the pet market. Films like The Lion King and others have romanticised meerkats and more and more people want them as pets, not knowing what they are in for. The truth is meerkats are sociable mongooses. They bond fiercely with their families and if you keep one in your home, you automatically become one of the tribe. The meerkat will bond with you, protect you and viscously attack anyone who comes near you - because that's what meerkats do. It will need to be with you 24/7, urinate on you to claim you as part of his/her tribe, and also urinate on everything in your house as being part of his territory. Alpha females will not tolerate anyone else in the family getting pregnant, and they will not tolerate anyone else mating/bonding with you.

title: BBC Seven Worlds One Planet
oneLiner: We go behind the scenes on an iconic wildlife series, and explore how David Attenborough and the BBC are using a celebration of natural wonder to inspire climate action
summary:
The Seven Worlds One Planet series divides the world into seven continents, with each 50 minute-long episode exploring the wonders great and small of each continent. We will focus on the ever more urgent question of climate change and human destruction of the natural world. We will ask what the BBC's production teams experienced and uncovered in terms of the challenges species are facing around the world, and the ways they are tackling those challenges. We will also go behind the scenes through the BBC's 'making of' clips, which show the extremes that film-makers face to bring these incredible stories to life for viewers. Some incredible ‘film firsts’ were achieved in making this series, including the largest aggregation of whales ever filmed, wolves hunting in the mountains of Italy, and multiple animal interactions captured in unprecedented detail thanks to the development of smaller, quieter drones. We will interview series Executive Producer Jonny Keeling about the BBC's newly strengthened stance on climate change. We will hopefully also interview a crew member or producer (possibly via Skype/sent from location) about the experience of shooting such an ambitious and groundbreaking project. We will also select one or two success stories the series tells about species brought back from the brink: whales almost hunted out, or pumas in Patagonia which are slowly recovering now that their habitat has been protected. We will hopefully interview one of the scientists involved in one of these projects, who can tell us the story of how to save a species. The gist of the Seven Worlds One Planet series and our story will be a celebration of our natural wonders alongside an awareness of how delicate these systems are and how vital it is to preserve them.

The BBC's latest natural history series launches in South Africa on 29 March 2020. Bringing the wonders of the natural world to our living rooms since the 1950s, the BBC's Natural History Unit has always been at the forefront of technological innovation and narrative drama in scientific storytelling. But both the production house and its iconic presenter, Sir David Attenborough, have long shied away from taking a stance on climate change and the destruction human beings are wreaking on the planet. Until now. This series is bigger and bolder than ever before, featuring animal behaviours never before captured on camera with brand new technology - but along with the marvels comes a message: we need to act now, or lose all this forever. We go behind the scenes on the making of a masterpiece.

title: Renal Roulette
oneLiner: Is the public health care rationing, of South Africans in dire need of dialysis, a death sentence for patients with chronic kidney disease?
summary:
The South African Health care system is bleeding dry when it comes to funding across the board, and never more so when it comes to patients who suffer from chronic kidney disease. For the most part the State is unable to provide adequate care for anyone needing dialysis treatment unless they are eligible for a kidney transplant, and even if they qualify, they may never get there and die in the process of waiting. The reasons for this are that each province has limited slots for dialysis, for example at Charlotte Maxeke, there are only 150 slots for Dialysis and the waiting list is over a thousand, but there may only be 40 kidneys available for transplant at any time.

Unlike in the private medical sector where dialysis is mostly available for patients suffering from chronic kidney disease, within the public sector the only way to get dialysis treatment is if you are eligible for a kidney transplant. If you are not eligible for a kidney transplant you will never get on the State dialysis programme. Many people who may not be eligible for transplant can live long and productive lives on dialysis. If these people do not receive dialysis the probability of them dying soon is high. But for patients who are eligible for transplant and are on the state’s list for dialysis, they may never get to the point of transplant or dialysis because the waiting list is too long, and they too may die soon. The reason for this is there are not enough organ donors to help the queues move faster. Moreover, even if you have a willing compatible donor you cannot skip the queue in terms of receiving much needed dialysis. So the probability that you may die soon is also high. People in need of dialysis but not necessarily a kidney transplant would however require this treatment for the rest of their lives, and at the cost of R 200 000 per patient per year, is it just too much of an ask of the already stretched public healthcare funds.

title: Forensic Nursing Debacle
oneLiner: A profession in peril” with a looming crisis in the nursing fraternity may leave specialised Forensic Nursing services in endless limbo.
summary:
The South African Nursing Council is responsible for regulating all nursing qualifications, institutions and overall policy making within the nursing sector. The council however has been lagging behind in ensuring that Forensic nurses are recognised as a specialised postgraduate course and profession. This forensic nursing postgraduate qualification was largely provided by the University of Free State, between 2011 and 2017. The university made claims to only 200 out of approximately 400 graduates of their F-Nursing program. This one year course was done outside of the SANC awarding the accreditation to the University of Freestate which has caused much warranted frustrations to the graduates of forensic nurses, some of which have more than eight to ten years working in hospitals and Thuthuzela Care Centres, around county without being accredited. With the acknowledgement of the much needed service Forensic Nurses provided, to sexual assault victims. Cyril Ramaphosa’s GBV emergency plan, stated that by March 2020, there should be a Forensic Nurse in each hospital nationally. However, the University of free State having a majority of students coming from their school, created a conundrum, which poses the question Firstly will the Council accredit the Forensic Nursing discipline in time to meet the March 2020 deadline? Secondly since there has been an phasing out of old the old curriculum, and postgraduate degrees, what does it mean for the 400 plus FNurses, who graduated under an uncredited course provided by the Free State university. Finally: What does the Regulatory body and the Minister of Health say about the All nursing postgraduate specialisation courses not being offered in 2020, and the looming gap of nursing within the public sector.

There is a looming crisis within the nursing fraternity. The phasing out of the old legacy nursing programs is a cause for great concern, for specialised nursing programs. All this is happening while the South African Nursing Council, lags behind in accrediting forensic nursing before the presidential deadline, to have one nurse in each hospital by March 2020. This story will demonstrate the ironic systematic failure between the nursing council and Department of Health and the failures to implement presidential mandate to address GBV in South Africa. Even though we have Forensic Nurses in South Africa. The South African Nursing Council still have not accredited this specialised nursings program that enables victims of Sexual assault and other crimes come closer to finding justice.
