title: Stellenbosch under siege?
summary:
Stellenbosch - the iconic university town with its oak-lined streets, cafes, boutiques and art galleries makes it a major tourist destination in the Western Cape. It’s surrounded by prestigious wine farms and home to some of the wealthiest people in the country, but on the outskirts are some of the poorest of the poor, in suburbs like Kayamandi and Cloetesville. The residents of Stellenbosch feel they are under siege, it has the 11th highest crime rate in the country, despite the relatively small population of 180 000 and over seven different security companies operating in town. It’s a story about how one small town, a microcosm of South Africa, is fighting back with private citizens challenging local municipalities to step up and protect them.

James Hayes is a successful businessman living in Stellenbosch. He grew up there, studied at the university and sees it as his home, but when he moved back there a few years ago he was horrified by the high level of crime and the municipalities apathetic approach towards protecting its residents. He could have sat back like most of us and just paid his subscriptions and attended the local ratepayers meetings. But as a former police reservist he is well versed with the law and how criminals operate. He recognizes the local police are over stretched and security companies have guards that are under paid and poorly trained. Angered by how tourists were being targeted by ATM gangs and the lack of effective policing James took it upon himself to drive them out of town by chasing them and driving into them. He was also angry by the lack of action against the gangs preying on hikers and students in the green belt so he put up a drone, tracked them down, and chased them with the help of local security company and caught 6 or the 7 heavily armed gang. James dedication and unconventional methods ruffle feathers. Nobody likes to be challenged by a private individual who is putting his body on the line to stop crime. He works closely with all the security networks and police and provides them with information from his well established network of informers. He is so disruptive to the gangs trade that they are trying to buy them off, or kill him.

title: Sextortion
oneLiner: Often it's young vulnerable girls that are taken advantage of in the online space, but Sextortion, an online catfishing crime is on the rise in South Africa and the victims are of all ages and sexes.
summary:
In South Africa incidents of Sextortion have been on the rise from 2016 and to date, more and more individuals are falling for it. It used to be that the primary targets and victims for such online attacks are young vulnerable females, but this has since escalated to older victims being blackmailed for cash. With online dating sites such as Tinder, Zoosk and Grinder more adults are targets of the scams. Unscrupulous individuals are lurking on the Internet ready to pounce on unsuspecting victims. Your computer webcam, cellphone and online chats can be hacked by an unknown stranger who will be able to access all intimate information about you. The unknown individual will then invite you to a social media platform, be it Watsapp, Facebook, etc. They would then proceed to blackmail you for money or to perform sexually explicit activities such as sending nude pictures, videos or such. They will then threaten you with publicizing your intimate information on the Internet or alerting your loved ones, church congregations and colleagues of all the information they have.

It’s the new form of sexual harassment. Sextortion refers to a form of blackmail in which sexual information or images are used to extort sexual favors and money from the victim. Social media and text messages are often the source of the sexual material and the threatened means, used to share it with others.

title: Transorbital surgery - a game changer
summary:
Her story starts 4 years ago, when she attended a medical conference and she saw a leading USA doctor perform transorbital procedures on a gadiva. But the doctor only spoke about the possibilities of this type of surgery and minor procedures that could be done. The Prof came back and shared her excitement with top SA neurosurgeon Prof Allan Taylor, who was initially sceptical and onthamologist Dr Hamzah Mustak. They trio spend 100's of hours working on gadivas and the operations began - not only did the team save patients from hectic surgery (cutting half the skull away) but in most instances patient's eye sight was saved. Recovery time - 3 days only. She also designed and developed, working in tandem with a top German instrument maker) a set of specialised instruments which have also just been introduced. She has also written a book with visuals for surgeons to learn the procedures.

43 year old Prof Darlene Lubbe is now recognised as the leading world expert in transorbital surgery. And over the last three years Groot Schuur hospital has done more of these operations than anywhere else in the world. it was standing room only last week when Prof Lubbe addressed the world's leading neurosurgeons in Europe.. She is the first ever to do this operation on a sphenoid wing meningioma, a tumour situated several centremers behind the eye and which leads to blindness.. Surgoens have to cut away the skull, and shift the brain to get to the tumour. This often puts pressure on the optic nerve leading to blindness. 1000's of SA's have this condition but doctors are loathe to cut away some of the skull ,. These cranitomies and the sugery that follows often lead to severe complications. So these ops are not performed which means that patients go blind. . Also recuperation is very very long. Now Dr Lubbe goes in through 8 pathways around the eyes and two in the nose.

title: Diabetes Warriors (#WeAreNotWaiting)
oneLiner: Citizen scientists hack their way to cutting edge diabetes treatment
summary:
Type 1 Diabetes is an auto-immune disease. At worst, it causes coma and death - at best, it means a lifetime of blood sugar monitoring, insulin injections and meal planning. It's increasingly diagnosed in children under 5, who are too young to check their own blood sugar levels or respond to dangerous lows or highs. This is a problem for parents, who wake up constantly every night to check levels, then send the child to school where they can't keep an eye on them. Medical technology helps: insulin pumps which constantly inject pre-programmed amounts of insulin into the bloodstream, and continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) which track blood sugar every five minutes, but is still lacking. The first CGMs sent data to a receiver that had to stay within range of the monitor, so when a child was at school, their data was unavailable to anyone not nearby. A growing band of tech-savvy parents has spent years working on their own solutions. John Costik created Nightscout, hacking his son's CGM to transmit its data to the cloud where he could access it from anywhere. And adult T1D Dana Lewis created the ultimate diabetes tech: she hacked her insulin pump, creating an algorithm that would respond on its own to unexpected or predicted highs and lows, adjusting the insulin delivery without Dana having to intervene. This is called closing the loop. These innovators have made all their programming and design available open-source online, so people around the world are using it. In South Africa, Jaco Cronje installed and improved Nightscout for himself, and has helped less tech-savvy people with theirs. 18 year-old Chloe Royston closed the loop on her own pump, which she says is allowing her to study overseas this year, away from her parents' watchful eyes. And finally tech companies are responding, bringing out CGMs that can be linked to an app, and last year, the first ever FDA-approved closed-loop artificial pancreas.

They call themselves Loopers. They go by the hashtag #WeAreNotWaiting. They're an international community joined by social media and open-source innovation, and they're creating the medical solutions they are tired of waiting for big tech companies to provide.

title: Stuck in the East
oneLiner: Having accepted job offers to teach English in China, some 50 South African youths are now the subject of a criminal investigation for working without permits, and stuck in the East
summary: Some 50 South African youngsters have all been scammed by a company called SANDA Youth International. This Chinese based company has been recruiting South Africans to teach English in China. The youths were promised that SANDA Youth International would sort out all their visa and work permit requirements for an upfront fee of R8000 and a cut of the salaries they would earn in China. Most of them flew to China on student visas, and handed over their passports to SANDA personnel on arrival, ostensibly so that there work permits could be obtained. But according to the youths, in the last week SANDA director and Chinese national Owen Wang was arrested. They have been interrogated by Chinese customs officials and told they were working illegally in China. Their passports have been confiscated. And they are now stuck in China at a university in Chan Chun province. They have been told not to speak to their parents about the investigation. They have also been told that they are welcome to stay on and study at the university at their cost. The parents have contacted the SA embassy in China as well as DIRCO but have been told, on email, that there is very little that can be done for their children.

title: Crisis in the Mediterranean - Journeyman Special
oneLiner: death and despair on the frontline of the Mediterranean refugee crisis
summary: As fewer NGOs aid refugees fleeing across the Mediterranean, and more power is given to the morally dubious Libyan coastguard, volunteer rescuers attempting to save lives face greater challenges than ever. As NGO intervention dwindles, so the number of bodies found drowned at sea has increased. Haidi Sadik is the Cultural Mediator for the volunteer organisation Sea-Watch, who scour the seas daily for survivors fleeing Libya. She observes that, "Some people are more traumatised than others, and some people are more clearly abused than others, but it's quite clear that anyone who comes through Libya has been through hell'. Now, Sea-Watch’s humanitarian mission is being challenged by the heavily subsidised Libyan coastguard, which seeks to transport escaped refugees back to Libya. Since they may face torture or slavery upon their return, for associate professor at Queen Mary's University Violetta Moreno-Lax, "co-operation with the Libyan coastguard is against HR law". Sea-Watch believes that the Libyan coastguard may even be lying to them, mis-communicating the coordinates of refugee boats, in order to carry out their mission. Putting such difficulties at sea aside, Sea-Watch's Head of Mission Julian Koberer maintains that, "other solutions need to be found. Political solutions. No one should get on boats."

title: Future Mobility
oneLiner: Self-driving cars will hit our shores soon -- is South Africa prepared for this and other innovations in mobility?
summary:
Though the idea of cars driving themselves is alarming to many, few realise that a car with cruise control or lane assist is already the first steps in autonomous driving. Though these vehicles are undoubtedly coming, it will be a long time before fully autonomous vehicles can operate on public roads in SA. Laws and infrastructure must be in place first. The Mobility Centre for Africa is an NPO that aims to bring all roleplayers together in order to prepare South Africa for innovations in mobility. Later this year, the Mobility Centre for Africa will start testing the first self-driving vehicle in South Africa (an electric shuttle by French manufacturer Navya) in various controlled areas such as the CSIR campus in Pretoria or the Durban beachfront promenade. It will gather data in order to help write regulations and prepare infrastructure for these vehicles. At the moment, there are no regulations that determine the nature and use of autonomous vehicles in SA. These vehicles use cameras, sensors and lasers to read its environment and it builds up memory of routes as it drives. It also maintains a satellite connection for navigation. It brings other unexpected complications such as the need to store and secure massive volumes of data. An autonomous vehicle generates up to 4 TB of data per day as it scans and logs its surroundings. In the long term we would require smart infrastructure, like sensors in road signs, lamp posts and lines on the road to ensure autonomous vehicles can read the surroundings. The biggest challenges to so-called e-mobility in SA are infrastructure, cost, cyber security and the impact on job security -- I will examine each of these.

How will a self-driving vehicle react on a South African road with its ample potholes, pedestrians and unpredictable minibus taxis? Who will be responsible in the case of an accident -- the owner or the manufacturer of the vehicle? The future in mobility is coming -- we can't hide from it and if we don't handle it correctly, there will be chaos. This is why mobility industry roleplayers are engaging with government and regulators to ensure that South African is ready for the future. The future where cars drive themselves and can even check your calendar to determine where to go is not as far away as we may think. The first fully autonomous vehicle will enter the country later this year, but to be used on a small scale only in order to gather data to prepare regulations for the vehicles. The idea of self-driving cars alarm many people, especially after a self-driving car recently hit and killed a pedestrian in the USA. I will examine what these autonomous vehicles look like, how they work and what is required in terms of regulations and infrastructure for them to operate in South Africa. I will also touch on innovations in electric vehicles. These vehicles may soon be able to travel 400 km or more before needing to recharge. It's also set to become more accessible to the general public.

title: Rubber Stamp Duke
oneLiner: Meet Bruce Murray: 12th Duke of Atholl: businessman, head of a private army, and... a South African.
summary:
This insert tells the story of Bruce Murray, the 12th Duke of Atholl. It will include a visit to the family's estate at Blair Castle in the Scottish Highlands, where his two sons, Michael and David, will take the salute on the Duke's behalf from the Blair Highlanders. This infantry regiment constitutes the only legal private army in the UK -an honour bestowed on the family by Queen Victoria. We have been granted permission to film at the castle by the estate's Trust, which includes a rare go-ahead for the use of a drone. Michael and David have also made themselves available for interviews. Further filming will be done in Louis Trichardt, where we'll film an interview with Bruce and the rest of the family. The juxtaposition of the Highlands and Limpopo should add additional texture to the piece.

Under normal circumstances, an interview with a member of the UK's landed gentry wouldn't inspire much excitement. But, Bruce Murray's story is anything but normal. As the 12th Duke of Atholl, able to raise the UK's only "private army", he has collected more titles than he can remember. He also happens to be a South African who, when not rubbing shoulders with Britain's "mink and manure" set, runs a humble rubber stamp business in Louis Trichardt.

title: Anatomy of Hope
summary: Anatomy of Hope is surgeon Jerome Groopman’s best seller on how people prevail in the face of illness and how hope can radically alter the out come. Why do some people find and sustain hope during difficult circumstances, while others do not? What can we learn from those who do and how is their example applicable to our own lives. His book Anatomy of Hope spans some thirty years of Groopman’s practice. Through encounters with many extraordinary people he sought to answer these questions. Using his background of science and the human factor Jerome explains how he distinguishes true hope from false and how this can essentially change or alter your diagnosis. Reach for a dream have been going for 30 years and decided on their 30th Birthday that they would bring out Jerome Groopman M.D precisely because his his book and it’s message is their own vision. We have been promised an exclusive interview…together with that we will weave case studies of two families whose children’s wishes and hopes have been granted by Reach for A Dream. Case Study 1 Lesedi Sekgolo is 16 years old and has been diagnosed with Ewings Sarcoma, a rare and difficult cancer that occurs around the bones. Lesedi loves to cook and her dream was to meet television personality Chef Siba. Case Study 2 Arabella van Rooyen is 6 years old and has Nephroblastoma cancer of the kidneys that typically occurs in children. Arabella’s dream was to have her own drum set.. These are not huge wishes to fulfil but what does it give to the patient when these dreams are fulfilled, what sort positivity or hope sets in that could play a part in a more positive out come for their future.

title: Winnie Mandela 2
oneLiner: A new documentary about her life has sparked heated debate about the tarnished reputation of Winnie Madikizela Mandela
summary:
The uncontested fact remains that Winnie Mandela was found guilty in a court of law for the abduction and kidnapping of Stompie Seipei, and received a 6 year sentence for the crime. On appeal that was eventually changed to two years suspended sentence. It is also a well known and uncontested fact that Mandela United FC were not choir boys, and while there is no evidence of just how much of what they did was actually under her orders, she didn't do anything to stop their reign of terror in Soweto. And that is really the crux of the story - while it is clear and quite frankly obvious that Mandela was the target of Apartheid propoganda and smear campaigns, and while she was treated inhumanly cruel by the regime, she was also a flawed character who was at least, according to the law, partly responsible for the death of Stompie.

The documentary, which has won an international award, has many believing that Madikizela-Mandela was completely innocent of the crimes she's long been under suspicion of committing. But it was a one sided story, told by a filmmaker and as was her right to do, it painted a very specific picture. Embarrassingly for the ANC, it has emerged that they were just as complicit in tarnishing Mandela's name.

title: Transnet Pensioners die of poverty as they wait for their day in court
summary:
In 2013 the Pensioners launched the largest class action in the country but it still hasn’t started to be argued in court as Transnet has successfully stalled the process. The case is Claim 1: Pensions to be increased as promised and pensioners to be compensated for arrears. ( Transnet challenged this and the Pensioners took it to the Constitutional Court in November 2017 and a ruling is expected any day) Claim 2: Transnet to pay the legacy debt of R17Bn plus interest. CLaim 3: Transnet to repay the R309M illegal donation plus interest to the Transport Pension Fund 20 000 pensioners have died since the start of the case. These pensioner range from train drivers, ticket collectors and firemen to top SAA pilots. The black pensioners don’t receive a pension at all- they got a lump sum pay-out. Top pensions are R24 000 a month, the lowest R1380. After deductions have been made for the medical aid some get as little as R600. 400 pensioners die a year, they fear it’s a waiting game for them all to die and the money returns to Transnet. Allegations of corruption continue, funds continue to go missing. 580 million was invested in Trillion and is yet to be paid back The fund is run by a board of 8 Trustees and a Chair- the Principle Officer. 4 of the trustees and the Principle officer are all Transnet employees 4 trustees are pensioners and Transnet Second Defined Benefit Fund pensioners and nominated by pensioners to represent them. Currently there is a 4.7 Million surplus in the fund which one Trustee Claire Fichardt is fighting to get paid out to the pensioners while they wait for the outcome of the court case. But Transnet say they need the money to fight the case. The reason there is a surplus is that so many have died and this money remains in the fund and because their pensions have only increased by 2% since 2003. Its a closed fund, Transnet makes no contribution anymore and the pensions say its their hard earned money and they are dying in poverty.

This is a fight that has been going on since 2003 and it’s a fight by the oldest and arguably weakest members of society- some 80 000 Transnet Pensioners. Many worked all their lives for the company and believed their old age was secure as the pension fund was arguably one of the strongest at the time. But it got plundered by the State, funds borrowed and not returned, bonds not repaid and since 2003 their pensions have been pegged at a 2% annual increase. They have marched, met with Parliament Portfolio committees and pleaded with their board. Nothing shifts. Today there are only 50 000 left and 14 000 are on full pension their widows some 37 000 live on 70% of the original amount.

title: Young Entrepreneur
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche: A teenager from Pretoria becomes the youngest commercial aquaponic farmers in the country and doing so with foresight and expertise.
summary:
Rikalise is a teenager with a passion for aquaponics and a drive to succeed. She started off with a home-made tank and 1000 fish at the age of 12. Today she has 88 000 Tilapia in her tanks and runs one of the four biggest aquaponic farms in South Africa at the tender age of 16. She has also invented a filtration system to clean ‘dirty’ water. This earned her a gold medal at the Eskom Science Expo for ‘own design on reuse of effluent water`. The system is called Decoupled Aquaponic System (DAPS) Through this technique she has cut her water consumption from 2 500 liters per day to 450 litres. In her greenhouse she houses 22 plant species (vegetables, herbs and sweet melons) which she sells to restaurants. She sells about 400 plants each week. What is amazing about her is that she makes enough money from her farming the she pays all her overheads herself, pay two salaries, buy fish food and electricity and still pump some money back into the business to buy more fry (baby fish). Her dad has taught her to build her own tanks, connect pipes and run the business by herself. She is an example of a young entrepreneur who have achieved in 4 years what most teenagers will only dream of.

Rikalize is a 16 year old teenager and owner of one of the largest aquaponic farms in South Africa. She does this without the help of her father. Instead the business is run from her cellphone during the week when she is at school and weekends she is hands on. She has a small team of reliable operating staff responsible for the day to day duties of growing fish and plants which she sells to restaurants and hotels in Pretoria.

title: TOXIC SNAKE PARK
oneLiner: With a (slowly) growing body of evidence linking heavy metal in the dust to disability and deformity Soweto activist Tiny Dlamini is waging a war to survival for the children of Snake Park
summary:
According to the peer reviewed REVIEW JOURNAL of AUTISM AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS, increasing evidence supports the role of industrial chemicals as contributors to the development of neurobehavioral disorders, including autism spectrum disorders, whose prevalence has progressively increased in recent years. Heavy metals, in particular, are recognized as neurodevelopmental toxins since they can be responsible of foetal damages which lead to neurological defects, developmental delays, learning disabilities and behavioral abnormalities. Most of the reviewed studies reported a relationship between exposure to metals during perinatal and early childhood periods and increased risk for autism. Moreover, the effects resulting from co-exposure to multiple metals should not be underestimated, especially in the assessment of children who live in developing countries or near heavily contaminated sites. Heavy metal contamination is one of the most severe threats for the environment and in unrehabilitated mining areas heavy metals in the environment occurs via a wide range of processes and pathways impacting on air, surface water, and soil quality. Due to the multiple sources of exposure, heavy metals represent also one of the most serious threats to human health (Arita and Costa 2009; Dufault et al. 2009; Szewczyk 2013). https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-014-0028-3 Even without the heavy concentration of poisonous mining compounds in the water, air and soil in one's immediate environment, city dwellers (all of us) are at risk of building up toxicity -- https://myersdetox.com/guide-sources-symptoms-toxic-metals/

It’s surreal to walk through the rows of well-established informal homes in Snake Park and the small farming plots of Doornkop, sandwiched between Roodepoort and Dobsonville, Soweto with Tiny Dlamini. Animated, passionate, well-spoken and well-loved in this area, Tiny's trained eye can pick out every child with cerebral palsy (CP) and every animal with spinal deformity and skin disease. The overwhelming number of suffering children and animals begs an explanation. We visit Snake Park on the day that French investigative filmmaker Martin Boudot presents findings from research that TV5 has just paid for -- a survey of the pollutants and chemicals that are found in Snake Park. Martin (who in 2016 released his investigation "Toxic Chemicals: Kids in Danger" on how our dependence of chemicals and pesticides harms children) has just spent 5 weeks in the the historic gold belt of Soweto and the West Rand to investigate the claims of deformity in animals, plants and birth defects in children. In addition to French scientists that specialise in environmental toxicity (www.kudzuscience.com) Martin collaborated with our own AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH COUNCIL to sample and record the elevated levels of toxic chemicals in human and animal hair as well as in the water and soil from Snake Park and the other nearby hotspot Lancaster Dam, in the Wonderfontein Spruit area (in the same minings rights area as Snake Park). TV5 spent over R120,000 on this research -- research that should be done routinely and should be informing epidemiological studies on a large scale in this area. When Martin presented his findings to the Snake Park community who worked with him on his study, the BENCHMARKS FOUNDATION -- a think tank on global corporate responsibility with whom Tiny has teamed up to help establish scientific ground for her concerns -- handed out wheelchairs to the CP kids of Snake Park. We filmed the disturbing picture of a community under siege by elements in their air, water and soil that they live with daily and from which there is no escape, nor for which they have any absolute explanations. Martin's study (he can explain basics in Skype itv) and David van Wyk will explain possible consequences for residents, indicated that in the water samples there was: Berillium that causes Intestinal lesions; Chromium that causes Allergic dermatitis; Nitrate -- infants below the age of six months who drink water containing nitrate in excess of the MCL could become seriously ill and, if untreated, may die. Symptoms include shortness of breath and blue-baby syndrome Copper --Short term exposure: Gastrointestinal distress; Long term exposure: Liver or kidney damage; Arsenic -- Skin damage or problems with circulatory systems, and may have increased risk of getting cancer Selenium -- Hair or fingernail loss; numbness in fingers or toes; circulatory problems Cadmium -- Kidney damage Barium -- Increase in blood pressure Mercury -- Kidney damage Thalium -- Hair loss; changes in blood; kidney, intestine, or liver problems Bishmuth -- Infants and children: Delays in physical or mental development; children could show slight deficits in attention span and learning abilities; Adults: Kidney problems; high blood pressure Uranium -- Increased risk of cancer, kidney toxicity This is also an opportunity to report back on the WHO-backed research spearheaded by he FSE and Northwest University on uranium deposits in hair that we reported on in 2016 -- the study has faced some scientific hiccups that we will highlight -- but in the end it proved that uranium does find its way from mine tailings dust, through local water courses and soil into the body (not just from inhalation by miners, as was previously shown in Native American uranium mining communities) -- and so the FSE and academics are pressing on for the WHO to promote and/or fund and/or insist on epidemiological studies from our government. With Tiny's help and that of her Benchmarks principal David van Wyk, we will also reflect on the Snake Park/Doornkop community is affected by the heavy metal toxicity of the environment as we attempt to extract accountability from the mines -- in this case DRDGold which has left wholly unrehabilitated, neglected, disintegrating dumps right next to Snake Park. DRDGold is the historical miner, that Benchmarks holds responsible. But we also want to confront the current mining rights holder, MINTAILS (listed on the Austraian ASX) to whom the mining right for the area stretching from KRUGERSDORP TO JHB was sold/transferred by the Minister of Mineral Resources. Astonishingly, just this week environmental management practitioners for WES WITS MINING (Australian Listed junior miner...but with "former" managers form DRD and Mintails) sent around information to the community and civil society that shows they intend to re-mine the dumps in this area even further. The gold price is low because of the strength of the rand; most of the gold reserves are too deep to safely mine; Eskom has increased in electricity costs, the proposed carbon tax is a burden, the new mining charter looms, royalties are high -- all these factors are making of gold mining increasingly non-viable within the Witwatersrand. Other mines are downscaling (e.g. Anglo Gold Ashanti’s Tau Tona, Maponeng and Savuka Mines have been placed on care and maintenance). It therefore surprising and shocking to the community that West Wits Mining considers their project to be economically justifiable. While walking around Snake Park with Tiny, we take Geiger counter readings -- in the area readings range from 20 to 27uSv/hr. A normal safe background reading for radiation varies roughly between 0.05-0.10. DRDGold has vociferously defended its community engagement in SOME communities where Benchmarks have done research, but for Doornkop and Snake Park, there's no forum or ongoing engagement. DRDGold has denied their culpability an the conditions they've left behind. DGD says it "at some stage" fenced off and signposted old dumps -- but it put them at odds with a community where kids drown in the sinkholes of their unrehabilitated dumps. DRD's arrogance toward the community is quite staggering -- it has also said that dust from its mine dumps ‘pose no health risk and negligible public nuisance’, and that ‘there is no credible evidence that the dust is toxic’ -- but has not engaged with the high prevalence of respiratory illnesses in the communities studied by Benchmarks. According to Benchmarks research more than half (56.1%) of residents identified respiratory ailments (cough, sinus, asthma and TB) as their most persistent ailment. This is compared to only 25.6% of residents of Danville, Mafikeng, likewise identifying respiratory complaints. (Danville was chosen as a control study because it is a township with asbestos roofs that in all ways approximates Riverlea, except that there is no mining in close proximity.) DRD has been accused by a leading scientist of of using an outdated and outmoded system of dust measurement. DRD admits to a single leak from one of its pipelines in the vicinity of the Russell Stream in February 2016. Given that the company itself reported 16 environmental incidents in 2011 alone, this admission to a single incident in 2016 is quite remarkable. According to Dept of Water Affairs since 2014 two DRD operations were operating without water licences and ostensibly no applications for authorisation had been received by DWS. MINTAILS has never even been hauled on the red carpet for the ongoing lack of rehabilitation now that they own the mining right -- it may be only about 10 years that the company has long been the target of the Human Rights Commission's investigations because it's essentially bankrupt and in business rescue. It holds the largest uranium reserved in the country but its gold mining has all but ground to a halt -- it just processes other small companies' ore. Equally, we should approach the new mining minister Gwede Mantashe for comment -- as there has been no intervention to stop housing development and enforce mine closure and rehabilitation despite ongoing directives and court cases. The health impact of mining pollution is not an easy story to understand and it's not an easy story to prove -- despite proof of elevated levels finding their way into human and animal bodies, the causal link to conditions like cancer and cerebral palsy and autism etc remains unproven. Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common motor disability in childhood. Population-based studies from around the world report prevalence estimates of CP ranging from 1.5 to more than 4 per 1,000 live births or children of a defined age range so while we can raise suspicions and ask questions, we will struggle to establish causation. We will however speak to international experts who do research in highly industrialised mining areas, like India. About 1 in 323 children has been identified with CP according to estimates from America's CDC’s Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network. So it's up to us to work with local experts to try and put a figure on the prevalence in Snake Park.

title: Human Rabies

summary:
A heartbroken father lost his three year old son when he was bitten by a stray cat on New Year’s Day at Palm Dune Resort in Blythedale on the Natal South coast. Greg Hayes and his wife and the rest of the family is devastated. At the time of the cat bite, Hayes had no idea that the cat had rabies. It took 6 weeks before the boy fell ill and died within one week. His death on the 17th of February led to an enquiry. Hayes then traced back their movements over the last 2 months to the cat which bit their little boy and they suspected had rabies. An autopsy confirmed his suspicion. For Npandbo Mchunu, a father from Richards Bay, the traumatic event of losing his 6 year old Ianda Nxosi was something he do not wish on any other father. The father tells the story: “The boy came back from visiting his relatives up north and he became ill thereafter. I took him to the local hospital in Empaneni and they kept him there, said he had the rabies disease.” He never came back home. He died in that hospital,” he says.

Why is rabies still a disease that we cannot control or stop. It is always fatal and no-one is spared. Why is the government not able to monitor and control the recent scourge that has led to the death of 4 people and a suspected 230 confirmed cases in KwaZulu-Natal alone.

title: SA Drone technology inventions
summary:
Capetonian inventor Richard Hardiman’s watched men in a boat scooping up waste that had been blown into the water with a pool scoop at the Waterfront in cape Town- an exercise in futility, no sooner had they scooped it up more blew in. To his surprise this method of was used in most harbours around the world. This was the inspiration for Wasteshark –using drone technology this autonomous floating device swallows up litter moving into places that people can’t. It can operate 16 hours a day sucking up 350 kg of trash. Richard’s invention was picked up by the Port of Rotterdam as part of an accelerator program for innovations in the management of harbours; suddenly an idea developed in his pool in Cape Town had international attention. Tested in Cape Town during the Volvo yacht race the Waterfront is now using two of the devices. But Wasteshark can do far more than collect trash, it also collects data on the quality of the water and scoops up invasive weeds and algae blooms. The 2nd drone application is called Aeroview- this uses the conventional aerial drone. Aeroview is a software program which uses a combination of satellite and drone images to map farm lands. The images are then converted into a software program that gives farmers detailed information of every tree on their farm. They monitor tree health noting changes over time. GPS co-ordinates of a specific trees are sent to the farm manager enabling the farmer to pin point the exact treatment required. Nedbank are using Aeroview on 200 of the farms that require Agri- Finance. Accurate yields can now be predicted by monitoring the canopy size and tree health. Accurate insurance cover is now possible giving banks more security on issuing finance to farmers. Aeroview was selected by Google Launch Pad as one of the most promising products in the emerging market

There is fierce competition in the ever expanding world of Drones. Two South African inventions have grabbed international support for their inventions,one assisting farmers and the other to clean up the water ways.

title: The first 1000 days
oneLiner: The first 1000 days of life set us up for the rest of our days - science now says it is so!
summary:
We look at the first 1000 days of a child's life - the tumultuous irreversible development of the brain in ways which are directly linked to parenting and relating styles. Recent scientific discoveries in brain development are reshaping our understanding of early childhood development. What makes recent findings so compelling are the enduring and largely irreversible ways in which social conditions and ways of relating are biologically woven into the brain in the first 1000 days. Most of adult mental ability is formed in the first three years of life, and about half of that before birth. There is overwhelming scientific evidence that the parent-child relationship, in particular responsive sensitive care in the early years of a child’s life, is critical to children’s development. The benefits of responsive caregiving are critical to healthy relationships later in life, in language skills and economic productivity in the adult years. We talk to experts in the field, neurologists, psychologists and early childhood development experts. We track the progress of babies in institutional care and travel with workers who educate women about their infants experience. The piece is intimate and accessible merging of science and relational care.

cutting edge research into the profound impact of parenting in the first 1000 days and it's implications for society at large.

title: VAT- An increase in the cost of living
oneLiner: With the majority of South Africans living below the poverty line, the recent increase in VAT by 1% will increase the cost of living. How will the poor compensate from their already empty pockets?
summary:
According to StatsSA poverty trends show the number of people falling into poverty has risen to about 55.5% in the country. 1 in 4 people in South Africa are living below the amount necessary to keep alive as many get to survive on less. While unemployment is soaring at 36% and about 45%, almost half of the country’s population is dependent on social grants. This is a clear assault on the poor. Pro- poor organizations and workers unions are up in arms with the minister’s budget speech highlighting that there isn’t enough done to help the poor, which are the majority in this country, to cope with the VAT increases. The number of zero-rated food items is not enough according to the Cosatu. Cosatu also believe all food, water and electricity should be zero rated and they are willing to strike for it. Similarly the SPII believes that buying power is being taken away from the already struggling vulnerable households in the country. According to PACSA people can not survive on zero rated food items alone as it not enough for an adequate nutritional diet. The Cost of living will get unbearable as it will not just be food and basic household items that will go up but transport, which is a daily need for many South Africans will be affected. Carte Blanche will highlight this through a trolley run in a supermarket. With a child support grant budget, we’ll fill the trolley up with zero-rated food items and a nutritional basket to emphasize how much buying power has been taken from the consumer.

For the first time in 25 years government has imposed a new VAT increase from 14% to 15%. Given the state of the country some believe tampering with tax was a necessary but it’s the poor and vulnerable households that will feel the effect of an increase in the cost of living.

title: THE CASE AGAINST JACOB ZUMA I
oneLiner: Former President Jacob Zuma's day in court could be drawing nearer. Media reports indicates that the NPA prosecution team unanimously recommended that 18 charges of fraud and corruption dating back mo
summary:
In April 2009, shortly before Jacob Zuma became the president of the country, then NPA boss, Mokotedi Mpshe announced that he was dropping the charges against Zuma. Since then, his decision has been the subject of one of the country's most drawn-out and longest-running legal battles. The DA relentlessly pursued Zuma and the NPA to make them reinstate the charges. The charges relate to the Arms Deal. The Pretoria High Court last year ruled that Mpshe was "reckless" in dropping the charges and this judgment was upheld by the SCA in Zuma and the NPA's appeal. NPA boss Shaun Abrahams allowed Zuma an opportunity to hand in recommendations on why he should not be charged. At the end of February, City Press reported that the team of five senior prosecutors who studied former President Jacob Zuma's recommendations to avoid his day in court have recommended that all charges against him be reinstated. Zuma is expected to face 18 charges of corruption, money laundering and racketeering, originating from 783 questionable payments he received.

Former President Jacob Zuma's day in court could be drawing nearer. Media reports indicates that the NPA prosecution team unanimously recommended that 18 charges of fraud and corruption dating back more than a decade be reinstated. NPA boss, Shaun Abrahams on Monday, 26 March 2018, indicated that he has made a decision on whether or not Jacob Zuma should be prosecuted. Many are questioning his timing - a week after Zuma resigned as president and only two days before Abrahams' own appeal against a December 2017 Pretoria High Court ruling that said Abraham's appointment was invalid and unlawful and should be set aside - was heard in the Constitutional Court. Abrahams announced that he will announce his decision on whether or not to prosecute Zuma by Thursday, 15 March - this depending on whether the Concourt gives judgment before then and depending what the outcome will be. There is a possibility that the Concourt may uphold the Pretoria High Court ruling that Abrahams' appointment was invalid and unlawful and should be set aside; and that former NPA head Mxolisi Nxasana should be reinstated in this position - or that an entirely new NPA boss should be appointed by President Cyril Ramaphosa all together. Council for the Helen Suzman Foundation (HSF) argued that it would be improper for Abrahams to announce whether or not Zuma is going to be prosecuted. He argued that the question is not whether Abrahams is independent, it's about whether he is perceived to be independent. The HSF points to Appeal Court ruling on Spy Tapes case, where judges questioned why NPA had tried to defend irrational decision to drop Zuma prosecution. High Court found Abrahams had aligned himself with Zuma legal strategies. And it criticized how he failed to act against Jiba. Adv Geoff Budlender, who argued for the lobby group Council for the Advancement of the South African Constitution (Casac) argued that the question is not just whether to prosecute (Zuma), but who should prosecute? These decisions need to be made by a person in whom the public has confidence. There are too many senior people in the NPA who carry toxic baggage. Justice Cachalia again asks Budlender if he realizes that not allowing Abrahams to announce his Zuma decision may delay the prosecution process by a year. Delay would be justified, Budlender says, nut he doubts it would take long for President Ramaphosa to appoint new NDPP.

title: AFTER ESIDIMENI
oneLiner: With the arbitration award announced, we ask the Esidimeni tragedy brought any change? We investigate the current conditions of Esidimeni survivors and other psychiatric patients in Gauteng.
summary:
In the aftermath of the Esidimeni tragedy, the survivors of the Gauteng Mental Health Marathon project were moved to psychiatric hospitals and other facilities. In general, their living conditions are much improved from the NGOs where they were starving and freezing. But the family committee raises concerns that they do not have access to service level agreements between the health department and facilities to see whwther they are satisfied with the level of care agreed upon for their loved ones. Some families complain that patients are not getting proper care. Some facilities are not fit for purpose and there is still a lack of linen, toiletries and other things. One family member told us that her sister's ID was still with the owner of the NGO until very recently - the department had not taken steps to collect the IDs and Sassa cards until she queried it. We talk to family members and plan to visit facilities to see for ourselves. Even though the former Esidimeni patients were moved, some of the NGOs where patients died, remain open and other patients are still living there. Peter Mentoor, who used to work as a security guard at an NGO in Cullinan, says he left because he ccould not stand the way patients were mistreated. He says he was made to sleep in the ward with the patients and there were no qualified care workers at night. He says male and female patients are housed together and patients are not being fed and clothed properly. Meanwhile, the police and the Gauteng health department are also still looking for some patients who had gone missing during the move. The health department had simply lost track of nearly 50 patients -- for months, no one knew where they were. Some of these patients have since been found still living at some of the "death NGOs" We track what happened to these patients who have been found, and question what could have happened to those still missing.

We unpack the arbitration award and reflect on the families' views of the outcome, while asking whether this experience has done anything to improve mental health care in Gauteng. After the Esidimeni tragedy, the surviving Gauteng state psychiatric patients were removed from the deadly NGOs and placed in state psychiatric hospitals or private facilities, some even into Life facilities. But are they better off now? There are complaints from family members that patients are still lacking proper care. The family committee says they want to have access to documents like the service level agreements between the provincial health department and the facilities - it is simply no longer good enough to hear that such documents exist. Meanwhile, other patients still remain at some of the NGOs where people died. Insiders tell us of the terrible conditions at two NGOs in Cullinan. Is the Gauteng Health Department just paying lip service when they promise to do betteR?

As a representative of the governing party and now president, the introduction of the NMW has been met with criticism from opposition parties and workers unions alike. It is a slap in the face of the workers considering the cost of living in South Africa. Unions like Numsa have coined the NMW as the “Poverty Wage” with some calling it a “slave wage”. title: Port St Johns
oneLiner: One way or another the community of Port St Johns is fighting to save their town!
summary:
The Mayor of Port St Johns, Ms Lindelwa Rolobile, promised salary increases to municipal workers in October last year. However, nothing has come of it. Now workers are angry about the lack of action and last week they dumped a truckload of the town's waste in and around the Town Hall and municipal offices. While the Port St Johns Tourism Forum have been hard at work to try and raise the town's profile and put it back on the tourism map, their plans could now be derailed by negative publicity of filth and waste on the streets of Port St Johns. In the meantime the Mayor and councillors of Port St Johns have been ordered to embark on a cleanup operation at their own cost. Source of order is being traced but comes from within the ANC.

Port St Johns on the SA Wild Coast falls under the OR Thambo Municipality. The local community is sick and tired of the town being mismanaged and have taken matters into their own hands. The Tourism Foundation has embarked on an aggressive "town beautification" project, new investment is earmarked for the town, and now municipal workers have started protesting, saying enough is enough! Municipal workers say they were promised an increase on 30 October 2017. MEC for Cooperate Governance and Traditional Affairs, Fikile Xasa was called upon to find a solution, but instead he sent someone from his office to deal with the matter. This angered the workers who to date have still not received their increases. At first they stopped collecting municipal waste, and when the mayor and councillors refused to remedy the situation they decided to dump all the town's rubbish on and in town hall and at the municipal's offices. They have also resorted to defacing the Town Hall with faeces.

title: OGIES STANDOFF
oneLiner: Despite our expose of the structural damage, noise and dust Glencore's coal mining has caused in Ogies, Glencore's operations have expanded and the residents are desperate.
summary:
Many of the issues the community is protesting, have not shifted in years. The standoff with Glencore seems deeper than ever. MEMORANDUM DEMANDS: 1) Inadequate and unfair economic exclusion of the hosting community and its residents in the continued mining activities of the mine. 2) Families relocated to Makause who still do not have water and electricity supply. 3) Compensation for forced removals and the relocation of graves without following traditional customs. 4) The mine and all its major contractors to demonstrate their local employment and skills development statistics, local Small Medium and Micro-Enterprises (SMME’s) that they are developing and are currently contracted directly with the mine or any of its major contractors. Show their local socio economic development initiatives. 5) Demand that all criminal charges and the court interdict against any of their leaders resulting from their many attempts to raise their concerns be immediately withdrawn. 6) Families relocated in order to allow for mining operations to take place be compensated and collectively explore a way in which they can benefit directly in the continued mining activities.

While the human rights lawyers attempt to get a court date to have the problems aired in court, it appears that Glencore has rapidly expanded their blasting on the edge of the town of Ogies -- making breathing and sleep virtually impossible. When the community protested against the dust last week -- they found themselves on the receiving end of police action. The community has been at logger heads with the mine for a long time now. As a result of many dissatisfactory engagements with some representatives of the mine, they took the step of protesting and drafting a memorandum to hand to Glencore. One of the leaders who has charges against him, Joseph Zikhali wants the community of Ogies and Phola to be the first group of people that benefit from the mining activities. “Charity must begin at home before the mine can look elsewhere. I want the charges against me to be dropped as I am not a criminal I am simply fighting for our rights. Until such time where people will be employed, compensated and benefit from the mine. We will not rest."

title: Day Zero unavoidable in Cape Town?
summary:
Day Zero plans have become more practical and accessible. JP Smith Councillor for Safety and Security spelt out for the first time how the collection points would function. But the 200 Day Zero water collection points have still not been revealed to the public as they have to ensure that they are on council or provincial land and if they are on private land they still have to get permission to access those site. Now it may be down to 160 sites and the mind boggles how the whole of Cape Town will be serviced by only 160 sites. Traffic congestion in the City is already out of control so the water collection points will have to be on good traffic nodes and they are talking about having drive through sites. Families of 4 can collect 100 litres at a time and water will be free , you will not have to show your ID and the points will remain open till late at night depending on the demand and the area. Informal settlements will not be switched off and very low income areas area will have water but at reduced pressure. The concern in poor communities is that people are already coming into the informal settlements to collect water from the free standpipes much to the frustration of the residents who have to cue and collect water. When Day Zero hits those surrounding formal houses which are right ontop of the informal areas will just collect water from free standpipes as they will be more accessible than Day Zero collection points. Industries water saving efforts and their contribution to distributing and bringing water into the City Why groundwater will not be ready before day zero The facts around desalination- it takes 5 years to build a 500 mill liter a day desalination and Grahamtek promises are all spin. Details on the desal commissioned this week WWF practical guide to how to survive Day Zero

The reality that Cape Town could hit Day Zero on 12 April has finally hit home. Capetonins went into panic mode and stripped the shelves 5 litres of bottled water and plastic containers to collect and store water. Bottled water is being collected around the country and sent to Cape Town to be distributed to old age homes and animal welfare centres. Then it was finally revealed that NONE of the alternative water augmentation would be online by Day Zero whether that April or May, and those that will be online are in very small quantities. The message moved from a well- run city will not run out of water to #Avoiddayzero – it’s entirely down to everyone using 50 litres per person day. It clear Cape Town was on its own and National Water Affairs and Sanitation is leaving them pretty much to their own devices quibbling about the term Day Zero

title: Water Crisis - Hotels
oneLiner: Cape Town is facing one of it's worst droughts in 100 years. How will this impact on the hotel industry when tourist flock to the city to enjoy their summer break? We go behind the scenes to find out
summary:
Cape Town is a top holiday destination visited by 1.2 million foreign tourists per year spending roughly R40 billion. Tourism makes up 9% of South Africa’s gross domestic product of which a quarter is generated in the Western Cape alone. “This industry is delivered by people. People that wake up at the crack of dawn to drive tourist busses, to man Robben Island gates, to stand at the top of Table Mountain. People's lives and jobs depend on this economy thriving," says Ravi Nadasen of the Tourism Business Council of SA. The hotel industry will therefore go to extraordinary lengths to keep their business going and staff employed. In our story we look at the impact of the drought on the hotel industry in Cape Town and the innovative ways that many establishments have resorted to in order to help save water and prepare for a future water crisis. We investigate with Law Enforcement Officers and the Department of Water and Sanitation officials whether hotels in the city have complied with the new water saving by-laws and visit a number of large to small establishments to find out what they are doing to save water.

When 1.2 million tourists flock to Cape Town each year, they spend roughly R40 billion and provide in excess of 200 000 jobs to the industry. Their is a misconception from both local and international visitors that by staying away they help to save water when in fact combined they only use 5%. However many bookings were cancelled and hotels felt the impact. To prepare themselves for a water scarce future, hotels have resorted to innovative ways to save water and think out of the box. One hotel is already completely off the water grid and a few more is soon to follow. Smaller establishments have all found a way to save water and still keep their doors open. We visit a number of hotels and find out what they are doing during this crucial water savings time in Cape Town.

Can he keep the Zuma faction under control in Kwa Zulu Natal - Zuma was making veiled threats on Wednesday afternoon but his departing message was no violence in my name? Will he remove Minister of Finance Malusi Gigaba before the budget speech? Can he pull the South African economy back from brink with of collapse?

One of the most dramatic weeks in South African political history unfolded this week. The President refused to resign and threatened the ruling party that they would regret it if they forced him to go as he had done nothing wrong. He finally resigned with an hour and half before the deadline holding the Nation to ransom to the last hour. Now his whole cabinet is dissolved. Parliament now elects Cyril Ramaphosa as the new president denying Julius Malema his moment of glory with the 9th Vote of No Confidence in the National Assembly. It will be the first State of the Nation address which will allow the President to proceed without major disruption from the opposition Cyril Ramaphosa will be sworn in as the new president of South Africa on Friday morning and deliver the State of the Nation address a few hours later- never before has South Africa seen a forced removal of President and the election of a new president over night

title: OTTO - THE LOAN SHARK
oneLiner: Meet a man who makes a living out of ripping off people desperate for finance – Otto van Tonder is not the finance guru you were hoping for – instead he’s just another low life conman.
summary:
What’s worse than a bad credit record when you desperately need to secure finance? Getting ripped off by the people who promise to help you. Once he has you conned, sorry I mean convinced, a deposit and admin fee is due – once it’s paid, there’s suddenly an issue with investors and the finance doesn’t arrive.

GOOD CONSUMER EDUCATION OPPORTUNITY IN TERMS OF GETTING FINANCE. A CROOK THAT PRESENTS HIMSELF AS A FINANCE GURU WILL GET SCHOOLED ABOUT THE LAW WHEN WE EXPOSE HIS DODGY DEALS. OTTO IS SO RIDICULOUS – HE’s FUNNY AND DISGUSTING AT THE SAME TIME…. EEEEIIIIUUUUWWW!

title: Cemair
oneLiner: Last week low cost airline Cemair was grounded by the Civil Aviation Authority over concerns about aircraft safety but that's only the beginning - we expose their lethal history
summary:
Cemair CEO Miles van der Molen has a particularly bad history in SA aviation. Three aircraft that we know of, and were flying under various companies van der Molen owns, have crashed and resulted in fatalities. One of those cases was an aircraft that fell at OR Tambo International killing the two occupants. Another case resulted in an aircraft crashing seconds after takeoff at Rand Airport, where the two pilots, one cabin crew and 13 passengers all died. The civil aviation authority found the aircraft to be overweight and not properly maintained. The latest drama has seen Cemair grounded for allegedly falsifying aircraft maintenance reports, having them signed off by unqualified individuals. It is clear that van der Molen likes cutting corners to protect the businesses bottom line, but in aviation that means putting lives at stake.

Last year three ex-Cemair pilots approached Carte Blanche about the malpractice in the company. They allege Cemair forces pilots to fly in dangerous conditions, and if they speak up about it they get the axe. Allegations range from aircraft being overweight prior to takeoff, a huge no-no in the aviation industry, to aircraft landing on runways they are not certified to land on, to lack of proper maintenance on the aircraft. They have supplied us with emails and documentation corroborating their stories.

title: MABUZA PROTECTION ORDER
oneLiner: Has one man's long lonely battle to build his dream Big-5 reserve inadvertently opened a way for ordinary people to hit back decisively against corruption?
summary:
This is a story of Fred Daniel’s breakthrough after 20 years of legal struggles – through the clever, lateral application of the relatively simple Protection from Harassment Act (17 of 2011) which came into effect in 2013 to stop and fix harassment and stalking behaviour which violate someone’s Constitutional right to privacy and dignity. After spending millions on legal representatives, investigations and getting nowhere, this Act provided for Daniel an inexpensive civil remedy to protect him from behaviour which may not constitute a crime but may impact negatively on various rights... All he had to do was fill out a simple form, available online, and put his case to a Magistrate – which Daniel did in Carolina. He didn’t even need legal representation. And his harasser didn't have to be present. The only risk...if Daniel is lying, he could himself face arrest. On Monday 29 January, the Carolina Magistrate granted Daniel his interim protection order, and the court has invited Mr Mabuza to court on 19 Feb to explain why the order shouldn’t be made permanent.

After 20 years of struggling through the courts, spending R18-million in legal fees to defend his actions to establish a luxury Big-5 game Nkomazi Game reserve, Cradle of Life, Mpumalanga businessman Fred Daniel has finally broken through against ongoing harassment and high-level corruption that have nearly scuppered his life’s work – by applying a simple, inexpensive and bold law. Conservationist Fred Daniel made his fortune in IT and dreamed of establishing a big-5 game reserve near Badplaas, Mpumalanga. He had all the partnerships and international deals in place to make it happen. Daniel bought up 98 failing farms near Badplaas – it had become impossible to cultivate grain here, and farmers were eager to sell up and get out. But since Day One, Daniel has found himself at the receiving end of administrative blockages, violence, victimisation and harassment, last year there was an attempted media smear campaign with false allegations that Daniel had to refute by opening his gates and books to the media. And he's even had a phone call from one David Mabuza, then MEC for Agriculture, to get out of Badplaas. He couldn’t get his Big-5 permits. He had his boundary fences cut. There were attempts to burn down his buildings. He woke up to violent protests on his doorstep. He had his animals removed and sold off with the money diverted to the Problem Animal Fund. And then there was the fraudulent land claim against his land -- the scandal that saw the department of rural development and land reform buying farms for claimant communities at rates that were up to 300% higher than market value. Daniel hired forensic investigators and exposed the fraudulent land claim (in 2003), with tentacles reaching into the then MEC for Agriculture, DD Mabuza’s office. If Daniel hadn't exposed it, the tax payer would have lost R600million. Since then Parliament have even passed the Restitution of Land Rights Amendment Act, 2014 which provides that anyone who lodges a claim with the intention of defrauding the state shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a fine and imprisonment. (Two years ago the Land Claims Court in Randburg ordered Rural Development and Land Reform Minister Gugile Nkwinti to take back the land that was given to a controversial trust and review the claim. The validity of the claim involving 105 farms worth R51 million in Mpumalanga’s Badplaas area had been contested over the past 12 years.) But none such provisions protected Daniel when he turned whistleblower. Daniel's whistleblowing, together with defrauded land claimants, resulted the scheme exposed and a R3.3 million fraud charge being laid by the EFF against Mpumalanga Premier David Mabuza (http://city-press.news24.com/News/r33m-haunts-premier-mabuza-20151212). But by then, Daniel's investors, and potential partners had vanished. But all hell broke loose. Harassment escalated sharply. Of 20 court cases where Daniel opposed the Mpumalanga tourism authorities’ administrative interference, he won 18. In the process he spent over R18-million. In forensic reports and court proceedings, all of which Daniel paid for, testimony emanated that officials had suffered immense political pressure, all the way to the Premier's office, to thwart Cradle of Life. Now, only two cases remain outstanding: - a R1,6bn damages claim against the government for the business he’s lost (mediation process is underway to try and settle this and restore relationships with new Tourism Authority management who are eager to help him). - an interim protection order against the same DD Mabuza – now Premier of Mpumalanga and Deputy President of the ANC.

title: CAR T-CELL THERAPY
summary: FDA approved 30 August 2017. This treatment is the collecting, reprogramming and multification of a patients’ own immune cells to treat their cancer. The CAR on the cell’s surface is composed of fragments of synthetic antibodies. These receptors recognized and binds to the antigen on the tumor cell. More than 80% of children diagnosed with ALL that arises in B cells will be cured by intensive chemotherapy. But for patients whose cancers return after chemotherapy or other traditional cancer treatment there are no options. Of the first 59 children and young adults treated during the human trial period since 2012, 55 (94%) had a complete response, meaning their cancer disappeared. Human trial started at CHOP in 2012 already and this approval of the therapy is a huge and dramatic development in cancer treatment and can be the beginning of many more similar treatments for other types of cancer as well. Mia Cara is at CHOP now and is undergoing strong chemotherapy today, 17 Jan ’18, and on Friday to get the cancer count down before her T-cell treatment. And she is also treated with steroids. The reason why she has not yet received her treatment: As part of their immune-related duties, T cells release cytokines, chemical messengers that help to stimulate and direct the immune response. It can lead to CRS (cytokine release syndrome). In the case of CRS, there is a rapid and massive release of cytokines into the bloodstream, which can lead to dangerously high fevers and precipitous drops in blood pressure. It is treated with steroids and immunoglobulin therapy, which provides them with the necessary antibodies to fight off infections. In her case she is not yet strong enough to withstand the high volumes of cytokines. Anything can happen between now and February. She might be strong enough by next week to undergo the treatment! The doctors have not given up on her and are positive and working on getting her strong enough to get the treatment! At the moment there is no hope for Mia Cara other than this treatment! Even if the worst happens before the treatment, this gave hope where there was none before and gives hope to other children in her position!

title: Knife attacks in Table Mountain Reserve
oneLiner: Horror attacks in the Table Mountain Reserve has spread fear amongst hikers. Tonight we bring you the story of a group of 9 hikers who were mugged at knifepoint in the Silvermine area.
summary:
It was a Saturday morning when forty-nine-year Michael Traut from Retreat in Cape Town joined a small group of hikers on the Silvermine trail. The group was led by an experienced hiker Anwar Adams who gave a brief tooltalk before they set out on a comfortable pace. The group consisted of mostly elderly people, amongst them a British couple, Dan and Yvonne Cormack. It was a perfect sunny day with little wind and breathtaking scenes along the path to make this the perfect hike. Michael made small-talk with Dan and took a memorable picture on route. Little did he know that their fate was about to change. Two men appeared from behind a bush. They were flicking their knives and shouted at the group to hand over their phones, cameras and rucksacks. Dan put up a fight and got stabbed multiple times as he tried to resist. His wife Yvonne picked up a stick and hit the attacker shouting “leave my husband alone”. The attacker retaliated and stabbed Yvonne in the arm. Michael was next. A rock struck his jawbone and he was stabbed in the hand. Michael threw down his phone, camera and wallet then fell on the ground in a dizzy spell. Anwar ran to a high point for cellphone signal and to call for help. The second attacker ran after Anwar and and stopped him in his tracks with a blow on the head. Anwar fell down. The attackers fled from the scene with their loot.

We track the story of a horrific attack on 9 hikers in the Silvermine area of Table Mountain Reserve when a peaceful walk turns into a nightmare. This is just one of many recent attacks that have the community and visitors up in arms. Why is this happening and what is SANPark who are the custodians of the park doing about the drastic escalation of crime stats in the Reserve.

title: Bubble Boy
oneLiner: Groundbreaking gene therapy offers hope for a rare immune condition.
summary:
Ayaan Ahmed Sheik has spent almost all of his two years of life in hospital, battling a series of infections that threatened to end his short life. He was born with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency, a rare condition that left him with no immune system at all - no defence against the hundreds of common infections that the rest of us brush off daily. Most children born with this condition die, because they are not diagnosed in time to rescue their embattled immune systems from common but - to them - life-threatening infections. SCID children who are diagnosed early enough receive a bone marrow transplant - this must be carried out within their first three months of life for maximum effect. In Ayaan's case, there was a long delay in tissue typing and searching for a donor. When a potential donor was found, it was only a partial match and his mother Shamaa considered the risk to be too high. In desperation, Shamaa reached out to St Jude Children's Hospital in Memphis Tennessee, where a clinical trial was testing ground-breaking new gene therapy for treatment of SCID. Ayaan was eventually accepted into the trial and after a long journey filled with stress and setbacks, he is now home in Cape Town, apparently able to start a normal life at last.

A South African first and a globally leading gene therapy clinical trial. Ayaan Ahmed Sheik, a Cape Town child has received cutting edge and apparently successful gene therapy for the rare condition, Severe Combined Immunodeficiency. This is a story that speaks not only to fascinating new technology, but to the question of whether newborn screening should be implemented in SA hospitals.

title: Darryn August a selfless hero
oneLiner: What happen to Darryn August the selfless hero who intervened in a train mugging which left him paralysed from the waist down?
summary:
Darryn’s story remains truly inspiring- coming from a poor working class family there was no safety net to help him with expensive re-hab but thanks to his friend Graeme DaleKuys who on hearing of his incredible bravery decided he had to step up. Through Back-a- buddy Graeme set out to raise R50 000 for Darryn and ended up raising half a million. Graeme and a few friends rode what they called the Everest Challenge – the 8884 meters from sea level to the Steenbras Dam viewpoint a ride that started at 4am and ended at 10pm with 46 trips up and down– the equivalent of Everest. Graeme campaign gave people a way to support Darryn for his bravery. Once he was out of rehab Darryn wanted to find and confront his attackers. The police investigation was not making progress so he started to visit the area where the gang had got onto the train, a small community called Macassar. After weeks of searching he finally sat down with the men that had robbed and thrown him from the train. They were grown men aged between 29 and 36. At first they were defensive and showed no remorse- robbing people was what they did, but after several hours these grown men were crying. All Darryn wanted from them was to confront what they had done to his life; he didn’t press charges because he knows prison doesn’t change people in fact it makes them better criminals. Darryn had grown up in a community filled with men like this and had no illusions about life. His mother -a rape survivor persuaded him not to press charges and inflict suffering in another life but to rather move on with his life. Darryn continues to work with street kids and youth at risk using his own life story to inspire them. But life as a disabled person is extremely tough especially in areas with pavements and roads that are poorly maintained. Darryn is campaigning to raise awareness for people with disability in poor communities and is assisting the Brandon Beack Foundation support people is disadvantaged communities.

Darryn August made headlines in April 2017 when he survived being thrown from a MetroRail Train early one morning while travelling to work. Nine men had boarded the carriage and were clearly there to rob people, as they approached two women, one whom was pregnant, Darryn intervened. He was severely beaten and thrown from the moving train. He lay on the side of the track for hours - paralysed and bleeding out. His life was saved by a City of Cape Town cleansing contractor who found him by chance. Darryn's selfless actions and terrible tragedy of being left paralysed from the rib cage down made headlines for weeks. But once the hype was over how did Darryn reconstruct his life?

title: Scholar Transport- Long Walk To School
summary:
Since 2014 activists from Equal Education have been advocating and campaigning for scholar transport for children in Kwa-Zulu Natal. For many children in rural KZN, getting to school means waking up in the wee hours of the morning and embarking on a long two and half hours walk just to get an education. These routes that they take are quite dangerous as the children run the risks of drowning in the rivers they have to cross or even get raped or abducted. The department of education in KZN has cried budgetary constraints to assist these learners with transport while nationally there was a promise from the minister to allocate grants for scholar transport but nothing has been forth coming. A court ruling in KZN was in favour of EE and has now forced the department of education in KZN to provide transport for this students and has given them a deadline of 1st April 2018 to present to the court a report that outlines how they will accommodate and assist all the children that are in need of scholar transport in KZN. The use of private scholar transport such as bakkies and mini taxis has also endangered the lives of the children as Omalume (drivers of private scholar transport) constantly overload their vehicles for extra money at the expense of these children’s lives. The department of transport has put out a law that prohibits the Omalume to transport school children but according to Jabulani Dladla from the KZN scholar transport association, business is still running smoothly in KZN atleats until January whilst they are still in negotiations with the department to help them acquire new vehicles that meet the regulatory standards.

There are over 1 million children in need of scholar transport in the country with some in the rural areas having to walk over 14 Kilometres Just to make it to class and back home. Is the safety of these pupil and their rights neglected?

title: Phantom pain
oneLiner: A local researcher is leading the fight against phantom pain
summary:
For years phantom pain was poorly understood and was treated using mirror therapy. However, this technique proved to only reduce pain by approximately 20%-30%; Kathlego's trial using Graded Motor Imagery - which involved teach patients a variety of techniques through the use of a free app has helped improved the pain reduction to 100% in virtually of of his test subjects. This is the first time this method is being trialled in Africa. Limakatso has already won an award for his work. The patients are based out of Khayelitsha, Somerset West and Victoria Hospitals. According to Limakatso the therapies are cheap and able to be performed anywhere which opens them up to a much larger portion of the population, rather than just those who can afford private medical aid cover. Eileen is one of his patients, from Somerset West, who described the sensation of phantom pain in her left as feeling like, "broken glass under her skin". After her amputation, due to diabetes, she couldn't sleep and was taking vast quantities of pain killers and sleeping tablets to simply be able to function. According to her pre-admission study her pain was rated as 9/10 using a universal medical pain scale. This rating means the pain is so severe it disables the patient and they are unable to perform "activities of daily living". Eileen says she is now totally pain free and says the treatment saved her life and she can live normally now and go back to work as a booking's agent for a cage-diving company. Limakatso says that after the success of this trial the team, including himself and several neuroscientists at Groote Schuur's Pain Management Unit want to roll this treatment method out to other sufferers of Chronic Complex Pain Syndrome which affects vastly more people.

Kathlego Limakatso is a physiotherapist is conducting a trial using a new technique, Graded Motor Imagery, for the first time in Africa to relieve phantom pain caused by amputations with virtually a 100% success rate.
