title: Abalone poaching
oneLiner: Rampant poaching of wild abalone could drive the shellfish to extinction in South Africa within a decade. Carte Blanche investigates.
summary:
It is Friday midday and yet another news story hit the newsstand: “Law enforcement officials confiscated abalone worth more than R700 000 and arrested 11 suspected poachers in Simon’s Town.” Almost weekly, news flashes appear in the media reporting on illegal poaching on our cape shores: From Pearly Beach to Houtbay, our seas are stripped clean to satisfy an ever growing demand in Asia for the product. An estimated 4000 tonnes of abalone is caught illegally every year in South Africa. This is 20 times over the limit (98 tonnes per year) set by the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. South Africa is one of the largest suppliers to the East where abalone is used as an aphrodisiac, for medicinal purposes and consumed as a delicacy. With their own seas stripped bare seafood suppliers will pay up to R1500 per kilogram of fresh abalone and plated in a Cantonese restaurant, roughly R3 000. Abalone is run by local and Chinese crime syndicates and gang members like the 26 and 28 gangs. They lure the local fishing community and their families into their network: from divers to spotters, collectors, drivers, sellers and buyers, the industry is highly organised and sophisticated as money is no object. Small communities and towns have been infiltrated and lately even drugs have been used to pay for the abalone which has had a devastating effect on the lives of people. On the Overberg coast in towns like Pearly Beach, Kleinbaai and Hawston poachers have become so brazen that groups of up to 20 divers will enter the sea during broad daylight and even give you the finger when trying to film them as seen here on a cellphone video clip taken from the deck of a B&B in Hermanus.

A booming illegal trade in abalone is fueling the social and environmental crisis in South Africa. It is estimated that illegal harvesting of abalone from South African shores comprise more than 90% of total abalone production with an estimated value, after processing, of more than R1 billion. Poachers are making 440 million dollars a year by trafficking these giant sea snails into Asia where they are valued as a delicacy. As a result the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries says that “only an appreciable reduction in removals can prevent a complete collapse in the wild within about a decade”.

title: Sewer Zama Zama's
oneLiner: Did you know there was hidden treasure in the sewers of Johannesburg? Called "Sewer Rats," or "Sewer Zama Zamas" we follow a team who find the things we lose down the drains in order to make a living.
summary:
In the sewage tunnels in Johannesburg is a trove of hidden treasure (items of value like jewellery or money), sifting through the sewage, storm water and everything else… are Zama Zama’s. There are various ways that they do this: They block the sewage pipe so that it overflows causing it to flood – then sift through it by adding sand to the water to dry it, or use gold pans sifting through the water for valuables, another method is to open sewage infrastructure like manholes, block to water flow if the manhole is full, or go through it with a magnet. We have several videos of how this is done. “Minister” is a sewer Zama Zama. He was retrenched in 2010 from his job as a plumber. He couldn’t find another job, and didn’t want to do commit a crime, and so thought outside the box. He noticed that as a plumber items often went down the drain and he would have to retrieve them so he began doing this. He said it’s a dirty job, and sometime he can come out with nothing, but more often than not he finds all sorts of treasures that flow down the pipes. He has found watches, rings, necklaces, cell phones, knives, guns, cutlery etc and then cleans them and sells them. There are obvious risks – health being one of them. The faecal matter contains ecoli and other pathogens that can be deadly if it infects an open cut or is consumed. Another is the risk of drowning or being caught by a current and being dragged under. Others are that when you retrieve your items you could be attacked for them – as is the situation with Gold Zama Zama’s.

We have footage of Zama Zama's doing this already. We have verified that they are real and not just a myth. The city of joburg is also going to go down with us and let us see the damage caused first hand.

title: Maternity UIF claims
oneLiner: How easy is it to claim your Maternity UIF benefits?
summary:
Giving birth is a financially stressful time in any woman's life. Many women do not get paid their full salary during their maternity leave and they rely on Maternity UIF payments to get them through this time. Suddenly there's an extra mouth to feed in the house and a string of unexpected expenses. By law a woman can claim Maternity UIF if she has been contributing to the fund. But this is a huge source of frustration for new moms. Many approach the Department of Labour themselves, only to be sent back because they have the wrong, or incomplete forms. Then they are told to wait 4-6 weeks. After that, they contact the Department asking for their first payment, only to discover the the DOL has lost a form, or an entire file and they need to start the process all over again. In most cases women only get paid out (if at all) once they are back at work. And that completely defeats the purpose of the Maternity UIF, since it is meant to alleviate financial pressure during maternity leave. Because of this struggle there are a host of UIF assist companies that assist mothers, but they too are struggling and in many cases fail to deliver on their promises. They simply take their fee and run. Companies like Moms Assist ask a fee of around R750, and for that they will submit your paperwork, stand in the queue on your behalf - basically make the whole process hassle free. However, companies struggle to deliver on their promises because of the chaos at the Department of Labour. We will speak to the Department about the problems the Department is experiencing as well as the private agencies, and whether or not they are being regulated to some extent.

The Department of Labour is struggling to keep up with UIF payments and many people are outraged because they are either not paid out, or they have to wait long for their payment. In addition, there are countless stories of paperwork getting lost and general inefficiencies within the Department. We speak to a group of women who have been trying for months to get what is due to them paid out. Along came UIF Assist centres, private businesses that were supposed to make life easier for the claimants. This meant that, in the case of pregnant mothers, women could pay a once-off fee and their claims would be processed hassle free. However, some of these companies could not deliver on their promises.

title: Report Card: Airport Followings
oneLiner: So-called follow-home robberies have been plaguing foreign and local tourists alike on the roads from OR Tambo. We revisit this issue to see what police have managed to do to stop the scourge.
summary:
July 2017: shortly after we put together our second story, several suspects are arrested in connection with airport followings, as a result of crime intelligence operations and increased security patrols. Police MInister Fikile Mbalula announces a new tactical security plan, including suspension of several police, airport and tourism officials, vetting of all airport staff and service providers, new police leadership at ORT, and increased security on routes to and from the airport. The plan, it is said, will be a blueprint for increased security in the country's other airports. August shows more promising results, with several arrests being made in connection with drug and rhino horn smuggling. IN September, ACSA announces a 10.8% profit increase for the year. Then, on 26 September, 36 elderly Dutch tourists are violently robbed on their way from the airport to their hotel, hours into a 3-week holiday. The bus driver and tour operator are tied up, several of the tourists are punched, and the robbers try to open fire on them. They are severely traumatised and leave the country immediately. Less than a month later, seven members of an Iraqi delegation are robbed on their way to their hotel. One is wounded and taken to hospital. The suspects make off with jewellery and cash. The next day, six suspects are arrested following a tip-off. One of them is the manager of a security company contracted to ORT and is wanted for crimes in Limpopo. Stolen items are recovered and a manhunt is launched for a seventh suspect who escaped. Mbalula is quoted as saying the days of airport followings are drawing to an end. But is this true? Despite a few arrests here and there, two daring, violent and large-scale robberies show that gangs are undeterred. Do these arrests mean the 'cracking' of at least one airport syndicate? What about the investigation of previous cases we showcased?

In June 2017, we exposed an alarming rise in the number of so-called airport followings, in which foreign and local arrivals at OR Tambo are followed home and robbed in their driveways, or along the side of the motorway. We showed that there are numerous syndicates operating from within the airport and spoke to a 'spotter' who helps criminals identify their targets. In July, we interviewed Police Minister Fikile Mbalula, who took responsibility for the issue and promised that the police would come down hard on these syndicates. In the last three months, SAPS has implemented a multi-layered security plan at OR Tambo, which showed promising early results. However, two recent high-profile robberies, followed by a much-lauded arrest of 6 suspects, have raised the profile of this issue again. Carte Blanche takes a look at how effective police intervention has been.

title: Pangolins
oneLiner: The Pangolin is the most trafficked animal in the world, and South Africa is one of the hotspots for smugglers.
summary:
Of the 8 species of Pangolin found throughout Africa and Asia, 2 are critically endangered, 2 are endangered and 4 species are listed as threatened. Traditional Asian medicine believes the scales are a cure for a whole host of medical conditions including cancer. The scales are actually keratin, the same stuff our nails and hair consist of, and hold no medicinal value. Some Chinese operations claim their product comes from farming, but this is also false and all Pangolin products found in Asia are as a result of the huge smuggling operations both their and in Africa.

We have a source who is in contact with a wildlife smuggling syndicate. Amongst other things the syndicate has access to Pangolins and regularly sells them on the black market, where a live animal can fetch up to R150 000. The source is willing to setup a sting with us, in which we will setup a "buy" with members of the syndicate, capture everything on hidden camera, and then have the relevant law enforcement arrest the sellers and one of the main players in they syndicate, as well as have the Pangolins removed and rehabilitated.

title: WEST CAPE FARMERS' WATER WARS
oneLiner: West Coast farmers not only have to contend with Eskom and fuel price increases, but drought has seen them cut back production for the last 2 years...now their neighbours divert their water
summary:
In the Matzikama municipality in the Western Cape, farmers have to plant their crops by October, but they are horribly short on water. The drought is hitting everyone hard, but for these farmers and their workers, their livelihood is disappearing. Depression has landed some in psychiatric institutions, and there have been suicides. Thousands of jobs stand to be lost if the farmers can only produce a fraction of their usual crops - the prediction right now if things don't change. Companies such as Tiger Brands, which has a tomato processing plant in the area, have warned of major job losses. Meanwhile, farmers are fighting about the little bit of water that's left. Those in Matzikama and the Clanwilliam area are accusing farmers upstream in the Citrusdal area of illegally damming up the Olifants River and robbing them of their fair share of the water. They have asked the Department of Water and Sanitation to take action, but to no avail yet. The Citrusdal Water Users Association has allegedly walked out of meetings meant to find a solution, and stated that the downstream farmers are not their concern. The Matzikama municipality has declared a disaster area, in the hopes of getting funding from donors and national government. They have a plan, but no way yet of pulling it off. Matzikama wants to access an underground aquifer, something they need R100 million for. They are currently raising funds for this. Meanwhile, farmers are also being squeezed from other sides with electricity price increases and fuel getting more expensive.

As the Western Cape drought continues, it's high drama for farmers on the West Coast, where jobs and lives are at stake. What will the impact on the economy really be if the rains don't come, and other plans for salvation don't succeed? Farmers are under serious pressure from increases in things like electricity and the fuel price, let alone the lack of water. We examine the big picture by looking at one municipality and its tireless battles as a case study. The Matzikama Local Municipality is waging the battle for water on a variety of fronts. It has an ambitious plan to extract water from an aquifer, but money is scarce. It is also tackling farmers upstream on the Olifants River for allegedly illegally damming up the river and taking more than their fair share.

title: Homeless
summary: Vaya the movie is inspired by untold stories of Johannesburg. It began 8 years ago, with the Homeless Writers Project, where filmmaker Robbie Thorpe agreed to work with a group of homeless people to create opportunities for their stories to be told. Robbie set up a weekly space for homeless people to share their experiences, to reframe them and write them down. It was here that the film script for Vaya was crafted in workshops, and based on the stories of David, Madoda, Tshaba and Anthony. David came to Johannesburg in the 90’s and joined homeless talk to eke out a living. He and Robbie initiated the Homeless writers project. He lives with friends or shares a room to keep a roof over his head. Madoda ran away from Giyani when he was 20 to find work in Johannesburg. Impeccably turned out, one would never imagine that he often sleeps at Park Station. He runs a soccer website out of McDonalds. Tsaba lived on the streets of Durban since the age of 12. In 2001 he came to Johannesburg on the promise of work from relatives, where he experienced betrayal and tough times. He runs a theatre group for street children. Anthony grew up in Soweto, and got involved with drugs and gangsterism as an adolescent. During that time he did hot have a permanent home. He cleaned himself up and in 2014 moved into an RDP house with his mother. He creates posters and business cards and runs a vinyl night each Monday in Braamfontien. We spend time with these four, exploring their histories and learning something of their traumatic and colourful lives on the streets. We visit their places of sleep, their working spaces and spend time with them at the Homeless Writers Project. The evolution of Vaya, and the true stories that make up the movie drive the narrative.

title: OSCAR PISTORIUS: THE STATE'S APPEAL AGAINST HIS SIX-YEAR SENTENCE
oneLiner: Just more than a year and four months since Oscar Pistorius was sentenced to six years in prison for murder, his future hangs in the balance again.
summary:
In yet another chapter of the protracted court case - dubbed the "Trial of the Century" - that has sustained global interest, Oscar Pistorius's future again hangs in the balance. It is the State's second appeal against the findings by Trial Judge Thokozila Masipa: first the successful appeal against the verdict of culpable homicide - overturned by the SCA in a unanimous judgment of a full bench of judges - to murder; and the State's second appeal against the six-year sentence Judge Masipa imposed on Pistorius for murder. The State will argue that the former athlete's sentence is "shockingly inappropriate for the crime of murder". The NPA will argue that Pistorius should have been handed the minimum term of 15 years behind bars. NPA spokesperson, Luvuyo Mfaku, said: "The State, in the papers, we stipulate that the sentence imposed is shockingly low. The presiding officer has the discretion to deviate from the minimum prescribed sentence when compelling and substantiate circumstances exist. But... with this matter, the presiding officer exercised that discretion in a very lenient manner." Pistorius's defence team lead by defence advocate Barry Roux, has always argued that Pistorius did not deliberately kill Reeva Steenkamp. Pistorius has always insisted the shooting was a mistake, saying he thought an intruder had entered his home and he feared for his safety. He fired four shots through a locked toilet door, hitting Reeva in the head, arm and hip. During his trial in 2014, Pistorius testified in court it was only when he battered down the door with a cricket bat that he realised who was behind it. The State will argue that the SCA extends the sentence to the imposed minimum 15-years for murder. The Defence will argue that the six-year sentence stays unchanged. A year after the Supreme Court of Appeal granted the State leave to appeal the six year sence

In December 2015, Supreme Court of Appeal Justice Eric Leach, who wrote and read the ruling on behalf of a five-judge bench unanimous in its verdict, opened the verdict with the following words: "This case involves the human tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. The young man overcomes huge physical disabilities to reach Olympian heights as an athlete. He meets a young woman of great natural beauty and a successful model. All is destroyed when he takes her life. The court found the accused to have been a very poor witness. One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. I have no doubt that in firing the fatal shots the accused must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that whoever was behind the toilet door, might die, but reconciled himself to that event occurring and gambled with that person's life. He ought to have been convicted not of culpable homicide on that count, but of murder." It is perhaps upon these words, that the NPA and the trial's chief state prosecutor, adv Gerrie Nel, said the sentence that Pretoria High Court Trial Judge, Thokozile Masipa, imposed on Oscar Pistorius on the charge of murder, is "shockingly inappropriate". And this is what the State will build its case on and argue in the Appeal Court in Bloemfontein on the 3rd of November. In July 2016, when Judge Masipa sentenced Pistorius for a second time, she sentenced him to six years imprisonment for the murder of Reeva Steenkamp, saying the mitigating factors outweighed the aggravating factors and therefore the prescribed 15-year minimum sentence for murder would be unjust. At the time, adv Nel said the sentence was too lenient and that the State would appeal it. In August 2016, Judge Masipa dismissed the State's application for leave to appeal the sentence she imposed on Oscar. In dismissing the application, Judge Masipa said she was not persuaded that there was a reasonable prospect of success at another court. Adv Nel then launched an application directly at the SCA, and in November last year the court ruled that the State and Defence would have to give oral arguments in the State's appeal against Oscar's sentence. These are the arguments that will be heard on the 3rd of November in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein - and this appeal, once again, let Oscar Pistorius's future lies in the balance: another chapter of a protracted trial that has sustained global attention.

title: Into the Light - assisting drug users
oneLiner: "Current Drug rehabilitation methods are failing dismally, indicating that in South Africa - we are certainly not winning the war on drugs – in fact we are just driving it further underground.
summary:
Currently in South Africa – According to the Medical Research Council - the success rate for heroin rehabilitation methods, across the board, at private and government provincial centers, is only + - 7%, leaving us with a daunting + - 93% failure rate.Hundreds of thousands of rand is spent by users and institutions annually, on ineffective treatment intervention methods, regardless of their “sophisticated” approaches.The first low threshold Opioid Substitution Therapy Project (OST) in South Africa has recently opened up in Durban. Unlike most rehabilitation facilities, heroin users are met where they are at, with recognition that they have human rights and that drug use is a public health issue, not a criminal one. The results are astounding. For the first time people who use drugs, who have joined this project feel that they can talk openly about their drug use habits, and receive assistance from a team that neither judges them nor has unrealistic expectations of abstinence. Equally importantly, the Durban OST Project provides heroin users with medical assistance (with carefully observed Methadone provision), which makes ‘detoxification’ less daunting, and provides hope for maintaining a life that they define as normal and healthy. Out patient programme - The fact that this is an outpatient programme is important. Beneficiaries are not taken away from their everyday environment and hidden from sight. Instead, the team at the Durban OST Project works together with support persons that are seen as invaluable to the success of normalisation of life for people with heroin use disorders.

The first low threshold Opioid Substitution Therapy Project (OST) in South Africa has recently opened up in Durban. Unlike most rehabilitation facilities, heroin users are met where they are at, with recognition that they have human rights and that drug use is a public health issue, not a criminal one.

oneLiner: In a rising tide of violent sex crime, the women of the Joburg DPP take us behind the scenes of their work and lives to show what it takes to put serial rapists behind bars.
summary: We have the unique opportunity to spend time on the job with 4 senior advocates...ordinary women -- wives, mothers, sisters -- who take on extraordinary evil, every day at the office of the Johannesburg Directorate for Public Prosecutions, as prosecutors of some of the country's most heinous serial rapists and murderers. I believe the women's personal stories provide a way of addressing the current narratives and trends around violence against women and children in SA in a way that is constructive, hopeful and inspiring. In March this year, one of two serial rapists dubbed the "Balaclava Rapists" had his face covered with a scarf in court when he was convicted on 53 charges of rape, compelled rape, assault, sexual assault and robbery with aggravating circumstances. His victims had been aged between 13 and 38. He had started his spree in 2007 and was arrested in 2015 (Carte B instrumental in solving the case after the community complained to us...then a SAPS unit was set up) and the case eventually landed in the pile of dockets on the DPP assignments desk . Senior State Advocate Michelle Bayat, a Randburg wife and mother of twin boys in her 30s was assigned the case -- to run it simultaneously with a heavy caseload of economic crimes. What haunts her is the total lack of remorse in the first convicted rapists' eyes. Since running the case, she even finds it hard to pass by women walking on the street without worrying for their safety. This case -- and the many other less famous ones like this -- has changed her. This coming week Michelle will be presenting arguments in aggravation of sentencing of a second man who was charged. The men have been linked to the crime by DNA evidence, but the second accused steadfastly denies guilt. Michelle draws much courage from her colleagues (who've become friends) in the DPP. -- Zarina Peck (38) is a petite woman who was a senior advocate for only a couple of years when she got the case of the "Caretaker Rapist" -- a caretaker at a school, where he used his access to kids to groom more than 40, from ages 13 to 16, using pornography and raped them. He had carried on for years before the crime was discovered in 2015. Zarina prosecuted the man on 33 dockets; some of the children had moved on and would not be deposed. Zarina speaks with passion of what it takes to win a child's trust -- she has 3 of her own at home. She had serious nightmares throughout the case, but despite the NPA's well-intended wellness programme and counselling offered, she had no time in the midst of her heavy caseload to attend sessions. In the end she turned to her Muslim faith, prayer and her colleagues to process the trauma. -- In her fifties, Phakanyisa Marasela is the oldest of the women and a quiet source of strength in the team. She feels she has a special insight into the psyche of women, which compelled her to complete a law degree after stating her career as a court translator in the 1980s. She worked her way up through the courts until she landed in the high-rise home of the DPP opposite the Joburg High Court ten years ago. Phakanyisa wants to share her struggle in getting a conviction in the case of two accused rapists who raped 6 women and murdered 5 before they were caught. To this day, Phakanyisa is driven by the brutal crime scene photos in her docket, and she's been struggling since 2012 to get justice for the woman (all of whom have since passed away). Accused Nr. 1 confessed and has already been sentenced -- the second remains in custody and the trial is set down for January 2018. All this time, Phakanyisa has been in contact with the children and families of the victims, and want to bring them closure. -- Ten years ago, Nerissa Muller begged the Joburg DPP for a job when she found herself as a public defender unable to defend "one more scumbag". Now she's become the "Mama" of al the kids that seemed to land in her caseload of late -- in particular the case of a man who raped 38 children (who could be traced) from Limpopo to Thembisa. Colleagues honour Nerissa's skill with children and in particular disabled kids -- she's found rapists target disabled kids precisely because they "won't talk" or possibly even understand what's happening to them...but Nerissa will spend days before trial, even weekends to play with the kids in the room where they're to testify, making it safe for them...and making it possible to nail the criminals. The work of these prosecutors is nothing like television court dramas. They have no interns, candidate attorneys or secretaries to make copies of documents or help them feed restless, traumatised children who have to spend long days in court. They do it all themselves -- and they want to do it all with excellence, so that none of the criminals they prosecute will get away on stupid technicalities. They've given us access to follow them around for a couple of days at the office, and in court, and have welcomed us into their homes -- (with the exception of their own children, who will not be part of any filming). They all speak extremely eloquently and their communications officer and managers have agreed to accommodate us.

experts: Mr. Adv Johan J du Toit

title: MIDSTREAM REPORT CARD
oneLiner: More than 6 months later, the FG Landfill is still operating. We give the DEA a report card.
summary:
In March, we reported on the community in Midrand's battle against the FG Landfill site, a large general waste dump owned by Interwaste. Residents complain of the bad odours and gases emanating from the dump and health effects such as respiratory problems, eye irritation and nausea. In February, the Department of Environmental Affairs issued a directive to Interwaste to close the FG Landfill site. But Interwaste appealed to the minister of environmental affairs and the directive was suspended pending the minister's decision. Submissions could be made until end March and the minister then had to make a decision within 90 days. But no decision has been made as yet. Interwaste and the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development are also still embroiled in a court case over the waste dump's licence. But in the meantime it's business as usual at the dump and the residents say things are worse than ever for them. The DEA has since commissioned two new reports. One models the air dispersion of the hydrogen sulphide and sulphur dioxide released from the dump. The other report examines the health effects of residents' possible exposure to hydrogen sulphide and sulphur dioxide. The air dispersion modelling report found that the average limit (DEA standards) of sulphur dioxide could possibly be exceeded within up to 600 m from the site and limits of hydrogen sulphide (WHO standards) within up to 419 m of the dump. It shows the gases could reach the southern boundary of the Midstream Estates in very low concentrations but would reach Glen Austin residents in high concentrations. The health effects report found that the sulphur dioxide concentrations were low and the health effects insignificant. But the levels of hydrogen sulphide were often high enough to cause eye irritations and respiratory effects in residents nearby and even complaints of headaches and nausea "can not be regarded as invalid". The odour threshold was also frequently exceeded.

Three months after the Minister of Environmental Affairs was due to make a decision on the future of the FG Landfill site in Midrand, the dump is still operating unhindered. It's unclear what the holdup is, while two new reports show that the complaints of nearby residents of respiratory problems and eye irritation are not unfounded. We give the DEA a report card for their handling of this matter.

title: Cell Phone Masts
oneLiner: There's no denying that cellphones have vastly improved our lives, but as masts go up seemingly around every corner across the country, do we have any say in where?
summary:
There are two cases identified to look at: in Craighall Park and Lonehill. In Craighall Park, residents are taking the COJ and the company who erected the tower, Atlas Tower, to court. Only Atlas Tower is opposing the case. Atlas seems to be a relatively small company from the States, which has rapidly expanded in SA, putting up 135 towers in 2 years. They seem to target schools and churches, institutions who have property and can use the rental income. Our case studies are battling a tower put up on the grounds of Old Apostolic Church. The residents have in writing an agreement from the church with residents saying they would duck out of the deal with Atlas if residents objected. Residents even offered to pay the R4000 a month rental income. But the 30m tower has gone up in anyway. It turns out the church has a nation wide agreement with Atlas to lease their properties to the firm. It seems public participation in the construction meant nothing, despite most residents objecting and handing in their written submissions, no hearing or resolution took place. In Lonehill, MTN are putting up smaller sized towers(only about 15m). These aren't disguised as trees. Residents have been waging war against MTN for the past 18 months. Apparently the MO for major service providers is to approach resident's associations with incentives like installing fiber etc in return for exclusive use by the service provider. In essence, bypassing the full public participation process. The bigger story here is that cellphone service providers are using a tender put out by City Power for cellphone airspace in the city to bypass public participation. These smaller masts are erected on street light poles, and city power does not need public participation to put up street lamps. in the 5 square km's that Lonehill consists of there are 15 MTN towers.

We want to look at how various companies seem to be able to erect cellphone towers with complete impunity in suburbs across the country. There are multiple cases of residents lodging complaints but the building going ahead in anyway. Most of the towers seem to be built without proper public participation.

title: Inner- City Darkness- Cable Theft

summary: In the past two weeks large parts of the Johannesburg city centre have been affected by electricity power outages that has put a grinding halt to businesses and left residents in the dark. This is due to a cable thieving syndicate in the inner-city that has led to 6 kilometers of copper cables being stolen from underground tunnels. A number of arrests have been made, and it is believed that members of City Power, possibly contractors, and possibly members of the SAPS all form part of this syndicate. This is a major robbery that will plunge the city into millions of Rands in repair costs.

title: Superstar the octopus
oneLiner: The story of a citizen scientist’s relationship with an octopus called superstar
summary: This is a story about a citizen scientist, these are people who want to serve the interest of wider society, who volunteer and who work under the collaboration of professional scientists. His name is Craig Foster, an internationally award winning film maker who moved to Simonstown 8 years ago and became interested in the kelp forests. He has spent 5 hours in the sea every day for the last 8 years and has developed the first ever tracking system for marine animals. He even discovered new species of shrimps, but it’s his relationship with an octopus whom he spent time with every day that has resulted in BLUE PLANET coming to SA earlier this year to do a full documentary feature on Craig and his work. Whilst diving Craig noticed traps set for Octopids and realized that these highly intelligent animals were being plundered from the sea with no idea if their slaughter was upsetting the ecology in the area. Craig who had started the NGO Sea Change which looks to the protection of marine life, then went to parliament to talk about the wisdom of the octopus. The SA govt has put forward a Marine Act which shows only .4% of the ocean is protected t for marine life. He cautioned MPS to make wise decisions that secure the long term future of SA’s ecological foundation upon which all economic and political activities rest.
caseStudies: Craig Foster Pippa Ehrlich

title: Bird Flu strikes an already struggling poultry industry
summary:
10 days ago Duck farmer Leon Groeneveld had a thriving Duck business. He had just received a huge order from the Seychelles and Pick and Pay had agreed to supply whole frozen ducks in it's stores. After 8 years of working very hard to expand his duck business things were looking good. Then overnight 11000 of his ducks dropped dead. Bird Flu had struck. Then on his parent breeding stock farm 5 kms away the ducks stopped laying eggs- from 1200 eggs a day to 234. They too had the flu. Yesterday he slaughtered 35 000 of his ducks, most perfectly healthy but his farm is under quarantine and there is nothing he can do with them. The parent breeding stock also had to be culled and for the next for 45 days his farm is a no go area as is every farm within a 5 km radius in the hopes it will control the virus from spreading. But its wild birds that are the biggest danger and you can't stop them and so we have seen the disease move from Zimbabwe through Limpopo right down to the Western Cape. “It’s like being hit by a train”

Poultry Farms look like toxic waste sites, farm workers have hazmat suits and have to go through several de-contamination chambers entering and leaving the poultry farms. Vehicles are sprayed and they have become no go zones. Bird flu strain H5N8 has struck and its the most deadly bird flu virus to hit SA so far rapidly spreading across the country. Currently there is no vaccine in the country and no insurance or compensation for farmers. 1 Million birds have been culled by the end of August and the figure is rising. Its hit 35 farms across the country 15 of which are commercial farms. Entire flocks are dying over night and although people cannot get sick from the virus, workers are loosing their jobs.
caseStudies: Leon Groeneveld Gary Arnold Julia Andrews Peter Stuart
experts: Ms. Charlotte Nkuna Dr. Eileen Pypers

title: GAUTENG HEALTH TROUBLES
oneLiner: Having its furniture seized to settle a legal claim may be a particularly low point, but it follows on years of bankruptcy in management and administration.
summary:
The Gauteng Health department, with a budget of R40.2 billion a year, has paid R1.017 billion in the 18 months from January 2015 to settle 185 medical negligence claims. But the department has more than R20 billion in claims pending against it. This is not something that is budgeted for and these claims could cripple a department already struggling to cope with staff shortages, lack of maintenance of buildings and machines and a high volume of patients. The department has asked the Constitutional Court change the law to allow it to pay medical negligence victims with installments or as and when they need medical attention. This request has failed before the courts in the past, but the department is making yet another last-ditch effort. The most medical negligence claims against the department originate in babies being brain-damaged at birth and by far the majority of claims originate at Chris Hani Baragwanath, where facilities are inadequate and understaffing endemic.

Last week the Gauteng health department had its furniture and office equipment seized to pay for a medical negligence claim of about R6,2-million. About 400 computers, 50 printers, 400 desks, 600 chairs, 200 filing cabinets, 10 fridges, 10 microwaves and three lounge suites have gone into storage -- keep in mind the total haul may not be worth more than about half a million rand. Keep in mind that the Department itself is now responsible to pay for the storage. Think about the replacement cost and new opportunities for graft as new tenders are issued to kit out the offices. Think of the time lost as staff reportedly sit on floors and commute to offices in Pretoria to be able to work. The seizure came after action was brought by Pretoria attorney Oloff Joubert, acting on behalf of a child who suffered brain damage when she was born at the Pholosong Hospital in December 2009. Joubert has confidentially informed us that he intends bringing further sheriff's action because of other unsettled claims -- in the interest of the children left behind. Joubert says his sense is that medical services may have improved in recent years and there seem to be fewer cases coming in, but many of the cases now crippling the system financially date back five years and more. He argues for a system similar to the private sector where doctors have insurance for negligence claims -- since negligence payouts are not budgeted for. (Keep in mind the national backdrop -- the South African Law Reform Commission is working on ways to stop the bleeding of the fiscus through lawsuits -- some very controversial suggestions are being put forward). But what about outstanding debts to suppliers? In May health MEC Gwen Ramokgopa conceded that the current R40.2bn budget was inadequate to cover requirements, largely due to substantial debt burden consisting of money owed to suppliers. Outstanding payments to suppliers dating back to previous years totalled R4.2bn. Commitments to long-term contracts took up R2.95bn, while possible payments for medical negligence amounted to R3.78bn. In 2016, the health department’s legal fees amounted to R569m, pushed up by burgeoning negligence cases since 2009. The department also reported that a total of R860m meant for hospital infrastructure had been withheld from the National Treasury pending submission and approvals of plans by the department. Of the total budget, R23.8bn was earmarked for the wage bill and R16.3bn for goods and services, while an estimated R6bn was allocated to accruals, the MEC said. "This budget is effectively not available," Ramokgopa said, "which means we have not been able to afford services in the past years and the service providers carried the public health system at a huge cost." The National Treasury’s fourth-quarter provincial budgets and expenditure report for the 2016-17 financial year released in April showed that provincial health departments spent 63% of their health expenditure on salaries. A meagre 4.4% of the total health expenditure went to capital expenditure. In 2016, the DEPT owed R300 million to 509 companies (mostly small and struggling...but some also large and struggling) according to answers to the DA's questions in the Gauteng Legislature. As of the end of January 2016, owed R296 million to 509 companies. In January 2017 the DEPT said: ​As the Gauteng Department of Health we wish to inform that we are paying all our suppliers but not full amount. This is due to prioritising payment as per demands which we cannot accede to because they are higher than what we budget for. This is compounded by the fact that the Department services other provinces and countries (which payment thereof is not consistent and sufficient). We are monitoring closely the stock management over what is available and what is needed at the facilities. This is to ensure we always have enough funds to pay suppliers. It is important indicating that Medico-Legal claims dating back 2009/10 and 2011 take bulk of the Department's budget. We wish to confirm that an amount of R11 billion has been paid to suppliers in this financial year (2016/17) and this will continue until the end of March 2017. All the outstanding amount will be settled in the new financial year. We asked where the money is going and who benefits.

title: MEAT WORLD
oneLiner: We investigate a chain meat supermarket called Meat World. We discover they are changing sell-by-dates, are unhygienic and their products have micro bacterial counts in the millions!
summary:
About the sources: Bernard (father) and Jason (son- 22) both worked at the Krugersdorp branch for 3 months. Although initially, Bernard’s wife, Bonnie, was also working for Meat World as a cashier – although she was fired on her first day. She says a customer complained about her and was fired on the spot, without giving her side. Obviously that would have upset them, and she took her story to the bargaining council because she was fired and never given a chance to make her case. (we need to be harsh with them and ask them if they did these things.) Bernard has several accreditations as a safety and cleaning expert – he was working for Pick n Pay and then sent him on several courses. He and his family moved down to Durban and then moved back this year. There were no openings at Pick n Pay at the time, so Bernard took a job at Meat World. His son was working packaging meat with him up until he Bernard was given an offer to go back to Pick N Pay, where he is now. Carte Blanche decided to do a process investigative. We wanted to see if their video and allegations were true. So we visited 9 of the stores and found “double label’s” at each store – we visited 4 stores 4 times and found double label’s at each. Not only did we find blood on the floors, meat just left in refrigerators, but we saw the employees handle the meat at several stores without gloves. We also noted that many of the fridges were not cold enough. At the main branch in Springs, there is no glass casing around the hanging meat carcasses, so anyone can sneeze on it, handle it etc… some products are not even kept in fridges. There are also large bins of sausages with no date – these are labelled R10 – if they aren’t sold that day, they still stay out there. Etc… We believe our sources are telling the truth from the evidence above. We then decided to take a step further… we have decided to test the meat.

In June a family came to Carte Blanche alleging that they had footage showing how a butchery/ meat market was: 1. Changing label dates (this is determined by the meat company – they go okay this meat can be packaged for 2 weeks before it goes off. So they put that label on: Expiry date: 14th, but then they try to take off the label and put a new one on that will then extend that date another 2 weeks – so it’s now outside of that company’s sell-by-date.) Our experts say this is fraud – and can be dangerous if the meat produce is an unstable product (mixed meat, pork/chicken/ sausage). 2. They re-wash and re-use poly-Styrofoam packaging/ trays (Experts say no amount of washing it with green soap will fix this – the bacteria’s don’t just go away and are often absorbed by the Styrofoam.) 3. They do not use hygienic cleaning products that they are supposed to use. Instead they use green soap (have photo’s). 4. They use sodium sulphate as a preservative. (This was made illegal back in the 1990’s – because it can cause cancer. South Africa follows the EU’s rules on food safety standards. According to our sources they use this in a bucket and paint it on the meat.) 5. They mix old mincemeat with new mincemeat (we do not have video of this) The butchery/meat market were revealed to be called “Meat World”. They have 14 stores, their main branch is in Springs. The stores are franchised, and every store also has a manager. As observed in the video, many of the products are unstable meat products – vienna’s, sausages, wursts etc The owner of “Meat World” is a man named Angelino Periera. We will call him and ask for an interview. The sources say they reported this to the manager of the branch, but no steps were taken. The source says they then reported it to the department of health, but nothing happened. It’s important to also say that the video shows that this meat goes from the back to the front of the store, and the source is told that the “boss says they must do it.”

title: No more lost aircraft
oneLiner: ...new technology to prevent aircraft from becoming lost
summary:
We all think aircraft are tracked with precision throughout the flight. It is not the case! On long haul flights over Africa and oceans, flights disappear from radar and tracking apps. The only way airlines know where their planes are, is to let the aircraft send their locations via radio every hour. If the electrical system on the plane packs up or if the device is switched off as in the Malaysia plane, nobody knows where the plane is. New technology developed in South Africa now offers a way to track planes so that they will never again get lost. It is something that will impact aviation globally.

New technology developed in South Africa that will impact aviation globally.

title: Meet the Venters
oneLiner: Meet a family taking on the unique challenge of communication between two blind parents and their two deaf children
summary:
Tanya Venter and her husband Johan are both almost completely blind, with only 3-5% vision each. Tanya's children from a previous marriage, Corban and Samantha, were both born so profoundly deaf that even a hearing aid is inadequate to allow them to hear the noises around them - including their parents' voices. This family faces the unique challenge of trying to communicate when the parents cannot see the sign language the children are using, while the children cannot use sound to speak to their parents or follow instructions and warnings. Several media houses covered the story of the Venters and their 'medical miracle' when, with the help of the Foundation for Children with Hearing Loss in South Africa, they managed to raise the R800 000 needed to provide Samantha and Corban with cochlear implants. The children were implanted in March 2017 and are now undergoing speech and hearing therapy to help them make sense of the new world they have entered. Both children are too old to expect a full acquisition of age-appropriate language - they may never develop more than a very limited vocabulary. But they will be able to gain information from the sounds of the world around them - traffic, alarms...and most importantly, the sound of their parents' voices calling their names.

Facing profound loss of hearing or sight can seem like an insurmountable challenge...but the Venter family is taking on an event more daunting task. Mom Tanya and stepdad Johann are both blind, while their children Corban (11) and Samantha (9) were born profoundly deaf - probably due to the same inherited mitochondrial disease that cause Tanya's loss of vision. Yet this tight-knit family communicates almost telepathically, with Corban and Samantha helping their parents navigate the world they can't see; and signing words into their hands to communicate. But now a modern medical miracle is opening new doors in the family's life - and bringing new challenges - as Samantha and Corban take on the task of learning to navigate life with a cochlear implant. Carte Blanche pays this extraordinary family a visit to find out how they're adjusting to their new lives together.

title: COJ Billing Blunders UPDATE
oneLiner: The City of Johannesburg keeps making promises to sort out the decade-long billing crisis, but is anything changing?
summary:
We revisit the case studies from Billing Blunders, who will all say the same thing... Their cases, which MMC Dagada undertook to solve personally are still in exactly the same situation. Carlos Siemos has had 2x pre-termination notices since our last broadcast and no joy in having his account fixed. He is being billed for the wrong meter (has been for the past 5 years). Soso Gwadiso is still fighting with the council to get his money refunded that his wife paid to get his electricity reconnected. Mike Lingwood's account keeps escalating despite the fact that we dug the meter up in May, which indicates the account reading is completely inaccurate. Mike is also struggling to get the COJ to write off some prescribed debt which dates back to the previous owner of the building. MMC Dagada promised this issue will be sorted by August. No joy there either. Despite numerous phone calls and emails and follow-ups on my part, the only intervention came when I contacted Mayor Mashaba himself, then all of a sudden the Van Niekerk's electricity was switched back on at 10pm on a Friday evening. Their water was reconnected the following week. Yet, their account is still in the name of the deceased mother which means that soon they will once again be disconnected since the account is in arrears. This account needs to be written off against the mother's estate and the Van Niekerk's need to be allowed to open their own water and electricity account with COJ. Despite having presented their mother's death certificate on various occasions and many letter and trips to the ombudsman, they are still struggling.

In May, MMC for Finance, Rabelani Dagada made on-screen promises to the Carte Blanche viewers about sorting out the billing crisis in the city. Three months later we revisit the cases to see nothing much has changed, despite Mayor Herman Mashaba's recent drive to solve the crisis once and for all.

title: COAL FIGHTS
oneLiner: Overwhelmed by the discomfort of a life choked by black dust and random startling explosions, businesses and residents from Ogies, Mpumalanga is fighting the mines around in a human rights case
summary: Louw Potgieter (80) is one of the oldest residents of Ogies -- in the last few years he started suffering chronic sinusitis or the first time in his life. Guest house owners Annemarie and Mike Muller (late 50s) permanently carry around tissues -- but their constant health problems are the least of their worries -- what gets to them is that they may never get back the R6-million that they sunk into developing two guest houses in Ogies, after cashing in their pensions to invest in the town. With mines booming around the town and another application pending that will take mining to within a few hundred metres of their yard, they should have made in killing in the business guest trade. In stead the town is slowly killing them. Their home and guest houses are cracking from the constant and untimely dynamite explosions to prepare the way for mining and the heavy-duty dragline crunches away day and night, disturbing the rest of residents and visitors. A thick layer of black dust hangs in the air all the time. Residents of the black township tell of being moved from one area to the next around town to make way for new stretches of opencast mining. Promises by the mines of proper housing result in stead in little concrete boxes without ventilation, electricity or water. The people of Ogies have roped in human rights lawyer Zehir Omar to help them fight three mines in their area (GLENCORE, ANGLO AMERICAN and SHAFT32) on human rights grounds. The DISRTESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES COMMITTEE that's been founded between the town and township, claims their right to a safe and clean environment is being destroyed, without them ever having been consulted on what was to come...now they sit with houses cracked and banks unwilling to touch the area, so they cannot sell up and leave. Uniquely, two local doctors are also willing to stick their necks out to confirm that a rising incidence of respiratory diseases in the area can be attributed to the intense pollution by coal dust. The group has had some minor success in court already this year when they managed to get a South Gauteng High Court innterdict to stop Glencore from privatising a public road for their own use...a move that would have cut off the town's access to the main school. Omar feels that the community's problems would be completely addressed and solved if only the Department of Mineral Resources would send an inspector to the area to look at the residents complaints. Having got nowhere with getting said inspector to the area, he's approached the Public Protector (that office should really be willing and able to investigate the abuse or neglect of state institutions to enforce residents' complaints)...but the Public Protector dismissed Omar and Ogies and threaten to lump them with costs, should they pursue the matter. For their part, all three mines deny any wrongdoing and have been fighting Omar in court. Glencore aims to mine an area of 113m2 for another 22 years -- it denies that it's encroaching on the town...we would have to get independent expert opinion but it certainly LOOKS to the naked eye that they're closer than the 1000m buffer zone they should be. I want to pull the focus a bit wider -- 67% of Mpumalanga is now covered by open cast coal mining -- this has cut the production of maize by a million tonnes. According to an often-quoted study by the Northwest University on behalf of West European governments that are considering whether to re-open certain mining areas in Europe, Witbank and surroundings -- up to and including areas like Ogies, are now THE most polluted in the world of any mining area that's been the subject of study. I want to investigate problems with breathing and water -- in Witbank (provincial capital, half hour away from Ogies) I have reports/case studies of black lung/mining tuberculosis in people who've never mined, but who live right next to mine dumps. This is all happening in a context where the area has already paid a heavy price for virtually unrestricted coal mining -- Anglo is paying a fortune to rehabilitate the town's drinking water and there have long been sink holes and burning earth from old and abandoned coal mines.

title: Adoption Crisis KZN
oneLiner: With over 1.2 million children in need of adoption, why is our adoption rate declining to 1500 a year and why did KZN province only grant eight adoptions in 2016? CB investigates
summary:
There are an estimated 3 million orphaned and abandoned children in South Africa with 1,2 million of them in potential need of adoption, of which at least 3 500 are abandoned babies. The country’s adoption rate has declined in recent years from an annual rate of 2500 adoptions to a mere 1600 begging the question, what happens to the rest of the these vulnerable members of society that are need of a loving family. In May 2016 the Department of social Development in the KZN brought a relative halt to adoptions in the province, sighting an unfounded threat of Child trafficking. As a result only 8 adoptions took place in 2016 whilst a host of them were put on ice and hamstrung by bureaucracy in a province estimated to have the highest number of orphans. Cultural perceptions have been cited by roll players, as one of the major reasons why adoptions have slowed down in the country. The majority of children being adopted are black, whilst the majority of adoptive parents are white, however there are cases where same race adoptions have also been frowned upon as in the case of Bonnie and Michael, who have been virtually coerced into fostering by the DSD in KZN, making this a complex issue. Do these intrinsic undertones form part of the KZN's DSD rationale when approaching adoptions? Carte Blanche investigates

Hundreds of thousands of South Africans are in effect 'adopting' children annually, but that doesn't reflect in our official adoption figures, and we are still facing an adoption crisis country wide. Are South Africa's orphans without any family the real losers? Carte Blanche investigates

title: Killer breast feeding hormone
summary:
Heart disease is on the increase in South Africa and alarmingly it’s affecting more young people. One of the heart conditions that often goes un-detected until it’s too late is Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM). It is a global phenomenon but in parts of Africa like in Nigeria it affects one in 300 new mothers. The rate of PPCM could be in fact be far higher than currently documented because maternal deaths are only recorded up to 6 months after a woman has given birth. Women can die within 12-24 months after the birth and so do not fall into the maternal mortality figures. PPCM is caused by a defect in the hormone prolactin which is responsible for milk production. The women are fine during their pregnancy and then weeks sometimes months after the birth they begin to experience extreme fatigue, a shortness of breath, their legs and face swell. All these ailments are often associated with the exhaustion of raising a young infant and so go un-diagnosed. Groote Schuur has a specialised Cardiac Maternal clinic where these women can be treated but most hospitals don’t and many of these women are treated at clinic and often misdiagnosed as having asthma rather than a chronic heart condition. One of the major problems of late diagnosis is that the damage to the heart has already been done and although the mother may get help she may only live for a few years leaving very young children. Some woman have had to have a leg amputated below the knee due to poor circulation and their life prospects are very poor. The treatment is quite simple and cheap and if the condition is picked up quickly woman recover well. If they have another pregnancy they can take a pill immediately after the birth and do not breast feed to prevent the condition developing. Some women have no problems with the first birth and the condition only presents after the second child.

Young mothers are dying in South Africa from a completely preventable heart condition brought on by breast feeding. 1 in 1000 mothers contract this fatal heart condition and 25% of those die from it within the first few years of giving birth. Tragically its completely treatable with a very inexpensive drug. They're dying because they go undiagnosed until its too late because their symptoms are similar to so many other associated with the early post-partum ailments. These are healthy young women who had perfect pregnancies- there were no warning signs until after the birth. It effects women of all races.

title: Illegal Roadblocks
oneLiner: Roadblocks legal and illegal: what everybody should know
summary:
Lobo das Neves contacted us about a case he is investigating on behalf of a family. Raymond Tzouganatos (30) was shot and killed at 20:00 on Wednesday 28 June by the Metro Police in Johannesburg. Thye initially reported that he was killed in a hijacking. Then the story changed to being killed in a shootout with the Police. Later on the story changed again when it was alleged that he was killed while tried to run over a Metro policeman. The JMPD officer involved have refused to provide statements as they are required by law, although Wayne Minnaar of the JMPD falsely said they did. It is all very fishy and it seems that the roadblock was an illegal one. Last week a young woman was stopped at men in Police uniforms at a roadblock and raped. She stopped when commanded – something most of us would do, and paid the price. All of the above speaks to the issue of police roadblocks and what is legal and illegal, and the rights of ordinary citizens in such cases. The big question is: Can a JMPD member or SAPS member stop anyone willy nilly? Is there something like “probable cause” in South African law? There are also cases where stops and roadblocks are illegal, for example in cases where there is no commanding officer present it is an illegal roadblock. SAPS and JMPD also claims that they are allowed to make “roadside stops”, but is that legal without “probable cause”? Lobo claims that the police actually have limited rights under the criminal procedures act, and that they cannot continue to do things as they are done currently. He also alleges that many illegal roadblocks are set up as a way to extort money from an unknowing public.

In the aftermath of the alleged murder of a young man at the hands of the JMPD at an illegal roadblock we examine issues surrounding roadblocks and the powers of the Police to stop and detain citizens. It is something we all have a vested interest in.

title: Emergency Services Shortage Crisis
oneLiner: When you dial 10111 in a medical emergency you rely on proficient care on the spot. New regulation on EMS personnel qualifications threatens to put your life, and their livelihoods on the line.
summary:
The new regulation has evoked concern amongst EMS practitioners and private Emergency service providers as well as private training academies, that it will limit progress for individuals already in the system with six weeks basic or even intermediary life support qualifications, as this means that in order to now get higher qualifications they would quit their jobs in order to attend a mandatory full time course for three years or more to get more qualified in the field. Paul Masita, a 50 year old Intermediary Paramedic fears his career advancement is over, he has a family and two children to support and full time study would be out of the question. The colleges currently running the short courses will have to close those programmes down and there is no light coming for accreditation from the HPCSA and SAQA. With only four universities currently running with the courses how are we going to get enough paramedic's into the field? The Department of Health is adamant that they want to professionalise the industry even if there is some collateral damage along the way. They assert that many of these colleges are cash cows, churning out basic paramedic's who may never find a job. In the mean time we may not have services that can effectively save lives or even worse they could end up costing the average citizen a lot more. Paramedic's with degrees are far more expensive to hire. A group of concerned Emergency Services providers and organizations are not taking this lying down and are planning on taking the Department of Health to court later this month. Carte Blanche investigates.

In January 2017 the Health Professionals council of South Africa and the Department of health introduced a new regulation that revokes recognition of the six-week basic life support, six-month intermediate life support and nine-month advanced life support courses for paramedics, that have been serving the industry up till now. A basic life support paramedic now has to complete a two-year course, and those wanting to become advanced life support paramedics must do a four-year degree. This could put the entire industry in jeopardy as well as put our live's in danger.

title: Steaming
summary:
Friends of Rail have restored an old station from which their excursions take place. The backbone of their operation is a trip that runs from Hermanstad in Pretoria to Cullinan. The trip runs along the main line in amoungst the current trains which is unusual. Sadly they have recently been the victim of the metal thieves- on a day trip to Cullinian with a fully laden train they derailed. Fortunately the metal thieves had cut both lines in the same place so instead of tipping over they ground to a rather sudden halt but remained upright. They stole the branch line from Rayton to Cullinan and although they have the railway line, skills and trolleys to do so, because the railway line is owned by the SA Railways so they can’t do the repairs themselves and have to wait for the bureaucratic wheels of SAR to turn. Now they have to bus people for the last 10 kms instead of steaming into the grand old station themselves It’s a professional operation with all the train drivers taking official drivers licence and being issued with safety certificates which qualify them to take the public on excursions. They are trained by an Ex SA Railways trainer and train driver and have to re-apply for their train licence on a regular basis. These men all have full time jobs or are retired and this is their hobby. The Cullinan line was built by Paul Kruger to get supplies so they did not have to use the British rail and he escaped to the Eastern Transvaal on this line. Winston Churchill also escaped on this line during the 2nd World War- lots of history on the tracks. There are many steam train trips around the country but these are all run by corporations and operate as businesses. Friends of the Rail is just a bunch of enthusiast who run the trains out of their own pockets and have fund raising drives. This will be a nostalgic day full of rich characters.

Steam Trains bring back the romance of yesteryear travel - the nostalgia of childhood train trips when many little boys saw the train steam down the tracks and dreamed of being a train driver. Friends of the rail is full of those little boys- except they are grown men who have a passion for Steam locomotives, they call it “Steaming”. Friends of the rail was established 25 years ago and from starting out watching videos and old movies they moved on to restoring old locomotives. One such example is the 19D built by Krupp in Germany in 1937 was rescued from the scrape dealers just in time, and restored lovingly over seven years and is still running today. Another was donated by the Transnet Museum – a rusty old class 24 which they refurbished over 4 years and became their first locomotive they could “Steam” with and start running excursions. Each locomotive has her own story, and history and this weekend we will be traveling on a 60 year old Diamond Express with passengers seated in old railway coaches dating back to the 1950's - plenty of lovely wood and vinyl seats. The coaches are on loan from The South African Railways who are still the official owners. Friends of the Rail is keeping the history of steam alive in SA instead of sitting in a museum or children’s play park , they are "living" museums. These men and woman love and care for them, maintaining them and making spare parts in their workshop because they are no longer around.

title: Aeroswift
oneLiner: cutting edge laser research promises to give the South African aersopace industry lift-off
summary:
Aeroswift represents the DST's response to the global boom of 3D printing, or Additive Manufacturing. Although 3D printers were initially used mostly to make prototypes and often dismissed as a novelty for hobbyists, their value in certain specialised industries is increasingly being recognised. 3D printing is perfect for the manufacture of low-output, highly complex components, and unlike traditional machining, allows for rapid change and flexibility in design. In South Africa, where our traditional manufacturing industry does not have a positive outlook, 3D printing represents an opportunity to get ahead of the curve in a disruptive new technology. Aerospace is the perfect application of 3D printing. It is a low-volume, high value industry that demands complex parts with the lightness, design flexibility and ability to track parts that 3D printing offers. The only challenge is that most printers are tiny - the biggest can produce parts 600x400mm. Those that can print larger items can't produce the complexity and fine resolution needed. So in an effort to fill the niche of large-scale printing at high resolution and complexity, Aeroswift was born. It uses an extremely high-powered laser to melt together thin layers of fine titanium powder, to form complex shapes and with a minimum of waste. The printer works 5-10 times faster than other similar printers and uses a new arrangement of laser and mirrors to overcome many of the challenges usually associated with 3D printing on a large scale. The machine is still at a research and design level, but it has produced its first parts which have passed quality control tests. Its first parts will be flight-tested in AHRLAC, a fully South African designed and made aeroplane, at the end of June. Aeroswift is working in partnership with Airbus and Boeing to get the machine into commercial production and make parts for these air giants' flagship aircraft within the next couple of years.

Researchers at CSIR, in partnership with aerospace company Aerosud and funded by the Department of Science and Technology, have developed what they say is the biggest 3D printer in the world. They are using it to print complex, specialised parts for aircraft - and our team will watch as they are flight-tested in the first-ever fully South African-designed and made aircraft, AHRLAC. We will also film the giant printer at work.

title: Renewable Energy boom crashes in South Africa - whats at stake?
summary:
Jeffreys Bay – the iconic surf mecca famous for its powerful winds - saw the first wind farm to be built in the Eastern Cape as part of round one. They brought in the turbines from overseas. Since then 16 wind farms have been developed across the Eastern Cape with several more planned as part of round 4. DCD Wind tower manufacturing plant is an entirely SA-owned firm and was established in the Coega Industrial Development Zone to supply wind towers for the wind farms commissioned in round 3, with the knowledge that round 4 would provide work for the next 10 years. They invested R400-million in establishing the factory and employed 172 people, many of whom found work for the first time in their lives. When round 4 was delayed, they downscaled to 135 core workers. The last tower left the factory in November 2016. Workers have been sitting at home on short pay for the last five months. Everyone was holding their breath after President Zuma promised in his SONA 2017 speech that the IPP agreements would be signed. The date set was the 10th April - that date has come and gone and nobody knows when they will be signed. The shareholders can’t hold out forever. Whole technical teams across the Eastern Cape who moved from one wind project to the next with the promise of work till 2027 have been laid off. Wind farm Project Manager Nico Schneider relocated to the Eastern Cape. He was told this week by the investors that “Renewable Energy is dead in South Africa”. They are moving elsewhere. The entire future of a boom industry of development, of manufacturing, technical skills development, employment and potential social investment hangs in the balance.

South Africa's renewable energy (RE) programme has been lauded as one of the most successful internationally. Over the three bidding rounds, the cost of renewable energy has consistently dropped and now wind and solar energy is cheaper than coal fired energy. It has attracted R195-billion in foreign investment, created 29 888 jobs in construction and seen manufacturing development in parts of the country that were desperately neglected. The RE programme was set to continue until 2030 with a focus on local procurement of up to 60% in round 4. In the light of this, the Renewable Energy Technology Centre was established at the Cape Peninsula University of Technology, CPUT, to provide skills to the industry. Wind turbine plants were built at Atlantis in the Western Cape and Coega Industrial in Port Elizabeth. The Northern and Eastern Cape have been the biggest growth areas, creating employment and social upliftment in areas of the country that are desperately under-developed with massive unemployment. One of the most important elements of the Renewable Energy contracts is that written into any commission is a 20 year commitment to social and economic investment into the communities within a 50 kilometre radius of the plants. The community trusts are a one third shareholder of every plant. R13.4-billion has already been invested into communities, creating infrastructure in places where the government was unable to provide. Essential areas for development like school teachers, health services and various social upliftment programs are being funded. Over the next 20 years, R6-billion rand will continue to go into these communities in dividends. Renewable Energy companies don’t establish social upliftment programmes, but invest in the NGOs that are already established in those areas.

title: The danger lies
oneLiner: Behind the posh and glamour of horseracing are the lesser known facts about the riders who steer these thoroughbreds. In Carte Blanche tonight we go behind the scenes to tell the story.
summary:
Summary: We track a legend who have made history, those who are at the top of their game and the newbie’s; fearless and part of a new generation of jockeys who are invited to compete overseas and taking the challenge. We talk to them and their family about the challenges, their coping mechanisms and how they manage to survive the challenges of weight control, injuries and suspensions - a reality they live with every day.

Behind the posh and glamour of horseracing are the lesser known facts about the riders who steer these thoroughbreds. In tonight’s episode of Carte Blanche we go behind the scenes and into the jockey’s changeroom on racing day, when shedding the last 500gram in the box (sauna) stands between you and being disqualified. When the scale becomes your enemy and your weight the controlling dial the price you pay to stay in the game takes its toll every step of the way. In the X-games of horses jockeys control half-ton thoroughbreds at neck-breaking speeds, leaving them open to injuries of the worst kind. From broken ribs to collarbones, feet and hands, these are common accidents on the race course every jockey face and those who survive get back into the saddle again. Stamina, capacity for pain, discipline on diet, a challenging lifestyle not cut out for the faint hearted. Jockeys have to have nerves of steel, make split second decisions and never think about the possibility that the beast they steer could stumble and fall, break its leg, tear a tendon, and all that at 60 kilometres per hour with no breaks to put on.

title: COJ Billing Blunders
oneLiner: One year on has the COJ billing crisis been resolved?
summary:
It's more than a year since our last story on this topic. During this time not one of the case studies' billing problems have been solved. And thousands of new disputes have been lodged. People getting wrong accounts, often running into millions of rands, face monthly cut offs of both water and electricity, unable to pay the exorbitant amounts the council claims they owe. To date, the council has lost every single case that went to court, and this in itself costs the residents millions. Problems include faulty meters, wrong meter numbers, months of estimated readings in stead of actual readings, prescribed and inherited debt issues, and large scale corruption spanning the spectrum from meter readers to those working in the billing department. Frustration amongst residents is at an all time high, and at the same time the council is getting less and less money coming in.

CoJ has had a new government for the past 9 months. They inherited a system where the infrastructure is on the verge of collapsing due to years of abuse and non-maintenance. To fix the problems they claim that they need R170billion, yet they only have R10billion. And yet, their main source of income, the payment of rates, taxes and basic services is in total chaos. The billing crisis in itself is now a decade old, and there still seems to be very little if any progress made in resolving the thousands of disputes between the council and the residents. In our investigation, we start at the bottom with case studies who have no option but to pay bribes to get water and electricity, and we take it all the way to the top (the mmc for infrastructure, the mayor etc) to try and get to the bottom of this crisis
