title: The Water Down Stream
oneLiner: A billion rand has been spent on cleaning up the Hartbeespoort dam, but why are we fixing the symptom and not the problem?
summary:
4.2 billion litre's of untreated waste water runs into our rivers everyday. Two years ago, the water in the Hennops was so bad that Afriforum laid criminal charges against Ekhuruleni municipality as there were around 50 leaking sewage pipes from Tembisa township alone. The sewage treatment facilities (Sunderland and Olifantsfontein) are both over capacity according to the last known water drop reports in 2014... who knows what it is 4 years later (it would have been tested in 2013). We went back and the river water is marginally better (awaiting tests), but the problem in Hartbeespoort is still very bad. Ivory park which is across the river from Tembisa falls under the city of johannesburg, and there we met a couple whose garden and home was literally on a broken sewage pipe that often leaks into their house. We interviewed them, and while doing the interview, the pipe across the street began as well. Is it that only on threat of legal action that these municipalities act? Julius Kleynhans who was at Afriforum, and now works at OUTA is considering building another case against the city of johannesburg. The case will be retrospective and he suggests we widen our story to incorporate the Jukskei river because when that meets up with the Hennops, together they form the crocodile river, which flows into Hartbeespoort. We would test the water by Alexandra, by the leaking sewage pipes by dainfern/steyn city and after the Northern sewage works, at the crocodile river, and in the dam near the water's abstraction point. Sewage water carries bacteria and disease causing bacteria and there have been several warnings in the Harties area regarding the use of their taps.

We are going to follow both the hennops river and jukskei river, where they join to become the crocodile river and into the Hartbeespoort dam. This river system supports Pretoria, and the entire NorthWest province. We will track the eColi count at several strategic positions and then see if the waste water treatment facilities are working properly. We already know they are over capacity, and the Department of Water Affairs admitted they had not even done the green drop report since 2014, and had UNDERspent by 2 billion rand! We have made a google map to show the different locations - we will interview case studies along the river and the department of north west water affairs regarding how Gauteng exports the problem downstream. The evidence we have already collected is good and shows that our water is in a dire condition.

title: Facebook: Cracking the Code - Journeyman Special
oneLiner: How has Facebook cracked the code of human interaction?
summary: "What's on your mind?" It's the friendly Facebook question which lets you share how you're feeling. It's also the question that unlocks the details of your life and helps turn your thoughts into profits. Facebook has the ability to track much of your browsing history, even when you're not logged on, and even if you aren't a member of the social network at all. This is one of the methods used to deliver targeted advertising and 'news' to your Facebook feed. This is why you are unlikely to see anything that challenges your world view. This feedback loop is fuelling the rise and power of 'fake news'. "We're seeing news that's tailored ever more tightly towards those kinds of things that people will click on, and will share, rather than things that perhaps are necessarily good for them", says one Media Analyst. This information grants huge power to those with access to it. Republican Party strategist Patrick Ruffini says, "What it does give us is much greater level of certainty and granularity and precision down to the individual voter, down to the individual precinct about how things are going to go". Resultantly, former Facebook journalist, Adam Schrader thinks that there's "a legitimate argument to this that Facebook influenced the election, the United States Election results".

title: Ben Ngubane and the Zululand Quarries
oneLiner: BEN NGUBANE AND HIS ZULULAND QUERRIES Ben Ngubane has been in the news a lot lately. He has just appeared before a parliamentary enquiry into the SABC where he faced a grilling, and he is also a key
summary: BEN NGUBANE AND HIS ZULULAND QUERRIES HUNTREX 305 Huntrex 305 is a company owned by Mr Ben Ngubane and his wife, that by itself is not unusual, but it’s the story of this company, that reveals much about the man installed as Eskom’s chairperson. Court documents reveal that Huntrex has defaulted on paying its loans, Ngubane has called upon his political connection, President Zuma to cover for him, and is now using the mining minister to delay court proceedings. Meanwhile court records reveal that he appears to have fraudulently forged false share certificates to hold onto a company that he hasn’t yet paid for. BEN NGUBANE BUYS A QARRY AND A SAND MINE The story begins in 2010 when Brikor, a brick company in Gauteng, ended up in a spot of financial bother. They were overdrawn on their overdraft facility by R30 million. FNB were unimpressed and wanted their money back. If not, they threatened Brikor that they would liquidate them. Brikor decided to free up some cash to repay FNB, by selling their STANGER operation for R50 million rand. The Stanger operation consisted of a sand mine and a quarry and the mineral rights for that. Enter willing buyers Mr Ben Ngubane and his wife Sheila. The Ngubane’s bought the entire operation and put it into what was a dormant company called Huntrex 305. Huntrex acquired all the assets of immovable property, the equipment and shares in Zululand quarries PTY LTD and Natal Sands PTY ltd. Presumably, they planned to operate the quarry and sand mining operation as a profitable business. It had a history of making a former rally driver very wealthy. Before Brikor owned the operation, it had been owned by rally driver called Jannie Habig, who had turned over R15 million rand a month and sold the business for R100 million to Brikor. NO MONEY HONEY But Ben Ngubane had no money to buy the business, so he approached the KZN provincial bank, Ithala for a loan of R30 million rand. The bank agreed. They funded the balance of R20 million in installments they would pay to Brikor who agreed to the terms, and the deal was sealed. THE HONEYMOON Now the Ngubane’s had themselves a quarry and sand mine, but with that came the repayments of the loan so they could call it their own. A million rand every month, R600 000 to Ithala bank and R400 000 to Brikor. For the first six months, they paid a million rand monthly, that they owed. Then after paying back less than 10% of the loan, they just stopped paying. ITHALA SAYS SHOW ME THE MONEY By the end of 2013 Ithala bank’s attorneys tell Ben and Sheila, that if they don’t pay up, the bank will liquidate Huntrex. The Ngubane’s responded by fighting back and bought an interdict to stop Ithala bank from liquidating them. In his application Ben Ngubane claimed that he had made a verbal arrangement with the CEO of Ithala bank that the loan wasn’t due and payable and therefore Ithala couldn’t liquidate! Ithala refuted this. TO COURT AND BACK AGAIN By Feb 2014 Ithala bank launched a counter application which included asking the court to provisionally liquidate the Ngubane’s company Huntrex. Its opposed. 2014 was spent backwards and forwards in a legal joust, until finally on the 31 March 2015 all the applications were set down to be heard. THE ESKOM CHAIRMAN, A CONVENIENT EXCUSE, AND AN UNWAVERING JUDGE Mr Ben Ngubane’s counsel stood up in court and told the judge that Mr Ngubane had been appointed as chairman of Eskom, he was busy with matters of national security and therefore the judge should postpone the matter indefinitely. But that didn’t wash with the judge, who said he didn’t care who the counsel’s client was, and without further ado he granted the provisional liquidation to ITHALA BANK. A FRONT POPS UP Four liquidators were appointed to manage Huntrex and keep the quarry going. One of the liquidators is an attorney at Stowell and Co. Attorneys, Mr Neil Button. “Our job was to preserve the assets” he told Carte Blanche. To ensure the business remained viable both Brikor and Ithala helped with some funding. The return date to put the company into final liquidation had been set down for August 2015, but the day before they were supposed to return to court, a lady called Janakey Reddy brought an application to put the company in Business rescue. She said she had sufficient funds to make it viable. But it turned out that Ms. Reddy was just the human resources manager at Huntrex ,who earned around R13 000 per month and had no other funding. She had been set up as a front by the NGUBANE’S. On the 10th December 2015, the court finally heard the two applications. The first was the case for business rescue which was defeated with costs, which is unfortunate for Mrs. Reddy as it meant she had to find the cost of several very expensive senior counsel. Then the liquidators fired her. MICHAEL HULLEY SWOOPS IN LIKE BEN NGUBANE’S ANGEL The second application heard on the 10th December was to confirm a date for final liquidation. Then counsel for Ithala bank makes a surprise admission. They tell the court that on the 9th December 2015, the day before they appeared in court, President Zuma’s attorney, Mr Michael Hulley, had arrived at ITHALA, convened a full board meeting of senior executives, and told them that the president had said they must “leave his man alone.” Ithala said no. Soon after Huntrex was put into final liquidation and Mr Hulley began to play a more prominent role. Mr Ngubanes original lawyer Mr Manogh Maharaj disappears. THE HOME STRETCH As per final liquidations, a process unfolds and a first meeting was held with creditors. The debts are discussed and by now they have ballooned to R75 million including interest: As at December 2015 HUNTREX owes: R34 million is owed to Ithala Bank R24 million to Brikor R1 million to the municipality in unpaid debts R4 million to the receiver for VAT R12 million to concurrent creditors Sandton Plant hire are keen buyers but they want to buy the whole bundle, the quarry, the sand mine, the mineral rights and the shares in Huntrex. But there’s a problem. Even though the shares in Huntrex have no value at that point, Ben Ngubane and Sheila are still shareholders. The liquidators put together a tripartite agreement and Mr Michael Hulley meets on Mr Ben Ngubane’s behalf. Meetings take place over the first six months of 2016 with Mr Hulley meeting the liquidators on behalf of Mr Ngubane who was away first in Brazil, then Nigeria, then the USA. Mr Hulley says in principle, Mr Ngubane will sell his shares. THE HOME STRETCH HITS A SNAG On the 15th June 2016 at the second meeting of the creditors it appears they are making progress. The liquidators have it recorded that they have received an offer of R30 million and Sheila Ngubane and her accountant adopts the report and sign the minutes. So far so good. Sandton Plant are ready to buy but then they encounter a problem. ZULULAND QUERRIES – A NEW SET OF SHARE CERTIFICATES The liquidators have a set of share certificates. But then suddenly Ben and Sheila produce another set of share certificate copies made out in their personal capacities. Ben Ngubane now refuses to sell his shares to the new buyer. THE MYSTERY OF ZULULAND QUERRIES The liquidators have both sets of share certificate and it appears the NGUBANE share certificates have been forged. The numbers are not consecutive as they should be; Zululand Quarries is spelt incorrectly as Zululand Querries, and instead of the shares being R1 each as they are in the originals they are recorded at one cent each. The shares should add up to 100 but instead one of the certificates has an adding mistake and reads 170 shares. Everyone is dumbstruck. Forging share certificates is a criminal offence under the companies act. Michael Hulley suddenly disappears from the scene and Mr Ngubane’s original lawyer Mr Maharaj enters the fray again. The liquidators ask the court for a declaratory order on the certificates but the Ngubanes oppose the declaratory order. MINISTER OF MINERAL AFFAIRS – GUPTA LINKED, MOSEBENZE ZWANE TO THE RESCUE. Currently there is an impasse. When the company was sold to the Ngubane’s the mineral rights changed hands without any problem. Strictly speaking, he should have had to reapply for a mining license due to the change of ownership. That didn’t happen, but now that the liquidators are trying to sell the business, the mining minister has intervened and said the new buyers must reapply for a mining right. The mining minister was supposed to file his affidavit by Tuesday this week. And that is where our story stands at present. Ngubane may yet hold onto an asset he has barely paid for, using the might of his political connections and the odd allegedly fraudulent share certificate.

title: Molefe returns
oneLiner: Did he resign? Did he retire? No-one knows ... but now Brian Molefe is back at Eskom as CEO
summary:
In November, then Eskom CEO Brian Molefe announced that he decided to leave Eskom "in the interests of good corporate governance". This after the former Public Protector Thuli Madonsela found, in her "State of Capture" report, that Molefe's ties to the Gupta family may have played a role in irregularities in dealings between Eskom and Gupta-linked companies. Fast-forward six months and Molefe will be back at the helm of Eskom after his R30 million pension payout was blocked and the Eskom board then reversed its "decision to grant him early retirement". But when Molefe left in November, there was no mention of early retirement - something he was too young to qualify for anyway. Even Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown called his departure a "resignation" in a statement. Now he will have to pay back some R7 million already paid out to him and he is set to complete his contract, which runs until September 2020. Brown has said that steps must be taken to ensure that pension packages at state-owned companies are in line with cabinet approved remuneration standards - yet Molefe and the Eskom board continue as if nothing happened. Brown has also reiterated her call for an investigation into allegations against Molefe, but says he is innocent until proven guilty and in the meantime he may return to run Eskom. This while the position of Eskom CEO was advertised and candidates apparently already interviewed by a recruitment company. The ANC has slammed the decision and called Brown to Luthuli House on Monday to account for it. The DA wants to apply for an urgent interdict to prevent Molefe from returning to Eskom.

By allowing the return of Brian Molefe as CEO of Eskom, after he left six months ago "in the interests of good corporate governance", has the board of this public entity executed its fiduciary duties, adhered to principles of good governance and complied with all the labour laws of the country? We ask the experts. Molefe's return comes after Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown blocked a pension payout of R30 million to Molefe, who only served as Eskom CEO (first acting, then permanent) for just less than 19 months. She sent the board back to the negotiating table with Molefe, and the board then decided to reverse all payouts to Molefe and reinstate him. Brown said it was a much better option than paying out R30 million - but is "the lesser of two evils" really the best solution for the country's crucial power utility? Molefe himself said, when he resigned in the wake of the Public Protector's state capture report alleging wrongdoing on his part in relation to Gupta-linked companies, that he was leaving "because it is in the interests of Eskom and the public it serves". No investigation has as yet been done into the allegations against him but he returns, while his name has not yet been cleared. We will interrogate Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown's assertion that Eskom will benefit from Molefe returning to the helm by compiling a timeline of Molefe's time at Eskom, punctuating the questionable dealings that took place in this period; and compiling a report card for Molefe, scoring his performance in areas such as electricity generation, finances, personnel and governance. The Molefe decision has also highlighted cracks within the ANC, with the party criticising pres. Jacob Zuma's government for its actions, and Brown called to account to Luthuli House on Monday.
experts: Mr. Zizi Kodwa Mr. Iraj Abedian Economist Mr. Michael Bagraim Mr. Chris Yelland Energy Expert

title: Stem-Cell Therapy for Autism - A Medical Conundrum
oneLiner: Desperate parents are sending their children to places like India for stem-cell therapy for autism. How effective are these therapies and what does the mainstream medical fraternity say about them?
summary:
Stem Cell therapy is a buzzword in the medical fraternity with practitioners hailing it as a medical breakthrough. In oncology in particular, stem cells have been used for decades to treat certain cancers such as leukemia through bone marrow transplants. Dr Alok Sharma from the Neurogen Brain and Spine Institute in Mumbai, India claims and believes that stem-cell therapy is a revolution for treating autistic people. The endorsement of stem-cell therapy has taken hold in the East and South America, especially in China, India and Panama. However, various applications of the treatment have been met with skepticism in the mainstream medical fraternity. Experts, such as Dr Lawrence Goldstein, Director at Sanford Stem Cell Clinical Center, suggest that stem-cell therapy for autism is a bogus treatment that has not been clinically proven and can be a fruitless and expensive exercise for desperate people. On the other hand, a number of parents who have put their children through this procedure vow that they can see and experience great improvements in their children. As well as interviewing medical experts, Carte Blanche gets to talk to some of these parents and care givers who swear by the treatment and say it could be the miracle they have been waiting for. Carte Blanche investigates, is this treatment bogus or is there real hope for the autistic?

Stem-cell therapy is growing in prominence in the medical world, reporting to effectively treat an increasing number of devastating and debilitating diseases, including autism. Desperate parents are sending their children to places like India for stem-cell treatment, but how effective are these therapies and what does the mainstream medical fraternity say about them?

title: Outbreak
oneLiner: 17 cases of measles are confirmed in Gauteng, linked to a family who chose not to immunise their children. We analyse cracks in the country's voluntary vaccination programme that put us all at risk.
summary:
Our proposal is to start with BATEMAN, to show the cracks in the immunisation programme -- then to look at the outbreak map that the National Institute of Communicable Diseases keeps (any instance of 3 laboratory-confirmed cases constitutes an outbreak). We will tell of 2 TYPES OF PATIENTS/CASE STUDIES who fall through the cracks -- the anti-vax child whose parents object for factual or religious beliefs; as well as the child who misses a dose due to vaccine stockouts, poor follow-up or unavailability of staff. We will show the history of some of the most dangerous illnesses successfully eradicated through vaccines and show the science "fixed" by Lancet after the damaging publication of the WAKEFIELD study in 1998. Turns out he wasn't interested in eradicating vaccines...but in replacing the vaccine in use with his own invention.

When Johann van den Heever, manager of South Africa's Extended Immunisation programme for 11 years resigned in protest over cracks in the programme early last year, the Department of Health slated him for speaking out about problems that he had said would make all South Africans vulnerable for diseases that should and could have been eradicated by now. The departing manager was interviewed by Science Writer Chris Bateman who published the interview in the South African Medical Journal that showed how severe understaffing, vaccine stock-outs and poor follow-up was causing children not to get the full complement of shots they should. Bateman will speak to us about the facts uncovered by his story a year ago -- the former manager was lambasted and runs scared of speaking out again. South Africa makes 11 antigens available in the extended immunisation schedule -- from measles, to the most recent HPV vaccine for protecting young girls agains caner of the cervix. Thanks to vaccines, polio and diptheria and whooping cough have been eliminated. But aside from measles, Kwazulu-Natal saw a resurgence of diptheria two years ago. Through outbreak data and case studies we can basically track and confirm problems in the system as one outbreak after another hits the headlines -- there have now been three measles outbreaks (from over 31 confirmed cases in Stellenbosch to JHB) before the winter season, traditionally outbreak season, has even started. Bateman warned in his article that missed vaccine doses were causing our herd immunity to be diminished, which would open doors to infections that could and should have been prevented. Add to this the growing, if misguided fear that vaccines cause illness and autism in children, and the country's promise to the world community that we would eradicate measles by 2020, after the WHO DECADE OF VACCINES, seems highly improbable. title: Karoo Uranium II
summary:
Carte Blanche first reported on plans to mine uranium and molybdenum in the Karoo in August last year. Nearly 10 months later, Tasman RSA Mines is pushing ahead with its application for mining rights in three areas between Beaufort-West and Aberdeen. The company also has pending prospecting rights applications for another five areas. Quaggasfontein, just outside Beaufort-West, is one of the areas subject to a mining rights application. This is where a borehole was planned to supply water for the town. Tasman RSA Mines admitted to us last year that there are concerns about this area and that they would have to make a plan to mitigate possible effects on water sources here - but no Environmental Impact Assessment is available for this area yet. The public had time until last month to comment on the draft Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for the mining in one of the areas - Kareepoort, about 60km east of Beaufort-West and 50 km west of Aberdeen. The draft EIA acknowledges that the area is a unique and sensitive habitat and home to a number of threatened and near-threatened animal and plant species. It also has a unique character and paleontological value. But any potential damage to the environment and character can be mitigated, the draft report says. The report also says the potential economic advantages for the area are great - this while the report states that only 16 permanent positions will be created in the mining operations here. One of the main criticisms raised by organisations opposing the mining is that the EIA only assesses the impact on this one area and does not take the cumulative effects into account.

Plans to mine uranium and molybdenum through open cast mining in the Karoo are still on the cards, with organisations fighting tooth and nail against it. The mining company's applications for mining rights in 3 blocks between Beaufort-West and Aberdeen are still pending, as are its applications to prospect in five more areas. A draft Environmental Impact Assessment report for one of the planned mining areas gives us a more accurate idea of how the mining company plans to mitigate the possible negative effects - and opponents are unimpressed. The mining company has no plans to preserve any of the normal vegetation but says it will remove and preserve the threatened plants, to be replanted during mine rehabilitation. It says it will educate mine workers not to kill the animals that live in the area. The area has high paleontological value but, since it is difficult to do any digging in the area, the mining may even make it easier for paleontologists to explore the area, the report states. It also says any radiation that people may be exposed to will be minimal. Philip McNaughton farms in the Kareepoort area, which is subject to a mining right application. Earlier this year, he discovered a tiny flowering succulent he had never seen before. Experts say that this is possibly a new species, and it may be under threat from the planned mining. Meanwhile, the Council for Geoscience also has plans to conduct a 3-year study that will involve the drilling of deep research boreholes near Beaufort-West to assess the effect that mining and exploration activities in the area could have and has on the deep & shallow ground water, seismicity, soil chemistry and gas emission. The planned uranium mining and fracking are often criticised because adequate data and analysis of the possible impacts are not available and the Council for Geoscience's research would address this.

title: the world's most endangered seahorse
oneLiner: a look at conserving the world's most endangered seahorse...
summary:
The Knysna Seahorse is the only seahorse in the world currently listed as endangered by the IUCN and its tiny habitat is continually being threatened by human development. Despite this being an iconic species in South Africa there is still a lot we don't know about it - however, one scientist is leading a research project in Knysna to learn more about the species and to help save it from possible extinction. According to the lead researcher: "It should be remembered that the Knysna Estuary is the most important estuary in South Africa in terms of biodiversity – and if active management of our estuary and its catchments are not done – we might be losing a national asset." She runs a research group called the Knysna Basin Project which is starting a pilot project commencing in late May where her and her team will be tagging seahorses underwater with tiny UV tags in order to understand the animals' home range which she hopes will lead to the creation of new seahorse reserves. She hopes that the Knysna Project can be used as a pilot project which other South African coastal towns can follow to help preserve their environments. The main threats to the seahorse are habitat loss due to human development but also other factors that go along with it - including how human activity affects the water quality - its the management of the areas that's crucial to the long term survival of the seahorse. But another point which the researchers are looking at is whether the seahorses are adapting...or indeed thriving...in the artificial waterways of Thesen Island, Knysna's biggest development. Additional voices I think could include a representative from local government about how the seahorse is consideration for further development in Knysna and the surrounding estuaries, a representative from industry who's developing the area and perhaps a town representative about the iconic importance of the seahorse to the town.

The Knysna Seahorse is only found in three estuary systems in South Africa, and is currently the only seahorse in the world listed as endangered by the IUCN. A team of researchers are hoping their research will allow the animal to be better protected...

title: Race against time
oneLiner: South Africa is banned from exporting racehorses directly to the overseas market. We witness the impact it has on the equine industry.
summary:
It has been nine years since our last report on Carte Blanche and there has been no visible improvement in controlling African Horse Sickness or AHS. A vaccine for AHS was developed in 1957 and the only subsequent work that’s been done to improve the efficacy was in 1995. In 2006 Horse-owners asked whether a new vaccine would be developed. Onderstepoort Biological Products promised there would be one in five years. No new product has been made available.From a potentially R1 billion industry per annum the horse racing industry trickled down to R200 00 and more than 75 000 people lost their jobs. In a race against time South Africa is fighting to get the horse export ban imposed by the European Union lifted. AHS is a highly infectious and fatal disease and as many as 70% of horses die within one week of the infection. It is spread through tiny midges. When a midge bites an infected horse it carries the virus to a non-infected horse. The incubation period of AHS infection is 7 – 14 days but may be as short as two days. Symptoms include swelling above the eyes, sounds gurgling in their lungs as they battle to breathe and eventually a painful death for the animal.South Africa was banned from the international racehorse export market for many years. In a pro-active move a controlled AHS zone was established in 1997 in the Western Cape, historically known for few outbreaks. It consisted of a protection zone, a surveillance zone and a free zone spanning a total of 300km. The last stop for horses leaving South Africa was at the free zone at the Kenilworth Racecourse in Cape Town where horses would spend 21 days under quarantine. South Africa now had access to the European, Middle Eastern and Asian horseracing circuit provided we had no outbreaks in the safe zone. Continued outbreaks of AHS from 1999 to 2014 led to new restrictions by the EU. Besides the 21 days at Kenilworth, horses now had to spend 60 days in Mauritius and 30 days in the UK under quarantine.

African Horse Sickness has brought the equine industry to it's knees. Horse Breeders, competitors and trainers are calling for change.

title: Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis
oneLiner: High-tech genetic testing allows prospective parents to avoid passing life-threatening genetic conditions on to their children.
summary:
Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis (PGD) is a genetic testing procedure that allows parents to 'select' healthy embryos and avoid giving birth to children who either carry or are affected by hereditary genetic conditions. First, genetic material (a cheek swab) is taken from both parents (who may be carriers of a recessive genetic condition, or affected by a dominant one). This material is used to design a test unique to that couple. Then the couple undergoes ordinary IVF: eggs are harvested and fertilised. At about 8 days, the embryos are biopsied: one or two cells are removed, the DNA is extracted and compared against the test for the genetic condition. An embryo that is neither affected by the condition nor (preferably) carries it is then implanted. The remaining healthy embryos may be frozen and used for later pregnancies, or donated to other couples. We have three wonderful case studies who have all battled different and terrible conditions, undergone PGD and had healthy babies.

We are closer than ever to the idea of 'designer babies': fertility specialists and geneticists are helping prospective parents avoid passing on the potentially life-threatening genetic conditions they carry on to their children. For some parents, the knowledge of the conditions they carry comes only when they give birth to a child affected by the condition.

title: Deep Brain Stimulation
oneLiner: In 2010 we brought you the story of young Dakalo, a girl from rural Thohoyandu who suffered from an sever movement disorder called Dystonia. Tonight we revisit her to see how she is doing.
summary:
Dakalo has lived with Dystonia since she was only three months old. She has never been able to eat, sit or walk independently. Dystonia can be described as an imbalance in the neurotransmitters leading to involuntary muscle contractions that force the body into abnormal, sometimes painful, movements and postures. There are several treatments available for the movement disorder, one being Deep Brain Stimulation or DBS. In DBS therapy, a small pacemaker-like device sends electronic signals to an area in the brain that controls movement. Although DBS does not cure dystonia, it can help manage some of its symptoms and subsequently improve the patient’s quality of life.

This is truly a feel good story of the benefits of Deep Brain Stimulation, the people who helped to make it possible and the results.

summary:
The organization snuck onto the plantations, and with the help of an informant called “Pierre” managed to capture video evidence of the following: 1. A boma-like cage (see video) in which they capture the baboons with hundreds of bones scattered around the area. 2. A mass grave site where hundreds of skeletons were found The trust has made a short video which includes a little of their evidence – it has around 400 views. But, they will give us exclusive access to their video footage of a newer second mass grave with 300 hundred skeletons – many of them babies (family troop), access to their informants and exlusive access to their new information – the permits which were issued (2 to SAPPI who said they weren’t invovled) show that they only had permits to capture the baboons with nets, not kill them. Therefore this was unlawfull and they did not have the required permits. Baboon Matters has already PAIA’d both departments for further information – which they expect this week. We would have all of this exclusively. My proposal would be to go to SABI – a day in advance of a presenter arriving – try and gain access to the plantations and the bones. (Need to check legally if we are allowed on property – Jeni explained that it is open, but there are defintely signs we aren’t supposed to be on their land.) We would interview the baboon matters people, and their informants with a presenter. We would request interviews with both departments and then go to the forrests and ask to all 3 of the pine plantations as well. (So that’s 5 sets of right of replys)

Baboon Matters Trust’s Jeni Trenhowan and Kathy Kelly have been investigating why beneath the pine plantations in Sabi, Mpumalanga are the skeletal remains of thousands of baboons. They first heard about the baboons being killed back in 2008, when resident reported it to their trust. Back then, only 200 had been killed by the owners of the pine plantations becauase they believe the baboons ruin the bark on the trees which they make products like ironing baords and paper. Baboon matter raised awareness and the killing stopped. But, towards the end of last year, and in January informants on the ground suspected something was amiss. Upon further investigation 3 plantations – York (who make domestic products), Kavanti Land (which is government owned), and Sappi (paper), have allegedly killed 4000 baboons. This accroding to the department of envrionment and forrestry departments records, and the company’s confirm this.

title: Midstream Air
summary:
Who ensures the quality of the air we breathe? This is a question that residents of the Midstream, Midlands and Randjiesfontein Estates in Midrand, Olifantsfontein and Tembisa are asking themselves in their battle for clean air. They say the Department of environmental Affairs (DEA) and the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (GDARD) is letting them down by not clamping down on Interwaste's FG Landfill site in Midrand. They say the landfill site is emitting dangerous gases and bad odours into the air and not taking the necessary steps to prevent harm to the health of people living in the area. The large private landfill site accepts waste from mining operations by Lonmin and possibly other mine groups. Let alone the bad smell, residents say they suffer respiratory illnesses, nose bleeds and more. They have to take their children to the doctor numerous time a month. Many have costly air purifiers in their homes. An online tracking tool developed by those spearheading the battle has recorded more than 4000 complaints in less than a year. Section 24 of the Bill of Rights in the South African Constitution guarantees everyone the right to an environment that is not harmful to their health or well-being. Residents first started complaining to the DEA and GDARD in 2014 but, dissatisfied with what they saw as a lack of action, a group of residents took their case to the Public Protector's Office, which facilitated an agreement between the parties in November 2016. But, say residents, the pollution is now worse than ever and the monthly feedback meetings promised by the DEA have not happened. The DEA and GDARD were also supposed to provide the Public Protector's Office with regular feedback. We aim to interview residents of the area, representatives of the DEA and GDARD, Interwaste (owners of the landfill) and an independent air quality scientist.

Residents of the upmarket Midstream, Midlands and Randjiesfontein Estates in Midrand thought they were buying into a dream lifestyle ... until gases and the stench from a private landfill site started affecting their quality of life and their health. Residents of these estates and surrounding areas in Olifantsfontein and Tembisa in Midrand, have been battling for more than two years to get Interwaste to address the dangerous gases emanating from its FG Landfill site in Midrand. The source of the problem is said to be mining waste from Lonmin and possibly other mines being dumped at the landfill site. The gases being emitted from the site include hydrogen sulphide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide. Those living in the area say the stench is so bad on some days that they have to fight the urge to throw up. They say they suffer regular respiratory illnesses and ailments such as nose bleeds. Lanette Hughes, who is spearheading residents' battle, says her two young children are often sick, her childhood asthma has returned and they have needed to buy air purifiers for their home. Another resident says her family suffers so much that they are nearly exclusively living in one room in their house that has an air purifier installed. Hughes and her team of volunteers are using technology to their advantage and have created an online tracker for people to record complaints. Between May 2016 and February 2017, there were a total of 4582 complaints logged. A record number of 919 complaints were logged from Midstream Estate between 1 and 13 February. They have also taken their woes to the Public Protector, where an agreement was reached in October 2016 and Interwaste, the Department of Environmental Affairs and the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development were asked to make commitments to address the problems. But residents say that the commitments are not begin honoured and the situation is now worse than ever. In an attempt to work with Interwaste to solve the problems, the developers of the Midstream Estate, Bondev, purchased machinery to measure the gases in the air. Residents say that the steps that have been taken to address the problems are not working because Interwaste is not taking the necessary steps. They say, for instance, that the flares installed to burn off the gases do not have the required scrubbers installed.

title: Three parent babies
oneLiner: ....we meet the docotr who created the first child with three biological parents
summary:
A five-month-old boy is the first baby to be born using a new technique that incorporates DNA from three people. The boy’s mother carries genes for Leigh syndrome, a fatal disorder that affects the developing nervous system. Genes for the disease reside in DNA in the mitochondria, which provide energy for our cells and carry just 37 genes that are passed down to us from our mothers. This is separate from the majority of our DNA, which is housed in each cell’s nucleus. Dr Johan Zhang developed a technique to replace the faulty mitochondria with healthy mitochondria from a donor. He removed the nucleus from one of the mother’s eggs and inserted it into a donor egg that had had its own nucleus removed. The resulting egg – with nuclear DNA from the mother and mitochondrial DNA from a donor – was then fertilised with the father’s sperm. The baby thus has 3 biological parents, and was born healthy.

Medical breakthrough

title: Water Rights
summary:
The right to water is protected in the South African Constitution and under the National Water Act of 1998. In SA, water does not belong to anyone but to everyone, and everyone has the right to use it reasonably. Under the old apartheid era water laws, farmers could divert all the water from waterways crossing their land to their own farms, leaving nothing behind for others downstream. But now, they are obliged to let through enough water to maintain the waterway and preserve its ecology. But is this being enforced by officials on the ground? The situation in the Barrydale region, where the small Lemoenshoek River runs, seems to show a lack of executive will to enforce the laws that protect our water sources. Large-scale commercial farmer Jan Crafford uses much of the Lemoenshoek River's water for his farms and, according to farmers downstream, leaves too little behind to reach their farms. These farms include that of Freek Willemse, a beneficiary of the government's land redistribution program. Court cases costing millions have been fought over access to the water in this river. In an attempt to highlight the issues around access to water, Richard Butt, who owns an olive farm in the area, is even producing a documentary on the so-called "water wars" in this area and others around the country -- he is making this footage available to Carte Blanche.

Freek Willemse is a beneficiary of the Government's land redistribution programme. He was given a farm near Barrydale in the Karoo, along the Lemoenshoek river. But land means nothing if you don't have enough water. No-one knows that better than his neighbour Jan Crafford -- who bought a large number of farms in the valley in 2001. Crafford's farms are upstream from the Willemse farm and Crafford diverted most of the water from the Lemoenshoek river into his dams ... because he could -- he had the money, and the know-how. Willemse, on the other hand, was stunned when Crafford asked a third neighbour, Richard Butt, for the right to convey water from the river across Butt's land to one of his dams. Butt refused, seeing clearly that the diversion would mean no water would reach farms like Willemse's and other communities downstream. What followed was a 7-year legal fight that has cost Butt almost R5-million, to preserve Willemse's right to water -- a right that's protected in the Constitution as well as the National Water Act of 1998. This past December, Crafford once again applied to increase his water supply from the river. This while the region is suffering the worst drought in living memory and the river has just about dried up completely. Willemse's meagre livestock is facing starvation. Meanwhile, the government that gave Willemse his land, is now seemingly failing to protect his right to water. Even though the Department of Water and Sanitation has underwritten a document detailing how much water should be let through in order to preserve the river for the use of Willemse and others downstream, department officials are accused of failing to enforce it. This situation in Barrydale seems to be only one example of a pattern playing out in different areas across the country, with similar accusations surfacing in Limpopo, the Free State, the Eastern Cape and elsewhere in the Western Cape.

title: From Para to Dakar
oneLiner: Last week, Joey Evans completed the gruelling 9000km Dakar Rally - a decade after he was told he may never walk again
summary:
A testament to human determination, the story of Joey Evans's journey from paraplegic to Dakar finisher is the story of a man who refused to give up on his passion. A lifelong motor sport enthusiast and competitor, Joey broke two vertebrae in a racing accident in 2007. After months in a wheelchair and painfully learning to walk again, he finally got back on a bike, determined to pursue his dream of completing the legendary Dakar Rally. The journey was far from smooth - another accident in 2014 left him with torn ligaments, fractures and lacerations, unable to ride for 6 months. The R1.5 million Dakar price tag was a further obstacle, and Joey embarked on a months-long fundraising campaign with support from friends, fellow racers and an impressive list of smaller donors who he recognised by printing their names on his bike. Finally, on 2 January 2017, Joey's dream of reaching the Dakar starting line in Paraguay became a reality - and the hard work really began. 14 days, 9000km, and 12 gruelling stages later, he finished - the only South African in the bike category to do so. We talk to Joey about his long journey back to racing health, his fight to reach the Dakar, and his experience of this most punishing race - from mechanical failure, to injury, to triumph.

Paralysed from the chest down in a motor racing accident ten years ago, Joey Evans was told he might never walk again. But not only did he prove doctors wrong - last week he completed the gruelling 9000km Dakar Rally...the only South African to finish in his category.

A micro example of how the city should operate is 1 case study - Hermanus where a borehole system taps into the upper reaches of the deep aquifer and supplies a third of the town's water. We will also look at planes to purify water from the lower lying Cape Flats Aquifer. I think the overall message is that cities and individuals are being forced into changing their perception that water is to be respected in terms of our ever increasing droughts and erratic weather patterns.

title: Millions Missing
oneLiner: Twenty to 30-million people worldwide have dropped out of life due to a mysterious illness that can't be cured, nor its origins traced. But is there finally hope after years of misdiagnosis?
summary:
CFS has been called a malingerer’s disease - it occurs in people of all ages, socio-economic levels and ethnic backgrounds, even toddlers as young as 2. Many doctors remain unconvinced of CFS as a genuine illness; no cause or diagnostic test exist. Much damage was done to the CFS cause when in 2011 British researchers announced a major breakthrough in the highly respected journal Lancet. The researchers reported that ‘PACE’, the largest treatment trial ever had been a great success and "found" that the best way of dealing with CFS was exercise and psychotherapy. Graded exercise therapy (GET) and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) would improve the symptoms and could even cure CFS. CBT would challenge patients’ beliefs that they have a physiological illness limiting their ability to exercise and so they need only to become more active and ignore their symptoms to fully recover. Headlines around the world shouted, “Got ME? Just get out and exercise, say scientists.” The medical profession, including American CDC, soon set PACE as baseline for treatment guidelines. Problem is, PACE was bad science. CFS sufferers realised it straight away. Science is only now catching up with exactly how bad. PACE contradicted patients' everyday experience that even mild exertion could increase all other symptoms and cause fatigue so profound that they could barely lift the sheets on their beds. It caused cognitive deficits, blood pressure problems, unrestorative sleep, neurological and immune dysfunction, among about 60 symptoms. At first, the "Missing Millions" had no way of challenging the science, because the data of the study hadn’t been released, but what they COULD do was send emails, chat online…and form a community that began to fight back against their physical and conceptual imprisonment. A five-year battle ensued to review the actual data underlying the $8-million PACE study.

Millions of very ill people are wrestling their lives back from misunderstanding and stigmatization around a crippling disease called myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME) or chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS). There’s no known cure for CFS and the origins are still poorly understood – to make matters worse, bad science that led to totally inappropriate understanding and treatment of the disease in the last five years very nearly became a prolonged death sentence for the millions of people living with CFS.

title: Energy Costs
oneLiner: Together with our country's leading scientific energy researchers we debunk the need for nuclear, and show the numbers government and Eskom SHOULD arrive at, if they were being honest with us.
summary:
A new 2016 IRP has been prepared but is not yet released for public comment. This was recently delayed indefinitely – possibly because the ministerial advisory committee told the minister that renewable energy is the way to go rather than nuclear and new coal. The CSIR has used the exact same model the DoE uses to generate the IRP to generate a revised energy plan for SA based on current data. They only changed one thing – removed the annual limit on building wind and solar power plants. It is unclear why this annual limit was included in the 2010 IRP. With this limit in place, renewable energy sources will never be a significant part of SA’s energy mix and we will need nuclear and coal power. But with this limit removed, the CSIR’s re-optimised energy plan shows that the most cost-effective plan for SA is to have 70% renewable energy sources by 2040. If this plan is implemented, we will be generating more energy at a lower cost. The CSIR is in the process of making their whole campus in Pretoria, and others around the country, energy independent. They are doing all sorts of interesting research to ascertain the best and most cost-effective ways to generate power. Countries like China, India and Germany are taking up renewable energy and experience in those and other countries have shown that the renewable energy sector also creates jobs, instead of destroying them as some have warned. It also makes economic sense – the money from the power sector will be more widely distributed across the country too. But in all cases, it is clear that energy transitions start from the top – political will and decisions from policy makers are required. Government says it is committed to renewable energy but yet it has not proven this by scratching the annual new-build limits on renewable energy sources.

This is a pivotal moment in SA’s history when this generation will make decisions on our energy future that will impact generations to come. Renewable energy sources are cheaper, cleaner, easier to decommission and does not create dangerous waste that needs to be stored forever. So why are we not jumping at it? Government’s insistence that we need to build new nuclear and coal-fired power stations to supply SA with the power we need is based on outdated data. And new research by the CSIR proves this. We are still operating on the assumptions in the Integrated Resource Plan on energy of 2010. Since then, the cost of solar PV panels and wind turbine technology has drastically fallen. Dawn in the desert and the boats travel out to the Jordanian side of the Dead Sea, past border point and the always present guards with their guns. It’s a 50 km swim that’s never been done before. (The reasonable cost should be no more than R29 million per kilometre.) And then still added the Contractors Ps & Gs – costs and profit margins. By 2013, all the contractors were found guilty of corruption in this regard with corrupt tender processes. The hearings were conducted by the Competition Tribunal in July 2013. The report from the CIDB was made public in September 2013.

In 2007 The Gauteng Freeway Improvement Plan (known as “G FIP”) was approved – a plan to update or newly construct several roads in Gauteng. The plan was then tendered, and several roads were meant to be done in time for the 2010 world cup. Initial costs were estimated at 8 billion. And the majority of the completion dates were from early to mid 2009. http://www.nra.co.za/live/content.php?Session_ID=80cb5df55518542ed007349d67f9b05d&Item_ID=260 In 2008 there was a public outcry regarding the costs of the 2010 FIFA world cup stadiums, and this lead to there being an investigation into GFIP. According to calculations done by an engineering contractor – SOURCE JONES with more than 48 years in the roads construction business, (the source is an industry professional in South Africa and the rest of Africa) - South African Tax Payers are paying 3 times the price for one of SANRAL’s roads than in anywhere else in Africa or the world. (We have comparisons of other African’s nations and other far more complicated projects in the world.) G FIPs roads are tolled and the project was to either build new roads, or update (repave/ widen) other roads – the amount km’s is in contention. 185km verse 201km both of which are in SANRALs own reports. Please see MAP that shows the intended areas. The various sections of the roads were split up into 15 different packages (like Ingula) and each package was given to a construction company. (2 more packages were later added but are also in contention as SANRAL has also not been forthcoming regarding their tender bid documents etc) In 2011, the competition commission reported that 15 companies were actually working together to up the prices and charge more – these consortiums were fined individually (each split up- and we have that report it totalled 1.4 billion rand in fines) depending on how guilty they were found of “unfair practices”. The following companies are the ones we will focus on, and these were their fines” Aveng: R306 million Basil read: R95 million Murray & Roberts: R309 million (A, B, E) Raubex:R59 million (reported to be the whistleblower company – were not named but given a fine – possibly look for that whistleblower.) WBHO: R311 million (package A, B, E) BUT THE BIG QUESTION HAS ALWAYS BEEN: HOW MUCH HAVE WE OVERSPENT? WELL THE ENGINEER HAS PAINSTAKENLY WORKED THAT OUT! We will take Nine of the 15 packages (the ones that had clear cut documents) : Total cost was R9.2 billion. The engineer found that R5.9 billion of that was actually “unfair value” meaning we should only have paid R3.3 billion. Package F was marked for concern as the value of the steel used for reinforcing was in excess of R679 million!!! SANRAL have said that only R700 million rand (tribunal only found R100 million was from collusion) of the project was collusion, but the engineer can prove that the number is closer R5.9 billion based on their own numbers. In excel spreadsheets, again extrapolated from SANRAL’s own documents were have spent 18 billion on this, and it was budgeted as only R8 billion. Where has the 10 billion gone?

title: Whistleblower Gamechanger
oneLiner: Risking life and limb to blow the whistle on corruption and abuse of power, South Africans who want come forward, can now do so safely.
summary: Surveys since 2007 by the Open Democracy Advice Centre in Cape Town and private organisations like PWC have shown that only 3 out of 10 South Africans believe the law will protect them if they blew the whistle and so there's been a steady decline in the number of people willing to shed the light on corruption. Despite 15 years of having a Protected Disclosures Act meant to protect them, whistleblowers still sacrifice everything to come forward. Three initiatives aim to change that. The first is by Parliament. Realising that the heroes of democracy find themselves in the cold after standing up in defence of truth, and that information brought to light seldom leads to change or the perpetrators being fired and prosecuted, Parliament has written the Public Disclosures Amendment Bill, which has this week been debated in the Parliamentary Justice Committee after a long period of public submissions. The Amendment Bill places a positive OBLIGATION on organisations to grab the bull by the horns when information on corruption and abuse it brought to light. The Amendment will put the power and security back in the hands of the whistleblower, even if the purse is on the side of their employer. We speak to Justice Committee chairperson Dr Mathole Motshekga about the mini policy revolution he's overseeing to plug the holes in policy. Second initiative is an online whistleblowing platform developed in Australia and adopted by independent civil rights groups OUTA (Organisation Undoing Tax Abuse). Not only is OUTA's platform hacker proof and stripes out user data to protect the anonymity of submissions, but it has been designed to elicit information in a particularly helpful. detailed way that will allow the organisation to take legal action against individuals perpetrating fraud and corruption. It's a true game-changer for whistleblowers who usually walk the road of coming forward alone and risk losing their livelihoods and sometimes even their lives. OUTA will follow their cases every step of the way and make sure that perpetrators are made examples of. Using the example of Zwai Sokupa (who is speaking to us on condition of anonymity) we show how his information is enabling OUTA to blow the lid off corruption in a key development parastatal, and how they will continue to support whistleblowers financially and legally who help them reach their aim of safeguarding taxpayers' money. But OUTA's initiative is limited to the parastatals where their investigations are focused -- for the moment ESKOM and SAA, although this will change as they get good information on other state owned enterprises. So the broader legal landscape still remains crucial to challenge, as the Amendment Bill will do -- to afford whistelblowers true protection. So, the final initiative is by the Open Democracy Advice Centre itself -- the NGO that's been working with whistleblowers since the dawn of democracy and that's been working to change policy through research and advocacy, because it believes effective whistleblowing mechanisms are a key part of good governance. ODAC counsels and guides whistleblowers who come forward to bodies like Corruption Watch or the Public Protector, to guide them through the complex legal, emotional, psychological and often physically hazardous process of blowing the whistle. Now, hoping to take whistleblowing to the next level, and making the new law practical, helping to implement it, ODAC is launching a CODE of good practice and taking it around the country, to government departments and companies alike, to help them implement the new legislation and help make the world safe for whistleblowers. ODAC has held the hands of families like Tlholo Phakoe's whose father Moss was gunned down in 2009 after a lengthy period of tying to raise serious corruption issues in Madibeng, North West with senior leaders of the ANC -- most notably President Zuma, whom he visited at home, with his damning dossier. The murder of Moss Phakoe remains unsolved, while COSATU and Corruption Watch still campaign behind the scenes today to have the prosecutions reopened. It was the case of Moss Phakoe that marked a change in whistleblowing -- not only could you get fired, you could die.

title: Philasande's mechanical heart
oneLiner: a ten year old boy becomes the first child in the world to be fitted with the life saving mechanical heart.
summary:
In November last year, Philasande contracted a flu and within weeks his condition deteriorated. Turned out that he had the coxsachie virus and it affected his heart and valves so badly, he was dying. Doctors operated on him and he was given a temporary mechanical heart called the Tandem - pioneered by Milpark Hospital - to help his body heal. Just a few weeks later, Philasande returned to the hospital and doctors realised he needed an immediate heart transplant. But at ten years old, he was too small to get a new heart and despite being placed on the Priority List for a heart, they couldn't find him one. Dr Cassel, his attending cardiac specialist suggested that he be fitted with a Heartware Valve Assist Device (HVAD) - a mechanical heart - that up until then had never been fitted to a young child. He had to be flown to Cape Town to be operated on by Dr Willie Koen - the only surgeon on the continent who performs this operation - and Philasande received his new heart. At the cost of R2million for the device and a total of R3million for the entire operation, doctors hope that the HVAD will keep Philasande going for the next few years until he is old enough to receive a heart big enough for his own body. In the meantime, Philasande is back to being a happy healthy child.

Philasande Dladla became the first child on the African continent to undergo a lifesaving operation where a “mechanical heart” was implanted to assist his damaged heart. He is also the first child in the world to have a mechanical heart implanted in him. Doctors at the Netcare Christiaan Barnard Memorial Hospital in Cape Town inserted a heart ventricular assist device (HVAD) in Dladla aged 10 from KwaZulu-Natal. Dr Willie Koen, a cardiac and transplant surgeon practising at the hospital, and a founding member and vice-president of the Pan African Society of Cardio-thoracic Surgeons, led the surgical team that implanted the hi-tech lifesaving HeartWare HVAD.

title: Whale entangelment
summary: Once driven to the verge of extinction, southern right whales have made a dramatic comeback and recovery since being given full protection in South African waters, their traditional breeding ground. And it’s not just southern rights – humpback whales, killer whales (Orcas), Brydes and other whale sub-species are increasingly visiting our coast. But with the increase in numbers, have also come an ever-increasing number of entanglements – whales getting caught in drifting broken pieces of fishing nets and ropes, and in rock lobster and octopus traps. If left entangled, they die a slow and excruciating death. There have been 25 entanglements in the last 2 months- the largest number ever, 15 was high in years gone by. It is now prime whale season in the Western Cape, as the southern right whales arrive from the Southern Ocean and Antarctic for the breeding season. Enter the South African Whale Disentanglement Network (SAWDN), formed in 2006 to deal with whale entanglements around the African coastline. A volunteer network, it is part of a global initiative to deal with entanglements. Spearheaded by The Department of Environmental Affairs’ Oceans and Coasts division, SAWDN volunteers also include the NSRI, the Police Dive Unit, But it is a dangerous business. Mature southern right females weigh up to 60 tons, and can reach 80 tons, and their tails and flukes pack a massive punch. Volunteers get as close as they safely can to the whale and then use razor sharp blades on long poles to cut the ropes piece by piece. Operations can last for several hours, and the whales do not always cooperate. The expensive disentanglement equipment, made in the US and Australia, if often lost or damaged during operations. The network relies extensively on reports from commercial fishing vessels to find and track down entangled whales, and the companies regularly volunteer their fishing boats and crews to assist SAWDN in disentanglement operations.

title: The Final Frontier: South African Space Agency
oneLiner: When you think of space, you think of Russia or America, think again. South Africa has had a space agency for 50yrs and we aren't just looking at the stars, but seeing what space can do for us!

We'll speak to a team of young black researchers who went to Antarctica for SANSA and what they did there and why it's so important to have a "hub" there. We will also interview the head of the weather department Mpho Tshisaphungo - she'll explain operation Phakisa and how we are using the information to accurately forecast unexpected weather - like droughts and floods. They have information dating back 50 years and can spot trends and problems.

Gladys Magagula is head of South Africa's mission control room at SANSA (South African Space Agency). She has seen us enter the space race in terms of satellite communication. Because of our prime position relative to space and weather conditions, South Africa is the communications choice for the USA, Russia and China. So much so, we were a part of the Apollo missions securing communication between South Africa and Houston's mission control, we transmitted "One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." But we have continued and made the space communication race our own. We have sent 3 satellites into space and have had successful launches (from other countries). The information from these is priceless - we can see South Africa in a different way - from weather (droughts etc) and land surveying we can see EVERYTHING from space. So not only are we making money from communicating with satellites for other countries, we are also exploring and making our own satellites.

title: Dam Pipe
oneLiner: Despite a year's fight and the crippling drought, the pipe that will take partially treated sewage effluent into the Vaal Dam is set to go ahead, as the Dam level drops by 10cm a day...
summary:
Deneysville’s activists discovered (at the end of August) that approval for the pipe’s Water Use Licence was given in April already without any feedback or notification after they were engaged in a public consultation process. Worst of all, the Water Use Licence seems to have been given for 5 years, while the sewage treatment works still have to be upgraded to handle the massive population increase in the area. For now, the effluent that is discharged in the Vaal is not compliant with legislated treatment levels. After the activists had worked to get the issue aired in the media, the local council came under severe pressure by the national Department of Water and Sanitation to fill highly dangerous open trenches and flooded pump stations. The hazardous trenches were filled and partially treated sewage is now diverted into a massive unfenced quarry -- in which a child drowned last year. But despite their initial doubts, the residents have come to accept the quarry and it would seem that the quarry holds water that is attracting bird life and might be suitable for cultivating grass and creating employment. They would prefer this to what they’ve now been told will happen: The pipe will be re-opened where it had hastily been installed and merely covered to allow for a consultation process that residents feel was a total waste of time. Residents accuse DWS and the local council of acting in bad faith by never giving the interested and affected parties who had attended the community meeting any feedback, and trying to hide the (hot potato) issue in the run-up to local elections and to prevent the residents from appealing the outcome – they would have had a limited time to appeal after the decision was made final. But what DWS and the municipality probably haven't bargained on is a Cape Supreme Court ruling that the 30-day appeal period can only start once the affected parties become aware of the decision; not from the day of the official decision.

After a year of fighting to prevent the construction of a pipeline from Deneysville’s sewage works into the Vaal Dam, residents have just discovered the shocking news that their objections have been steamrollered and the pipe will go ahead – precisely where it had been laid in secret, and poorly constructed to boot. Now the pipe will stay where it's been laid because there's ostensibly no money to move it...but where it enters what used to be the Vaal Dam, is now dry land, thanks to the drought. The Vaal Dam holds the drinking water for the country’s most densely populated economic heartland is only 33% full and the water level drops by 10cm a day. Not only is the precious resource threatened by the drought but what little water is left is threatened by what residents feel will be wilful pollution by the local municipality. But not only is it Deneysville's pipe and partially treated effluent that's affecting the Vaal Dam, sewage treatment works all along the catchment, up to Villiers, that have been the subject of Carte Blanche scrutiny, have come in for pressure to fix faltering treatment works. But while construction work in Standerton and Frankfort give reason for hope, Villiers is in a worse state than ever, and new reports are emerging. In August 2015 Minister of Water and Sanitation Nomvula Mokonyane announced the construction of the Sedibeng Regional Sewer System – a mega sewage plant to take care of sewage spills at the three existing, old and overworked sewage plants in the South of Johannesburg. It would have been up and running within three years. Identified by the Presidential Infrastructure Coordinating Council as early as 2005, it now appears that the mega waterworks has now been postponed. The United Nations Environment Programme last week issued a report on the Vaal River basin -- flagging it for salinity from acid mine drainage, eutrophication and pollution from microbiological causes -- like defunct sewage works. The Department of Water and Sanitation's way of dealing with pollution has always been to dilute it out, by releasing water from the dam to flush the Barrage and Vaal as it proceeds into the Free State and flows into the Orange River, but with the persisting drought and the unrelenting pollution of sewage works, as well as acid mine drainage from mines along the Upper Vaal, and the release of partially treated AMD back into the Vaal and Crocodile rivers, what has long been predicted is now reality -- the Vaal Dam is losing its dilution capacity and it's only a matter of time before consumers bear the brunt of increased treatment costs. DWS DG Margaret-Ann Diedricks promised Carte Blanche a road-trip to show off their progress in fixing problems in the Upper Vaal by April this year, but all that happened, despite numerous attempts to arrange this interview, is that the Director-General was ousted from her post, the Minister of Water is being investigated by the Public Protector on various corruption allegations, and in Deneysville the ANC municipality lost its hold on the council in the municipal elections -- the town is now under a DA-led coalition. In this story we aim to recap what's happened to the pipe -- asking the new municipal leaders to open the books and tell us where things went so wrong; holding accountable the environmental practitioners that promised to keep the community informed; and the contractor who is accused of shoddy workmanship on the pipe. We will try to present the best forecasts of what weather patterns say about coming rain and what the drought and pollution levels mean for the Vaal in coming months. The Vaal's fate is at a critical point and we will analyse the big picture of how problems like Deneysville contribute to the degradation of the Vaal system.

title: Albino killings in Malawi
oneLiner: The UN has declared that people with Albinism in Malawi are at risk of "total extinction" unless radical action is taken to protect them
summary: Malawi has an albino population of 10 000, in May this year the UN announced that this population is at risk of extinction due to kidnappings and attacks for their body parts. 18 Albino's haven been killed and 64 attacked over a 2 year period. Edna Cedrick's 2 year old Albino son was kidnapped in May this year, his twin brother is all she has left. She tells us the story of the day he was taken and how she fears for him every single day. We have made contact with a man who worked in the black market of Albino body parts. For two arms, two legs and a tongue you can get 75000$, which is way more than the fine or small sentences handed down for alleged Albino body part trading. He is willing to speak, he is out on bail so we will have to hide his identity. We would also want to speak to the head of the traditional healers association about how these parts are being used in traditional medicine and magic. What is the ideology behind it and why are they condemning those that are still practicing this? In Tanzania they have lowered these type of killings by registering all Albino's in the country, monitoring them and offering safe houses. In Malawi there is no such protection and it is feared that the increase in attacks in Malawi is because of these tighter regulations in Tanzania. The traders are crossing the borders. Is this happening in SA? Not on this scale at all. But, the Albinism society of South Africa is willing to be interviewed and speak about the threat to people living with albinism in South Africa. We have one case study in SA, but that is all. The biggest problem on the continent at the moment is in Malawi

title: The internet of "things"
oneLiner: Your car, your house and even your pace maker may be susceptible to hacking as they are all NOW connected to the internet.
summary:
Keitumetsi - spoke about how hackers work with ransomeware and the fact that soon we will need our own security people - like chubb for online etc she also speak about how hackers work - black and white hat, ransomware Evan speaks about the car example, the thermostat example and others. Rika Butler said the number one danger for 2016 is medical implants being hacked like your pacemaker. I can script her, if you think it's similar to use all of the experts from previous story.

We will go to an online house with an expert and will be shown how the "things" in it will...Same people as password story, but obviously on the "internet of things." These are all the "things" that are now connected to the internet and making sure our audience is aware of their connection and the worst case scenario of what may happen. We will find a case study - and scare them regarding everything that is online... so their car could be hacked through bluetooth, their home thermostat could be held for ransom, and the newest hackable target for hackers who want a ransom are medical implants - like pace makers. We have real world examples of all of these things and we are going to bring it home to South Africa by interviewing a south african whose house is online. I think it could be a great 5-6 minute story on the threats that this poses. NOTES FROM BRON: "The internet of things is not only about hacking. We will need to include, the pros and the cons as well as the what this means for advertising in your homes, push notifications, in-appliance purchases that could come with your home being online and such connectivity abused. What about knowing your movements throughout the home (sensors) and when you’re out. How does this impact on privacy as well? We’ll need to touch on further applications like intelligent transport, smart grids and smart cities – with overseas EGs (or African if there are). Experts estimate that the IoT will consist of almost 50 billion objects by 2020. What are the possibilities – what’s next and where are we on this timeline? I know you already have your car, thermostat and pacemaker egs, but let’s keep this in mind: "Things," in the IoT sense, can refer to a wide variety of devices such as heart monitoring implants, biochip transponders on farm animals, electric clams in coastal waters, automobiles with built-in sensors, DNA analysis devices for environmental/food/pathogen monitoring or field operation devices that assist firefighters in search and rescue operations. Legal scholars suggest to look at "Things" as an "inextricable mixture of hardware, software, data and service". These devices collect useful data with the help of various existing technologies and then autonomously flow the data between other devices. Current market examples include smart thermostat systems and washer/dryers that use Wi-Fi for remote monitoring. As well as the expansion of Internet-connected automation into a plethora of new application areas, IoT is also expected to generate large amounts of data from diverse locations, with the consequent necessity for quick aggregation of the data, and an increase in the need to index, store, and process such data more effectively."

title: Skype Music
oneLiner: Students from Soweto inspired and taught by renowned musicians from United Kingdom
summary: Njabulo ,a music student from South Africa, who has talent but no means to reach for the sky and develop her gift. A musician from United Kingdom’s Birmingham Conservatoire. Two totally different worlds, which now have the opportunity to interact. This is Arco a collaborative music project between Soweto’s Morris Isaacson School and Birmingham Conservatoire Strings department. Twenty four gifted students from Soweto were selected at the beginning of this year to participate in weekly instrumental Skype lessons given by teachers at Birmingham Conservatoire – this is in addition to their music lessons in South Africa. Their aim: to provide life-changing inspiration of music to children who would never normally have access in their belief that music is a tool transcending both language and cultural boundaries. To provide support and opportunity to students at who may not readily have access and exposure to such a rich international cultural exchange of this caliber. These 24 students are only coached and mentored by students and alumni of the Conservatoire but have access to live event streaming of master classes, workshops and performances taking place in the Strings Department at the Conservatoire and have been inspired, exposed and participated in music and performance at a top international level. The teachers in Birmingham on their apart have gained valuable experience in teaching, chamber music coaching, technical videoing skills and a cultural awareness outside their normal life. It is a two way street.

He was paralysed, to all intents and purpose, a quadriplegic . But Brandon and his family were determined not to give up. Through intensive rehabilitation, iron-will and hard work he has not only regained use of his arms but is now competing internationally at Olympic level in a number of disciplines. He has set a new South African and African record for the Men's 100m wheelchair sprints But that’s probably not the most impressive thing about Brandon Beake, he was able to afford (with medical aid help) extensive rehabilitation at one of the best centres in the world in Atlanta Georgia – where Christopher Reeve went -and came back determined to help less fortunate South Africans.
